# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first argument is clear. There is no doubt that just as men can kill with God's permission, so too can they truly and actually remove that member <note>the male organ</note> or others. However, in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now being made. Through this, the solution to the second argument is also clear. But as for the point that because God permits the generative power to be bewitched more often for certain reasons, He therefore also permits that member to be truly and actually removed: this does not hold as a general rule. This is because it would not be done by way of a glamour <note>original: "maleficii"</note>, nor do witches desire this when they perform such works, for they wish to retain the power of restoring the member when they please and know how. From this it is clear that it is removed not in truth, but by a prestigious art <gloss>the art of illusion or glamour</gloss>. Regarding the third argument concerning the transformation of Lot's wife: we say it was a real transformation and not done by prestigious art, whereas we are now speaking of prestigious art. Regarding the fourth argument, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said regarding the magicians of Pharaoh that they produced true serpents. Demons can produce certain effects regarding some imperfect creatures with the help of some other agent, which they cannot do regarding men, for whom God has greater care. According to the scripture: Does God have care for oxen? Nevertheless, as has been said, they can always harm men truly and actually, or even by prestigious art, provided God permits it. Through this, the solution to the final argument is also clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into bestial forms through prestigious art.
</margin>

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared where men are also transformed into beasts. Regarding how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to be done. In the twenty-sixth book, question five, of the Canon *Episcopi* from the Council of Ancyra: Whoever believes that any creature can be made, or changed for the better or worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is beyond doubt an infidel and worse than a pagan. Let us also use the arguments of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the second book of the *Sentences*, distinction eight: Whether demons can make impressions on the bodily senses by deluding them with glamours. Here he first argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must be somewhere; but it cannot be only in the sense, because the sense does not possess any species <gloss>mental image or form</gloss> except that which is received from things. And there is no true beast present, according to the authority of the canon cited above. Nor, again, can it be in the thing which is seen—as when a woman appears to be a beast—because two substantial forms cannot exist in the same thing at one and the same time. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen can be nowhere, no prestigious illusion can occur in the eye of the beholder, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. Furthermore, if it is said that the form is in the surrounding air, this cannot be: first, because air is not capable of receiving any form or figure; second, because the same air cannot always remain around that person due to its fluidity, especially when the person moves; and third, because such a transformation would then be seen by everyone, which does not happen, for demons are not seen to deceive the visions of holy men, at least. Furthermore, the sense of sight or the visual power is a passive power; but every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportioned to it. Now, the active thing proportioned to the sense is twofold: one which, as it were, originates the act, namely the object; the other which, as it were, conveys it, such as the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor even the medium that conveys it. Regarding the first, it cannot be the object because it cannot be taken from any real thing, as touched upon in the preceding argument, since it is not in the sense as something accepted from a thing, nor in the thing itself, nor even in the air itself as a conveying medium, as was touched upon in the third argument. Furthermore, if a demon moves the inner cognitive power, he does this either by presenting himself as an object...

<summary>This page discusses whether the removal of male organs by witches is a physical reality or a sensory illusion, concluding it is usually an illusion. It begins a new inquiry into whether witches can transform humans into animals, citing Canon Law and Thomas Aquinas to argue against the physical possibility of such changes.</summary>
<keywords>glamour, prestigious art, transformation, Thomas Aquinas, Canon Episcopi, sensory illusion, generative power</keywords>

<note>Verse 3-4</note> ... <note>Manuscripts</note> S, U, and many others, along with Latin versions b, e, f, g1, ff1, and the Syriac Peshitta, Coptic, and others agree here. <note>Manuscripts</note> C, D, E, F, H, K, Delta, Pi and many others read "you are able" <note>original: "dynasthe"</note>. Manuscripts G, M, U and others read "you are able to discern" <note>original: "dynasthe dokimazein"</note>. Latin versions vary between "to know" <note>original: "scire" or "nosse"</note> and "to recognize" <note>original: "cognoscere"</note>. Manuscript L reads "discern" <note>original: "dokimazete"</note>.
4. **and adulterous** <note>original: "kai moichalis"</note>: Found in b, c, f, q, and the Vulgate, as well as Origen. Omitted in D, a, e, ff1, ff2, and Prosper. **seeks a sign**: Manuscript B reads "asks for" <note>original: "aitei"</note>. Manuscript D reads "a sign seeks" <note>original: "zetei semeion"</note>. **Jonah**: Found in Codex Sinaiticus (aleph), B, D, L, and several Latin and Coptic versions. The received text <note>indicated by the symbol ς</note> adds "the prophet" <note>original: "tou prophetou"</note> following manuscripts C, E, F, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, and others.
5. **had come**: Latin versions a, b, c, ff2, g1, and Hilary read "when he had come". **the disciples**: Found in aleph, B, C, D, and others. The received text adds "his" <note>original: "autou"</note> following E, F, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Pi.
6. **Jesus**: Omitted in ff1, g2, k, and the Vulgate. **See and**: Omitted in a, b, e, ff2, q, and Irenaeus. **and Sadducees**: Omitted in U and some others. In manuscript k, several words are lost between 16:1 and 5, then it continues: "and they forgot to put in loaves, and since they had only one loaf in the ship, he broke it for them saying, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of the Herodians."
7. **And they**: D, a, b, c, e, ff2 read "Then they" <note>original: "tote"</note>. **saying**: Omitted in K and the Curetonian Syriac. **we took**: The Curetonian and Sinaitic Syriac read "they took".
8. **said**: Found in aleph, B, D, K, L, M, S, X, Delta, Pi, and many others. The received text adds "to them" <note>original: "autois"</note>. **among yourselves**: Manuscript L reads "among them". **you took**: Found in C, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi. However, aleph, B, D, and others read "you have" <note>original: "echete"</note>, likely following the parallel in Mark.
9. aleph omits "nor remember". D and Delta read "remember when" <note>original: "mnemoneuete hote"</note>. D reads "to the five thousand".

the means with God in this unity <margin>How noble this unity is.</margin> we are received by the Holy Spirit, and we receive the Holy Spirit and the Father and the Son and the divine nature all together, for one cannot divide God. And the enjoyable inclination of the spirit, which seeks rest in God above all likeness, obtains and possesses supernaturally in its essential being all that the spirit ever naturally received therein. All good people have this, but how that is remains hidden to them all their lives, unless they are inward and empty of all creatures and enlightened with spiritual understanding. In the same <margin>As soon as man turns from sin, he is received by God.</margin> moment that man turns from sin, he is received by God into the essential unity of Himself, in the highest part of his spirit, so that he may rest in God now and always. And he receives grace and a likeness of God in the property of his powers, so that he may always grow and increase in virtues. And as long as that likeness exists in charity <note>original: "charitate"</note> and in virtues, so the unity exists in rest, and it may not be lost except through mortal sin.

# SOCRATES SCHOLASTICUS BOOK 6

<note>The text continues describing Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop of Constantinople.</note>

heretical <note>original: "αιρετικόν"</note> often fled from his skill in debate. Regarding his lifestyle, he was not simple, yet he practiced a refined moderation within extreme self-control. He lived luxuriously in white clothing and continued to bathe twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he bathed twice a day since he was a bishop, he replied, "Because I cannot manage a third time." On another occasion, when he went to pay his respects to Bishop Arsacius, he was asked by one of Arsacius's attendants why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said, "You tell me first where it is written that a bishop should wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question by saying, "You will not be able to show that a priest must dress in black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels is shown using white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah wearing white to the apostles." Having said these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia <note>original: "μικρᾷ Γαλατίᾳ" Little Galatia</note>, was taking away a church from the <term>Novatians</term> <gloss>a rigorist Christian sect</gloss> and was visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him and pleaded for him to return the church. Leontius answered warmly and said to him, "You Novatians ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance and shut out the loving-kindness of God." When Leontius said these and many other such things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "And yet, no one repents as much as I do." When Leontius asked again, "How do you repent?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you." 

Once, when Bishop John <note>John Chrysostom</note> was accusing him and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "Indeed it does not." When John became angry and said, "Do you see that you wish to be the only bishop?" Sisinnius said, "I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, though I am one to everyone else." John, being annoyed at what was said, said, "I will stop you from preaching, for you are a heretic." To this, Sisinnius replied gracefully, "I would even pay you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor." John, softened by the reply, said, "I will not stop you from preaching if speaking grieves you so much." 

Sisinnius was thus ready and graceful in his replies. To write and record all the things said by him would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown what kind of man he was through a few examples, thinking them sufficient. I say this: he was famous for his education. Because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Furthermore, all the prominent members of the Senate cherished and admired him. He composed many books, but he is a hunter of words in them and mixes in poetic expressions. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writing. For grace attended him in his face, his voice, his dress, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all the religious sects, and especially by Bishop Atticus. Such are the matters concerning Sisinnius.

they warn of God and command that he be worshipped everywhere. But those of an unlearned and impious nature, to whom fate has truly not granted the ability to obtain gifts from the gods, nor to have a conception of immortal Jove <note>Jupiter, the supreme Roman deity</note>, do not listen to either the gods or divine men. They have indeed rejected all the gods; yet they have chosen not to pursue the forbidden demons with any hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those acts through which alone God is adored. For God, as the father of all, stands in need of nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through the imitation and seeking of him. For the seeking of him purifies, he says, and the imitation of him deifies the affection by working toward him. He indeed preached well concerning God the Father and spoke of the character with which he should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, where the life of the saints is either praised or blamed. But among Christians, there was only as much, or he only slanders as much as the demons wish, whom he considers gods. As if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were performed in theaters and temples in service to the gods, and to observe what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God, and from this to understand where the building up and where the ruin of morals lies. Who told him this or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, with such a vain and open lie: that the Christians revere rather than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped forbids sacrifice even to the holy celestial angels and the powers of God, whom we, as fellow citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love as most blessed. He forbids it, thundering in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people, and introduced it with a great threat, saying: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out. And lest anyone should think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom that man calls the least or lesser gods—since in the holy scriptures they themselves are called gods, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations—the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> placed this clearly in a psalm, saying: For all the gods of the nations are demons. Therefore, lest anyone should think it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, but permitted to sacrifice to all or some of the celestial beings, he immediately added: except to the Lord alone; that is, only to the Lord. This was said lest perhaps someone might believe that the sun is the Lord to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made, because he said "to the Lord alone" <note>A play on the Latin words "soli" meaning "alone" and "sol" meaning "sun"</note>. That it is not to be understood this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher bears such significant testimony, gave a law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but now made famous among all nations. In this law it is written: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only. What need is there to search out many things on this matter in his law and his prophets? Indeed, there is no need to search; for they are not hidden or rare. Rather, one should collect the open and frequent passages and place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and highest God willed that sacrifice be made to no one at all except himself. Behold this one thing said briefly, or rather grandly, threateningly, but truly by that God whom their most learned men preach so excellently: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the rooting out follow the disobedient. He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, he says, except to the Lord only. Not because he has need of anything, but because it is profitable for us that we should be his possession. For to him it is sung in the holy writings of the Hebrews: I have said to the Lord, you are my God, for you do not need my goods. Moreover, we ourselves are his most noble and best sacrifice. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets' oracles proclaimed that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the nations would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun to its setting, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine argues that the God of the Hebrews demands exclusive worship and forbids sacrifice to demons or lesser gods. He asserts that true worship consists of virtue and the imitation of God rather than external rituals or the veneration of spirits.</summary>
<keywords>sacrifice, demons, Hebrews, Christians, idolatry, Septuagint, City of God, virtue, worship</keywords>

We have established that everything is small <note>referring to the limited human perception of the vast divine structure</note>. **Rabbi Elazar said**: Come and see that Jacob emerged from the side of harsh Judgment <term>Din Kasya</term>, for Isaac held harsh Judgment as his portion. **Rabbi Shimon** said to him: Is that so? Behold, Isaac himself emerged from Mercy <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss>. Thus, all Judgment emerges from Compassion <term>Rachamim</term>, and Compassion emerges from Judgment. Abraham inherited the inheritance of Mercy; from Mercy, Isaac emerged in Judgment. Jacob emerged in Compassion from the side of harsh Judgment. So it is above: one from the other, and one is nourished by the other, until it is known that all is one. All things hang upon the One, and all is found to be one; blessed be His Name forever and ever.

**Rabbi Elazar said**: It is known that there is no perfection except when one attribute grasps the other, and a third grasps them both to complete the whole, such as Jacob <note>representing the central pillar of Balance</note>. This is what is written:
> Passing through from end to end. <note>Exodus 26:28; interpreted here as the unifying force connecting the extremes of the divine emanations</note>

We have learned: This "vessel" is only called so from our perspective. From our side, everything is made known, but above, everything rises in one balance <term>matkala</term>. Nothing changes or shall ever change, as it is written:
> I am the Lord, I change not. <note>Malachi 3:6</note>

**Rabbi Yehuda said**: All the lamps <note>the Sefirot or divine lights</note> shine from the One and hang from the One. These lamps are all one and must not be separated. Whoever separates them is as if he separated himself from the Life of the Worlds. **Rabbi Isaac said**: It is written:
> And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them. <note>Isaiah 3:4</note>

This relates to what is written: *And you shall make two Cherubim of gold*, and it is written: *He who sits upon the Cherubim*. It is also written: *And He rode upon a Cherub and did fly*. "He who sits upon the Cherubim" refers to when the Divine Presence dwells in perfection. <note>Another version: when it is found in perfection</note>. "He rode upon a Cherub" <note>singular</note> refers to when the King is not settled upon His throne. "He who sits upon the Cherubim" <note>plural</note> refers to two. **Rabbi Yose said**: Woe to the world when one Cherub turns its face away from its fellow, for it is written:
> And their faces shall look one to another. <note>Exodus 25:20</note>

This occurs when there is peace in the world. **Rabbi Isaac said**: We have learned, *The nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother you shall not uncover*. Woe to the one who uncovers their nakedness <note>by causing a separation between the divine masculine and feminine principles</note>. In this manner, it is written of Jacob: *Passing through from end to end*. Happy is the portion of Israel, for the Holy One, blessed be He, glories in their praises as it is done above, as it is written:
> Israel, in whom I will be glorified. <note>Isaiah 49:3</note>

We have learned that **Rabbi Isaac said**: In former days, a man would say to his fellow, "Tell me one word of Torah and take a hundred pieces of silver." Now, a man says to his fellow, "Take a hundred pieces of silver and labor in the Torah," and there is no one who pays attention or inclines his ear, except for those few holy supreme ones in whom the Holy One, blessed be He, glories, as it is written:
> And your people shall all be righteous, they shall inherit the land forever; the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, that I may be glorified. <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

Woe, *the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be silver*. **Rabbi Isaac said**: Woe, the "hooks" <term>vavim</term> <note>the Hebrew letter Vav, which means 'hook' and has the numerical value of six</note> of the pillars! I have said that all those who are attached to the upper knots are called "the hooks of the pillars," and all those below hang from those hooks. What are these hooks? Six within six <note>referring to the six directions or Sefirot</note>, and they are joined and watered by the spinal cord <note>the central channel of divine flow</note> that stands over them. In the *Book of Concealment* <term>Sifra Detzniuta</term>, we learned: there are hooks above and hooks below, and they all rise in one balance. What is the "Concealment of the Book"? **Rabbi Shimon said**: There are five chapters included in a Great Palace <term>Heikhal</term> that fill the whole earth. **Rabbi Yehuda said**: If they are included thus, they are superior to everything. **Rabbi Shimon said**: So it is for one who enters and exits <note>the mystical pardes or orchard of knowledge</note>, but for one who does not enter and exit, it is not so.

There is a parable of a man whose dwelling was among the mountains and who knew nothing of the dwellings of the city. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat in its raw state. One day he entered the city. They offered him good bread. The man said, "What is this for?" They said, "It is bread, to be eaten." He ate it and it was very pleasant to his palate. He asked, "What is this made of?" They said, "From wheat." Later, they offered him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said, "And what are these made of?" They said, "From wheat." Later, they offered him royal pastries <note>trikas</note> kneaded with honey and oil. He said, "And what are these made of?" They said, "From wheat." He said, "Truly, I am the master of all these, for I eat the essence of all these, which is the wheat itself." And because of that...

<summary>This page explores the interconnectedness of divine attributes, emphasizing that Mercy and Judgment are not separate but emerge from one another. It concludes with a famous parable of a villager who mistakes raw wheat for the finished delicacies made from it, illustrating how the uninitiated fail to see the sophisticated layers of divine manifestation.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob, Isaac, Cherubim, Sifra Detzniuta, Parable of the Wheat, Unity of God, Sefirot, Balance</keywords>

Whoever has a portion in the holy people sits in the shadow of faith to receive the <term>Ushpizin</term> <gloss>divine guests</gloss>, to rejoice in this world and in the world to come. Therefore, one must bring joy to the poor. Why? Because the portion of those guests who are invited belongs to the poor. If a person sits in this shadow of faith and invites these supreme guests, the guests of faith, but does not give them their portion <note>by feeding the poor</note>, they all rise up from him and say:
> **Do not eat the bread of one who has an evil eye...** <note>Proverbs 23:6</note>

It turns out that the table he prepared is his own, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is not upon it. Concerning him it is written:
> **I will spread dung upon your faces, the dung of your festival sacrifices...** <note>Malachi 2:3</note>

It says "your" festivals, and not "My" festivals. Woe to that person when these guests of faith rise from his table. Rabbi Abba said: All his days, Abraham would stand at the crossroads to invite guests and prepare tables for them. Now that people invite him, and all the righteous, and King David, yet do not give them their portion, Abraham rises from the table and calls out:
> **Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men...** <note>Numbers 16:26</note>

And they all ascend after him. <term>Isaac</term> says:
> **...but the belly of the wicked shall want.** <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>

<term>Jacob</term> says:
> **The morsel which you have eaten, you shall vomit up.** <note>Proverbs 23:8</note>

And all the other righteous ones say:
> **For all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean.** <note>Isaiah 28:8</note>

<term>King David</term> spoke and completed the judgment, as it is written: "And it came to pass about ten days after, that the Lord smote Nabal, and he died." Why is this mentioned? Because David asked of Nabal and acted as a guest toward him, but Nabal did not want him, did not invite him, and gave him no portion. During those ten days when King David judges the world, that person who acts this way is judged more harshly than Nabal. Rabbi Eleazar said: Therefore, the Torah does not burden a person more than he is able, as it is written: "Every man shall give as he is able." Let a man not say, "I will eat and be satisfied and drink first, and what remains I will give to the poor." Rather, the first of everything belongs to the guests. If he gladdens the guests and satisfies them, the Holy One, blessed be He, rejoices with him, and Abraham calls over him:
> **Then you shall delight yourself in the Lord...** <note>Isaiah 58:14</note>

And Isaac calls over him:
> **No weapon that is formed against you shall prosper.** <note>Isaiah 54:17</note>

Rabbi Simeon said: King David says this <note>the verse from Isaiah 54</note> because all the King's weapons and the King's battles were entrusted into David's hands. However, Isaac says: "His seed shall be mighty upon earth... wealth and riches shall be in his house." Jacob says: "Then shall your light break forth as the morning." The other righteous ones say: "And the Lord shall guide you continually, and satisfy your soul." King David says: "No weapon that is formed against you shall prosper," for he is appointed over all the weapons of the world. Fortunate is the portion of the person who merits all this. Fortunate is the portion of the righteous in this world and in the world to come; concerning them it is written:
> **Your people also shall be all righteous...** <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

-> **And you shall take for yourselves on the first day...** <- <note>Leviticus 23:40</note>

Rabbi Simeon opened: "Every one that is called by My name: for I have created him for My glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him." "Every one that is called by My name" refers to Man, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, called by His name, as it is written: "So God created man in His own image." Furthermore, he is called by His name when He brings forth truth and judgment in the world and is called <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God/Judge</gloss>, as it is written: "You shall not revile the judges <note>Elohim</note>." He called him by His name, as it is written: "So God created man in His own image." And we have well established that it is written: **"Let us make man in our image, after our likeness"**; this was said at the time of union. And so it is in the union of both, in image and likeness, and Man emerged as male and female. "So God created man in His own image." In the book of King Solomon, we find that at the time of union

**This commandment** is to take the <term>Lulav</term> <gloss>palm branch</gloss> on that day with its specific species. > At the arrival of the clouds <note>the monsoon season</note>, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew away to Lake Manasa. One-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge toward a forest of land-growing lotuses. O young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great affection in the water adorned with tender lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of swans in that flock. 3

**Sentence Structure:** O young girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth part flew from the water's edge and went to a forest of land-lotuses. And three pairs of swans were seen eager for play in the water shining with young lotus stalks. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** O beloved, sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. From among them, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root went to Lake Manasasarovar. One-eighth part flew from the shore of the water and went into a forest of land-lotuses. And three pairs <note>six swans</note> were seen playing very lovingly in water beautiful with tender lotus stalks. So tell me, how many swans were in that group? 3

**Statement of the Problem:** <term>Mulaguna</term> <gloss>the multiplier of the square root</gloss> is 10. The <term>ashtamsha</term> <gloss>eighth part</gloss> is 1/8. The <term>drishyam</term> <gloss>visible or known quantity</gloss> is 6. Since it was stated <note>in a previous rule</note> that the quantity should be increased or decreased by the fractions, here we divide the visible quantity and the square root multiplier by one minus the fraction <gloss>1 - 1/8 = 7/8</gloss>. The resulting visible quantity is 48/7 and the square root multiplier is 80/7. Half of the multiplier is 40/7. The square of this <gloss>1600/49</gloss> is added <note>to the visible quantity</note> resulting in 1936/49. The square root of this is 44/7. Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the total number of swans is 144.

**Expansion:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse, the eighth part 1/8 was subtracted from one. Thus 1 - 1/8 = 7/8. This was used to divide the visible quantity 6. Thus 6 divided by 7/8 becomes 48/7, which is the adjusted visible quantity. Similarly, the square root multiplier 10 was divided by 7/8. Thus 10 divided by 7/8 becomes 80/7, which is the adjusted square root multiplier. Now, taking 48/7 as the visible quantity and 80/7 as the square root multiplier, the operation was performed according to the method mentioned in the previous verse. That is, half of the square root multiplier is 80/14. Reducing this by a factor of 2, it becomes 40/7. Squaring this results in 1600/49. This is then added to the visible quantity 48/7...

# Against Celsus IV. 30. 31.

<margin>5</margin> Celsus says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt, and that they never performed any noteworthy deed, nor were they ever of any account in terms of fame or number. Regarding the claim that they were not fugitives, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had settled in Egypt as sojourners, we have already spoken in the preceding sections. If he thinks he can prove they were of no account in fame or number because their history is not widely found among the Greeks, we shall say this: if anyone were to look closely at their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were <margin>10</margin> men who displayed a shadow of the heavenly life upon earth. Among them, no other was recognized as God except the One over all, and no maker of images was permitted to be a citizen. For neither painter nor image-maker existed in their commonwealth, as the law expelled all such people from it, <margin>15</margin> so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues—an activity that attracts the attention of foolish men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, among them a law to this effect: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved image, any likeness of a form, male or female, the likeness of any beast that is upon the earth, the likeness of any <margin>20</margin> winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 4:16-18.</note> And the law intended that by associating with the truth of each thing, they should not fashion other things contrary to the truth, which would give a false representation of the truly male or the truly female, or <margin>25</margin> the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or of creeping things, or of fish. Noble and magnificent also was their command: "Lest, when you look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, the whole host of heaven, you be led astray and worship them and serve them." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 4:19.</note>

<margin>30</margin> What a constitution this was for an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for an effeminate man <note>original: "thelydrian," referring to men who adopted feminine traits or roles</note> to be seen! It is also wonderful that the provocations of the young, namely prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of the most just men, who had long given proof of a healthy life.

<summary>Origen defends the Jewish nation against Celsus's insults by highlighting the moral and spiritual superiority of the Mosaic Law, specifically its prohibition of idolatry and its promotion of a "heavenly life" on earth.</summary>

# Through meditation on the Supreme, that which is hidden is revealed; for from Him come both bondage and liberation. (3.2.5)

3.2.5

Now, a further point may be raised: the <term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss> is indeed a part of the Supreme Self, just as a spark is a part of a fire. This being the case, just as the fire and the spark possess the same powers of burning and lighting, so too should the individual soul and the Lord possess the same powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Therefore, by virtue of this inherent knowledge and sovereignty, the soul should be able to create chariots and other objects in dreams by its mere will.

To this, we reply: Although there is a relationship of part and whole between the individual soul and the Lord, it is a matter of direct perception that the soul possesses characteristics opposite to those of the Lord. Does this mean that the soul does not possess characteristics identical to the Lord at all? No, it is not that they do not exist; rather, though existing, they are hidden <note>original: "tirohita"</note> by the intervention of ignorance and other factors.

That hidden nature, however, is revealed to one who meditates on the Supreme Lord and exerts effort, whose darkness has been dispelled. Just as the power of sight, when obscured by a cataract, is restored through the potency of medicine, so too does this nature manifest in someone who has attained perfection through the grace of the Lord. It does not manifest naturally in all living beings. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, come the bondage and liberation of this soul. Bondage results from the lack of knowledge of the Lord's true nature, while liberation results from the realization of that nature. As the Scripture says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of afflictions, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, there is a third state at the dissolution of the body: universal sovereignty, absolute unity, and all desires fulfilled" <note>Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note>.

# Or, that hidden state results from connection with the body. (3.2.6)

3.2.6

Why, then, does the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It would seem more logical for these powers to remain unhidden, just as the burning and lighting powers of a spark are not hidden.

We reply: This is true; however, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs due to its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the burning and lighting powers of fire are hidden when it is latent in wood <note>original: "arani"</note> or covered by ashes, so too is the soul's knowledge and sovereignty obscured. This obscuration is caused by the error of non-discrimination resulting from the soul's connection with the <term>upadhis</term> <gloss>limiting adjuncts</gloss> such as the body, which are produced by name and form through ignorance.

The word "or" <note>original: "va"</note> in the aphorism is intended to dispel the doubt that the soul is entirely different from the Lord. One might argue: "Let the soul be something entirely different from the Lord, since its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden; why bother imagining a connection with the body?" We say no, because the difference of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. The Scripture begins with "That Divinity thought," and continues with "Entering with this living soul, which is my Self," using the word "Self" to refer to the soul. Furthermore, it teaches the soul its identity with the Lord: "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That Thou Art, O Shvetaketu."

Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden due to the connection with the body. Consequently, the soul's creation of chariots in dreams by mere will is not possible. If such creation were possible by will, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is unpleasant. As for the argument that the scriptural comparison to the waking state proves the reality of dreams, that comparison is not intended to assert reality. It would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the Scripture itself shows the absence of chariots in dreams. Rather, the comparison is made because dreams, being constructed from the impressions of the waking state, appear similar to it. Therefore, it is established that the dream state is <term>mayamatram</term> <gloss>mere illusion</gloss>.

# The absence of that <note>dreaming</note> takes place in the channels and in the Self, as is known from the Scripture. (3.2.7)

The Discussion on the Absence of Dreams (Deep Sleep)

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep <note>original: "sushupti"</note> is examined. Regarding deep sleep, there are several scriptural passages. In one place it is said: "When a man is so asleep that he is completely serene and knows no dream, he has then entered into these <term>nadis</term> <gloss>subtle channels</gloss>." Elsewhere, referring to the same channels, it says: "Having moved through them, he rests in the <term>puritat</term> <gloss>pericardium/membrane surrounding the heart</gloss>." In another place, following the mention of the channels, it says: "In them he then rests; when he is asleep and sees no dream, he then becomes one with the <term>prana</term> <gloss>vital breath/life-force</gloss>." Elsewhere: "He rests in the space within the heart." Again: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with the Existent, he has gone to his own Self." And also: "Embraced by the conscious Self, he knows nothing without and nothing within."

A doubt arises here: Are these various places—the channels and so on—different, independent locations for deep sleep, or are they related to each other as a single location? What is the initial view? That they are different. Why? Because they serve the same purpose. When things serve the same purpose, they do not usually depend on one another...

<summary>Shankara explains that the soul's divine powers are hidden by its physical embodiment and ignorance, rendering dream creations illusory. He begins an inquiry into deep sleep, questioning whether the various scriptural locations for sleep are independent or unified.</summary>

# Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras

## From that comes speed of mind, the state of being beyond instruments, and mastery over the primary cause. 48

The body gaining an unsurpassed speed of movement is <term>manojavitvam</term> <gloss>speed of mind</gloss>. The state of being beyond instruments <note>original: <term>vikaraṇabhāvaḥ</term></note> is the ability of the senses to function independently of the physical body, reaching any desired place, time, or object. Mastery over the primary cause <note>original: <term>pradhānajayaḥ</term></note> is the power to control all manifestations and transformations of nature. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like</gloss>. These are attained from the mastery over the five forms of the sensory organs. 48

## For one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the purity of the intellect and the Self, there comes supremacy over all states of being and omniscience. 49

When the purity of the intellect <note>original: <term>buddhisattva</term></note> is cleansed of the impurities of passion <note>original: <term>rajas</term></note> and darkness <note>original: <term>tamas</term></note>, and when the yogi dwells in the highest clarity and the highest state of self-mastery, they become established in the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the Self <note>original: <term>sattvapuruṣānyatākhyāti</term></note>. This leads to supremacy over all states of being. All the qualities <note>original: <term>guṇas</term></note>, which constitute the essence of all things, present themselves as objects of perception...

<column-break/>

He explains the accomplishments resulting from the mastery over the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, the state of being beyond instruments, and mastery over the primary cause.** The state of being beyond instruments means the functioning of the senses without the physical body. Place refers to regions such as Kashmir; time refers to the past and so on; objects refer to subtle things. Mastery over the primary cause is the power over all natural transformations arising from the mastery of the senses along with their underlying connections. Those who are experts in the Yoga scriptures call these accomplishments <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like</gloss>. It might be asked: through the mastery of the senses, the senses and their objects may be controlled, but how does this affect their causes like the primary matter? He answers: **And these...** from the mastery of the five forms of the instruments <note>the senses</note>, such as perception. This means these accomplishments do not come from mastering the senses alone, but from mastering the five forms, which include the primary matter within them. 48

These meditations <note>original: <term>saṃyamas</term></note> are the causes of powers in the form of knowledge and action. Through the faith produced by the achievement of these powers, he shows the secondary glories of that discernment of the difference between the intellect and the Self, which is the ultimate goal: **For one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the purity of the intellect and the Self, there comes supremacy over all states of being and omniscience.** Clarity comes from washing away the filth of passion and darkness. From that comes the highest state of self-mastery. Indeed, the mind-stuff was not under control when overwhelmed by passion and darkness; but when these are subsided, it is under the control of the master yogi. For the yogi established in the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the Self, there is supremacy over all states of being. He explains this further: **All the qualities...**

<margin>Su Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin> Those who do not know the Tao but devote themselves to learning find that their knowledge and observations increase daily. Yet, they have no way to unify this information, and it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: To hear much, select what is good and follow it; to see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Tao and look back upon your past actions, you will see that every one of them was false and delusional. To remove delusion and return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I have one thread that strings it all together. To remove delusion in order to seek a return to nature can be called decreasing. However, the mind that seeks to remove delusion still remains. Only when one forgets even this mind, leaving only pure nature without residue, can one act in all things without losing the state of non-action <term>wuwei</term> <gloss>effortless action or non-interference</gloss>. All people have the desire to grasp the affairs and principles of the world. Therefore, they create complications and seek results. This intention is visible externally, and things resist it; thus, they can never truly succeed. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no such intentions in his heart. This is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Although he does not try to grasp the affairs of the world, the affairs of the world follow him and find peace.

<margin>Lü Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a high-ranking official and reformer known for his commentaries on Daoist texts.</note></margin> One who pursues learning is one who has not yet heard the Tao. Seeking it without having heard it, one must be broad in study; thus, there is a daily increase. One who pursues the Tao is one who has already heard the Tao. Having heard it and acting upon it, one aims only for non-action. Thus, there is a daily decrease. But the act of decreasing itself still involves some effort. One must decrease even the act of decreasing until one reaches non-action. Non-action means being still and unmoving. "Doing nothing left undone" means being moved by a stimulus and then penetrating all the causes under heaven. To pursue the Tao and reach this state is called "ending learning and having no worries." It is called "the spirit has no fixed direction and the Changes have no fixed form." Who but the most divine in the world could achieve this? From this, we see that taking hold of the world is always done through non-action. When one resorts to forced action, it is clear that it is insufficient to take hold of the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai Commentary <note>Huang Maocai was a Southern Song dynasty scholar.</note></margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires daily increase. Only after what has been increased is transformed can one speak of the Tao; therefore, the Tao desires daily decrease. That which is increased can be sought through progress, but that which is decreased is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only those with the highest clarity can suddenly let everything drop away and reach the realm of non-action. Thus, they can do everything, and their applications are inexhaustible. They apply themselves to the world with ample room to maneuver.

<margin>Xizhai Commentary <note>Xizhai is the art name of Li Kan, 1245 to 1320, or potentially a later commentator using the same name.</note></margin> Pursuing learning is the means to seek knowledge; therefore, it increases daily. Pursuing the Tao is the means to remove delusion; therefore, it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, then the decrease will not be complete. Thus, daily increase provides the ground for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. Upon reaching non-action, every action is essentially non-action. This cannot easily be discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its peak, though the world is vast, one thread unifies it. If one creates trouble through meddling, even a single object before one's eyes will become entangled and confused, let alone the vastness of the world.

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own heart. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good. Thus, virtue is goodness. To those who are trustworthy, I give my trust. To those who are not trustworthy, I also give my trust. Thus, virtue is trust. Are Being and Substance different? Is Being something stripped of all other things, while Substance is Being along with the others: motion, rest, sameness, and difference? And are these the elements of Substance? In that case, the whole is Substance, while each of those is something specific: one is Being, another is motion, and another is something else. Motion, then, is Being by accident; but is Substance also accidental? Or is it a completing part of Substance? Or is Substance itself, and everything there <note>referring to the intelligible realm of true reality</note>, Substance? Why then is it not the same here <note>referring to the physical world of the senses</note>? Is it because there, all things are one, but here, the images having been separated, one thing is this and another is that? Just as in a seed all things are together, and each part is the whole, and a hand is not separate, nor is a head separate; but here, they are separated from one another, for they are images and not true realities. Shall we then say that qualities there are substances, being differences concerning substance, or concerning Being, and creating different substances in relation to one another, and substances in general? This is not absurd. But regarding the qualities here, some are differences of substances, such as being two-footed or four-footed; while others, not being differences, are called qualities in this sense alone. And yet the same thing can be a completing difference in one case, and not a difference in another, where it does not complete the substance.

This is how it stands with poetry in relation to philosophy. For what else is poetry but philosophy? In time, it is ancient; in harmony, it is metrical; in thought, it is mythological. And what else is philosophy but poetry? In time, it is more recent; in harmony, it is more unencumbered <note>original: "euzonotera," literally well-girded or lightly equipped for movement</note>; in thought, it is clearer. Since these two things differ from one another only in time and outward form, how could anyone judge the difference between them? In both cases, both the poets and the philosophers say something concerning the divine.

Or let us say this inquiry is like the following: it is as if someone, considering that original art of medicine in comparison to the new art prescribed for modern bodies, were to look for what is better or worse in each. Asclepius <note>The god of healing and medicine</note> would answer him that time does not transform the other arts. For those things whose use is always the same, the works are likewise similar. But medicine must follow the temperament of bodies, a thing that is not stable or consistent, but is altered and shifted by the foods in one's diet. It must find remedies and regimens for the body, different ones at different times, suitable to the current nourishment.

Therefore, do not think that my sons, the famous Machaon and Podalirius <note>Homeric healers and sons of Asclepius</note>, were any less skilled at healing than those who later applied themselves to the art and discovered these wise and manifold remedies. Rather, at that time, the art dealt with bodies that were not pampered, nor complex, nor entirely weakened, and so it handled them easily. Their work was a simple matter: to cut out arrows and spread soothing herbs <note>A reference to Iliad 11.515</note>. But now, as bodies have slipped away into a more complex diet and a corrupted temperament, the art itself has become complex. It has changed from its former simplicity into a manifold form.

Come then, let both the poet and the philosopher together answer like Asclepius on behalf of their practices. The philosopher would be greatly distressed if anyone should think that Homer and Hesiod, or by Zeus, Orpheus, or any other of the men of that time, were any less wise than Aristotle.

First, let the fisherman be both swift and strong in body and limbs, neither too fat nor lacking in flesh. For it is often necessary for him to struggle against powerful fish being hauled in, which possess immense strength as long as they are tossed about in the embrace of their mother, the brine. He must be able to leap from a rock and spring back onto a rock with ease. He must be able to travel quickly through the long paths of the deep when the labor of the sea is extended, to dive into the deepest parts, and to remain among the swells as if on land, lingering over the tasks in which men of enduring spirit compete within the sea.

The fisherman should have a soul of many shifts and a keen mind, since fish devise many varied schemes when they encounter unexpected snares. Let him be especially daring, fearless, and temperate. Let him not love the satiety of sleep, but let him watch with a sharp heart and wide-open eyes. Let him bear well both the winter storms of Zeus and the thirsty season of the Dog Star <note>Sirius, associated with the peak of summer heat</note>. Let him desire labor and love the sea. In this way, he may be successful in the catch and dear to Hermes.

Hunting is strongest in the evening during the autumn seasons, and also when the Morning Star <note>the planet Venus</note> rises. When the god had revealed these things, all the maidens of the race of the Aepytidae <note>a royal Messenian dynasty</note> immediately cast lots. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. However, Epebolus the seer forbade her sacrifice, saying she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus; he claimed that Lyciscus's wife, being unable to bear children, had secretly substituted the girl as her own. While the seer was explaining these matters, Lyciscus took the maiden and fled to Sparta. When the Messenians became disheartened upon learning of Lyciscus's escape, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytid lineage who was more distinguished than Lyciscus in general reputation and especially in matters of war, offered his own daughter for sacrifice of his own free will. 

But human ambition is often obscured by destiny, just as a pebble is covered by the silt of a river. Even then, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, fate brought the following obstacle. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not record) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was already intending to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since Aristodemus had betrothed her to him, he was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, as the betrothed, had more authority over her. Secondly, when he saw that this argument was not succeeding, he turned to a shameful story, claiming that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. 

Finally, he provoked Aristodemus to such an extent that, driven mad by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and demonstrated that she was not with child. Epebolus, who was present, then ordered that someone else must provide a daughter; for he claimed that the death of Aristodemus's daughter counted for nothing, as her father had murdered her, rather than sacrificing her to the gods whom the Pythia <note>the priestess of the Oracle at Delphi</note> had commanded. When the seer said this, the Messenian multitude rushed to kill the girl's suitor, as he had brought a useless defilement upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain. 

However, this man was a very close friend of Euphaes. Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the death of the girl, and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. While he was saying this, all those of the Aepytid race agreed that he spoke the truth; for they were eager to be rid of the fear for their own daughters. Thus, obeying the king's exhortation, they dissolved the assembly and turned from it to sacrifices and a festival of the gods. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, hearing of the oracle given to the Messenians, were also disheartened, and their kings were hesitant to begin a battle.

In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians—since their sacrifices had become favorable—marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to no longer be present with them. The allies of the Messenians were also late. For the Spartans were already viewed with suspicion by other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly from the Lacedaemonians, acting more on their own than by a common decree. The Arcadians had been openly forbidden from the campaign, and they too were not present. The fame of the oracle led the Messenians to risk battle even without allies. For the most part, nothing happened differently than in the previous battle; the daylight failed them while they were still fighting. That we should not go up to the Chosen House <note>the Temple</note> on a festival without an offering, as it is said: and they shall not appear before Me empty-handed.

### **Torah** is light. These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah refers to the commands of "do not add" and "do not subtract," which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers have said: a thing that is perfectly complete cannot be subject to deficiency or excess. For if it were deficient, it would not be complete, and if it could receive an addition, it would mean it was not previously finished. Therefore, the definition of the complete is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is dependent on His Great Name, which is <term>YHVH</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>, as it is written: "The Torah of <term>YHVH</term> is perfect," as I have elaborated on this in my commentary on Tractate Shevuot in the chapter "Torah Or." And as it says in the Zohar on the verse "This is My Name and this is My Memorial": the letters <term>Yod-He</term> with "My Name" <note>in Hebrew numerology</note> equals 365 <note>the negative commandments</note>, and <term>Vav-He</term> with "My Memorial" equals 248 <note>the positive commandments</note>. And it is written: "I am the first and I am the last." He is the absolute perfection, without subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God," which is a warning against erasing the Name or breaking a stone from the Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are the house in which He, blessed be He, dwells, as is the Temple. It is written: "I am the Lord, that is My Name"; the Holy One is one and His Name is one. The letters are like a body or a house, and His Name, blessed be He, is the soul within them. One who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service <note>Divine Service/Sacrifice</note> comprises most of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came to have a fixed place specifically in the Chosen House, and the reason was given: "To His dwelling place you shall seek, and there you shall come." "To His dwelling" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>YHVH</term>, as it is written: "And <term>YHVH</term> is in His holy palace," which is the secret of the Name <term>Adonai</term> <gloss>Lord</gloss>, which is the <term>Shekhinah</term>. For in the Temple, the Glory is united with the Beauty of His strength, and this is "to place His Name there," which the Targum translates as "to cause His Presence to dwell." And "around the place of holiness the wicked walk," referring to the <term>Kelipah</term> <gloss>husks/shards of evil</gloss>; therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see."

### **And sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inside. This is the secret of the commandment to occupy oneself with bringing the sacrifice from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch is returned to its root, and it is written regarding them: "There you shall offer," meaning there they shall have an elevation and not outside. Since the holiness is in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we were commanded to "turn away from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. Our Sages hinted at this secret: "Gentiles outside the Land are not true idolaters." The matter is that gentiles in the Land of Israel, who are under the dominion of the Honorable Name, worship by "cutting the plantings" <note>heresy/spiritual damage</note>, and this is true idolatry. However, those outside the Land are under the dominion of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against breaking a single stone of holiness, so conversely it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate a "Condemned City" and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Likewise, one who entices or misleads others to idolatry must be uprooted and eradicated, for he is from the impurity of the ancient Serpent who was an enticer. The Holy One immediately said, "Cursed is the Serpent," therefore we do not seek merits for an enticer. The command came not to love him but to hate him, as was said of the Serpent: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman." A false prophet is also like an enticer. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the First Fruits <note>Bikkurim</note>, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the First Fruits, being the "beginning," indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there the priests, who are holy to their God, shall take them and eat them in Jerusalem. The secret of "Lesser Sanctity" offerings and the Second Tithe is that their consumption is in Jerusalem. This is like the grain, wine, and oil, which are the "fathers of fathers" of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat Lesser Sanctity offerings until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul, and afterward the body is permitted for enjoyment. Know that just as the Service, which is the sacrifice, is an offering to God, so too is the worshiper. For the essence of the service is that a person offers himself, in the secret of "When a man <note>Adam</note> brings an offering from among you." The burnt offering is entirely consumed because it comes to atone for the thoughts of the heart, which are spiritual, and it burns all night because "he devises iniquity upon his bed." Lesser Sanctity offerings represent the perfection of the soul and the body.

### **The secret** of the unblemished firstborn is the secret of "Holy Israel," who are called "My firstborn son, Israel." They are "Tam" <gloss>perfect/simple</gloss>, the complete congregation, and are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating consecrated animals when they have fallen into blemish and been redeemed is that Israel is holy, and Israel is called "Adam" <gloss>Man</gloss>. He was holy, but afterward a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," yet he has a redemption, in the secret of "And I will give a man <note>Adam</note> in your stead." This was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>the scapegoat</gloss> and "he shall bear their iniquities," which the Sages interpreted as the "iniquities of the perfect one" <note>a play on words between 'avonot' and 'avot'</note> which fall upon his head and his people. But we are commanded not to intentionally cause a blemish in consecrated animals in order to eat them, for then one casts a blemish into holiness by his own choice. Also, the prohibition of working or shearing consecrated animals exists because even the "broken tablets" of the Law remain holy.

### **The general principle** is that the Service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the human being. Likewise, his soul is offered after his death on the Altar on High, and Michael is the High Priest. All of this is the secret of "For in the image of God He made man." Therefore, the warning is very strong to be careful in capital laws, not to put a person to death except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then he dies "by the hand of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the witness, He is the judge," for God is a true witness and a true judge. So must the Sanhedrin be: just as they are judges of truth, they must have witnesses of truth. I mean that the truth of the testimony must be clarified to them with absolute clarity through inquiry and investigation. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones."

### **And since** death is precious in the eyes of the Lord—because Israel is holy from the side of their souls, and after death the souls cleave above—therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness, etc., for you are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the nations; cutting and baldness are among their statutes, for it is appropriate for them since in death they go to destruction and have no portion in this world or the World to Come. We, however, are children of God. When we are absent from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, on the contrary, we have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or to perform these acts.

### **Let us return** to the matter: the person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it says, "When a man brings an offering from among you." There is a further secret in this: for it happens that a person is offered even below, namely in the secret of <term>Gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation</gloss>, as in "Man and beast You save, O Lord." Therefore, even in the eating of non-consecrated meat <note>meat of desire</note>, we were commanded regarding ritual slaughter <note>Shechitah</note> with a great warning against a nick in the blade, for then it becomes "carrion" <note>nevelah</note>, and "a vile thing <note>nevalah</note> is done in Israel." For who knows what reincarnation might be within it? "Love your neighbor as yourself"—choose for him a beautiful death, namely slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies on its own, the power of impurity spreads and takes hold of it. But when one slaughters it while it is healthy, and there is a spark of holiness in the pure animal, beast, or bird, then its soul departs in purity.

### **And one who eats** a limb from a living animal is like one who eats the flesh of his brother when a reincarnated soul is present. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure animals, beasts, and birds all indicate the spark spread within them, whether it is from the "Side of Impurity" or the "Side of Holiness." I have elaborated on this in the portion of Shemini. When Israel conducts themselves with holiness, it is written of them: "And they shall make for Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell within them." For they themselves are the Tabernacle, as man consists of three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies, the heart to the Holy Place, and from the belly downward to the Courtyard of the Sanctuary, as I elaborated in the portion of Terumah. When one eats foods that are from the side of holiness, they are like sacrifices offered upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages said: "Now, a man's table atones for him," as I have elaborated in its place.

### **Regarding** the matter of the commandments of the Festivals and their sacrifices, I have written about each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals and to go up for the pilgrimage: "Three times a year all your males shall appear." Our Sages said: "Just as he comes to see, so he comes to be seen." Therefore, if one wishes to be seen in the Temple where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. For otherwise, it is forbidden to gaze upon a wicked person; how then could he wish to appear before Him, blessed be He, bringing a burnt offering of appearance? Then he himself becomes a sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. And it says, "Three times a year he shall appear"—Isaac, who was a "perfect burnt offering"...

<header>Description of Lima, City of the Kings.</header>

<margin>Appearance of the city of Lima.</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some of them are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one may also see into every corner, and on both sides the open fields. Through the majority of the houses run canals, bringing fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort to the citizens, who may thereby water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they keep beautiful and pleasant. Also,

<margin>Many watermills, with which they grind their corn.</margin>
there lie in this river many watermills after the manner of our own land, where they grind their corn; in short, there live here very wealthy citizens, some of whom possess 150,000 <term>ducats</term> <gloss>gold coins</gloss>. And from this city ships sometimes depart carrying a value of 800,000 ducats, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which stands a crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their cattle, as well as their dovecotes and their vineyards—though the grapes are not good due to the nature of the land—and beautiful gardens, filled not only with all kinds of fruits of that country, but also

<margin>Description of the fertility of the land.</margin>
those of Spain, such as figs, pomegranates, limes, lemons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar canes, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. Truly, to pass a human life with joy, were it not for the scandalous disagreements and wars, this place is surely one of the most beautiful in the entire world. For the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the entire year there is neither excessive heat nor harmful cold. Also, it has never been seen that hunger or plague occurred there, nor any rain, or claps of thunder, or lightning from heaven

<margin>Why the City of the Kings received its name; it was built in the year 1535.</margin>
striking. On the contrary, there is always a clear, bright, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535 and is named the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Epiphany <note>original: "drie Coningen dagh", the feast of the Three Kings</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as meat and fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less an abundance of wheat and grain. During the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet it is not unhealthy like ours; those who have pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase in population and wealth, although many years ago there were already over 500 houses,

<margin>The width and length of the houses of Lima.</margin>
and the city is built very spaciously, so that 2,000 might well stand there, for the streets are wide and the market square is large. Each house has a plot of 80 feet in width and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for within two or three years it is eaten away by worms—the houses are built with only one story, yet very

<margin>Appearance of the houses.</margin>
costly and magnificent with many chambers, halls, and parlors, suitable for living and for lodging foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials which they bake together very thickly and fill with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen; all around and on top

<column-break/>

of the walls they make small arbors of greenery where they shelter from the sun. They do not need to worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where Bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trujillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popayan, Carchi, St. Michael, and St. Francisco. It was mentioned previously that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea, we have dealt until now, beginning from the Equator <note>original: "Linea"</note> and Cape Passao to this point. It should also be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima but much further south, the sea coast is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places, where for a distance of ten miles it neither thunders, lightens, nor rains; but beyond those ten miles it does, or as far as the mountains lie from the sea. There are also in this flat land no springs or wells, but rather four or five standing waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which originate from the snow and rain falling in the mountains, not from springs, of which there are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers have been partly described before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from one another, though mostly 7 or 8, by which traveling people regulate their journey because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, for a mile's width or even wider, sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the layout of the land, there are various fertile trees and corn lands which are cultivated and sown by the people, which they may do throughout the entire year. Also, many kinds of wild trees grow near these rivers: cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises, etc. And since the Spaniards have taken the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through certain canals which they lead out of these rivers. Because these rivers run swiftly down from high mountains, one can hardly cross them without help, and many have drowned therein. Those who make their journey along the flat land generally stay so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and rains heavily, it is dangerous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either with certain rafts they have for that purpose, or with a net which they fill tightly with gourds, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out, while one of the Indians swims ahead, pulling that net or raft with a cord, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of greenery. The men wear shirts and cloths over their knees and extending beyond, and an upper garment like a cloak. The women wear a garment of cotton according to the length of the body; and although the fashion of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nonetheless some distinction in the head-dress. For some wear single cords, some braided, some of one color, others of various colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, all distinguished according to the custom of the land.
