<meta>continues from previous page: the soul</meta> holds together all mundane essences; how it harmonizes the entire cosmos through its own harmony; how it contains all cosmic forms and shapes within its own shape; in what manner it is able to perfect all natural powers, as well as all rational or technical powers, through the powers within itself; and how it awakens mundane productions through its own activities. Why, then, did he not call the soul the middle point between intellect and sense-perception? Because, he says, intellect and sense-perception are certain cognitive powers; but he wishes to hand down the middle-status inherent in their essences, not that which is in their powers. And why did he not call it the middle between the Idea <note>the archetypal Form</note> and things formed according to species? Because his purpose now was not to teach what kind of form it has, but rather its essence; and it is not the same thing to speak of the essence of something and its form; he presents it as such an essence. Why did he not place it as the middle between intelligible and sensible numbers? Because he will provide the account of harmony in the following passages, according to which the soul holds the middle-status between the separate numbers and separate harmony, and the sensible numbers and the harmony inseparable from their subjects. For the soul is neither Harmony-itself nor is it among things harmonized, at least according to the thought of Plato; rather, Harmony-itself is uniform, separate, and exempt from all things harmonized in any way, being only that very thing which is called harmony; whereas the harmony in harmonized things belongs to others and is naturally moved by others; but the harmony of the soul is the middle between both; for this is the "primarily harmonized" thing. Therefore, it also imparts harmony to others; for that which is able to impart something to another is either the Form itself, or it has participated in it primarily. It is, therefore, subordinate to intelligible harmony and subordinate to intelligible numbers; and by surpassing sensible harmony, it also surpasses sensible numbers. And if one must speak briefly about each of these, each exists in four ways: for number is first the divine, second the essential, third the psychic, and last the natural; the first is of the nature of the One, the second is immovable, the third is self-moving, and the fourth is moved by another. Harmony, too, is first that in the gods, second that in truly existing things, third that in souls, and last that in things harmonized by others. If, then, it were Plato's present purpose to speak about psychic harmony, he would have said that it is the middle between indivisible and divisible harmony; but since the discourse at present is about essence, he says that it <unclear>has occupied</unclear> the middle of Sameness, Difference, and Essence. One must also observe this: that just as he has made a return in these matters from the progressions of the psychic essence back to the principles; for since the form of mixtures is twofold—one being established by the mixing of the extremes,

<column-break/>

as we have in the case of essence, sameness, and difference, and the other being established by the gathering of the middle terms back into a single whole—in the former case he began from essence and ended at difference, but in the second case he did the reverse: he harmonized difference with sameness first, then both with essence, and ended at essence, from which he started during the progression. Everywhere, moreover, he holds to the two principles after the One; for even when he made the soul out of the indivisible and the divisible, he placed the indivisible analogous to the Limit, and the divisible to the Infinite; <unclear>for the Infinite is the cause of multiplicity</unclear>, and the Limit is the cause of union. And when he used Difference as it is among the genera of Being, it belongs to the series of the Infinite, while Sameness belongs to that of the Limit. And when he mixed these with Essence; for Essence is uniform, while these are dyadic and opposed to one another; and he did not stop gathering the multiplicity until he revealed the whole as one; for the One is superior even to Essence itself and to the two principles. Since the mixture is twofold, as we said—one being the constitutive mixture of the elements themselves, the other being the mixture of the product of the elements—Porphyry rightly inquired whether he made both of these in the Mixing Bowl <term>krater</term> <gloss>the vessel used by the Creator to mix the soul</gloss>, or one outside the bowl and the other within it. And he judged that he mixes the elements without the bowl <unclear>acting</unclear>; since the generation of the middle terms occurred through the meeting of the extremes, the extremes were not able to come together into the same thing at all. But when completing the product from all the middle elements, he uses the bowl, casting the elements into it and mixing them, so that the soul might become all things in all, one and of the same color as itself and of like parts, all the genera having pervaded through the whole, and so that the soul might receive its form, which comes from the bowl. For the form of each thing depends on the whole, so that reasonably, the bowl being the "soul-maker," he produces the wholeness of the soul within it. Therefore, the second mixture is in the bowl alone. Our teacher <note>likely Syrianus, Proclus' predecessor</note> was also pleased with this distinction. Plato also seems to indicate this in his discourse on particular souls, saying: "and again into the former bowl, in which he had blended and mixed the soul of the universe, he poured the remains of the previous ingredients, mixing them." He says the soul of the universe was cast into this bowl, but not its elements, and in the case of our souls, the remains of the previous ingredients are mixed in it. These were the middle terms, clearly meaning that the second mixture occurs in the bowl <unclear>after another</unclear> of the first according to the demiurgic cause, and the second also according to the life-generating cause, already making a soul out of the middle genera. For it was necessary for the Demiurge <note>the Creator</note> to act both before the bowl and with the bowl, just as he acts after the bowl, using the demiurgic divisions and the other activities concerning the soul; for after the wholeness of the soul come the

### On the shame sought from unworthy praise.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you later condemn, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Pain:* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.
<note>A large ornamental initial L marks the beginning of the response from Reason.</note>
*Reason:* That which is an evil often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people believe others to be such as they are themselves. Hence they are even more prone to praising than is fair. And although I admit it is an evil to praise the unworthy, it is much worse to disparage the undeserving.

*Pain:* I praised an unworthy man.

*Reason:* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another, but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Pain:* The praise of another turns into my own infamy.

*Reason:* Rather, it is either your fault or your ignorance. For no infamy, just as no praise, truly comes from what belongs to another.

*Pain:* I grieve deeply for having praised an unworthy man.

*Reason:* See to it then that you do not have cause to grieve for this same thing often. Beware of leaping forward rashly to praise or to disparage. For there is a lust for both things and, to speak accurately, a disease and a certain itching of a restless tongue that knows no quiet. The restraint and guarding of the tongue are numbered among the works of extraordinary perfection, as the Scripture says:

I say, therefore, that in the first method, which is that festive narration, there is no need for any art, because nature itself creates and forms men capable of narrating pleasantly, giving them the face, the gestures, the voice, and the appropriate words to imitate whatever they wish. In the other method involving witticisms, what can art do? For that salty saying must have come out and hit the mark before it appears that the one who says it could have thought about it; otherwise, it is cold and has no merit. Therefore, I estimate that the whole thing is the work of talent and nature. Then Messer Pietro Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo, 1470 to 1547, was a prominent Venetian scholar, poet, and later a Cardinal, known for his influence on the Italian language</note> replied and said: The Lord Prefect <note>Francesco Maria della Rovere, the Duke of Urbino and Lord Prefect of Rome</note> does not deny what you say, namely that nature and talent play the primary roles, especially regarding <term>inuentione</term> <gloss>invention or the finding of ideas</gloss>. But it is certain that in the mind of everyone, no matter how talented a man may be, there are born good and bad concepts, some more and some less; but judgment and art then polish and correct them, making a selection of the good ones and rejecting the bad. Therefore, leaving aside what pertains to talent, explain to us what consists of art, namely concerning the <term>facetie</term> <gloss>facetiae or humorous anecdotes</gloss> and the <term>motti</term> <gloss>mottoes or quick jests</gloss> that induce laughter. Tell us which are appropriate for the Courtier and which are not, and at what time and in what manner they should be used, for this is what the Lord Prefect asks of you. Then Messer Federico <note>Federico Fregoso, a diplomat and cleric who participates in the dialogue</note>, still laughing, said: There is no one here among us to whom I do not yield in everything, and especially in being witty, unless perhaps the foolish things that often make others laugh more than fine sayings were also accepted as witticisms. And so, turning to Count Ludovico <note>Ludovico di Canossa</note> and to Messer Bernardo Bibiena <note>Bernardo Dovizi da Bibiena, author of the comedy La Calandria</note>, he said: Here are the masters of this.

raw wool <note>original: "succida"</note> applied as a compress. Olympias of Thebes added hyssop and soda <note>original: "nitru"</note>. Ash of stag's horn is taken in a drink. It is also used for a laboring womb. An application of bull's gall with opium in the amount of two obols is also effective. It is beneficial to fumigate the womb with the hair of a stag. They report that hinds, when they feel themselves to be pregnant, swallow a small stone; this stone, found in the excrement or in the womb (for it is found there too), is kept and tied on as an amulet to preserve the fetus. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb which are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. Regarding the pumice-like stone found in the uteri of cows in a similar way, we have already spoken in the section on the nature of cattle. Wolf's fat applied as an ointment softens the womb. Their liver relieves pains of the same. It is beneficial for those about to give birth to have eaten wolf's flesh, or if it is near the woman when she begins to labor, provided someone else has eaten it; it is so powerful that it even works against harmful ointments. However, for a wolf to come upon her is considered perilous.

The use of the hare is also great for women. The dried lung taken in a drink aids the womb. The liver taken with Samian earth in water helps with discharges. The rennet <note>original: "coagulum"</note> helps with the afterbirth. They should avoid bathing the day before. An application of it with saffron and leek juice, applied on a fleece, expels a dead fetus. If the wombs of hares are taken in food, it is thought that they conceive males. This is also achieved by their testicles and rennet. A fetus taken from the uterus of a hare is said to bring restored fertility to those who have ceased to bear children. But for the sake of conception, the lung of a healthy hare is also given to the husband to drink. Likewise, nine grains of its dung are given to a virgin so that her breasts may stay firm forever. This is also done with the rennet. For this reason, they smear it with honey on the skin where they do not want pulled hairs to grow back. For flatulence of the womb, it is beneficial to apply the dung of a wild boar or a pig with oil. It stops it more effectively if dried and turned into flour or sprinkled in a drink, or if pregnant women or those in childbirth are suffering from cramps. Pig's milk drunk with honey-wine aids the delivery of women. Drunk by itself, it refills the failing breasts of nursing mothers. If the breasts of a young girl are smeared with the blood of a female pig, they grow less. If they are painful, they are soothed by drinking ass's milk. This, taken with added honey, also aids their purgations. The seasoned fat of the same animal heals ulcerations of the womb, and applied on a fleece, it softens hardness of the womb. By itself, whether fresh or seasoned, applied with water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>a hair-removing agent</gloss>. The seasoned spleen of the same animal applied with water causes an abundance of milk in the breasts. It corrects the womb by fumigation. The hooves of an ass, when used for fumigation, hasten the birth, even to the point of inducing abortion; it is not used otherwise, as it kills a living fetus. The dung of the same animal, if applied fresh, is said to wonderfully stay the flow of blood. Likewise the ash of the same dung, which is also beneficial to the womb when applied.

If horse foam is applied for forty days before they are born, the first hairs are suppressed. The same is done with a decoction of stag's horn; it is better if the horns are fresh. The womb is aided by being washed with mare's milk. If a dead fetus is suspected, the spleen taken in sweet water ejects it. Likewise, a fumigation of the hooves or dried dung. Infused butter stays a prolapsed womb. A hardened womb is opened by bull's gall mixed with oil of roses, with a fleece and turpentine resin applied externally. They also say that a fumigation of dung from a male ox represses a prolapsed womb and aids the fetus. Conception is aided by drinking cow's milk. It is certain that sterility can be caused by the distress of childbirth. Olympias of Thebes asserts that this is corrected by bull's gall, serpent's fat, and verdigris with added honey, applied to the parts before coitus. Calf's gall, if used during purgations and sprinkled on the womb during coitus, both softens the hardness of the belly and diminishes discharge when the navel is pricked, and is generally beneficial to the womb. They set the measure of the gall at the weight of a denarius mixed with a third part of smallage and as much almond oil as seems sufficient; they apply this on a fleece. The gall of a male calf ground with half as much honey is preserved for the womb. If they eat calf's flesh roasted with aristolochia <note>birthwort</note> around the time of conception, they are destined to bear males. Calf's marrow boiled in wine and water with tallow is beneficial for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise, fox fat and cat's excrement applied with resin and rose oil.

They think it most useful to fumigate the womb with goat's horn. The blood of wild goats with sea-palm removes hair. The gall of other goats, however, softens the callus of the womb when sprinkled on, and facilitates conception after purgation. In this way also, the power of a hair-remover is achieved; it is kept applied for three days after the hairs are pulled. Midwives promise that even an immense discharge is stayed by drinking goat's urine, and if the dung is applied. The membrane of goats, seasoned and taken in wine after a birth, expels the afterbirth. They think it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. In a discharge of blood, the rennet is drunk or applied with the seed of henbane. Aeschines says that if the loins of a woman are smeared with the blood of a wild black ox, a loathing for sexual intercourse is produced. He also says that love is induced by drinking goat's urine mixed with nard to mask the smell.

Nothing is more useful for infants than butter, by itself or with honey, especially during teething and for the gums and mouth ulcers. A wolf's tooth tied on as an amulet prevents the terrors of infants and diseases of teething. A wolf's skin provides the same. Indeed, their largest teeth, when tied to horses, are said to provide an untiring gallop. An infant's bowels are stayed by hare's rennet applied to the breast. Ass's liver mixed with a little panacea and dripped into the mouth protects infants from the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and other diseases. They prescribe this to be done for forty days. An ass's skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that horses lose first, when tied on as amulets, provide easy teething for infants, more effectively if they have not touched the ground. Ox spleen is eaten in honey and applied for pains of the spleen. For running ulcers, it is used with honey. Calf's spleen boiled in wine, ground, and applied, heals small ulcers of the mouth. Goat's brain, passed through a gold ring before milk is given to infants, is dripped in against the falling sickness and other infant diseases. Goat's dung tied in a cloth restrains restless infants, especially girls. Gums smeared with goat's milk or hare's brain make teething easy. Cato thinks that sleep is produced by taking hare in food. The common people also believe it brings beauty to the body for nine days—a frivolous claim, yet there must be some underlying reason for such a strong belief. The Magi say that sleep is induced by the gall of a sacrificed goat, provided it is smeared on the eyes or placed under the pillow. Ash of goat's horn smeared with myrtle oil inhibits sweats. Sexual intercourse is stimulated by an application of wild boar's gall, or by a draught of pig's marrow. Likewise, ass's fat mixed with the fat of a male goose. Also, from the coitus of a horse, according to Virgil...

In this manner, the eighth theorem will convert <note>original: ἀντιστρέψει</note> with the fourth. For the one says that under equal sides and angles, equal bases subtend; while the other says that on equal bases, equal sides being placed contain equal angles. Of these, the conclusion of the former was "on equal bases," while "equal sides being placed" was one of the hypotheses previously assumed in that one. Since there are two types of conversions, the leading type is simple and definite, while the other is varied and proceeds into a great number of theorems, converting not in one but in many because of the multitude of hypotheses in the composite theorems. Often, even when starting from two or more hypotheses, we convert one, whenever the hypotheses are not all definite but some are indefinite.

It is necessary to observe in these matters that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions. For example: every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangular number is a hexagonal number. The cause is that the one is more general, while the other is more specific.

In this way, although ships may travel with full sails, they nevertheless seem to stand still. Someone will eventually demonstrate in which parts of the heavens the <term>Cometæ</term> <gloss>comets</gloss> wander, why they travel so far removed from the others, and how great or of what kind they are. We are content with what has been discovered; let posterity also contribute something to the truth. 

One might say, "We do not see further things through the stars, but we transmit our sight through comets." First, if that happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself consists of thick and solid fire, but where a thin splendor runs out and is dispersed into hair <note>The Latin "crines" refers to the tail of the comet, from which the word "comet" (long-haired) is derived.</note>. You see through the gaps in the fires, not through the fires themselves. 

"All stars," he says, "are round; comets are elongated, from which it appears they are not stars." For who will grant you that comets are long, when their nature is indeed a globe like the others? However, the brightness is extended just as the sun sends its rays far and wide. Yet the form of the sun itself is one thing, and the form of the light flowing from it is another. Thus the body of the comets itself is rounded, but the splendor appears longer than that of the other stars. 

Why, you ask? Tell me first, why does the moon receive a light so unlike the sun, since it receives it from the sun? Why is it sometimes red, sometimes pale? Why does it have a livid and black color when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have faces somewhat unlike each other, and most different from the sun. Just as nothing prevents them from being stars even if they are not similar, so nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same condition as the rest, even if they do not have a similar face. 

Furthermore, if you consider the world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in <term>Leo</term> <gloss>the Lion</gloss> and scorches the earth with heat, but in <term>Aquarius</term> <gloss>the Water-bearer</gloss> it binds the winter and closes the rivers with frost? Yet both this star and that are of the same condition, though dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time <term>Aries</term> <gloss>the Ram</gloss> <margin>† rises</margin> is passed through, while <term>Libra</term> <gloss>the Scales</gloss> sinks most slowly; and yet this sign and that are of the same nature, though the former ascends in a brief time and the latter is brought forth for a long duration. 

Do you not see how contrary the elements are to one another? There are heavy and light things, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it like the others. But you see, that star which returns to its place in the thirtieth year <note>A reference to the orbit of Saturn.</note> is very similar to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not perform her work according to a single form, but boasts in her own variety. She made some things slower, others swifter than the rest. Some she made stronger, others more temperate; some she led out from the crowd so they might proceed as individuals and be conspicuous, while some she sent into a flock. 

He is ignorant of nature's power who does not think she is permitted at any time to do anything except what she does most often. She does not show comets frequently; she assigned to them another place, other times, and movements unlike the others. She wished to honor the magnitude of her work through these things, whose appearance is too beautiful for you to think them accidental, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more burning than the others. Indeed, the face of a comet has something remarkable and singular, not cast into a narrow space and cramped, but let down more freely and embracing the region of many stars. 

Aristotle says that comets signify storms and the intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge that to be a star which announces future events? For this is not a sign of a storm in the same way that oil sparking and rotten fungi forming are signs of future rain, or in the way it is an indication of a raging sea if the sea-coots play on dry land, and the herons desert the familiar marshes and fly above the high cloud. Rather, it is like the equinox turning the year toward heat or cold, or like those things the <term>Chaldæi</term> <gloss>Chaldeans/Astrologers</gloss> chant regarding what a star determines as sad or joyful for those being born.

# Zechariah

Since I have already seen the visions which are a hint to the four kingdoms, if so, what are these? For what purpose did I see them?

And the angel answered and said to me: These are the four winds of heaven, going out from standing before the Lord of all the earth. The one in which are the black horses goes out to the north country, and the white ones go out after them, and the spotted ones go out to the south country. And the strong ones went out and sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth; and he said: Go, walk to and fro through the earth. So they walked to and fro through the earth. Then he cried out to me and spoke to me, saying: Behold, those who go out to the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country.

**And he answered:** These are the four winds. This is like saying "to the four winds." Similarly, "and he came Jerusalem" <note>2 Chronicles 1:1</note> is like "to Jerusalem," and "son of Saul" <note>2 Samuel 4:1</note> is like "to the son of Saul," and similar cases. It means to say that these four chariots go out to the four winds of heaven, meaning to give permission to the four kingdoms to rule in the four winds, each one in its time; that is to say, in the entire world which has four sides. **From standing before the Lord of all the earth:** Meaning, by the mission of God who sent them for this, just as it says: "And the sons of God came to stand before the Lord" <note>Job 2:1</note>.

**The one in which:** The black ones. He did not mention the red ones because the kingdom of Babylon had already passed. The kingdom of Media and Persia went out first to the north country, which is Babylon, to destroy it, and afterward they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth. **And the white ones:** Which is the kingdom of Greece <note>Hebrew: Yavan</note>, went out after them because their kingdom grew strong. For Alexander of Macedon, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him, and he and those who came after him ruled afterward over the whole world.

**And the spotted ones went out to the south country:** Which is the land of the south <note>Hebrew: Teiman</note>. Because Rome is northern, and Julius Caesar, who ruled over Rome, began to fight against the kingdom of Greece. At the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is southern, and at that time the sons of Greece were ruling in all those lands. This Julius Caesar overcame them; he transferred the kingdom from the sons of Greece and returned it to the Romans.

**And the strong ones:** These are a hint to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>The Islamic Caliphates</note> who strengthened themselves on their own to seek a kingdom in whatever place it might be. Therefore, he did not designate a specific wind for them. This is what is meant by: "And they sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth."

**And he said:** Meaning, He gave them permission to walk about and conquer lands.

**Then he cried out:** Meaning, he called to me with a loud voice and said to me: **Behold, those who go out to the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country.** This refers to the black horses that went out to Babylon to destroy it.

A pilot has his sailors, and a ship-owner has his pilot, who know well how to handle the tiller at the stern and how to tighten the yard-arm when the wind rises. An architect has assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work but will help labor it to perfection. But the political man, being a master-craftsman <note>original: "aristotechnas"</note> according to Pindar, and a creator of good law and justice, will not immediately choose friends who share his same passions as assistants and fellow-enthusiasts for what is noble. Instead, he often finds himself bent unjustly and violently by one person or another toward different needs. In this, he will seem no different from a builder or a carpenter who, through ignorance and error, uses crooked squares, rulers, and plumb-lines, by which the work was bound to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking tools of political men. One must not slide down with them when they transgress, but rather take care that they do not commit errors even through ignorance.

This very thing brought shame upon Solon and discredited him before the citizens. For when he intended to lighten the burden of debts and introduce the <term>seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking off of burdens</gloss>—which was a polite name for the cancellation of debts—he shared this plan with his friends. They committed a most unjust act: they anticipated the law by borrowing a great deal of silver, and a short time later, when the law was brought to light, they were seen to have purchased splendid houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon bore the blame for joining in the injustice, though he himself had been wronged.

Agesilaus, in his zeal for his friends, became most weak and humble in his own character; like Euripides' Pegasus, he crouched down, yielding more than he perhaps <margin>should .H.</margin> wish. By helping them in their misfortunes more eagerly than was proper, he seemed to make himself a partner in their injustices. Indeed, he saved Phoebidas when he was on trial for seizing the Cadmea <note>the citadel of Thebes</note> without orders, saying that such deeds should be done spontaneously. He also acted for Sphodrias when he was fleeing a trial for a lawless and terrible deed—for he had invaded Attica while they were friends and allies—and managed to have him acquitted, having been softened by the "erotic" entreaties of his son. A short letter of his to a certain ruler is also circulated: "If Nicias is not guilty, release him; if he is guilty, release him for my sake; in any case, release him."

But Phocion would not even join his son-in-law Charillus in court when he was on trial regarding the Harpalus affair, but said, "I made you my kinsman only for what is just," and went away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not dissuade his brother from tyranny by teaching and entreaty, joined with those who put him to death. For one should be a friend "only as far as the altar" <note>meaning: not to the point of perjury</note>, as Pericles once said, but only as far as law, justice, and the public interest allow. When this is overlooked, it leads to great and common harm, as happened when Sphodrias and Phoebidas were not punished; for they, more than anyone, plunged Sparta into the Leuctrian War.

The political reason does not compel one to be harsh toward the moderate failings of friends. It even allows one, once the most important public matters are placed in safety, to help friends from one's surplus of influence, and to stand by them and labor with them. There are also favors that do not provoke envy, such as helping a friend toward an office, or rather putting into his hands some honorable administration or a benevolent embassy—one that carries the honors of a leader or involves a mission to a city for the sake of friendship and concord. If there is a laborious but illustrious and great deed to be done, one should first appoint oneself to it and then choose the friend as an associate, as Diomedes did: "If you indeed bid me choose a companion myself, how then could I forget godlike Odysseus?" And Odysseus in turn returns the praise appropriately: "The horses, old man, are newly arrived, of which you ask, Thracian ones; and their king was slain by brave Diomedes, and beside him twelve companions, all the best." ### Precepts of Statecraft

yielding to friends does not adorn those being praised any less than those who give the praise. But "willfulness," as Plato says, "is the companion of solitude." Furthermore, in matters of noble and benevolent favors, one should give friends a share of the credit, and bid those who have benefited to praise and love them, as having been both the causes and the counselors of the deed. But base and absurd requests should be pushed away, not bitterly, but by teaching and encouraging them gently <margin>the base .H.</margin> that such things are not worthy of their virtue and reputation.

Epaminondas acted best of all men when he refused Pelopidas' request to release a certain peddler from prison; yet a little later, when his mistress made the request, he released him, saying, "Pelopidas, such favors are fitting for little mistresses to receive, not for generals." Cato, however, acted harshly and willfully when Catulus the Censor, who was a very close and intimate friend, requested the release of someone being tried by Cato while he was quaestor. Cato said, "It is a shame that you, who ought to be disciplining us young men, are being driven out by our own subordinates." For it was possible to refuse the favor in deed while removing the harshness and bitterness from the speech, showing that the unpleasantness was brought about not willingly but by the necessity of law and justice.

There are also ways of helping friends in politics toward financial gain that are not ignoble. For instance, Themistocles, after the battle, seeing a corpse wearing gold necklaces and bracelets, passed by himself, but turning to his friend said, "Pick these up, for you have not become Themistocles." For circumstances often give the political man such opportunities for his friends—for not all are like Menemachus. To one, entrust a paid legal advocacy for a just cause; to another, introduce a wealthy man who needs care and protection; for another, help him obtain a contract or a lease that offers profit. Epaminondas, when a friend came to him, told him to ask a certain wealthy man for one talent, saying that he himself had ordered it. When the man who was asked came to inquire the reason, Epaminondas said, "Because this man is honorable but poor, while you are rich because you have embezzled much from the city." And Xenophon says of Agesilaus that he took pride in enriching his friends while being himself superior to money.

Since "every lark must have a crest" according to Simonides, and every political life brings certain enmities and differences, it is especially fitting for the political man to have considered these matters. Most people praise Themistocles and Aristides because they would lay aside their enmity at the borders whenever they went out on an embassy or a military campaign, and then take it up again later. Some are also exceedingly pleased by the conduct of Cretinas of Magnesia. For when he was a political rival to Hermeias—a man who was not powerful but was ambitious and noble in spirit—and he saw the city in danger when the Mithridatic War broke out, he urged Hermeias to take the command and manage affairs while he himself withdrew. Or, if Hermeias wished him to lead, then Hermeias should depart, so that they might not destroy the city by competing with one another. The challenge pleased Hermeias, and saying that Cretinas was more skilled in war, he departed with his children and wife. Cretinas then escorted him out, giving him from his own property whatever is more useful to those in exile than to those under siege, and by leading the city excellently, he unexpectedly saved it when it had come within a hair's breadth of destruction.

For if it is noble and of a great spirit to cry out, "I love my children, but I love my fatherland more," why is it not even readier for each of them to say, "I hate so-and-so and wish to do him harm, but I love my fatherland more"? <term>Venesection</term> <gloss>bloodletting or phlebotomy</gloss> is the evacuation specific to the blood itself. As for the evacuation specific to a <term>humor</term> <gloss>one of the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, or black bile</gloss> that has increased in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is different from venesection. Every excessive evacuation causes fever in most cases. If the cessation of a habitual discharge—such as earwax or nasal mucus—causes an ailment due to blockage, then restoring that evacuation usually cures it. Know that leaving a remnant of the matter that needs evacuation is less harmful than being excessive in evacuation to the point that the patient's strength fails. Nature often dissolves that remnant itself. As long as the humor is of the type that should be removed and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to evacuate until the patient faints.

For those whose strength is robust but whose bad humors are plentiful, evacuate them little by little. Do the same if the matter is very stubborn or heavily mixed with the blood and cannot be evacuated all at once, as is the case in <term>sciatica</term>, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that <term>purgation</term> <gloss>laxative treatment</gloss> draws from above and uproots from below; thus it is suitable for both "contrary attraction" <note>drawing fluids away from the site of disease</note> and "direct attraction," and it is also suitable after the matter has settled. If the matter is below, purgation draws it in the opposite direction and uproots it from its place. <term>Emesis</term> <gloss>vomiting</gloss> performs attraction and uprooting in the reverse manner. The state of venesection varies according to the sites from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who least need evacuation are those with a good diet and good digestion; likewise, inhabitants of hot countries have little need for evacuation.

### Chapter Four: On Common Rules for Vomiting and Purgation and an Indication of How Purgative and Emetic Medicines Attract

We say: it is recommended for whoever wishes to purge or vomit to divide their food, taking the daily amount in several portions and making them of different foods and different drinks. This state causes the stomach to desire to expel what is in it, either upward or downward. However, if a single type of food is consumed upon another, the stomach becomes stingy with it, grips it tightly, and holds it fast, especially if the amount is small. Those with naturally loose bowels should not do this at all.

Know that the need for vomiting, purgation, and the like does not occur in those who follow a good regimen; they require what is lighter than these. Often, exercise, massage, and bathing are sufficient for them. If the body becomes full, and most of that fullness is of the best humor—meaning blood—then venesection is what is needed for cleansing, rather than purgation. If necessity dictates both venesection and evacuation with something like <term>hellebore</term> or strong medicines, one must begin with venesection. This is among the counsels of Hippocrates in the book <term>Epidemics</term> <note>original: "Abidhimia"</note>, and it is the truth. This is also the case if phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are viscous and cold, venesection might increase their thickness and viscosity; in that case, one must begin with purgation. In general, if the humors are equal, perform venesection first, then evacuate if any excess remains. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are balanced, then perform venesection.

Whoever takes medicine before venesection when venesection should have come first may suffer for a few days. For one who has recently undergone venesection and needs evacuation, drinking medicine is more suitable. Often, drinking medicine when venesection was required results in fever and agitation; if it does not subside with sedatives, know that venesection should have preceded it. Not every evacuation is needed due to excessive fullness; rather, the severity of the disease or the fullness in quality <note>the "badness" of the fluid</note> rather than quantity may demand it. Often, improving the regimen suffices instead of the venesection required at the time.

Sometimes a cause calls for evacuation but an obstacle opposes it; in such a case, there is no remedy except fasting, sleep, and correcting the <term>dyscrasia</term> <gloss>imbalance of temperaments</gloss> caused by the fullness. Some evacuations are performed as a precaution, such as for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in spring. One needs to take precautions before the time and perform the evacuation specific to the disease, whether it be venesection or purgation. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done for those with <term>dropsy</term> <gloss>edema or fluid retention</gloss>.

You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor to be evacuated in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> when you need to evacuate yellow bile. In that case, you must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purgation, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <note>original: "al-halilaj"</note>, to correct any dyscrasia that might occur afterward. In those with inflammation of the internal organs, their purgation and vomiting are weakened; if forced to do so, use for them things like <term>bindweed</term> and <term>safflower</term>. As for <term>polypody</term> and <term>purging cassia</term> <note>original: "khiyar shanbar"</note> and the like, Hippocrates said: whoever is thin and responds easily to vomiting, it is best to cleanse them using emesis in summer, spring, or autumn, but not winter. Whoever is of a moderate build, purgation is better for them; if a cause calls for evacuation by vomiting, let them wait for summer and avoid it when not necessary.

Before purgation and vomiting, one must first thin the humor intended for evacuation and widen and open the passages; this protects the body from exhaustion. Know that habituating the nature to looseness and responding easily to the desired purgation or vomiting before using strong medicine is a successful management strategy. Purgation and vomiting while the abdominal walls are thin is difficult, exhausting, and dangerous. An emetic medicine may turn into a purgative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk during intense hunger, if the drinker has a "slippery" stomach <note>chronic diarrhea</note>, if they are unaccustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is of a heavy substance that descends quickly. Conversely, a purgative becomes an emetic due to weakness of the stomach, extreme dryness of the stool, the medicine being repulsive, or the person having indigestion.

Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge or purges something "unripe" <note>undigested or not ready for expulsion</note>, stirs up the humor it was meant to purge and spreads it through the body. It then overcomes the body and other humors transform into it, increasing that humor in the body. Some humors respond most quickly to vomiting, such as yellow bile; others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile; and some vary, such as phlegm. For a person with a fever, purgation is more appropriate in itself. For those whose humor is already descending, such as those with <term>lientery</term> <gloss>a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</gloss>, making them vomit is impossible. The worst purgative medicines are those composed of drugs with widely different evacuation times; they cause agitation, and the first drug may purge the second before the second has acted, or the first may even purge the second itself.

If someone undergoes purgation or vomiting while their body is clean, they will inevitably suffer from dizziness, colic, and distress; whatever is evacuated will be expelled with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating waste, there is no agitation; when agitation begins, it is evacuating something other than waste. If the humor evacuated by vomiting or purgation changes to another humor, it indicates that the body is cleansed of the humor intended for evacuation.

Question 85, Article 3: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

<column-break/>

The third article asks whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third article, we proceed as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition. For those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known to us. But universals are prior according to nature, because that from which the sequence of being does not return is prior <note>original: "prius est a quo non conuertitur subsistendi consequentia essendi"; a reference to Aristotle's definition of priority in the Categories</note>. Therefore, universals are posterior in the cognition of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things. But universals are simpler; therefore, they are known later by us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the Physics that the defined thing falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition. But more universal things are parts of the definition of less universal things, just as "animal" is part of the definition of "man." Therefore, universals are known later by us. Furthermore, we arrive at causes and principles through effects. But universals are certain principles. Therefore, universals are known later by us.

On the contrary is what is said in the first book of the Physics: that one must proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensory cognition. And because the senses are of singulars while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior for us than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potentiality to act. Everything that proceeds from potentiality to act reaches an incomplete act—which is midway between potentiality and act—before reaching a perfect act. Now, the perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete knowledge, through which things are known distinctly and determinately. The incomplete act, however, is imperfect knowledge, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known partially in act and in a way in potentiality. Hence the Philosopher says in the first book of the Physics that "what is first manifest and certain to us are rather confused things; later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly."

It is manifest, moreover, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both a universal whole <note>the genus</note> in which parts are contained potentially, and also an integral whole <note>the physical object</note>, can be known. For either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in a universal whole is to have cognition of a less common thing. For example, to know "animal" indistinctly is to know animal insofar as it is an animal. To know "animal" distinctly is to know animal insofar as it is rational or irrational, which is to know a man or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "man." The same reasoning applies if we compare any more universal thing to a less universal thing. And because the sense moves from potentiality to act just like the intellect, the same order

<column-break/>

of cognition appears in the sense. For according to the sense, we judge the more common before the less common, both according to place and according to time. According to place, as when something is seen from a distance, it is first perceived to be a body before it is perceived to be an animal; and it is first perceived to be an animal before it is perceived to be a man; and first a man before Socrates or Plato. According to time, because a child from the beginning first distinguishes "man" from "non-man" before he distinguishes this man from another man. And therefore, children from the beginning call all men "fathers," but later they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the Physics. And the reason for this is manifest: because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potentiality to knowing the principle of distinction, just as he who knows the genus is in potentiality to knowing the difference. Thus it is clear that indistinct cognition is the medium between potentiality and act. It must therefore be said that the cognition of singulars is prior for us than the cognition of universals, just as sensory cognition is prior to intellectual cognition. But both according to sense and according to intellect, cognition of the more common is prior to cognition of the less common.

To the first objection, therefore, it must be said that the universal can be considered in two ways. In one way, according as the universal nature is considered together with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality—namely, that one and the same thing has a relationship to many—proceeds from the abstraction of the intellect, it must be that in this way the universal is posterior. Hence in the first book On the Soul <note>De Anima</note> it is said that "the universal animal is either nothing or is posterior." But according to Plato, who posited subsistent universals, the universal would be prior according to this consideration, because particulars, according to him, do not exist except through participation in subsistent universals which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself, namely of "animality" or "humanity," as it is found in particulars. And thus it must be said that the order of nature is twofold. One is according to the way of generation and time, according to which those things that are imperfect and in potentiality are prior. In this way, the more common is prior according to nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For an animal is generated before a man, as is said in the book On the Generation of Animals. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior according to nature than potentiality, and the perfect prior to the imperfect. In this way, the less common is prior according to nature than the more common, as man is prior to animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a man.

To the second objection, it must be said that the more common universal is compared to the less common as a whole and as a part. As a whole, insofar as in the more universal there is contained not only the less universal in potentiality, but also others; as under "animal" not only man but also horse is contained. As a part, however, insofar as the less common contains in its definition <note>ratio</note> not only the more common but also other things; as "man" contains not only "animal" but "rational." Thus, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man." But "man" is prior in our cognition to the fact that "animal" is a part of his definition.

To the third objection, it must be said that a part can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing prevents knowing the parts before the whole, as stones before a house. In another way, according as they are parts of this whole, and thus it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we first know the house with a certain confused cognition before we distinguish its individual parts. Thus it must be said that defining elements considered absolutely are known before the defined thing; otherwise the defined thing would not be made known through them. When the Lion woke the next morning, the Judge and a group of his prominent companions entered his presence with a written record of what Dimna had said in his excuses. The Lion took the document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read that document to her. It distressed her, and she said: "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said: "I shall not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not see you recognizing what harms you from what benefits you. I believe that by prolonging your consideration of Dimna's case, he will stir up against you a trouble that you will be unable to withstand, whether sitting or standing."

Then she stood and left in anger. When the next day came, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the <term>Ulama</term> <gloss>scholars and learned men</gloss> regarding him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him: "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have united in the belief that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after this accusation has taken root in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than confessing your guilt. By doing so, you may escape the consequences of the afterlife, and a good reputation may return to your case for two reasons. The first is your ability to find ways out and fabricate excuses to defend yourself. The second is your confession of guilt, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: Death in what is honorable is better than life in what is base."

Dimna answered him, saying: "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have learned that suspicion is no substitute for the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself better than you do, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty beyond doubt. My situation has only become ugly in your eyes because you suspect that I have acted as a slanderer."

<summary>The Lion's mother warns him against delaying Dimna's judgment while the Judge pressures Dimna to confess his crimes to save his soul. Dimna defends himself by arguing that legal judgment must be based on certainty rather than collective suspicion.</summary>

A commotion fell upon the entire court, and a great anxiety seized the mind of the Sultan. The hearts of both the elite and the commoners of the city were lost in worry, wondering what distress or calamity had occurred. They thought: "Either a powerful enemy is intent upon us, or a deadly plague has arisen from the Unseen."

For Dalqak <note>A famous court jester or "wise fool" figure</note> had arrived, riding harshly and killing several Arabian horses along the way. The people gathered at the King's palace, asking why Dalqak had arrived in such a frantic rush. Because of his haste and his excessive exertion, a clamor and agitation fell upon the city of Termez. One person struck their hands against their knees in grief, while another cried out "Woe!" in terror. From the outcry, the turmoil, the fear, and the threat of punishment, every heart wandered into a hundred kinds of imagination. Everyone cast an omen based on their own conjecture, wondering what fire had fallen into the wool.

The King quickly sought a path and granted him entry. When Dalqak kissed the ground, the King said to him: "Hey, what happened?" To anyone who asked him about the situation, that sour-faced man would merely place a finger to his lips, signaling: "Silence!" His behavior only increased the King's apprehension; everyone was stunned and bewildered by his agitation.

Dalqak made a sign: "O generous King, allow me a moment to catch my breath, so that my intellect might return to me for a second, for I have fallen into a strange world." After an hour, during which the King's throat and mouth became bitter from worry and suspicion—for he had never seen Dalqak in such a state, and there was no companion more pleasant than him—he waited. Dalqak used to always raise up stories and jests; he kept the King happy and laughing. He would make him laugh so much in the assembly that the King would hold his stomach with both hands. From the strength of the laughter, his body would break into a sweat, and he would fall on his face from laughing so hard.

Yet today, he was so pale and sour, placing his hand on his lips as if to say: "O King, be silent." Worry upon worry and imagination upon imagination—what punishment did the King think was coming? For the King's heart was already filled with grief and caution, because the Khwarazm-Shah was a great shedder of blood. That stubborn ruler had killed many kings of that region, either through trickery or through sheer power. The King of Termez was already in fear of him, and Dalqak's antics only increased that fear.

The King said: "Speak quickly! What is the matter? From whom does this turmoil and agitation of yours come?"

Dalqak replied: "I heard in the village that the King had a herald announce at every crossroads: 'I seek someone who can gallop in three days to Samarkand, and I shall give him treasures. I will give him hoards of wealth in exchange once the purpose of his message is achieved.' I rushed to you for this reason: to tell you that I do not have that capability! Such agility does not come from someone like me; do not spin the thread of this hope upon me."

<meta>continues from previous page: the commentary on the significance of a friend bringing news</meta>

Of women with parted hair <note>original: "simantininam"</note>, meaning wives. The <term>Amarakosha</term> <gloss>a famous Sanskrit lexicon</gloss> states: "A woman is called <term>simantini</term> or <term>vadhu</term>." Having arrived through a friend <note>original: "suhridupanatah"</note>, meaning received through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is used here to remove any fear of deception or bad news. The news of the beloved <note>original: "kantodantah"</note> means the tidings of her lover. The <term>Amarakosha</term> says: "News, report, account, and tidings are synonyms." This news is only slightly less than an actual meeting <note>original: "sangamat kincidunah"</note>, meaning it brings almost as much joy as the physical contact of the beloved.

Now he delivers the message:

O Long-lived One, speak thus to her both on my behalf and to do yourself a kindness: "Your companion, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, is alive and, though separated from you, asks after your welfare, O frail one. For this is the first thing to be asked of living beings whose misfortunes are easily met." (Verse 41)

To her: O Long-lived One <note>original: "ayushman"</note>. The suffix here implies praise, meaning one whose life is praiseworthy because of service to others. On my behalf <note>original: "vachanat"</note>, meaning from my words of request, and also to do yourself <note>original: "atmanah"</note> a kindness. This means to make yourself fulfilled through the act of helping others. Although "self" is the object of the act of helping, the use of the genitive case <note>grammatical possessive</note> is not incorrect here, as it expresses a general relationship. As the poet Bharavi says: "That wealth is useful which serves others." Sriharsha also says: "To help the virtuous, to see wealth, to travel through the sky." Therefore, the claim by the commentator Natha that the second case <note>accusative</note> is seen everywhere is a claim without support. You should speak to that beloved in this way. What should you say? "O frail one <note>original: "abale"</note>, your companion and husband stays in the hermitages of Ramagiri <note>identified here as Chitrakuta</note>." He is not dead <note>original: "avyapannah"</note>. He gives the reason for mentioning life: "Though suffering from separation, he asks after your welfare." The verb "to ask" <note>original: "pricchati"</note> takes two objects here. Indeed, for living beings whose calamities occur without effort, welfare is the very first thing that must be inquired about. The grammatical suffix used here denotes necessity.

With his thin body, your thin body; with his fevered body, your fevered body; with his tearful body, your tear-drenched body; with his longing body, your longing body...

Xiangling said, "I simply love Lu Fangweng's <note>the poet Lu You</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Daiyu said, "You absolutely must not look at such poetry. Because you do not yet understand poetry, you love it when you see something shallow and accessible like this. Once you enter that mold, you will never be able to learn your way out of it. Just listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have here the <term>Wang Mo-jie Quanji</term> <gloss>The Complete Works of Wang Wei</gloss>. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and study them until you have thoroughly grasped and memorized them. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems, followed by one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three men as your foundation, then take a look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin, and Bao Zhao. Since you are such an exceptionally clever and quick-witted person, in less than a year's labor, you need not worry about not becoming a true poet!"

Hearing this, Xiangling smiled, "In that case, dear Miss, please take the book out for me. I will take it back and it will be good to recite a few poems at night." Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-character regulated poems of <term>Wang Youcheng</term> <gloss>Wang Wei</gloss> and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at those with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Recite them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>Alkaid Court, the residence of Xue Baochai</gloss>. Ignoring all other matters, she simply began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her to go to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her such dedication, Baochai had no choice but to leave her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, she saw Xiangling coming in with a beaming smile to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. Daiyu asked with a smile, "How many do you remember in total?" Xiangling laughed, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any insight from them?" Xiangling smiled, "I have indeed gained some insight, but I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you about it."

Isa ibn Hisham told us, saying:
I turned with a group of my companions to the courtyard of a tent, seeking hospitality <term>qira</term> <gloss>the meal offered to a guest</gloss> from its people. A short, sturdy man came out to us and said: "Who are you?" We said: "Guests who have not tasted a morsel for three days." He cleared his throat and said: "What is your opinion, O young men, of a portion of <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of butter and dried curd</gloss> as large as the head of a bald man, in a wide bowl, crowned with the pressed dates of Khaybar from the sides of a great, firm palm tree, a single one of which fills the mouth? It is for a group of hungry, thirsty men, in which the tooth disappears, and whose pits are like the tongues of birds. They scoop up the <term>nahida</term> with cups of milk milked from sturdy, old, well-fed camels. Do you desire it, O young men?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" The old man guffawed and said: "And your uncle <note>referring to himself</note> also desires it!"

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O young men, of fine white bread <term>darmak</term> like pieces of silver ingots, gathered on a leather table-spread that smells of mimosa bark? A brisk, clever, and light youth among you leaps to it and kneads it without shaking or making a sound, smoothing it without a soft touch. Then he mixes it thoroughly with diluted milk or water, then turns it and leaves it in a corner of the stony ground until it softens without becoming sour. Then he goes to the wood of the <term>ghada</term> tree and ignites a fire. When its flame dies down, he prepares its pit, then takes his dough and flattens it after thoroughly coating it. He flings it upon the embers and covers it. When it has risen and hardened, he heaps upon it such glowing stones that the two heats meet. When he covers them in the matching hot ashes with a lid, and it cracks open, its crust resembling thin bread, and its redness like the redness of the Hijazi dates known as 'Mother of Rats' or 'Ibn Tab's Cluster,' then white honey like snow is poured over it until it sinks into the crevices of the fat, and the heart of the fine bread drinks what is poured upon it. It is then presented to you, and you swallow it like the swallowing of Juwayn or Zankal <note>names of famous gluttons</note>. Do you desire it, O young men?"

He said: Every one of us craned his neck at his description, our mouths watered, and we smacked our lips. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" He said: The old man guffawed and said: "And your uncle, by God, does not hate it!" Then he said: "What is your opinion, O young men, of a young she-goat from Najd, high-bred and wild, that has eaten the mimosa blossoms, the Najdi wormwood, the yarrow, and the dry herbage? She has sipped the remains of rain-water and filled herself with desert truffles until her marrow is rich and her fat is thick. She is slaughtered fresh and then hung in an oven <term>watis</term> until she is cooked through without being scorched or underdone. Then she is presented to you, her skin stripped away from white fat, on a table arranged with thin loaves like spreading Egyptian linen or fine white cloth. She is soaked in bowls containing mustard sauce and various seasonings. She is placed before you, dripping with fat and overflowing with broth. Do you desire it, O young men?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" He said: "And your uncle, by God, dances for it!" Then one of us leaped at him with a sword and said: "What..."

If a man leaves two sisters and a wife, and bequeaths to a man as much as the portion of a sister less one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy, the calculation for this is that you establish the legal shares <note>original: al-faridah</note> out of twelve shares. Each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains, together with the legacy, equals the portion of a sister. One-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy, plus the legacy, equals the portion of a sister. This is one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The whole estate equals three-eighths of the estate plus three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the whole estate, and five-eighths of the estate remains, equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The whole estate then equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. Thus, the estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons. He bequeaths to a man as much as the portion of one of his sons, and to another man one-fourth of what remains of the third. <margin>Traps prepared for the tiger.</margin> Necessity being the mother of invention, a method was finally devised to make the animal pay the penalty for shedding so much blood. After scouting the narrow paths through which it was accustomed to emerge from its cavernous dens at night to seek prey, the path was cut open. They dug a pit, covered it with hurdles and the excavated earth, and scattered the excess soil <margin>concerning the tiger</margin> so it would not be noticed. Coming along incautiously, a male tiger fell into the pit and was impaled on sharp stakes fixed at the bottom of the trench. With its roaring, it deafened the entire neighborhood, and the mountains echoed with the sound. It was killed by huge rocks thrown down from the edges of the pit onto its body where it was fixed upon the stakes. Even as it was being broken into a thousand splinters and a thousand pieces, it continued to shatter the spears aimed at it and those hurled from above with its right paw. Half-dead and drained of blood, it still filled those watching with terror; one can only imagine what it might have done if it were free and unharmed. # Section 44: The Superintendent of Courtesans

A courtesan who refuses to go to a man at the command of the King shall receive one thousand lashes with a whip, or pay a fine of five thousand <term>panas</term> <gloss>the standard silver coin of the period</gloss>.

If a courtesan, after receiving her fee, shows hatred toward the client, she shall be fined twice the amount of the fee.

If she refuses to provide lodging after receiving the fee, she shall pay eight times the amount of the fee, unless the client suffers from a disease or possesses physical defects.

For a courtesan who kills a man, the punishment is burning on a funeral pyre or drowning in water.

Anyone who steals a courtesan’s ornaments or her fee shall be fined eight times the value of the stolen items.

The courtesan shall report to the authorities her income, her future earnings, and the identity of her clients.

By these rules, the conduct of the wives of actors, dancers, singers, musicians, storytellers, bards, rope-dancers, jugglers, and wandering minstrels, as well as women who live in secret, is explained.

Foreign musical troupes shall pay five <term>panas</term> as a license fee for each performance.

Women who live by their beauty <note>original: "rupajiva"</note> shall pay one-sixth of their income to the state.

The state shall provide a livelihood from the royal treasury to those who teach courtesans, female slaves, and actresses the arts of singing, playing instruments, recitation, dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing the lute <note>original: "vina"</note>, flute, and drum, reading the thoughts of others, preparing perfumes and garlands, shampooing, and the arts of the courtesan. The sons of courtesans and chief actors shall be trained to be the leaders of all musical and dramatic performances.

Women who are proficient in various languages and signals should be employed, along with their kinsmen, to detect foreign spies and to cause the destruction or negligence of enemies.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, The Superintendent of Courtesans, in the section concerning the Activities of Superintendents. This is the forty-eighth chapter from the beginning of the work.

Other episodes occurred in this prison, some planned as traps, others happening by chance, which were not yet of great importance or worthy of my serious attention. Damis, I believe, mentioned them so as not to omit anything; but as for the matters worth recording, it was evening, and he had been imprisoned for five days. A man who spoke Greek entered the prison and asked, "Where is the man of Tyana?" Taking him aside, he said, "The Emperor will speak with you tomorrow." It seemed he had heard this from Aelianus <note>Casperius Aelianus, the Praetorian Prefect who was secretly a friend to Apollonius</note>. "I understand," he replied, "the secret message. "You act kindly," he said, "but I lead the same life here as I do outside. I converse about whatever happens to arise, and I lack for nothing." "Do you not even need someone to advise you," the man asked, "on how you should speak to the Emperor?" "By Zeus," he said, "unless he should try to persuade me to flatter him." And Apollonius said, "Odysseus, however, when entering the cave of Polyphemus, though he had not heard beforehand how large he was, nor what he ate, nor how his voice thundered, took courage against him, even though he was afraid at first, and he left the cave having proven himself a man. "To whom then should I say these things?" he asked. "To those who will lead me," he said. "For I suppose I must go as one from a prison." "These orders have been given to them as well as to me," he said, "and I shall arrive at the proper time. I have come now to give you notice, for these orders were given late in the evening." # We have set the distance

from the point of midday <note>original: "nisf al-nahar"</note> because the adjustment <note>original: "al-ta'dil"</note> for the birth <note>the moment of the lunar conjunction or Molad</note> is easier by this method than by working with horizons. The hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and a fraction. The Jewish method using seasonal hours <note>term: "al-sa'at al-zamaniyya" gloss: hours that vary in length depending on the season</note> would only be accurate if the conjunction for the beginning of Tishrei <note>the first month of the Jewish civil year</note> occurred exactly at the autumnal equinox <note>original: "al-i'tidal al-kharifi"</note>. However, it never occurs exactly then; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously.

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews, or by the table we have analyzed according to their views, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the start of the year and the determination of its character: whether it is deficient, regular, or complete <note>referring to the three possible lengths of the Jewish year: 353, 354, or 355 days for common years; 383, 384, or 385 days for leap years</note>. We already know whether the year is common <note>original: "basita"</note> or a leap year <note>original: "ubur"</note>. We then look in the Table of Limits <note>original: "jadwal al-hudud"</note> for a duration of weekdays whose two boundaries and sides contain the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look on the leap year side if it is a leap year, and on the common year side if it is common. When we find it, we find alongside it the day of the week for the start of the year and its specific character. Once we know the start of the year and its character, and combine that character with its status as common or leap, we can determine from that the beginning of the following year.
