### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The goal of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>
...destined, they may penetrate. From these things, conclude that it is necessary to proceed according to my prescription, and not at all according to yours. Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still thunder many things against me: nevertheless, my Monarchy shall stand, while yours goes to ruin. I do not write so at length about Alchemy in vain, but I do so with this mind and purpose: that from these things you may nearly and solidly learn what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended by this, that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it: but rather, care must be taken that through it <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret remedies</gloss> are uncovered, and the deceptions of the <term>seplasiarii</term> <gloss>perfumers or sellers of ointments</gloss> are exposed, by which the unrefined common folk are deceived, while these men provide for one florin what they would not redeem for a single penny. So "precious" are their secrets.

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is forced to admit this. If this is true, then I ask you now: must not the poison be separated from the good and useful? And the good be taken, the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If therefore it must be: I pray, tell me, how is it separated in your workshops? For among you, all things remain mixed together. But so that you may protect your simplicity, if you are convicted into admitting that poison lies hidden there, and you are asked where it finally goes: then you bring forth I know not what concerning "corrections" which supposedly drive out and take away the poison,
<margin>The correction of Physicians is examined.</margin>
just as they "correct" Quince, then Scammony <note>a purgative resin from the root of Convolvulus scammonia</note>, and then the substance called <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>prepared scammony juice</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it escape to?
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
It remains in the <term>Diagridium</term>. Test it, if you are wise: exceed the limit, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it quite quickly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>the root of Operculina turpethum, used as a purgative</gloss>, and you call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would be fit for peasants, and should be given to pack-horses. Make a trial by exceeding the limit and increase the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison.
<margin>What "to correct" means to Physicians.</margin>
*To correct is to take what has been corrected.* He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; the power lies within the substances themselves, not within you. Now indeed, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation: as, for example: a serpent is poisonous: and yet it is adopted as food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely that a similar separation is needed. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation: unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will have remained.

Now therefore, at last, if the true foundation is required, which takes away the poison, let us see how Alchemy performs it. For it is necessary that it be done in such a way that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars is removed; and if Saturn is found in Venus, it is separated from her <note>Paracelsus uses planetary names to refer to metals: Mars for iron, Sun for gold, Saturn for lead, and Venus for copper</note>. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies also exist in them. But those bodies which are contrary, it is entirely necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and from the good, the evil which you seek to avoid is removed.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire: so a Medicine is much less useful which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through fire into a second generation, by which it ought to benefit and help man. And should this not deservedly be judged the upright foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to employ poisons, but rather <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret essences</gloss>.
<margin>Workshops rebuked.</margin>
However, all those preparations of the apothecary shops, as many as there are, do not contribute even a tiny letter to this doctrine: but they are occupied simply in "correcting," just as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were suppressed either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room afterward just as much as before? And although it may not be perceived by the sense of smell: is it therefore permitted for anyone to say the stench has been separated and no longer remains? On the contrary, it is present, but corrected by the fumigation. Thus the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Of such a kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who blunt an <term>Aleopaticum</term> <gloss>a bitter aloetic medicine</gloss> with sugar, so that it inflicts no harm. Thus sugar and honey are their <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery or highest work</gloss>. Thus they also "correct" gentian with theriac. Are these not truly the works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the Physicians of princes. Who indeed is so stupid that he does not immediately smell that these things are worthless? What else, I ask, can they boast of their remedies, except to say, *This Electuary is sweet, made of spices, sugar, and honey*?

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the true purpose of alchemy is the medicinal separation of poisons from pure essences rather than the transmutation of gold. He critiques contemporary pharmacists for merely masking the unpleasant or toxic qualities of drugs with sugar and incense instead of chemically removing them.</summary>

The answer to the first argument is clear. As for the point that because God further permits the generative power of witches for the sake of <note>certain reasons</note>, it is therefore also permitted that the member be truly and actually removed: this is not valid as a general rule. Regarding the third argument about the conversion of Lot's wife: we say that it was real and not by deceptive art, but here we are speaking of deceptive art. Regarding the fourth argument, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore also remove them: it is said regarding the magicians of Pharaoh that they made real serpents. It often happened that his skill in debate escaped him <note>meaning his wit was so natural it seemed effortless</note>. Regarding his lifestyle, he was not simple, yet he practiced great moderation within a luxurious manner of living. He delighted in wearing white clothing and continued to bathe in the public baths twice a day. Once, when someone asked him why he, being a bishop, bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I cannot manage a third time." On another occasion, while visiting the bishop Sergius, he was asked by one of the associates of Arsacius why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said, "You first tell me where it is written that a bishop should wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question by saying, "You would not be able to show that a priest must dress in black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels is shown using white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles wearing white." Having said these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia <note>modern-day Ankara, Turkey</note>, took away a church from the <term>Novatians</term> <gloss>a rigorist Christian sect</gloss> while he was visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him and urged him to restore the church. Leontius answered warmly <note>here meaning with heat or anger</note> and said to him, "You Novatians ought not to have churches, you who do away with repentance and shut out the loving-kindness of God." When Leontius had said these and many other such harsh things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "Indeed, no one has ever repented as much as I have." When the other asked again, "How have you repented?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you."

Once, when John <note>John Chrysostom</note> was accusing the bishop of something and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "Indeed it does not." When John became angry and said, "You see that you alone are a bishop by your own will," Sisinnius said, "I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, though I am one to the ears of others." John, being provoked by what was said, cried, "I will stop you from speaking, for you are a heretic!" To this Sisinnius wittily replied, "I would even give you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor." John, softened by the response, said, "I will not stop your freedom of speech if speaking is truly a burden to you."

Such was the readiness and grace of Sisinnius in his replies. To write and record all his sayings would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown through a few examples what kind of man he was, having been considered worthy to lead. I say this: everyone knew him for his learning, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Furthermore, all the prominent members of the Senate cherished and admired him. He composed many books, using a refined style in them, and he mixed in poetic expressions. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writing. For there was such grace in his face, his voice, his posture, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all the religious sects, and especially by the bishop Atticus. And such are the matters concerning Sisinnius.

But the unlearned and those of a base nature, for whom a true fate from the Lord did not proceed to obtain gifts, nor to have a notion of the immortal Jove <note>Jupiter, used here as a name for the supreme deity</note>, not listening to either the gods or divine men, have indeed rejected all the gods. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things alone through which God is adored. For God, as the father of all, stands in need of nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction concerning him. For instruction purifies, he says, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward him. He indeed preached well concerning God the Father and spoke of the morals by which he is to be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, where the life of the saints is either praised or censured. But among Christians, there was only that which the demons—whom they think are gods—either desire or calumniate as much as they wish. As if it were difficult for anyone to recall what filthy and disgraceful things were performed in theaters and temples in service to the gods, and to observe what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building up and where the ruin of morals lies. Who, then, told this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, with such a vain and ready lie: that the Christians revere rather than hate the demons whose worship is forbidden by the Hebrews? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped—and whom we, as citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love along with the holy celestial angels and the powers of God—forbids sacrifice, thundering in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people. And he introduced it very threateningly, saying: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out. And lest anyone should think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom that man <note>Porphyry</note> calls the least or minor ones—who in the holy scriptures are themselves called gods, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations <note>the Gentiles</note>, as the seventy interpreters <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> evidently placed it in the Psalm, saying: For all the gods of the nations are demons. Lest anyone, therefore, should think that while it was forbidden to these demons, it was permitted to sacrifice to all or some of the celestial beings, he immediately added: except to the Lord alone. That is, except to the Lord only, lest perhaps he who says "to the Lord alone" might believe that there is some other god to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made. That this is not to be so understood is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher <note>Porphyry</note> offers such great testimony, gave a law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew tongue; not obscure and unknown, but now spread abroad among all nations, in which law it is written: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only. What need is there to search for many things on this matter in his law and his prophets? Indeed, there is no need to search; for they are not hidden or erased, but are clear and frequent to collect and to place in this my disputation. By these it appears clearer than light that he willed sacrifice to be made to no one at all except to himself, the true and supreme God. Behold this one thing, briefly yet grandly, threateningly yet truthfully spoken by that God whom the most learned of them preach as so excellent: let them hear, let them fear, let them fulfill it, lest eradication follow the disobedient. He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, he says, except to the Lord only. Not because he has need of anything, but because it is expedient for us that we should be his possession. For to him it is sung in the sacred writings of the Hebrews: I have said to the Lord, you are my God, for you have no need of my goods. Moreover, we ourselves are his most noble and best sacrifice. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets sounded oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting would offer one sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

# Against Celsus Book IV, 30–31

<margin>5</margin> Celsus says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt who never performed any noteworthy deed, and were never of any account either in reputation or in number. Now, regarding the claim that they were not fugitives and were not Egyptians, but were Hebrews who had settled in Egypt as sojourners, we have already spoken in the preceding sections <note>referring to Book III, chapters 5–8</note>. But if he thinks he can prove they were of no account in reputation or number because almost no history of them is found among the Greeks, we shall say this: if anyone were to dwell upon their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were men who displayed a shadow of the heavenly life upon earth <note>referring to Job 8:9 and Hebrews 10:1</note>. Among them, no other was recognized as God except the one over all, and no maker of images was a citizen. For there was neither painter nor sculptor in their commonwealth, as the law expelled all such people from it <margin>15</margin> so that there would be no pretext for the construction of statues. Such things attract the attention of foolish men and drag the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, among them a law to this effect: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved image, any likeness of a form, male or female, the likeness of any beast that is on the earth, the likeness of any <margin>20</margin> winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth" <note>quoting Deuteronomy 4:16–18</note>. And the law intended that they, by associating with the truth concerning each thing, should not fashion other things contrary to the truth, which would give a false representation of the truly male or the truly female, or <margin>25</margin> the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or of creeping things, or of fish. Also solemn and magnificent among them is the command: "Lest you look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, the whole host of heaven, and be led astray to worship them and serve them" <note>quoting Deuteronomy 4:19</note>.

<margin>30</margin> What a constitution this was for an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for an effeminate man <term>thelydrian</term> <gloss>a man who has been feminized or weakened by luxury</gloss> to be seen! It is also wonderful that the fuel for the passions of the young—prostitutes—were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of justice composed of the most righteous men who had given much proof of a healthy life.

<summary>Origen defends the Jewish nation against Celsus's insults by highlighting the moral and spiritual superiority of the Mosaic Law. He emphasizes the Jewish prohibition of idolatry and their focus on the one true God as evidence of a heavenly lifestyle on earth.</summary>

# But by meditating on the Highest, that which is hidden is revealed, for from Him come bondage and liberation. (3.2.5)

3.2.5

Now, a further point may be raised: the individual soul <term>jiva</term> <gloss>the living being or individual consciousness</gloss> is indeed a part of the Highest Self, just as a spark is a part of a fire. This being the case, just as the spark and the fire share the same powers of burning and lighting, so too should the individual soul and the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>the Supreme Ruler or God</gloss> share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Therefore, by the force of this knowledge and sovereignty, the individual soul should be able to create chariots and other objects in dreams simply by its will.

To this, we reply: although there is a relationship of part and whole between the individual soul and the Lord, it is a matter of direct perception that the individual soul possesses characteristics opposite to those of the Lord.

Does this mean that the individual soul does not possess the same characteristics as the Lord at all? No, it is not that they do not exist; rather, though they exist, they are hidden <term>tirohita</term> <gloss>concealed or obscured</gloss> due to the intervention of ignorance <term>avidya</term> and other factors. That which is hidden, however, becomes manifest in some rare individual who has perfected themselves through the grace of the Lord, who strives and meditates upon the Supreme Lord, and who has shaken off their darkness. This is like the power of sight, which may be obstructed by a cataract but is restored by the power of medicine. It does not happen naturally for all living beings. Why? Because from Him, that is, from the Lord, come the bondage and liberation of this individual soul. Bondage results from the lack of knowledge of the Lord's true nature, while liberation results from the realization of that nature. As the scripture <note>referring to the Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note> says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of afflictions, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, there is a third state at the dissolution of the body: universal sovereignty, where one is absolute and has all desires fulfilled."

# Or that concealment results from connection with the body. (3.2.6)

3.2.6

But why is it that the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, has its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It would seem more reasonable for these powers not to be hidden, just as the burning and lighting of a spark are not hidden.

We reply: this is true, but the concealment of the individual soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of its connection with the body <note>original: "deha-yoga"</note>, that is, its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the fire that is inherent in a piece of wood <note>original: "arani", the wooden block used for friction-fire</note> has its powers of burning and lighting hidden, or as fire covered by ash is obscured, so too is the soul's knowledge and sovereignty hidden due to its connection with the limiting adjuncts <term>upadhi</term> of the body, which are produced by name and form and set up by ignorance. This leads to the error of failing to distinguish between the soul and the body.

The word "or" <note>original: "va"</note> in the sutra is intended to dispel the doubt that the individual soul is something other than the Lord. One might argue: "Let the individual soul be entirely different from the Lord, since its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden; why bother imagining a connection with the body?" We say no, because it is not possible for the individual soul to be different from the Lord. The scriptures begin with "That Divinity thought..." and continue with "entering with this living soul <term>jiva-atman</term>," using the word "Self" <term>atman</term> to refer to the individual soul. Furthermore, the scripture instructs the individual soul on its divine nature: "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That Thou Art, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the individual soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty become hidden through its connection with the body.

Consequently, it is not possible for the individual soul to create chariots in dreams by its mere will. If a dream-creation were subject to one's will, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is unpleasant. As for the argument that the scripture compares the dream state to the waking state to show its reality, that comparison is not intended to assert its ultimate reality. Such a view would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous light and the fact that the scripture itself shows the absence of real chariots in dreams. The comparison is meant to show that dreams appear similar to the waking state because they are caused by the mental impressions <term>vasana</term> arising from waking life. Therefore, it is established that the dream state is mere illusion <term>maya-matra</term>.

# The absence of that dream occurs in the channels and in the Self, as is known from the scriptures. (3.2.7)

The Section on the Absence of Dreams (3.2.7)

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep <term>sushupti</term> is examined. Regarding deep sleep, there are several scriptural passages. In one place it says: "When a man is so asleep that he is completely serene and knows no dream, he then sleeps in these channels <term>nadi</term>." Elsewhere, referring to the same channels, it says: "Having crept back through them, he rests in the pericardium <term>puritat</term>." In another place, after mentioning the channels, it says: "In them he remains when, being asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one with the vital breath <term>prana</term> alone." Elsewhere: "He sleeps in the space within the heart." Again: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with the Existent <term>Sat</term>, he has gone to his own Self." And also: "Embraced by the conscious Self <term>prajna-atman</term>, he knows nothing without and nothing within."

A doubt arises here: are these various places—the channels and so on—different locations for deep sleep that are independent of each other, or do they together constitute a single location for deep sleep? What is the initial view? That they are different. Why? Because they serve the same purpose. It is not common for things serving the same purpose to be dependent on one another...

# From that comes speed of mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over the primary cause. 48

The attainment of unsurpassed speed of movement for the body is <term>manojavitvam</term> <gloss>speed of mind</gloss>. The attainment of the functioning of the senses of the bodiless ones <note>referring to those who have achieved a state of existence independent of the physical body</note> in relation to any desired place, time, or object is <term>vikaraṇabhāvaḥ</term> <gloss>the state of being without organs</gloss>. Mastery over all transformations of nature is <term>pradhānajayaḥ</term> <gloss>mastery over the primary cause</gloss>. These three perfections are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like</gloss>. These are acquired from the mastery over the five forms of the instruments of perception <note>the senses</note>. 48

# For one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the pure intellect and the Self, there comes supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience. 49

For the pure intellect <note>sattva</note> whose stains of activity <note>rajas</note> and inertia <note>tamas</note> have been washed away, and which exists in the highest clarity and the highest state of self-mastery, there is supremacy over all states of existence for one established in the discernment of the difference between the pure intellect and the Self. The <term>guṇas</term> <gloss>qualities of nature</gloss>, which constitute the essence of all things, appear as objects of determination...

---

He describes the perfections resulting from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over the primary cause.** The state of being without organs is the functioning of the senses for those who are bodiless. Place refers to regions such as Kashmir; time refers to the past and so on; objects refer to subtle things and so on. Through the mastery of the senses in their generic form <note>anvaya</note>, there is mastery over all transformations of nature, which is mastery over the primary cause. These perfections are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like</gloss> by those well-versed in the science of Yoga. It might be asked: through the mastery of the senses, the senses and their objects may become controlled, but what does this have to do with the primary cause <note>pradhāna</note> and its other origins? To this he says: **And these...** from the mastery of the five forms of the instruments, namely the senses, beginning with the act of grasping. This is what is meant: these perfections do not come from the mastery of the senses alone, but from the mastery of the five forms, and the primary cause is included within them. 48

These various concentrations <note>saṃyama</note>, which are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action, lead to the goal for which they were intended—the discernment of the difference between the pure intellect and the Self—by means of faith produced through the achievement of their own perfections, both directly and indirectly. He shows the intermediate powers of that discernment: **For one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the pure intellect and the Self, there comes supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience.** Clarity comes from the washing away of the stains of activity and inertia. From that comes the highest state of self-mastery. Indeed, the mind-stuff, when overwhelmed by activity and inertia, was not under control; but when these are subsided, it is under the control of the Yogi who is the master. For that Yogi, who is established in the form of the discernment of the difference between the pure intellect and the Self, there is supremacy over all states of existence. He explains this very point: **The qualities of nature, which constitute the essence of all things...**

<meta>This page contains commentaries on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The commentators include Su Zhe, Lu Huiqing, Huang Maocai, and Li Xizhai. The text discusses the contrast between worldly learning and the cultivation of the Tao.</meta>

<margin><term>Su</term> <gloss>Su Zhe, 1039–1112 AD</gloss> notes:</margin> Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>The Way</gloss> but strive for learning find that their information increases daily, yet they have no way to unify it. This inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the <term>Tao</term>, you will look back at all artificiality and false actions as nothing but delusion. To remove delusion and return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one principle." To forget the mind in order to purely return to nature is called decreasing. When delusions no longer remain and one reaches the point of forgetting even this mind to return to nature completely, then one discards "doing" and does not fail to reach "non-doing." Everyone has the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Therefore, they create tasks and seek results. Their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them; thus, they face difficulties and fail. The Sage practices <term>wu-wei</term> <gloss>non-doing or effortless action</gloss> and therefore has no business in his heart. This is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Although he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world follow him and find peace.

<margin><term>Lu</term> <gloss>Lu Huiqing, 1032–1111 AD</gloss> notes:</margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Seeking it without having heard it requires breadth, hence it is called "daily increase." Practicing the <term>Tao</term> is for those who have already heard it. Having heard it, one must act through non-doing, hence it is called "daily decrease." To decrease and further decrease means one has not yet avoided "doing." Only when one decreases even the act of decreasing does one reach <term>wu-wei</term>. <term>Wu-wei</term> refers to being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" refers to being stimulated and then penetrating all the causes under heaven. Reaching <term>wu-wei</term> through <term>wu-wei</term> is called the Constant Path. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the <term>Tao</term>. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this, we see that taking the world is always achieved through <term>wu-wei</term>. If one relies on "doing," it is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin><term>Huang Maocai</term> <gloss>Song Dynasty scholar</gloss> notes:</margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; thus, learning desires daily increase. Only after being able to do nothing can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>; thus, the <term>Tao</term> desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly drop everything and reach the realm of <term>wu-wei</term>. Thus, they can leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, spreading through the world with ample ease.

<margin><term>Xizhai</term> <gloss>Li Xizhai, a Yuan Dynasty commentator</gloss> notes:</margin> Practicing learning is for seeking knowledge, hence "daily increase." Practicing the <term>Tao</term> is for removing delusion, hence "daily decrease." If knowledge is not perfected, then the decrease is not complete; therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then there is <term>wu-wei</term>. Upon reaching <term>wu-wei</term>, every action is essentially non-action; this cannot easily be discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When <term>wu-wei</term> reaches its peak, though the world is vast, one unifies it. If one creates trouble by being meddlesome, even a single thing becomes entangled and chaotic, let alone the vastness of the world.

The Sage has no fixed heart; he takes the heart of the people as his own heart. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good; thus, virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I trust. To those who are not trustful, I also trust; thus, virtue is trust. The Sage lives in the world in a state of muddled simplicity, making his heart murky for the sake of the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes on him; the Sage <note>The text breaks here and continues on the next page.</note>

In this way, poetry relates to philosophy. For poetry is essentially an alternative form of philosophy: ancient in its timing, metrical in its harmony, and mythological in its intent. Philosophy, on the other hand, is a distinct form of ethics: more recent in its timing, more direct <note>literally: less bound by meter or complex harmony</note> in its harmony, and clearer in its intent. Therefore, since time alone is the factor and they are carried along together, how could one distinguish the difference in what each says about the divine—both the varied poets and the philosophers? Or how should we consider the similarity? Let us speak in this way: it is as if someone, considering the medicine of the past in relation to the new medicine now applied to diseases, were to look at each to declare which is better or worse. Asclepius <note>the Greek god of healing and medicine</note> would surely answer him. For time does not alter simple arts; where the need is simple, the works are also very simple. But in medicine, it is not possible to follow a single course for the body, nor is it agreed upon; rather, as the nature of our nourishment changes and shifts, the healing arts must find sufficient remedies, offering different treatments at different times suitable to the current diet. Do not think it was because the ancient surgeons were less skilled at using the knife or treating gout than those who later applied themselves to the art and these wise, diverse remedies of sharp mixtures. Rather, when the art dealt with bodies that were not over-indulged or complex, nor entirely weakened, it handled them easily; the work was simple, using mild applications or soothing drugs. But now, as the art treats bodies that have become softened and possess a more complex and sickly constitution, it has become complex itself. It changed from its former simplicity into a multifaceted state. So let both the poet and the philosopher answer, like another Asclepius, on behalf of their practices. One would be indignant on behalf of the suffering if someone ignored Homer and Hesiod, or Orpheus, or any other who spoke of the same things, or if one thought himself wiser than Aristotle.

First, let the fisherman be well-shaped in body, both lean and tall, swift and strong, neither lacking in fat nor burdened with excessive flesh; for it is often necessary for him to struggle against powerful fish being hauled up by force, which possess immense strength as long as they are tossed about and shaken in the arms of their mother, the brine. Let him be quick to leap from a rock and to spring up again easily, and let his hand be steady when stretched by the labor of the deep. He must quickly perceive the long path of the fish, dive into the deepest parts, and remain beneath the waves, performing his tasks as if on dry land, toiling in the sea with a steadfast heart.

The soul of the fisherman must be versatile and intelligent. For fish devise many and varied schemes when they encounter unexpected snares. Above all, let him be patient, silent, and temperate. Let him not be a lover of excessive sleep, but keep a sharp watch with a calm heart and wide-open eyes. Furthermore, let him endure both the winter and the freezing season of the dog-star <note>the heat of midsummer associated with the star Sirius</note>, let him be a lover of toil, and let him love the sea. For in this way, he will be strong and a friend to Hermes.

The morning hunt is best in the seasons of late summer and when the morning star <note>the planet Venus appearing at dawn</note> rises. In winter, one should set out when the rays of the sun are spreading, but in the blooming spring, the entire day is favorable for all kinds of catches.

When the god had revealed these things, all the maidens of the lineage of the Aepytidae <note>The royal house of Messenia, descended from Aepytus</note> immediately cast lots. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. However, Epebolus the seer forbade her sacrifice, claiming she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus. He asserted that Lyciscus's wife, being unable to conceive, had secretly substituted the child as her own. While the seer was explaining this matter, Lyciscus, taking the girl with him, fled to Sparta.

When the Messenians learned of Lyciscus's escape, they were deeply discouraged. At this point, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytid lineage who was more distinguished than Lyciscus in general reputation and especially in matters of war, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed willingly. 

Human ambition is often obscured by destiny, just as a pebble is hidden by the silt of a river. Even then, as Aristodemus strove to save the Messenians, a certain obstacle arose. A Messenian man (whose name they do not record) happened to be in love with Aristodemus's daughter and was soon to take her as his wife. At first, he disputed with Aristodemus, arguing that since the girl was betrothed to him, her father no longer had sole authority over her. When he saw this argument was failing, he turned to a shameful claim: that he had already been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. 

Finally, he provoked Aristodemus to such a degree that the father, driven mad by rage, killed his own daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and demonstrated to those present that she was not with child. Epebolus the seer, who was present, then ordered that someone else must provide a daughter for sacrifice. He argued that the death of Aristodemus's daughter counted for nothing, as her father had murdered her rather than sacrificing her to the gods as the Pythia had commanded.

When the seer said this, the Messenian multitude rushed to kill the girl's suitor, believing he had brought a useless stain of blood upon Aristodemus and made their hope of salvation uncertain. However, this man was a very close friend of Euphais <note>The King of Messenia</note>. Euphais persuaded the Messenians that the oracle was fulfilled by the girl's death and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. As he spoke, all those of the Aepytid lineage agreed, for they were relieved of the fear for their own daughters. Following the king's advice, they dissolved the assembly and turned to sacrifices and a festival for the gods.

The Lacedaemonians <gloss>Spartans</gloss>, hearing of the oracle given to the Messenians, were themselves discouraged, and their kings were hesitant to begin a battle. In the sixth year after Lyciscus's flight from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians—their omens finally being favorable—marched against Ithome. The Cretans were no longer present to help them, and the Messenians' allies were also late. The Spartans were already viewed with suspicion by other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to come secretly to help the Messenians, rather than by a public decree. The Arcadians had openly refused the campaign, yet they too failed to arrive in time. 

The Messenians were led to risk battle even without allies by their faith in the oracle. For the most part, the engagement did not differ much from the previous battle; the daylight failed while they were still fighting. ### **Torah** Or <gloss>Torah Light</gloss>
These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service, and Acts of Loving-kindness. 

Torah is represented by the commands "do not add" and "do not subtract," which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers have said: a thing that is perfectly complete cannot be said to be lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be complete; and if it could receive an addition, it would mean it was not previously finished. Therefore, the definition of the "complete" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is dependent on His Great Name, which is <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term>, for "The Torah of the Lord is perfect," as I have elaborated in my commentary on Tractate Shevuot in the chapter "Torah Or." And as it is written in the Zohar on the verse "This is My name and this is My memorial": the letters <term>Yod-He</term> with "My name" <note>Hebrew: Shemi</note> numerically equal 365 <note>the negative commandments</note>; the letters <term>Vav-He</term> with "My memorial" <note>Hebrew: Zikhri</note> numerically equal 248 <note>the positive commandments</note>. It is written, "I am the first and I am the last," and He is the absolute perfection, without subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God," which is a warning against erasing the Name or tearing down a stone from the Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are like the house in which the Blessed One dwells, and so too is the Sanctuary. It is written, "I am the Lord, that is My name"; the letters are like the frame of the house, and His Name is the soul within them. One who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God."

Divine Service <note>Avodah</note> comprises most of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command was given to have a fixed place, which is the Chosen House, and the text gives the reason: "To His habitation shall you seek, and there you shall come." "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term>. Do not fear that she dwells there, for in the Sanctuary the Glory is united with the Beauty of His people. This is "to place His name there," which the Targum translates as "to cause His Presence to dwell." And "around the place of holiness the wicked walk," referring to the <term>Kelipot</term> <gloss>husks/shards of evil</gloss>; therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see."

### **Sometimes**
sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inside. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborn offerings from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written of them, "There you shall offer," meaning there they shall have an ascent <note>Hebrew: Aliyah</note> and not outside. Since the holiness resides in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we are commanded to "turn away from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. The secret of this hints that the ten nations are not merely idolaters; rather, the nations in the Land of Israel, being under the dominion of the Honorable Name, worship God by "cutting the saplings" <note>a metaphor for heresy</note>, which is true idolatry. However, outside the Land, they are under the dominion of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against tearing down a single stone from the holy, so conversely it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate a "Subverted City" <note>Ir HaNidachat</note> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Likewise, one who entices or misleads <note>to idolatry</note> must be uprooted, for he stems from the impurity of the ancient Serpent who was an enticer. The Holy One immediately said, "Cursed is the Serpent," therefore the powers of <term>Samael</term> <note>the angel of evil</note> are never appeased. The command follows not to love him or listen to him, as was said of the Serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman." A false prophet is also like an enticer. 

Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first-fruits <note>Bikkurim</note>, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first-fruits, being the "beginning," indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there they take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. This is the secret of "lesser" holy offerings and the Second Tithe, whose consumption is in Jerusalem. This is the blessing of "grain, wine, and oil," which are the primary ancestors of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat lesser holy offerings until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul, and only afterward is there permission to enjoy the physical benefit. Know that just as the service of the sacrifice is an offering to God, so too is the worshiper, for the essence of the service is that one sacrifices himself, in the secret of "When a man <note>Adam</note> brings an offering from among you." The burnt offering is entirely consumed, for it comes to atone for the straying of the thought, which is spiritual, and it is burned all night so that the Serpent cannot hinder it. Lesser holy offerings represent the peace of the soul and the body.

### **The Secret**
of the firstborn is the secret of "Holy Israel," who are called "Israel My firstborn." He has pity on them and guards them, and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, the firstborn animal is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating holy things corresponds to those with blemishes. For Israel is holy and Israel is called "Man" <note>Adam</note>. He was originally holy, but afterward a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," yet he has a redemption, in the secret of "I will give a man in your stead." This was the secret of the <term>Azazel</term> goat, "and it shall bear their iniquities"; their iniquities fall upon its head and upon its people. But we are commanded not to cause a blemish in a holy animal in order to eat it. For if one intentionally blemishes holy things, he also violates the prohibition of working or shearing them, for even the "broken tablets" remain holy.

### **The General Principle**
is that the service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the person. Likewise, his soul is called to the "Altar Above" after death, and Michael is the High Priest. This is the secret, for "in the image of God was man made." Therefore, the warning comes to be careful during his life regarding damages to souls, not to kill a person except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then he is "dead by the hand of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the witness, He is the judge," for the Lord is a true witness and a true judge. So must the Sanhedrin be; just as they are judges of truth, they must have witnesses of truth. I mean they must clarify the truth of the witnesses with total clarity through inquiry and investigation, and then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death" <note>of His pious ones</note>.

### **Since**
death is precious in the eyes of the Lord—because Israel is holy from the side of their souls, and after death the souls cleave above—therefore the command comes: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness," etc., "for you are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the other nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, as is fitting, since at death they go to perdition and have no portion in this world or the world to come. We, however, are children of God. When we depart from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, we instead have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or perform these acts.

### **Let us return**
to the matter that the person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it is said: "When a man brings an offering from among you." There is a further secret in this: for a spark of a soul can be found even below in a person through the secret of <term>Gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation</gloss>, as in "Man and beast You save, O Lord." Therefore, even in the eating of non-sacred meat <note>meat of desire</note>, we were commanded regarding slaughter <note>Shechitah</note> and great caution against any nick in the blade, for then it becomes a carcass <note>nevelah</note>, and "a disgrace <note>nevalah</note> is committed in Israel." For who knows what reincarnation is within it? "Love your neighbor as yourself"—choose for him a "beautiful death," namely, slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies on its own, the power of impurity takes hold of it. But when one slaughters it properly, and there is in the animal or the pure bird a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **One who eats**
a limb from a living animal is like one who eats the flesh of a person when a reincarnated soul is there. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure animals, beasts, and birds all indicate the spark spread within them—whether it is from the "Side of Impurity" or the "Side of Holiness." I have elaborated on this in the portion of Shemini. When Israel conducts themselves with holiness, it is written of them: "And they shall make for Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell within them." For they themselves are the Tabernacle, as man is divided into three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies; the heart corresponds to the Holy Place; and from the belly downward corresponds to the Courtyard of the Sanctuary, as I elaborated in the portion of Terumah. When one eats foods from the side of holiness, they are like sacrifices offered upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages said: "Now, a man's table atones for him," as I have elaborated in its place.

### **Regarding**
the commandments of the Festivals and their sacrifices, I have written about each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals and to go up on the pilgrimage: "Three times a year shall all your males appear." Do not read it only as "appearing" <note>to see</note> but also "being seen." Therefore, if one wishes to be seen in the Temple where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. Otherwise, it is forbidden for a wicked person to enter the hall; how could he wish to be seen before Him and bring a burnt offering of appearance? Then he himself becomes a sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. It says "three times a year he shall appear"—referring to Isaac, who was a "perfect burnt offering."

### Description of Lima, City of the Kings.

<margin>
Appearance of the city of Lima.
</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one can see into every corner, and on both sides the flat fields. Through most of the houses run canals, bringing fresh water from the river, which is a very great commodity and convenience for the citizens; through this they can water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they have in beautiful and pleasant condition. Also,

<margin>
Many watermills, with which they grind their corn.
</margin>
in this river lie many watermills after our country's fashion, where they grind their corn. In short, very wealthy citizens live here, some of whom possess 150,000 <term>ducats</term> <gloss>gold coins</gloss>. And from this city, ships sometimes depart carrying a value of 800,000 ducats, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which stands a crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their cattle, as well as their dovecotes and their vineyards—though the grapes are not good due to the nature of the land—and beautiful gardens, full not only of all kinds of fruits of that country, but also

<margin>
Description of the fertility of the land.
</margin>
of the Spanish varieties, such as figs, pomegranates, lemons, citrons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar canes, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. Truly, to pass human life with joy, if the scandalous disagreements and wars were not there, this place is surely one of the most beautiful in the entire world. For the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the whole year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. Also, it has never been seen that hunger or plague occurred there, nor any rain, or claps of thunder, or lightning from heaven

<margin>
Why the City of the Kings received its name, and it was built in the year 1535.
</margin>
striking. But on the contrary, there is always a clear, bright, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535 and is named the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Epiphany <note>Three Kings' Day</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as meat and fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. During the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet it is not unhealthy like ours; those who have pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase in people and wealth, although many years ago there were already over 500 houses,

The width and length of the houses of Lima.

and the city is built very white, so that 2,000 might well stand there, for the streets are wide and the market square large. Each house has 80 feet of property in width and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for within two or three years it is consumed by worms—the houses are built with only one story, yet very

<margin>
Appearance of the houses.
</margin>
costly and magnificent with many rooms, halls, and <term>faletten</term> <gloss>galleries or balconies</gloss>, suitable for living and lodging foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials which they bake together very thickly and fill with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen; all around and on top

<column-break/>

of the walls they make arbors of reeds where they shelter from the sun. They do not need to worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where Bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trujillo, Guanuca, Chachapoia, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Catchi, St. Michael, St. Francisco. It was previously said that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea we have dealt until now, starting from the <term>Linea</term> <gloss>Equator</gloss> and Cape Passao to this point. It should also be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima but much further south, the sea coast is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places, where for ten miles inland it neither thunders, lightens, nor rains; but beyond those ten miles it does, or as far as the mountains lie from the sea. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but there are four or five standing waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which originate from the snow and rain falling in the mountains, not from springs, which are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers have been partly described before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from each other, though mostly 7 or 8, by which traveling people regulate their journey because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, for a mile's breadth or even more, sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the situation of the land, there are various fertile trees and corn lands which are cultivated and sown by the people, which they may do throughout the entire year. Also, many kinds of wild trees grow near these rivers: cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises, etc. And since the Spaniards took the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through certain canals which they lead out of these rivers. Because these rivers run swiftly down from high mountains, one can hardly cross them without help, and many have drowned therein. Those who make their journey along the flat land commonly keep so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and rains heavily, it is perilous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either with certain rafts they have for that purpose, or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds, upon which the traveling man must lie stretched out, and one of the Indians swims in front, pulling that net or raft forward with a rope, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of branches. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to and over the knees, and an upper garment like a cloak. The women wear a garment of cotton according to the length of the body; and although the fashion of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nonetheless some distinction in the head-dress: for some wear a single small cap, some braided, some of one color, others of various colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, all distinguished according to the custom of the land.

### On the shame sought from unworthy praise.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you later condemn, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Pain:* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.
<note>A large ornamental initial L marks the beginning of the response.</note>
*Reason:* That which is an evil often springs from a good root. For good and innocent people believe others to be just as they are themselves. Hence they are even more prone to praise than is fair; and although I admit it is an evil to praise the unworthy, it is much worse to criticize the undeserving.

*Pain:* I praised one who was unworthy.

*Reason:* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another, but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Pain:* The praise of another turns into my own infamy.

*Reason:* Rather, it is either your fault or your ignorance. For no infamy, just as no praise, truly comes from what belongs to another.

*Pain:* I grieve greatly for having praised the unworthy.

*Reason:* See to it then that you do not have cause to grieve for this same thing often. Beware of leaping forward rashly to praise or to criticize. For there is a lust for both things and, to speak accurately, a disease and a certain itching of a restless tongue that knows no quiet. The restraint and guarding of the tongue are numbered among the works of extraordinary perfection, as the Scripture says:

In this manner, the eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth. For the fourth says that bases subtended by equal sides and angles are equal, while the eighth says that equal sides placed upon equal bases contain equal angles. In these, the statement regarding equal bases was the conclusion of the former theorem, while the statement regarding equal sides being placed was one of the hypotheses previously assumed in that one. Since there are these two types of conversion, the first kind is simple and definite, while the other is varied and proceeds into a great number of theorems, not converting in one way but in many, due to the multitude of hypotheses in complex theorems. Often we also convert from a starting point of two <insert>or more</insert> hypotheses, whenever the hypotheses are not all definite but some are indefinite.

It is necessary to observe in these matters that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions. For example: every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangular number is a hexagonal number. The reason is that the one is more general, while the other is more specific.

# Zechariah

For I have already seen the kingdoms, which are an allusion to the seven <note>likely a scribal error or specific symbolic count for the four world empires</note> kingdoms. And so, "What are these?" <note>Zechariah 6:5</note> refers to the living beings through which I exist.

And the angel answered and said to me: "These are the four winds of heaven, going out from standing before the Lord of all the earth. The one with the black horses goes out toward the north country, and the white ones go out after them, and the dappled ones go out toward the south country." And the strong ones went out and sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth; and he said: "Go, walk to and fro through the earth." So they walked to and fro through the earth. Then he cried out to me and spoke to me, saying: "Behold, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."

**And he answered.** "These are the four winds." This is like saying "to the four winds." Similarly, "And he came Jerusalem" <note>2 Kings 18:17</note> means "to Jerusalem." Another interpretation: "to the son of a black man" is like "to a black son," and similar cases. This refers to the division of the four chariots, which go out to the four winds of the heavens. This is to give permission to the kingdoms to rule in the four winds, each one in its time. This applies to the whole world, which is characterized by strength. "From standing before the Lord of all the earth" means they act as messengers of God, who gave them dominion over this. It is like the verse: "The sons of God came to stand before the Lord" <note>Job 2:1</note>. <margin>Job 2</margin>

**The one with.** "The black ones." He mentions the black horses because the time of the Babylonian kingdom had already passed. The kingdom of Media and Persia would go first to the north country, for they were destined to destroy it, and afterward they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth. "And the white ones," which refers to the kingdom of Greece <note>original: "Yavan"</note>, went out after them when that kingdom broke forth. For Alexander of Macedon <note>original: "Alexandros Makdon"</note>, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingship from him, and he and his successors ruled afterward over the whole world.

**And the dappled ones go out toward the south country.** These represent the Roman faction, for Rome is <unclear>shnunith</unclear>. This is proven by Caesar, who ruled over Rome and began to fight against the Greek kingdom. At the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is in the south. At that time, the Greeks ruled in all those lands, but Caesar prevailed over them, transferred the sovereignty from the Greeks, and restored it to the Romans.

**And the strong ones.** These are an allusion to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>referring to the Islamic conquests</note>, who exerted themselves on their own initiative to seek dominion, to find a place for themselves where they might have spirit. This is why it says, "and they sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth."

**And he said.** That is to say, He gave them permission to travel and to conquer lands.

**Then he cried out.** Meaning, he called to me with a loud voice and said to me: **"Behold, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."** This refers to the portion of the black horses that went to Babylon to destroy it.

<margin>One for one task, another for another.</margin> A pilot needs a helmsman, and a ship-owner needs a pilot; for one knows how to tighten the stern-cable and the other how to manage the prow or work the capstan. Likewise, an architect requires assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work but will labor alongside him to complete it. So too the statesman, as a master-craftsman and a creator of power and justice, will not immediately choose friends who merely share his passions, but rather assistants and those who will strive with him toward what is noble. We must choose different men for different needs, rather than those who would act unjustly or violently. For he said it makes no difference whether a builder or a carpenter uses corners, rulers, and plumb-lines with ignorance and error, by which the work is bound to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking tools of statesmen. One must not join them in their transgressions, but rather take care that they do not commit errors even through ignorance.

<margin>Friends.</margin> This is what moved and distressed Solon regarding his friends. For when he intended to lighten the debts and introduce the <term>Seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking off of burdens</gloss>, and his plan was to bring in a cancellation of debts, he shared this with his friends. But they committed an injustice: they anticipated the law by borrowing a great deal of silver, and a short time later, when the law was brought to light, they were seen to have purchased splendid houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon was blamed for participating in this scheme, though he was actually a victim of it. Being ignorant of his friends' eagerness, he became the weakest and most humble of men, just like Euripides' Pegasus, who cowered more than he wished to yield. By helping them in their misfortunes more than was proper, he seemed to be a partner in their injustices. For even those who save someone lying in a ditch might be pushed by the rolling fire. 

When Phocion's son-in-law, Charicles, was on trial regarding the money from Harpalus, Phocion did not join him in court, but said: I made you my son-in-law only for what is just; and he went away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not dissuade his brother from tyranny by teaching and entreating him, joined those who put him to death. For a man should be a friend only as far as the altar <note>meaning: as far as his religious and moral oaths allow</note>, as Pericles once said, not joining in perjury, but remaining a friend only as far as law, justice, and the public good allow. If this is overlooked, it brings great harm to the community, as when they failed to punish Sphodrias or Phoebidas; for these men, by their actions, brought war upon Sparta. 

While the statesman should not be harsh in attacking the moderate failings of his friends, he should, after securing the most important public interests, use his surplus influence to help his friends, stand by them, and labor with them. These are favors that do not provoke envy: helping a friend toward an office, or rather handing over some administration to him, or an honorable embassy that carries the prestige of a leader, or a mission to a city for the sake of friendship and concord. For this is a proper trust, and a visible and great deed for them. First, he should manage his own affairs, then go on an embassy with a friend, as Diomedes did: If you indeed bid me choose a companion myself, how then could I forget godlike Odysseus? And Odysseus in turn gave him equal praise. There are also those who, like Diomedes, slew twelve of the best Thracians among their comrades. For

this yielding to friends does not less adorn the one praised than those who praise him. But stubbornness, as Plato says, is the companion of solitude. Furthermore, one should combine these noble favors of kindness with those that are less pleasant; he should not bid them to praise or love those who are not present as if they were the causes and tokens of success, but rather set aside mean or absurd demands—not bitterly, but by gently teaching and comforting them, showing that such things are not worthy of their virtue or reputation. 

Epaminondas acted best in this regard: when he refused to release a certain prisoner at the request of Pelopidas, but released him shortly after when a common girl asked for him, he said that such favors were for girls to receive, but for Pelopidas to receive treasurerships or generalships. And Cato the Censor acted with weight and dignity when his friend Catulus, who was then Censor, sought to intervene for someone being audited by him as treasurer; Cato said: It is a shame that you, who ought to be disciplining us young men, are being driven out by our own subordinates. For by refusing the request with spirit, he removed the abruptness and bitterness from his words, so that the pain did not seem to come from his own will but from the necessity of law and justice. 

There are also ways for friends to profit from political life that are not ignoble. For instance, after the battle, Themistocles saw a corpse wearing gold bracelets and a necklace; he passed by himself, but turning to a friend, he said: Pick these up, for you have not become a Themistocles. For circumstances often give the statesman such opportunities for his friends; for not all men are of a single mold. If one is not able to help in a matter of justice, he may assist a friend by giving him charge of a contract or a partnership in some public work, or by providing the benefit of a loan. 

When a friend came to Epaminondas asking for a talent of silver, he ordered him to ask a certain wealthy man for it, saying that Epaminondas ordered it. When the man who was asked came to inquire why, Epaminondas said: Because this man is honest but poor, while you are rich from having embezzled much from the city. And Xenophon says that it is a great thing to be able to benefit friends while remaining superior to money. 

Since every position of leadership and every public career brings certain enmities and differences, it is especially necessary for the statesman to know how to handle this. Most people praise Themistocles and Aristides because they would lay aside their enmity at the border whenever they went out on an embassy or a military command, and then take it up again afterward. Some are also exceedingly pleased by the conduct of Cretinus of Magnesia. He was a political rival of Hermias, a man of ambitious and brilliant spirit. When the war with Mithridates broke out and he saw the city in danger, he proposed that Hermias take over the command and manage affairs while he himself withdrew; or, if Hermias wished him to lead, that Hermias should step aside so they would not destroy the city by competing with one another. The challenge pleased Hermias, and saying that Cretinus was the better soldier, he withdrew with his wife and children. Cretinus then escorted him out, giving him money from his own funds, as it was more useful to those in exile than to those under siege; thus he unexpectedly saved the city which had come to the brink of ruin. 

For if noble and wise men say: I love my children, but I love my country more, why should it not be even readier for each of them to say: I hate this man and wish to best him, but I love my country more? For to be unwilling to settle an enmity for the sake of things for which one ought to give up even a friend is a terribly savage and bestial trait. But...

<margin>By the fullness of it, they use the heart and tongue of Egypt.</margin>
A divine water-jar <note>original: "Θεία δ’ ὑδρεία"</note>, or a jar gushing forth water to represent heaven and earth, is depicted by likening the water-vessel to a heart that possesses a tongue. They use the heart because, among them, this is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. They use the tongue because it always exists in moisture and they call it the producer of what is good. There are two water-jars, neither more nor less, because the process of the Nile's rising is twofold according to them. They assign one to the land of Egypt, since Egypt is capable of generating water by itself. They assign the other to the Ocean, for water also comes from it into Egypt at the time of the inundation. They also attribute the grain to the rains which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia at the time of the Nile's rising. That Egypt itself generates the water can be learned from this: in the rest of the world's climates, the flooding of rivers is completed in the winter.

<summary>This page explains the hieroglyphic symbolism of the water-jar as a representation of the Nile's inundation, comparing the river's governance of Egypt to the heart's governance of the body.
