# Original Wings of Laozi: Volume Two
### Page Twenty-Three

Su's Commentary: Those who do not know the <term>Dao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning find that their information and observations increase daily. Without a way to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much and select what is good to follow; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day a person knows the Way and looks back upon artificial actions, they see that everything is false. Removing the false to return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zi Gong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zi Gong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one principle." By removing falsehood to purify nature and returning to nothingness, one achieves "decreasing." Yet, the mind that intends to remove falsehood still remains. Only when one also forgets this very mind, leaving nothing but pure nature, can one reach the state where nothing is done, yet nothing is left undone. All people have desires and the mind to grasp the affairs of the world; thus, they create complications to seek them. Their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them, so they never succeed. The Sage practices <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action</gloss> and thus has no ulterior business. His mind is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Although he does not grasp at the world's affairs, the world's affairs follow him and find peace.

Lu's Commentary: Those who practice "learning" are those who have not yet heard the Way. Not having heard the Way, they seek it but do not find it; because they do not find it, they seek broadly, and thus "increase daily." Those who practice the Way have already heard the Way. Having heard it, they act upon it but find nothing except the need to reach non-action; thus, they "decrease daily." This decreasing is still not free from "doing." Only when one decreases the very act of decreasing does one reach non-action. Non-action means being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means being stimulated and then penetrating all the causes under heaven. Reaching this state of "nothing left undone" is called "ending learning and having no worries." It is the cause of the spirit, just as the Changes <note>referring to the I Ching</note> have no physical form. Who but the most spiritual in the world could achieve this? From this, we see that one can know how to take hold of the world; if one relies on "doing" things, it is clear that one is insufficient to take hold of the world.

<column-break/>

Huang Maocai's Commentary: Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires daily increase. That which increases can progress toward transformation. Only then can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires daily decrease. However, that which increases can eventually fall away. As for reaching non-action, it is perhaps difficult to achieve through force. Only those with ultimate clarity can suddenly break free, and then the whole world becomes spacious and easy.

Xizhai's Commentary: Practicing learning is the means to seek knowledge, hence the daily increase. Practicing the Way is the means to remove falsehood, hence the daily decrease. If knowledge is not exhausted, then the decreasing is not complete. Therefore, daily increase is the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until falsehood is gone and truth is complete, then one reaches non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even if things exist, they are as if they do not; this state cannot easily be discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its peak, even with the vastness of the world, one unifies it with a single thread. In this way, I also hold that poetry relates to philosophy. For what else is poetry but philosophy? In time it is ancient, in harmony it is metered, and in thought it is mythological. And what else is philosophy but poetry? In time it is more recent, in harmony it is more like prose, and in thought it is clearer. Therefore, since these matters differ from one another only in time and form, how could anyone separate the difference between them? In these things, what do both the poets and the philosophers say about the divine? Or what is this inquiry like? Let us speak of it in this way: it is as if someone, considering that earliest form of medicine in comparison to the new medicine prescribed for bodies today, were to examine which of the two is better or worse.

Asclepius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note> would answer him that time does not transform other arts. For those things for which the need is always the same, the works also remain unchanged. But it is not enough for medicine to follow the nature of bodies, which is a thing that does not stand still nor remain consistent. Instead, as the body is altered and changed by the nourishment of its diet, medicine must invent remedies and diets, different ones at different times, suitable to the current nourishment.

Therefore, do not think that either those men of old, or the famous Machaon and Podalirius <note>The sons of Asclepius, mentioned in Homer as healers of the Greek army at Troy.</note>, were at all wiser in healing than those who later applied themselves to the art and invented these wise and manifold remedies. Rather, at that time, the art dealt with bodies that were not over-nourished, nor complex, nor entirely weakened, and so it handled them easily. Their work was a simple matter, bringing the sick to rest with gentle medicines. But finally now, as bodies have slipped away from the art into a more complex diet and a poor temperament <note>The balance of bodily humors.</note>, the art itself has become more complex and has changed from its former simplicity into a manifold form.

Come then, let both the poet and the philosopher together answer on behalf of their practices, just as Asclepius did. This man is gentle in his thoughts, should anyone suppose that Homer and Hesiod, or even Orpheus, or any other of the men of that time, were less wise than Aristotle.

O Hermes of famous counsel, the fishermen propitiate you above all others; therefore, with cries shared among the gods of the wild, I would come to you after the fame of the gathered catch.
First, let the fisherman have a body and limbs that are both swift and strong; let him be neither too fat nor, on the other hand, wasted in flesh. For it is often necessary to battle against powerful fish being hauled in, which possess overweening strength as they are whirled and shaken in the embrace of their mother, the brine.
He must be able to leap from a rock and spring back up onto a rock with ease. He must be able to track a long path quickly through the deep-stretching toil of the sea, to dive into the deepest parts, and to remain amidst the swells as if he were lingering over labors on the land, as is fitting for a man of enduring spirit competing in the sea.
Let the fisherman’s soul be full of craft and wise; for fish devise many and varied schemes, escaping by unexpected deceits.
Let him be especially daring, fearless, and temperate. Let him not love the satiety of sleep, but let him look sharply, waking with his heart and with wide-open eyes.
Furthermore, let him endure the winter storms of Zeus and the parching season of the Dog Star <note>The star Sirius, associated with the peak of summer heat</note>, being steadfast in his desire for labor and loving the sea.
In this way, he would be both valiant and dear to Hermes.
Hunting <note>fishing</note> in the evening is best during the autumn seasons, and again when the Morning Star <term>Heosphoros</term> <gloss>the bringer of dawn</gloss> rises.
In winter, one should set out together with the spreading rays of the sun; but in the blooming spring, the work is aided by all kinds of breezes throughout the entire day.

When the god had revealed these things, they immediately cast lots for all the maidens who were of the race of the <term>Aepytidae</term> <gloss>a royal Messenian dynasty descended from Aepytus</gloss>. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. However, Epebolus the seer forbade them to sacrifice her, claiming she was not actually the daughter of Lyciscus; he asserted that Lyciscus's wife, being unable to conceive, had secretly substituted the child as her own. While the seer was explaining these matters, Lyciscus took the girl and fled to Sparta. The Messenians were deeply discouraged and were extremely angry with Lyciscus. Thereupon Aristodemus, a man of the race of the Aepytidae—who was more distinguished than Lyciscus both in reputation and in military matters—offered his own daughter to be sacrificed of his own free will.

But the god does not least of all hide the destined end of human affairs according to these things, and the pebble <note>referring to the voting or lot-casting process</note> having fallen by the river Illyus. Where even then, a struggle arose for the Messenians that hindered Aristodemus from saving them, for an obstacle of this sort occurred. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was about to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since Aristodemus had betrothed her to him, he was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, as the betrothed, had more authority over her. Secondly, when he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameful story, claiming that he had already been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him.

Finally, he provoked Aristodemus to such an extent that, driven mad by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and demonstrated that she was not with child. Epebolus the seer, who was present, then ordered that someone else must give up a daughter; for he said that the death of Aristodemus's daughter was of no use to them, because the father had murdered her, but had not sacrificed her to the gods whom the <term>Pythia</term> <gloss>the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</gloss> had commanded. When the seer said this, the multitude of Messenians rushed to kill the girl's suitor, believing he had brought a useless stain of blood upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of safety uncertain.

However, this man was a very close friend to Euphanes <note>the King of the Messenians</note>. Euphanes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle was fulfilled by the death of the girl, and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the race of the Aepytidae agreed that he spoke the truth; for each of them was anxious for his own daughter, and so, obeying the king's advice, they dissolved the assembly. From there, they turned to sacrifices and the festival of the gods.

The Lacedaemonians <gloss>Spartans</gloss>, hearing of the oracle given to the Messenians, were themselves discouraged, as were their kings, and they hesitated to begin a battle. But in the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (for the omens had become favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to no longer be present with them. The allies of the Messenians were also late. For the Spartans were already viewed with suspicion by other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. ### Torah is Light
These commandments mentioned in this Torah portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service <note>sacrificial or prayer service</note>, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah refers to the commands: Do not add and do not subtract, which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers say: a thing that is perfectly complete cannot be subject to deficiency or excess. For if it were deficient, they would say it lacks beauty, and if it were excessive, they would say it was not truly finished. Therefore, the definition of the "complete" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is suspended upon His Great Name, which is <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>, as it is written: The Torah of the Lord is perfect <note>Psalm 19:8</note>, as I have elaborated in my work on Tractate Shevuot in the chapter "Torah is Light." And as it is written in the Zohar on the verse: This is My Name and this is My Memorial <note>Exodus 3:15</note>. The letters <term>Yod-He</term> with "My Name" <note>in Hebrew gematria</note> equals 365 <note>the number of negative commandments</note>. The letters <term>Vav-He</term> with "My Memorial" equals 248 <note>the number of positive commandments</note>. And it is written: I am the first and I am the last. He is the absolute perfection, without subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: You shall not do so to the Lord your God, which is a warning against erasing the Name or breaking a stone from the Holy Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are the "house" in which He, may He be blessed, dwells. So too is the Temple. It is written: I am the Lord, that is My Name; either the letters are a covering for the revelation of His Name, or His Name is the soul within them. One who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of: You shall not do so to the Lord your God.

Divine Service <note>Avodah</note> comprises most of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command was given to have a fixed place specifically in the Chosen House, and the reason for the matter is: To His habitation shall you seek, and there you shall come. "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is a palace for the Lord, as it is written: The Lord is in His holy palace. That the Divine Presence should be in the Temple, so that the Glory may be unified with the Triumphant Beauty <note>the sefirot of Hod and Tiferet</note>. This is the meaning of "to place His Name there," which the Targum translates as "to cause His Presence to dwell." And "around the place of holiness the wicked walk," referring to the <term>Kelipah</term> <gloss>husks/evil forces</gloss>; therefore: Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see.

**Sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inside. This is the secret of the commandment to occupy oneself with bringing the offering from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the "flatterer" <note>the spark</note> returns to its root, and it is written of them: There you shall offer. Meaning, there they shall have an ascent, and not outside. Since the holiness is in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we are commanded to "turn away from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. Our Sages of blessed memory said: Gentiles outside the Land are not truly idolaters <note>they merely follow ancestral custom</note>. The matter is that gentiles in the Land of Israel, who are under the dominion of the Honorable Name, worship God by "cutting the shoots" <note>heresy</note>, and this is actual idolatry. However, those outside the Land are under the dominion of the external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against breaking a single stone of holiness, so conversely it is a great commandment to destroy and lose a "Subverted City" <note>Ir HaNidachat</note> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. So too with the "Enticer" <note>Mesit</note> and "Misleader"—one must uproot and eradicate him, for he comes from the impurity of the ancient Serpent who was an enticer. The Holy One, blessed be He, cursed the serpent; therefore, we do not seek merits for an enticer. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, similar to the enmity placed between the serpent and the woman. A false prophet is also like an enticer.

Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the commands that the priests have no permission to eat until they are within the Chosen House. For the First Fruits <note>Bikkurim</note>, which are the "beginning," indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere; therefore, they must go to the holy place and from there receive their vitality. They are holy to sustain them, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. This is the secret of the "Lesser Sanctity" offerings and the tithes of grain, wine, and oil, which are the "fathers of fathers" of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat Lesser Sanctity offerings until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul <note>nefesh</note>. Afterward, the body is permitted to benefit. Know that just as the Service, which is the sacrifice, is an offering to the Lord, so too is the worshiper. For the essence of the service is that a person offers himself, according to the secret of: When a man <note>Adam</note> brings an offering from among you. The burnt offering <note>Olah</note> is entirely consumed because it comes to atone for the thoughts of the heart—the secret of thought which is spiritual. It is offered all night because darkness does not rest upon its bed. Lesser Sanctity offerings represent the perfection of both soul and body.

**The secret** of the unblemished firstborn. And the secret of the remnant of Israel who are holy, whom He called: My firstborn son, Israel. They are the holy congregation and are called: The sheep of My pasture. Therefore, it <note>the firstborn animal</note> is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating consecrated items when they have acquired a blemish and are redeemed: for Israel is holy, and Israel is called "Man" <note>Adam</note>. He was a holy living being, but then a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," yet he has a redemption, in the secret of: I give a man <note>Adam</note> in your stead. This was the secret of the <term>Azazel</term> goat which carries their sins. Our Sages said: they are "brazen ones" <note>Azut</note> who depend on "the strength <note>Oz</note> of His people." But we are commanded not to intentionally cause a blemish in consecrated animals in order to eat them, for that would be a blemish in their holiness by one's own choice. Also, the prohibition of working or shearing consecrated animals remains, for even if they have fallen <note>become blemished</note>, they are still holy.

**The general principle** of the ascent of the Service is the sacrifice; the inner sacrifice is the person. Likewise, his soul is offered after his death on the Altar Above, and Michael is the High Priest. This is the secret of: For in the image of God was man made. Therefore, the warning is very strong to be deliberate and quick in capital cases, not to put a man to death except after thorough searching and inquiry. Then he dies by the hand of Heaven, according to the secret that He is the Witness and He is the Judge. For the Holy One, blessed be He, is a True Witness and a True Judge. So must the Sanhedrin be; just as they are true judges, they must have true witnesses. I mean that the truth of the witnesses must be clarified to them with absolute clarity through searching and inquiry. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and it shall be "right in the eyes of the Lord" on the Altar.

**Since** the sealing <note>of the soul</note> is precious in the eyes of the Lord, and because Israel is holy from the side of their souls—which after death cleave above—therefore the command came: You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note>, for you are children to the Lord your God. This is not the case for the nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, as is fitting for them, since at their death they go to perdition and have no portion in this world or the World to Come. But we are children of the Lord. When one is absent from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, we instead have a permanent dwelling above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or to perform these acts.

**Let us return** to the matter: the person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it says: When a man brings an offering from among you. Furthermore, there is a hidden matter: for it is prepared to be offered even below, namely in the secret of <term>Gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation</gloss>—"Man and beast You save, O Lord." Therefore, even when eating non-sacred meat out of desire, we are commanded regarding ritual slaughter <note>Shechitah</note> with a great warning against any nick in the blade. For if there is a nick, it becomes a carcass <note>nevelah</note>, and then "a vile thing <note>nevalah</note> is done in Israel." For who knows what reincarnation is within it? "Love your neighbor as yourself"—choose for him a beautiful death, which is slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies on its own, the power of impurity spreads and takes hold of it. But when one slaughters with a sharp blade and inspection, and there is in the domestic animal, wild beast, or bird a pure spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

**One who eats** a limb from a living animal is like one who eats human flesh when a reincarnated soul is present. This is the secret of: You shall not eat the soul with the flesh. Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure animals, beasts, and birds all indicate the spark spread within them—whether it is from the "Side of Impurity" or the "Side of Holiness." I have elaborated on this in the portion of Shemini. When Israel conducts themselves with holiness, it is written of them: And they shall make for Me a sanctuary and I will dwell within them. For they themselves are the Tabernacle, as they are "Man" divided into parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies, the heart to the Holy Place, and from the belly downward to the Courtyard of the Sanctuary, as I elaborated in the portion of Terumah. When one eats foods that are from the side of holiness, they are like sacrifices offered upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages said: Now, a man's table atones for him, as I have elaborated in its place.

**Regarding** the matter of the commandments of the Festivals and their sacrifices, I have written the meaning of each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals and to go up on the pilgrimage; three times a year all your males shall appear. One should not appear <note>to see</note> except in the way one comes to be seen. Therefore, if one wishes to be seen in the Holy Temple where the Glory dwells, he must turn from evil and do good, being a faithful servant to his Creator. For without this, it is forbidden to gaze upon a wicked man; how then could he wish to be seen before Him, may He be blessed? He brings a "Burnt Offering of Appearance," and then he himself becomes a sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. It says: Three times a year he shall appear. In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one may also see into every corner, with the open fields on both sides. And through the greater part of the houses run canals from the river bringing fresh water, providing great convenience and comfort to the citizens, who may thereby water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they keep beautiful and pleasant. Also,

And from this city, ships sometimes depart carrying goods worth 800,000 ducats, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which stands a crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their livestock, as well as their pigeon houses and their vineyards—though the grapes are not good due to the nature of the land—and beautiful gardens, not only full

Truly, to pass human life with joy, if it were not for the scandalous discord and war there, this place is surely one of the most beautiful in the entire world. For the landscape thereabouts is so temperate that throughout the whole year there is neither excessive heat nor terrible cold; also, it has never been seen that hunger or plague occurred there, nor any rain, thunder, or lightning from heaven

It was founded by the Admiral <term>Don Francisco Pizarro</term> in the year 1535 and is named the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Epiphany <note>Three Kings' Day</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and river, as well as the lasting fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. And during the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet it is not unhealthy like ours; for those who have pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase in people and wealth, although many years ago there were already over 500 houses

on the walls they make arbors of reeds where they shelter from the sun. They do not worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trujillo, Huanuco, Chachapoyas, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popayan, Catchi, St. Michael, and St. Francisco. It was mentioned before that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea, we have dealt until now, beginning from the <term>Linea</term> <gloss>Equator</gloss> and Cape Passao to this point. It should also be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima but much further south, the sea coast is very dry and full of large desolate sandy places, where for a distance of ten miles inland it neither thunders, lightens, nor rains; but beyond those ten miles it does, or as far as the mountains lie from the sea. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but rather four or five standing waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which originate from the snow and rain falling in the mountains, not from springs, which are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers have been partly described before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from one another, though mostly 7 or 8. Travelers regulate their journeys by this, because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, for a mile's breadth or even more, sometimes more, sometimes less depending on the layout of the land, there are various fruitful trees and cornfields which are moistened and sown by the people; which they may do throughout the entire year. Also, many kinds of wild trees grow near these rivers: cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and flags, etc. And since the Spaniards took the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through certain canals they lead out of these rivers. Because these rivers run swiftly down from high mountains, one can hardly cross them without help, and many have drowned therein. Those who travel along the flat land usually stay so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and rains heavily, it is dangerous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers one must cross, either with certain rafts they have for that purpose, or with a net filled tightly with gourds, upon which the traveler must lie outstretched, while one of the Indians swims ahead, pulling the net or raft forward with a rope, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of reeds. The men wear shirts and cloths to the knees, and over that an upper garment like a cloak. The women wear a garment of cotton according to the length of the body; and although the fashion of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nonetheless some distinction in the head-dress: some wear single bands, some braided, some of one color, others of various colors, and there is no one who does not wear a cap on the head, all distinguished according to the custom of the land.

containing all the mundane lives so that, after the sensible things, the harmony of the whole world might be joined together. And so that by this middle state, the things that already exist and the bodies containing certain cosmic elements might be shaped, though they are not able to do this by themselves. It is capable of all natural powers and every rational psychic art. Those things in their proper order persuade the mundane seats. For this reason, he did not say "the soul" <note>referring to the specific psychic substance</note> between the [intelligible] and perception. For he says that perceptions are not themselves certain cognitive powers. He grasped the perception of both the essence and of them, and it seems to me he handed it over to its own particular middle state. And because he says the same of the essence being generated and of the form.

Such an essence he presents; why did he not place it in the middle of the intelligible and sensible numbers? Because he wishes to follow his own harmony with [mathematical] ratios, according to which he holds the middle state. He will deem worthy both the middle numbers and the harmonies of the "tunic" <note>a metaphor for the soul's vehicle or outer layer</note> and the sensible numbers and their harmonies as underlying subjects. For the same harmony is not in souls as it is in mundane things, according to the breadth of the intellect. But since the sensible harmony is uniform, the soul also, having been raised up all at once just as the whole world, has been harmonized; and to it alone he says this, that the harmony is such as has been harmonized for them. It is excessive, and where it is naturally placed at the peak, it is always necessary for a middle to be in the harmony of the soul. For he calls that very thing "the harmonized." Wherefore they will also impart the harmony; for he imparts to it as much as it is able to receive. And he calls that "form." That which participates in it receives its lot. By those intelligible harmonies and numbers, it touches the bodies, and surpassing the sensible harmonies later, of which sensible numbers I also [speak] regarding each of the systems from each rank; for indeed there are actions of melody-making.

It is of an essential nature. Just as the soul is the last essence, yet being within, whence it is incapable because it is self-moving in the subject at hand, but the harmony again is not the forms. Further, he says that it is of such a kind. That which is in the soul is the last, but that which is in the world is as if in the breadth of the subject concerning which the soul is the harmony. From it, along with the indivisible and divisible numbers. And the forms are the essence among the wholes. Theology appointed this as sovereign; he says it attains it and there he contemplates that before the forms there is a turning in the intelligibles, the psychic progression, and it completes the principles of this form of the mixture and the melody, and the benefit of the extremes.

### DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you have praised unjustly,

In this manner, the eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth. For the fourth says that bases subtended by equal sides and angles are equal, while the eighth says that equal sides placed upon equal bases contain equal angles. In these, the statement regarding equal bases was the conclusion of the former theorem, while the statement regarding equal sides being placed was one of the hypotheses previously assumed in that theorem. Since there are two types of converses, the primary type is simple and definite, while the second type is varied and proceeds into a great number of theorems; it does not convert in a single instance but in many, due to the multitude of hypotheses in complex theorems. Often, we also convert one conclusion from two <insert>or more</insert> hypotheses, whenever the hypotheses are not all definite but some are of an indefinite nature.

It is necessary to observe in these matters that many converses turn out to be false and are not strictly converses. For example: every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangular number is a hexagonal number. The reason is that one is more general, while the other is more specific <note>The text breaks off here, likely continuing with the explanation that the more specific property does not necessarily imply the more general one in reverse.</note>

He says, "We do not see the things beyond through the stars, but we transmit our sight through the comets." First, if that happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself is made of thick and solid fire, but where the thin splendor runs out and is dispersed into the hair <note>original: "crines", referring to the comet's tail</note>. Through the intervals of the fire, it appears that they are not stars. For who will grant you that comets are long, when their nature is indeed a globe like the others? However, the brightness is extended just as the sun sends its rays far and wide. Yet the form of the sun itself is one thing, and the form of the light flowing from it is another. Thus the body of the comets itself is rounded, but their splendor appears longer than that of the other stars.

"Why?" you ask. Tell me first, why does the moon receive a light so unlike the sun, since it receives it from the sun? Why is it sometimes red, sometimes pale? Why does it have a livid and black color when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have faces somewhat unlike each other, and most different from the sun. Just as nothing prevents them from being stars even though they are not similar, so nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same condition as the rest, even if they do not have a similar face.

Furthermore, if you consider the world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in Leo and parches the lands with heat, but in Aquarius it binds the winter and closes the rivers with frost? Yet both this star and that are of the same condition, though they are dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time Aries <margin>rises</margin> is completed, while Libra sinks most slowly; and yet this star and that are of the same nature, though the former ascends in a brief time and the latter is brought forth for a long duration. Do you not see how contrary the elements are among themselves? There are heavy and light things, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire harmony of this world consists of discord <note>original: "concordia ex discordia", the concept of harmony arising from opposing forces</note>.

You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it like the others. For you see, that star which returns to its place in the thirtieth year <note>the planet Saturn</note> is very similar to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not perform her work according to a single form, but boasts in variety itself. She made some things more sluggish, others swifter than the rest. Some she made stronger, others more temperate; some she led out from the crowd so they might proceed as individual and conspicuous things, while some she sent into a flock. He is ignorant of nature's power who does not think she is permitted at any time to do anything except what she does frequently.

She does not show comets often; she assigned them another place, other times, and motions unlike the rest. She wished to honor the greatness of her work through these things, whose appearance is too beautiful for you to think them accidental, whether you consider their magnitude or their brightness, which is greater and more burning than the others. Indeed, their appearance has something remarkable and singular, not cast into a narrow space and cramped, but let down more freely and embracing the region of many stars.

Aristotle says that comets signify storms and the intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge that to be a star which announces future events? For this is not a sign of a storm in the same way that oil sparking and rotting fungi forming are signs of future rain; or in the way it is an indication of a raging sea if the gulls <note>original: "Fulicae", likely referring to coots or sea-birds</note> play on dry land, and the well-known marshes are deserted, and they fly above the high cloud. But it is a sign in the way the equinox marks the year turning toward heat or cold; or in the way those things which the Chaldeans <gloss>astrologers</gloss> chant, regarding what a star determines as sad or joyful for those being born.

So that you may know this is so: the rising of a comet does not immediately threaten winds and rains, as Aristotle says, but <margin>The rising of a comet makes the whole year suspect.</margin> it makes the entire year suspect. From this it appears that it has not drawn signs from the immediate vicinity to give for the immediate future, but has them stored up and compressed by the laws of the world. That comet which appeared in the consulship of Paterculus and Vopiscus <note>60 AD</note> brought about those things which were predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. For there were very great and continuous storms everywhere; and in Achaea and Macedonia, cities were overthrown by earthquakes.

# Zechariah

And the angel answered and said to me: These are the four winds of heaven, going out from standing before the Lord of all the earth. The one with the black horses goes out to the north country, and the white ones go out after them, and the spotted ones go out to the south country. And the strong ones went out and sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth; and he said: Go, walk to and fro through the earth. So they walked to and fro through the earth. Then he cried out to me and spoke to me, saying: Behold, these that go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country.

**And he answered.** These are the four winds. This is like "all my winds." Similarly, "and he came Jerusalem" <note>original: "ויבא ירושלם"</note> is like "to Jerusalem."
**The black ones.** All these four chariots go out as the four winds of heaven. That is to say, to give authority to the four kingdoms to rule in the four directions, each one in its time, over the entire world.
**From standing before the Lord of all the earth.** All of them act on the mission of God, who rules over this. It is as it says: "And the sons of God came to stand before the Lord" <margin>Job 2</margin>.
**Which in it.** The black ones. He mentions the black ones even though the kingdom of Babylon had already passed. The kingdom of Media and Persia went out first to the north country, for they were in Assyria and ruled over a portion of all the kingdoms of the earth.
**And the white ones.** These were the kingdom of Greece <note>original: "Yavan"</note>. They went out after them, for the kingdom was broken. For Alexander of Macedon, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him, and he ruled over the whole world.
**And the spotted ones.** They went out to the south country. These were the holy portion <note>referring to the Roman Empire</note> because Rome is southern. Julius Caesar, who ruled over Rome, began to fight the kingdom of Greece. At the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is in the south. In all the provinces where the Greeks ruled, Julius Caesar prevailed over them. He transferred the kingdom from the Greeks and returned it to the Romans.
**And the strong ones.** These are a hint to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>the Islamic Caliphate</note>, who exerted themselves on their own to seek a kingdom, so that there would be a place belonging to them. This is why it says: "And they sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth."
**And he said.** That is to say, He gave them permission to walk and to conquer lands.
**And he cried out.** That is to say, he called to me with a loud voice and said to me: "Behold, those going out to the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country." This refers to the portion of the black horses that went out to Babylon to destroy them.

Thinking he ought to do such things, and providing intensity in what is right <unclear>...</unclear> for he cast into the fire the dishonor of himself and his allies, and having acted unsparingly through his positions before he was softened, and toward a certain ruler <unclear>...</unclear> brings him wealth. Nicias, if he does not suffer injustice, neither does he do injustice <unclear>...</unclear> but entirely through fear. But Phocion did not even help his son-in-law Charicles when he was on trial regarding the money brought from <term>Harpalus</term> <gloss>the treasurer of Alexander the Great</gloss>, but saying, "I made you my son-in-law for all just things," he went away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not dissuade his brother from tyranny by entreaty, cooperated with those who killed him. For a friend should be a friend "only as far as the altar" <note>meaning as far as does not require breaking an oath to the gods</note>, as Pericles once said, but rather as far as every law and justice and the common good. If this is overlooked, it leads to great harm for the public, as was shown by the failure to punish Sphodrias or Phoebidas, for these men especially drew the city of the Lacedaemonians into war. Since the political reason does not compel one to be harsh toward the moderate failings of friends, but even to place them in safety, one should grant friends the greatest of public benefits from the surplus, and stand by them and labor with them. There are also favors that are not envied, such as helping a friend toward an office, or rather entrusting him with some administration, a glorious embassy, or a mission of goodwill, such as one carrying the honors of a leader, or to a city for the sake of increasing friendship and concord. For this is the object of hope, and their great deed is manifest when arranged thus, so as to send a friend on an embassy as Diomedes did: "If indeed you bid me choose a companion for myself, how then could I forget godlike Odysseus?" And again, this is better than praising one's own citizens: "The horses are old <unclear>...</unclear> which you will lean upon, Thracian indeed <unclear>...</unclear> noble Diomedes killed all fourteen of the best among the companions." For this

<column-break/>

<margin>To the base.</margin>
yielding to friends is observed no less in those who praise than in those who are praised. But "obstinacy," as Plato says, "is the companion of solitude." Furthermore, in using noble kindness, one should contribute through friends, not by commanding those who have received benefits to praise or love them as having been the cause and counsel, but in the case of base and absurd requests, one should lead them away, not bitterly, but teaching and comforting them gently, showing that such things are not worthy of their virtue or reputation. Epaminondas was the best of them; when he went to Pelopidas to ask for the release of a prisoner from the beginning, and not long after <unclear>...</unclear> he said, "O Pelopidas, such services are fitting for porters." But the general <unclear>...</unclear> and the heavy or the obstinate, since he was not like the censor, being a friend in the highest degree, or the familiar who seeks to humble those who are <unclear>...</unclear> by him, said, "It is shameful that you, who ought to make us young men temperate, are being cast out by our servants." In anger that pours out insolence <unclear>...</unclear> one should remove brevity and bitterness from the speech, as if bringing the pain of the action not willingly but by necessity because of the law and justice. There are also agreements in the state for the making of money that are not ignoble for friends in need, such as Themistocles, who after the battle saw a corpse cast aside wearing gold and a necklace; he himself passed by, but turning to one of his friends, said, "Take these for yourself, for you have not become Themistocles." For the affairs of the political man are often like stones and fire toward friends, and one should not <unclear>...</unclear> they are for everything, to one he will entrust help for the sake of justice, to another a careful recommendation and protection when needed, to another cooperation in some contract, or a share of profit. When Epaminondas was approached by one of his

<margin>Commanding.</margin>
friends, he ordered him to ask for a talent, as if his servant had commanded it. When the man who was asked came and inquired the reason, he said, "Because you are a good man, he is poor; and you are rich, having embezzled much from the city." And Xenophon says that he prided himself on making his friends wealthy with things better than money. Since in all peaks one must be a <unclear>...</unclear> for misfortunes, and every state produces certain enmities and differences, it especially belongs to the political man to moderate these. Most people praise Themistocles and Aristides because they laid aside their enmity whenever they went out on an embassy or a military command, and then took it up again. But the conduct of Cretinus the Magnesian is exceedingly pleasing; who, though a political rival of Hermias, a man not brilliant but ambitious and of a noble soul, when he saw the city in danger from a war that had been engineered, he urged Hermias to take the command and manage affairs while he himself withdrew. Or if Hermias wished him to be general, he himself would go out of the way, so that by competing against each other, they might not destroy the city. The challenge pleased Hermias, and since his nature was more warlike, Cretinus withdrew with his children and wife. Hermias escorted him and gave him honors from his own money, so that they might use the resources in the besieged city, and the city was unexpectedly saved by the generalship of the man who remained. For if noble and prudent men say, "I love my children, but I love my country more," why should it not be more ready for them to say, "I hate so-and-so, but I love my country more"? For to be unwilling to be reconciled with an enemy for the sake of which one loves a friend is terribly savage and bestial. My other...

<summary>Plutarch discusses the ethics of friendship in political life, emphasizing that a statesman must choose capable allies and balance personal loyalty with justice and the public good. He uses historical examples like Solon, Phocion, and Epaminondas to show that true friendship should never supersede the law or the safety of the state.</summary>

# Tractate Parah <note>The Red Heifer</note>

### Chapter 1
**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A heifer <term>eglah</term> is one year old, and a cow <term>parah</term> is two years old. But the Sages say: A heifer is two years old, and a cow is three or four years old. Rabbi Meir says: Even a five-year-old is valid, though they do not wait for it to get old lest it grow black hairs and become disqualified. Rabbi Joshua said: I have only heard the term "tripled" <term>shlishit</term>. They said to him: What does the term "tripled" mean? He said to them: I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it; if you say "third" <note>shlishit</note> it refers to its place in a sequence, but when you say "tripled" <note>meshuleshet</note> it means three years old. Similarly, they spoke of a "fourth-year" vineyard <unclear>etc.</unclear>

<column-break/>

<gloss>Fourth-year: They said to him, what does the term "fourth-year" mean? He said to them: Thus I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it; if you say "fourth" it refers to its place in a sequence, but when you say "fourth-year" <term>revai</term> it means four years old. Similarly, they spoke of one who eats in a house afflicted with leprosy: a <term>peras</term> <gloss>half-loaf</gloss> of three to a <term>kav</term>. They said to him: Say "eighteen to an ephah." He said to them: I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it; if you say "three to a kav" it does not include the dough-offering <term>challah</term>, but when you say "eighteen to an ephah," the dough-offering reduces its size.</gloss> **2** Rabbi Yose the Galilean says: Bulls are two years old, as it is said: "And a second bull, a young of the herd, you shall take for a sin offering." But the Sages say: Even three years old. Rabbi Meir says: Even four or five years old are valid, but they do not bring old ones out of respect <note>for the altar</note>. **3** Lambs are one year old, and rams are two years old; all are measured from day to day <note>from birth</note>. One that is thirteen months old is not valid as a ram nor as a lamb. Rabbi Tarfon calls it a <term>palgas</term> <gloss>half-breed/middle-aged</gloss>. Ben Azzai calls it a <term>noked</term>. Rabbi Ishmael calls it <term>perach-degma</term>. If he sacrificed it, he must bring the drink-offerings of a ram, but it does not count toward his obligation. If it is thirteen months and one day old, it is a ram. **4** Communal sin offerings and burnt offerings, the individual's sin offering, the Nazirite's guilt offering, and the leper's guilt offering are valid from the thirtieth day onward, and even on the thirtieth day itself. If sacrificed on the eighth day, they are valid. Voluntary offerings, vows, the firstborn, the tithe, and the Passover offering are valid from the eighth day onward, and even on the eighth day itself.

### Chapter 2
**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A Red Heifer that is pregnant is valid, but the Sages disqualify it. Rabbi Eliezer says: It may not be purchased from Gentiles, but the Sages permit it. Not only this, but all communal and individual sacrifices may come from the Land of Israel or from outside the Land, from the new crop or the old, except for the <term>Omer</term> <gloss>barley offering</gloss> and the Two Loaves, which must come only from the new crop and from the Land of Israel. **2** <gloss>Chapter 2: One may trim—meaning cut like shearing—a heifer whose horns and hooves are black. The eye, teeth, and tongue do not disqualify the heifer by their size. A dwarf heifer is valid. Rabbi Yohanan says: If it has a hump, it is disqualified. Rabbi Simeon says: Any place where a hair is pulled and does not grow back a red hair, it is disqualified.</gloss> **3** A heifer born by Caesarean section, or given as a harlot's hire, or the price of a dog, is disqualified. Rabbi Eliezer permits it, as it is said: "You shall not bring the hire of a harlot... into the house of the Lord your God," and this heifer does not enter the House <note>it is slaughtered on the Mount of Olives</note>. All blemishes that disqualify consecrated animals also disqualify the heifer. If one rode upon it, leaned on it, hung from its tail, crossed a river with it, folded its lead-rope over it, or placed a cloak upon it, it is disqualified. But if he tied it with a lead-rope, or made it a sandal so it would not slip, or spread a cloak over it because of flies, it is valid. This is the rule: anything done for its own needs, it remains valid; for the needs of another, it is disqualified. **4** If a bird rested upon it, it is valid. If a male mounted it, it is disqualified. Rabbi Judah says: If the person brought the male up, it is disqualified; if it happened on its own, it is valid. **5** If it had two black hairs...

Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, the youthful prince, spoke to the Blessed One: "Lord, it is difficult, extremely difficult, what these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings seeking enlightenment</gloss> and <term>Mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> have undertaken out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, Lord, should this <term>Dharma-paryaya</term> <gloss>religious discourse or method of the law</gloss> be proclaimed by these great beings in the later times, in the final age?"

When he had spoken, the Blessed One said to the youthful <term>Manjushri</term>: "A <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> who is established in four qualities should proclaim this discourse in the later times and the final age. Which four? Here, <term>Manjushri</term>, a great being established in proper conduct and proper sphere of activity <note>original: "achara-gochara"</note> should proclaim this discourse in the later times.

And how, <term>Manjushri</term>, is a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> established in proper conduct and sphere of activity? When a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> is patient, gentle, has reached the stage of self-control, is not terrified or easily frightened in mind, and is not envious. When a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> does not dwell upon any phenomena <note>original: "dharma"</note> but observes the true nature of things as they really are. That which is non-apprehension and non-conceptualization regarding these phenomena is called the proper conduct <note>original: "achara"</note> of a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term>.

They represent three water jars, or heaven and earth gushing forth water, by likening the water jar to a heart possessing a tongue. They use a heart because, among them, this is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. They use a tongue because it always exists in moisture, and they call it the producer of existence. They use three water jars, neither more nor less, because the process of the rising <note>the annual flooding of the Nile</note> is threefold according to them. They assign one for the land of Egypt, because Egypt is productive of water by itself. They assign another for the ocean, for water comes from it into Egypt at the time of the rising. They assign the third for the rains, which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia at the time of the rising of the Nile. That Egypt produces the water itself can be learned from this: in the rest of the regions of the world, the floods of the rivers are completed in the winter <note>the catchword indicates the sentence continues on the next page</note>

Other substances should not be mixed with it. One who has undergone evacuation <note>original: <term>istifragh</term></note> must not rush to consume large amounts of food or fatty substances, lest the <term>nature</term> <gloss>the body's innate healing intelligence</gloss> attract them while they are undigested. If such food is necessary, it must be taken little by little, step by step, so that it is introduced gradually and the substances entering the body are well-digested. The goal is a balanced and specific evacuation. As for an evacuation that targets a specific humor <note>original: <term>khilt</term></note> in excess or solely in its quality, that is not the primary goal. Every excessive evacuation usually causes a fever. 

If the cessation of a habitual bowel movement causes an illness, then resuming that evacuation usually cures it. For example, if the cessation of a nosebleed, ear discharge, or nasal mucus causes blockages, then their return removes the ailment. Know that the consequences of leaving a remnant of the matter that needs evacuation are less dangerous than being excessive in evacuation to the point that the patient's strength fails. Often, <term>nature</term> dissolves that remnant on its own. As long as the humor is of the type that should be expelled and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to evacuate until fainting occurs. 

For those with strong physical power but whose humors are many and corrupt, evacuate them little by little. Do the same if the matter is highly matured <note>original: <term>nadj</term></note> or heavily mixed with the blood, such that it cannot be evacuated all at once, as is the case in sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that diarrhea <note>original: <term>ishal</term></note> draws from above and uproots from below; it is suitable for drawing from both the opposite and the same direction, and it is also suitable after the matters have settled. If the matters are below, it draws them in the opposite direction and uproots them from where they are. Vomiting <note>original: <term>qay</term></note> performs drawing and uprooting in the reverse manner. Bloodletting <note>original: <term>fasd</term></note> varies in its effect according to the sites from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who least need evacuation are those who have a good diet and good digestion. Residents of hot countries also have little need for evacuation.

### Chapter Four: On the Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and an Indication of How Purgative and Emetic Medicines Draw Humors

We say: it is recommended for whoever wishes to take a purgative or an emetic to divide their food, consuming the daily amount in several portions. They should vary the types of food and drink. In such cases, the stomach may feel an urge to push its contents upward or downward. However, when uniform food is eaten on top of other food, the stomach becomes stingy with it, holds onto it, and grips it tightly, especially if the quantity is small. For those with naturally loose bowels, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not occur in those who follow a good regimen <note>original: <term>tadbir</term></note>, unless they require something more serious. Often, exercise, massage, and the bath are sufficient for digestion. If the body becomes full, and most of that fullness is of the best of humors—namely blood—then bloodletting is what is needed for purification, rather than purging. If necessity dictates both bloodletting and evacuation with something like hellebore <note>original: <term>khurbaq</term></note> or strong medicines, one must begin with bloodletting. This is among the recommendations of Hippocrates <note>original: <term>Abiqrat</term></note> in the Book of Epidemics <note>original: <term>Abidhimya</term></note>, and it is the truth. 

Similarly, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood, bloodletting might increase their thickness and viscosity if the humors are viscid and cold. In that case, one should begin with purging. In general, if the humors are equal, perform bloodletting first, then follow with evacuation if needed. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are balanced, then perform bloodletting. Whoever gives medicine before bloodletting when bloodletting should have come first has committed an error. 

If someone has recently undergone bloodletting and needs evacuation, taking medicine may cause it to stop. Often, taking medicine when bloodletting was required leads to fainting and agitation. If it does not settle with sedatives, know that bloodletting should have preceded it. You should not perform an evacuation required by extreme fullness gently when the severity of the illness demands otherwise; fullness is judged by quality, not just quantity. Often, improving the regimen suffices instead of the bloodletting required at the time. 

Sometimes a cause calls for evacuation, but an obstacle arises; in such a case, the only remedy is fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance <note>original: <term>su' mizaj</term></note> caused by the fullness. Some evacuations are precautionary, such as those needed by people accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at specific times, especially in spring. They need to take precautions before the time comes and undergo the evacuation specific to their disease, whether it be bloodletting or purging. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done for those with dropsy <note>original: <term>istisqa</term></note>. 

You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor to be evacuated in quality, such as scammony <note>original: <term>saqmunya</term></note> when you need to evacuate yellow bile <note>original: <term>safra</term></note>. In that case, it must be mixed with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as myrobalan <note>original: <term>halilaj</term></note>, to correct any imbalance that might occur afterward in those with internal organ inflammations, which weakens their purging and vomiting. If forced to do so, use things like bindweed <note>original: <term>lablab</term></note> and safflower <note>original: <term>qartam</term></note>. As for polypody <note>original: <term>basbayij</term></note> and cassia fistula <note>original: <term>khiyar shanbar</term></note> and the like, Hippocrates said: "He whose constitution easily responds to vomiting, it is better to purify him using vomiting in summer, spring, or autumn, but not winter." 

For those with a moderate complexion, purging is better. If a reason calls for evacuation by vomiting, let him wait for summer and avoid it when not necessary. Before purging or vomiting, one must first thin the humor intended for evacuation and widen and open the channels; this protects the body from exhaustion. Know that habituating the nature to milk and responding easily to the desired purging or vomiting before using strong medicine is a beneficial procedure. 

Purging and vomiting during extreme emaciation is difficult, exhausting, and dangerous. An emetic medicine may turn into a purgative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk during intense hunger, if the drinker has a sensitive stomach or naturally loose bowels, if they are unaccustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is heavy in substance and quick to descend. Conversely, a purgative becomes an emetic due to stomach weakness, extreme dryness of the stool, the medicine being repulsive, or the person having indigestion. 

Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge or purges before the humor is mature, stirs up the humor it was meant to evacuate and spreads it through the body. It then overcomes the body and other humors transform into it, increasing that humor in the body. Some humors respond more quickly to vomiting, such as yellow bile. Others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile <note>original: <term>sawda</term></note>. Some vary, like phlegm <note>original: <term>balgham</term></note>. For a person with a fever, purging is more appropriate. For those whose humor is descending, such as those with chronic diarrhea <note>original: <term>zalaq al-am'a</term></note>, making them vomit is impossible. 

The worst purgative medicines are those composed of drugs that vary greatly in their time of action, which causes agitation in the bowels; the first may purge the second before the second has acted, or the first may purge the second itself. Now Radha, distressed by separation, speaks regarding the moon: **In separation.** <term>Aye</term> is a tender address. O friend, this moon <note>literally: the "disturbed one" or "the moon"</note> extends great love-agony in my heart. Of what kind is it? It is the friend of the Mind-born One <note>Kamadeva</note>. She speaks by remembering the state of Murari in separation. Of what kind is the moon? Its luster is like the luster of the lotus-face of Murari, which is pale due to separation. Therefore, even while concealing the pain, it acts this way. The meaning is this: Previously, by having the beauty of Murari's face pale from separation from me, it destroyed my pain; but now, being the friend of Love, it certainly causes pain. Because of not attaining him, and because he was once waiting for her, there was no sorrow; but now, knowing him to be attached to another, I am unable to remain.

<note>Commentary from the Rasamanjari:</note>
<term>Hamsalilakah</term> <gloss>The play of the swan</gloss>. The <term>Amarakosha</term> defines <term>lava</term>, <term>lesha</term>, and <term>kana</term> as small fragments. **Spoken by Sri Jayadeva.** May the pleasure-play of Hari <note>Krishna</note> spoken by Sri Jayadeva destroy the sins of the Kali age for the listeners and readers. Now she says that even this moon causes excessive pain: **In separation.** <term>Aye</term> expresses dejection. This visible moon expands the pain of love in my heart to an even greater degree. Of what kind is it? It has the luster of the lotus-face of Murari, which is pale and greyish due to separation from me. The idea is that by seeing the moon which resembles Krishna's lotus-face, the memory of Krishna's face arises, causing extreme agony. What does it do? It even conceals the pain. By seeing the moon, one's discrimination is uprooted, and the mind remembers only Krishna, even though he has committed an offense. He gives the reason for it being a cause of agony: **Of the Mind-born.** It is the friend of the Mind-born One <note>Kamadeva</note>. Since I did not follow Krishna even when he was near, I have transgressed the command of Love, and Love has become my enemy. The moon, wishing to help its friend, also causes pain. This is because the moon is born from the mind of Krishna, and Love is famously "mind-born." Because they are both born of the mind, they are like brothers and have friendship. Thus the term "Mind-born" is used for Kamadeva. As the <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>Scripture</gloss> says: The moon was born from his mind, and the sun was born from his eyes. # Kalila and Dimna

When the lion woke the next morning, the judge and a group of his prominent companions entered his presence with a written record of what Dimna had said in his defense <note>original: "mu'adhirihi," meaning his excuses or justifications</note>. The lion took the document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read that document to her. It distressed her, and she said: "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The lion said: "I shall not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not see you recognizing what harms you from what benefits you. I truly believe that by prolonging your consideration of Dimna's case, he will stir up against you a trouble that you will be unable to withstand, whether sitting or standing."

Then she stood up and left in anger. When the next day came, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the learned men <term>ulama</term> <gloss>scholars or men of knowledge</gloss> regarding him, but they said nothing.

The judge said to him: "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have united in the belief that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after this accusation has taken root in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt. By doing so, you may be freed from the consequences of the afterlife, and a good reputation may return to you for two reasons: first, your ability to find ways out and fabricate excuses to defend yourself; and second, your voluntary confession of your sin, choosing safety in the hereafter over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: Death in what is honorable is better than life in what is shameful."

Dimna answered him, saying: "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have learned that suspicion is no substitute for the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself better than you do, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty beyond doubt. My situation has only become ugly in your souls because you have suspected that I acted as a slanderer."

A man who has just taken a wife stays outside the court and is no longer sent on official duties. When the King had finished the delicious foods, he set the wine flowing and prepared a banquet of joy.

The host replied, "May the King live forever; may the <term>Kawsar</term> <gloss>a river in Paradise</gloss> be his wine and the <term>Houri</term> <gloss>celestial maiden</gloss> his cupbearer.
This is no wonder coming from me, for I am a man; how could I grow weary of such steps?
The wonder is that there is a girl, beautiful as the moon, soft and delicate as the King's silk and ermine.
She takes a bull, massive as a mountain, upon her neck when it is time for it to eat its fodder.
She carries it up the sixty steps in one go, without stopping to rest on any step.
A bull, and what a bull! It is like an elephant; a single hair of it weighs more than a mountain.
By God, if anyone in this land could even lift it for a single breath from the ground, it would be a feat.
That a woman should carry it up a sixty-step fortress—how could this not be a marvel?"
When the host told this story to the King, the King pressed his fingertip beneath his teeth in amazement.
He said, "How can a deed of this kind be possible? It is not real, or if it is, it must be sorcery.
I will not truly believe this word until I first see it with my own eyes."
Then he requested of the host to prove the truth of his claim.
When the host heard this, he went down and told the story of the Lion <note>referring to the King</note> to the bull-carrier.

# The Latter Cloud <note>original: "Uttara-megha"</note>

of women <note>original: "sīmantinīnām"</note>, of wives. The lexicon of Amara states: "A woman is called a <term>sīmantinī</term> <gloss>one with a parted hair-line</gloss> or a <term>vadhū</term> <gloss>bride/wife</gloss>." **Brought by a friend** <note>original: "suhṛdupanataḥ"</note> means having arrived through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is used to remove any suspicion of a deceptive separation. The news of the beloved <note>original: "kāntodantaḥ"</note> is the tidings of the lover. Amara states: "News, report, account, and tidings <note>original: "udanta"</note> are synonyms." This news is only slightly less than an actual meeting <note>original: "saṃgamāt kiṃcidūnaḥ"</note>, meaning it brings almost as much joy as the physical contact of the beloved.

Now he delivers the message:

->O Long-lived One, speak thus to her both in my name and to do a favor to yourself:<-
->Your companion, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri,<-
->being alive, asks after your welfare, O frail one, in this separation;<-
->for this is the first thing to be said to living beings whose misfortunes are easily met. (41)<-

Regarding the verse beginning with "Her" <note>original: "tām"</note>: O Long-lived One <note>original: "āyuṣman"</note>. The suffix <term>matup</term> is used here as praise. It means one whose life is praiseworthy because of helping others. **From my word** <note>original: "vachanāt"</note> means from my request, and also for the sake of doing a favor to yourself <note>original: "ātmanaśca upakartum"</note>. This means to make yourself successful through the act of helping others. Although "self" is the object of the action of helping, the use of the genitive case <note>original: "ātmanaḥ"</note> is not incorrect when only a general relationship is intended. As Bharavi says: "She assists <note>original: "upakurute"</note> the fortune by which others are helped." Likewise, Shriharsha says: "To help the virtuous, to see fortune, to travel through the sky." Therefore, the statement of Natha <note>original: "nāthavacana"</note> that the second case <note>original: "dvitīyā"</note> should be used everywhere because it is seen in some places is a statement without authority <note>original: "anāthavacana"</note>.

Speak thus to that beloved. What should be said? He says: O frail one <note>original: "abale"</note>, your companion and husband, staying in the hermitages of Ramagiri <note>original: "rāmagiryāśramasthaḥ"</note>—which refers to Chitrakuta. He is not dead <note>original: "avyāpannaḥ"</note>. He gives the reason for his survival: though suffering in separation <note>original: "viyuktaḥ"</note>, he asks after your welfare <note>original: "kuśalaṃ pṛcchati"</note>. The verb "to ask" <note>original: "pṛcch"</note> takes two objects. For this indeed is the first thing to be said <note>original: "pūrvābhāṣyam"</note>, the first thing that must necessarily be asked of living beings whose misfortunes occur without effort <note>original: "sulabhavipadām"</note>. The suffix <term>ṇyat</term> is used here in the sense of necessity.

->With his limbs he joins your limbs: the thin with the very thin, the heated with the scorched,<-
->the tear-filled with those flowing with tears, the constantly longing with the yearning...<-

### In the Srimad Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda

The bears, lions, boars, buffaloes, elephants, and deer, terrified by that sound, fled in fear in all ten directions. There stood a tall peak of Mount Trikuta <gloss>the three-peaked mountain</gloss> that seemed to touch the sky. It was entirely covered in flowers and shone like great silver. It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> <gloss>a measurement of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles</gloss> in width, pure and beautiful to behold. It was smooth, majestic, and vast, difficult even for birds to reach. It was impossible to ascend even in thought, let alone by the actions of men. Situated on that peak was the city of Lanka, protected by Ravana. It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> wide and thirty <term>yojanas</term> long. That city was adorned with high gate-towers that resembled white clouds. It was beautified by a golden wall and silver ramparts, and Lanka was further decorated with palaces and celestial chariots <note>original: "vimanas"</note>. It looked like the middle path of Vishnu <gloss>the sky</gloss> when clouds depart at the end of the rainy season. In that city, a palace adorned with a thousand pillars, shaped like a peak of Mount Kailasa and appearing to scrape the sky, served as the ornament of the city for the King of the Rakshasas <gloss>demons</gloss>. It was constantly guarded by a full hundred of the Rakshasas. Rama, the fortunate elder brother of Lakshmana, together with the monkeys, beheld that prosperous city of Ravana, filled with forests, graced by mountains of various colorful minerals, adorned with gardens, echoing with the cries of various birds, inhabited by various animals, covered in diverse flowers, and populated by various Rakshasas. Seeing that city crowded with great houses, resembling the city of the immortals, the heroic elder brother of Lakshmana was filled with wonder.

Then Rama, accompanied by Sugriva and surrounded by the leaders of the monkey troops, ascended the summit of Mount Suvela, which spanned a circumference of two <term>yojanas</term>. On the top of a gate-tower in that city, he saw the difficult-to-approach King of the Rakshasas. He was flanked by white fly-whisks and graced by the umbrella of victory. ### The Maqama of the Nahida

Isa ibn Hisham told us, saying:

I turned with a group of my companions to the courtyard of a tent to seek hospitality from its people. A short, stout man came out to us and said: "Who are you?" We said: "Guests who have not tasted a morsel for three days." He cleared his throat and then said: "What is your opinion, O young men, of a <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of butter and dried curd</gloss> as large as the head of a bald man, in a wide bowl, crowned with choice pressed dates from the clusters of a great palm tree, a single one of which fills the mouth? It is from a group of camels that have gone five days without water, in which the tooth disappears, as if their pits were the tongues of birds. They scoop the <term>nahida</term> with bowls of milk drawn from old, sturdy, well-fleshed camels. Do you desire it, O young men?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" The old man chuckled and said: "And your uncle <note>Referring to himself</note> also desires it!"

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O young men, of fine white bread like pieces of ingots, carved upon a silken table-cloth smelling of mimosa? A brisk, elegant, and light youth among you springs to it, kneading it without shaking it or making it dry, smoothing it without a soft touch. Then he mixes it thoroughly with diluted milk or water, then turns it and leaves it in a corner of the stony ground until it settles without being meager. Then he goes to the wood of the <term>ghada</term> tree and sets fire to it. When its fire dies down, he prepares its pit, then takes his dough and flattens it after having smeared it well. Then he tosses it upon the embers and covers it. When it has risen and rounded, he heaps upon it heated stones until the two heats meet. When he covers them on the matching embers with a lid, and it cracks open with fissures, its crust resembling thin bread, and its redness like the redness of the Hijazi dates known as 'Mother of Rats' or 'Ibn Tab's Cluster,' he pours over it white honey like snow until it sinks into the crevices of the fat. The heart of the fine bread drinks what is upon it of honey. I present it to you and you swallow it like the morsels of Juwayn or Zankal. Do you desire it, O young men?"

He said: Each of us craned our necks at his description, our mouths watered, and we smacked our lips. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" He said: The old man chuckled and said: "And your uncle, by God, does not hate it!" Then he said: "What is your opinion, O young men, of a young she-goat from Nejd, high-bred and wild, that has eaten the mimosa blossoms, the Nejdi wormwood, the yarrow, and the dry herbage? She has sipped the spring water and filled herself with truffles until her marrow is rich and her fat is thick. She is slaughtered fresh and then inverted in an oven until she is cooked without being scorched or underdone. Then she is presented to you, her skin stripped away from white fat, on a table arranged with thin cakes like spread fine linen or dyed cloth. She is surrounded by small bowls containing mustard sauce and various dips. She is placed between you, dripping with fat and flowing with gravy. Do you desire it, O young men?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" He said: "And your uncle, by God, dances for it!" Then one of us leaped at him with a sword and said: "What..."
