If a man leaves two sisters and a wife, and bequeaths to a man as much as the share of a sister less one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy: the calculation for this is that you establish the legal shares <note>original: al-faridah</note> out of twelve shares. Each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals the share of a sister. Thus, one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy, plus the legacy, equals the share of a sister. This is one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The whole estate equals three-eighths of the estate and three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the whole estate, and there remains five-eighths of the estate equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The whole estate then equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. The estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the share is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons. He bequeaths to one man as much as the share of one of his sons, and to another man one-fourth of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is only taken from the third.

Its Sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>original: "Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman"</note>. This city previously belonged to his brother Musa, who ceded it to King al-Nasir <note>the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent an emir and an army there, but Sultan Badr al-Din later seized control of it, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this Sultan outside the city as he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my animal for him, so he dismounted from his animal and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands <note>Anatolia</note> that if a traveler dismounts for them, they dismount for him; they admire this gesture and increase their hospitality toward him. However, if a traveler greets them while remaining mounted, they take offense, and it becomes a reason for the traveler to be denied favor. This happened to me with one of them, which I shall mention later. When I had greeted him and we both remounted, he asked about my circumstances and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered excellent accommodations for me. He used to send abundant food, fruit, and sweets on silver trays, along with candles. He also gave me clothing and a horse, treating me with great kindness. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray <note>original: "Aqsara"</note>.

Aksaray is among the most beautiful and well-constructed cities of the land of the <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia/the Eastern Romans</gloss>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and gardens on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through the houses. It contains many trees and grapevines, with numerous gardens inside the city itself. The famous carpets named after this city are manufactured there from sheep's wool; they have no equal in any other land. From here, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq <note>the Ilkhanid Mongol ruler</note>. We stayed there at the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>hospice or lodge</gloss> of Sharif Husayn, who is the deputy there for Emir Artau Arta. This Emir is the representative of the King of Iraq over the conquered territories of the land of the <term>Rum</term>. This Sharif is one of the <term>fityan</term> <gloss>members of the youth brotherhoods or Akhi organizations</gloss> and has a large following. He showed us ultimate hospitality and acted even more generously than those before him.

Then we traveled to the city of Nigde <note>original: "Nakda"</note>. It is part of the lands of the King of Iraq. It is a large, heavily populated city, though some parts of it are in ruins. It is bisected by the river known as the Black River, which is one of the great rivers. It has three bridges, one inside the city and two outside. # The Superintendent of Courtesans

A courtesan who refuses to go to a man at the command of the King shall receive one thousand lashes with a whip <note>original: "śiphāsahasraṃ"</note>, or pay a fine of five thousand <term>panas</term> <gloss>the standard silver coin of the period</gloss>.

If a courtesan accepts payment <term>bhoga</term> <gloss>enjoyment fee or earnings</gloss> but then shows hatred or refuses the client, she shall be fined double the amount of the payment.

If a client stays at her house but withholds the payment, he shall pay eight times the amount as a fine, unless there was a valid reason such as the client having a disease or some other personal defect <margin>original variant: "puruṣabhyaḥ" referring to defects in the men</margin>.

A courtesan who kills a man shall be burnt alive on a funeral pyre or drowned in water.

Anyone who steals the jewelry or the earnings of a courtesan shall be fined eight times the value of the stolen goods <margin>original variant: "bharaṇamarthaṃ" regarding the maintenance or wealth</margin>.

A courtesan must report her earnings, her future income, and the identity of her clients to the Superintendent.

By these rules, the conduct of the wives of actors, dancers, singers, musicians, storytellers, bards, rope-dancers, jugglers, and wandering performers who trade in their women, as well as women who live in secret <note>clandestine prostitutes</note>, is explained.

When such performers arrive from abroad, they shall pay five <term>panas</term> as a performance license fee.

Women who live by their beauty <term>rūpājīvā</term> <gloss>independent prostitutes who do not belong to the royal establishment</gloss> shall pay a tax to the state amounting to two days' earnings per month.

The state shall provide a livelihood from the royal treasury to those who teach courtesans, female slaves, and female performers the following arts: singing, playing musical instruments, recitation, dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing the lute <term>vīṇā</term>, the flute <term>veṇu</term>, and the drum <term>mṛdaṅga</term>, reading the thoughts of others, preparing perfumes and garlands, shampooing <note>massage and grooming</note>, and the arts of the courtesan <term>vaiśikakalā</term> <gloss>the sixty-four arts of pleasure</gloss>. These teachers shall also train the sons of courtesans and the chief performers in all types of musical rhythms and theatrical techniques <margin>original variant: "tālāpachārāṃścha" regarding rhythmic errors or variations</margin>.

Standing in the valley itself is not permitted; whoever leaves it before sunset must offer a blood sacrifice <note>as an expiation</note>. On the border of Arafah are white markers. In the prayer place is a pulpit made of brick, and behind it is a large cistern. Two miles before it are the Mazamayn <gloss>The Two Narrow Passes</gloss>, which mark the boundary of the Sanctuary <note>the sacred precinct of Mecca</note>. Batn Muhassir is a valley between Mina and Muzdalifah, and it is the border of Muzdalifah. Al-Tanim is a place with mosques around the Mosque of Aisha and water-dispensaries on the road to Medina. From there, the residents of Mecca enter the state of ritual consecration <term>ihram</term> for the lesser pilgrimage <term>umrah</term>. The Sanctuary is surrounded by white markers. From the western road, Al-Tanim is three miles away; from the Iraq road, nine miles; from the Yemen road, seven miles; from the Taif road, eleven miles; and from the main highway, ten miles. Dhu al-Hulayfah is a village near Yathrib <gloss>Medina</gloss> with a flourishing mosque and nearby wells, though no houses are seen there. Al-Juhfah is a populated city inhabited by the Banu Jafar. It has a fortress with two gates and a few wells. Two miles away is a spring and a large pool; water may sometimes be scarce there, though it is a significant place.

On the following day, he discoursed to himself on suitable topics, for not a single listener to his lectures was left to him, as they had all been shut out by Domitian. But the witness whom the Emperor had sent—and who, as he claimed, posed a great danger to him—possessed a tongue that was not uneducated, being one of those sycophants who can toss out eight or ten rhetorical flourishes. Apollonius, however, keeping his own counsel, spoke of things that did not benefit the spy. For he reminisced to those present about mountains, and described wild beasts and trees; some were charmed by these tales, while others merely looked on. When the man tried to lead him into slandering the tyrant, Apollonius said, "My good man, you may say whatever you wish, for you will not be informed upon by me; but as for whatever I find fault with in the Emperor, I shall say it to his face." Other episodes occurred in this prison, some involving plots, and others generally so significant that they are worthy of my serious attention. In the evening, so as not to omit anything, he recounted them to us. These were the matters worth recording.

He had been sitting there for five days. A man who spoke the Greek language entered the prison and asked, "Where is the man of Tyana?" Taking him aside, he said, "The Emperor will speak with you tomorrow." It seemed that he had heard this from Aelianus <note>Aelianus was the Praetorian Prefect who was secretly friendly toward Apollonius</note>. One must understand the secret nature of this; for he alone was supposed to know it. "Furthermore," he said, "the prison warden has been told to provide you with everything you might need for your comfort." "You do well to say so," I replied, "but even in such a life as this, I do not require any of these things. I will speak on behalf of those who have fallen into trouble, and I ask for mercy." "Do you mean," he asked, "that you will speak to the Emperor not as a counselor but as a victor?" "By Zeus," he said, "unless the gods are to be punished! Why," he asked, "do you look down on him, and why do you not fear his pride?" "You advise me well," he said, "and I have already persuaded myself of this."

Running along with the conversation, the man said, "I am glad to see you prepared in a measured way. But you must be prepared for the Emperor's voice and for the harshness of his face. For he speaks with a heavy tone, even if he speaks mildly; and his brow hangs over the character of his eye. His cheek is full of bile, for this is what shows most of all. Let us not be terrified by these things, O man of Tyana. For they are more a matter of nature and are always the same." And Apollonius said, "The impious <term>Paionios</term> <gloss>healer/singer</gloss> in the song of Polyphemus <note>A reference to Homer's Odyssey</note>, even when he first approached him, did not fear what he ate nor how his voice thundered, and he took courage before him, even though he had feared his power at first and it destroyed him; but a man who is better than I and self-sufficient will save both myself and the companions for whom I am in danger." Having spoken such things to the newcomer, and having reported them to those he ought, he went to sleep.

Around dawn, a secretary from the imperial court arrived and said, "The Emperor commands you, Apollonius, to come to him when the market is full <note>around mid-morning</note>, not yet to make your defense, but because he wishes to see who you happen to be and to meet with you alone." "Why then," he said, "are you speaking to me about these things? For is it not he who should speak?" "By Zeus," said the man of Tyana. "To whom then should I say these things?" "Tell those who are to lead me. For I must surely go as one from a prison." "These things have been commanded to them in addition to this," he said. "And I shall come in due time. I came to announce it to someone. For these things were strictly commanded to him."

The man then departed. Apollonius, resting himself on the bed, said, "I have need of sleep; I must. For the night has been difficult for me, as I wished to remember things I once heard." And I was somewhat ashamed, as if I should have used the time better, and he to himself as if announcing something so great. "And how could I ask," I thought, "not even knowing what he will ask you? For will you not say something about your life?" "By Zeus," he said, "I must. For I should not use anything of his; but let him who always remembers speak well. I wish to go through this with you. For it will be useful and will seem right to you also. Regarding lions, and how men tame them, Phraotes <note>The Indian King mentioned earlier in the biography</note> commands neither to play with them—for they remember injuries if played with—nor to serve them, for they become arrogant by nature; but rather to call them while stroking them, to lead them into obedience. We shall not think this is about the training of beasts, but rather when dealing with tyrants; if one uses this, he would not fall out of measure with them." "This discourse," he said, "is excellently spoken regarding the characters of tyrants. But there is also in Aesop a lion in a cave. Aesop says he was not sick, but seemed so to the beasts who visited him and did not return. How then, O Apollonius? What shall we do with this one, from whom no one escapes, and the tracks of those going out are not left?" And Apollonius said, "But I would consider the fox wiser if, having entered inside, she was not caught, but came out of the cave and showed her own tracks."

Having said these things, sleep stopped him for a very short time, just enough to close his eyes. When day came, having prayed to the Sun, as is fitting in a prison, he discoursed with those who approached him on whatever they asked. And so, when the market was full, the secretary arrived and said it was time to open the doors, "lest we be summoned even sooner." But he, saying "Let us go," went forward with an impulse. While he was feared, four bodyguards followed him, and many people approached.

# We have only set the distance

from the point of midday <note>original: "nisf al-nahar"</note> because the adjustment <term>ta'dil</term> <gloss>correction or equation</gloss> for a birth is easier using it than working with horizons. The hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and a fraction. Therefore, the Jewish method using seasonal hours <term>al-sa'at al-zamaniyya</term> <gloss>hours that vary in length based on the season</gloss> is only correct if the conjunction <term>al-ijtima'</term> <gloss>the New Moon</gloss> for the beginning of the month of Tishrei occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. However, it never occurs exactly then; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously.

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their opinion, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year and the determination of its quality—whether it is deficient, regular, or complete. We already possess the knowledge of whether the year is ordinary <term>basita</term> <gloss>a common year of 12 months</gloss> or leap <term>kabisa</term> <gloss>an embolismic year of 13 months</gloss>. 

We then look in the Table of Limits <term>jadwal al-hudud</term> for a duration of weekdays whose two boundaries encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look on the side for leap years if it is a leap year, and on the side for ordinary years if it is an ordinary year. When we find it, we find alongside it the weekday for the start of the year and its specific quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as ordinary or leap, we can determine the start of the following year.

destined for them, they may penetrate. From these things, conclude that it is necessary to proceed according to my prescription, and not at all according to yours. Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still hurl more thunderbolts against me: nevertheless, my Monarchy shall stand, while yours goes entirely to ruin. It is not in vain that I write so extensively about Alchemy, but I do so with this intent and end: that from these writings you may clearly and solidly learn what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood.

<margin>The end of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>
Nor should you be offended by this, that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it: but this rather must be carefully seen to, that through it <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret remedies</gloss> are uncovered, and the deceptions of the <term>seplasiarii</term> <gloss>perfumers or sellers of ointments</gloss> are exposed, by which the unrefined common people are deceived, while these men administer to them for one florin that which they would not redeem for a single penny. So "precious" are their secrets.

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is compelled to confess this. If this is true, I now ask of you whether the poison ought not to be separated from the good and the useful? And the good accepted, the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If therefore it must be: I pray you, tell me, how is it separated in your workshops? For among you, all things remain mixed together. But so that you may protect your simplicity, if you are convinced to confess that poison lies hidden there, and you are asked where it finally goes: then you bring forth I know not what concerning "corrections," which they claim drive out and take away the poison, just as Quince corrects Scammony <note>a harsh purgative resin</note>, which is then called <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>purified scammony</gloss>.

<margin>The correction of Physicians is examined.</margin>
But what kind of correction is this? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it escape to? It remains in the <term>Diagridium</term>. Test it, if you are wise: exceed the limit, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it soon enough.

<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
In this way you also correct Turbith <note>a medicinal root</note>, and you call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would be fitting for peasants, and should be given to pack-horses. Make a trial by exceeding the limit and increase the dose: you will see whether you do not feel the poison.

<margin>What it is for a Physician to correct.</margin>
*To correct is to take that which is already corrected.* He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections of yours; the power lies with the substances themselves, not with you. Now indeed, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation: as, for example, a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted as food. If you remove the poison from it, you will eat with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely that a similar separation is needed. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation: unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will have remained. Now then, at last, if that true foundation is required which takes away poison, let us see how Alchemy provides it. For it is necessary that it be done in such a way that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars is removed; and if Saturn dwells in Venus, he is separated from her <note>Paracelsus uses planetary names to refer to metals: Mars for iron, Sol for gold, Saturn for lead, and Venus for copper</note>. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies also exist in them. But those bodies which are contrary, it is absolutely necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is removed from the good which you seek. Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire: so Medicine is much less useful which does not pass through the fire.

<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
For it is necessary for all things to pass through fire into a second generation, by which they ought to benefit and help man. And should this not rightly be judged the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to apply poisons, but rather <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret, purified essences</gloss>.

<margin>Workshops are rebuked.</margin>
However, all those preparations of the workshops, as many as there are, do not contribute even a single letter to this doctrine: but they are occupied simply in "correcting," just as if a dog has farted in a room, and that stench is suppressed either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room afterward just as much as before? And although it may not be perceived by the sense of smell: may I therefore be allowed to say the stench is separated, and no longer remains? On the contrary, it is present, but corrected by the fumigation. Thus the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who blunt <term>Aleopaticum</term> <gloss>an aloe-based medicine</gloss> with sugar, so that it may inflict no harm. Thus sugar and honey are their mastery. Thus also gentian "corrects" treacle. Are these not the works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the Physicians of princes. Who is so stupid as not to smell instantly that these things are worthless? What else, I ask, can they boast about their remedies, except to say, *This Electuary is sweet, made of spices, sugar, and honey*?

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine requires the alchemical separation of poisons from healing agents through fire, rather than merely masking unpleasant or toxic qualities with sugar or incense. He critiques contemporary pharmacists for their superficial "corrections" of drugs, which he views as deceptive and ineffective.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, poison, separation, arcana, Diagridion, correction, Physician, fire, Pharmacists, spagyric art</keywords>

But if the power of a greater natural heat should reach that quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> before it is formed to its end, namely into the form of silver, so that it is reduced into the pure and red sulfur of Nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver. Quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, which we have just mentioned, is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and moisture. If it is made pure and separated from all superfluity, then no further thickness can be mixed with it, such that it could be reduced back into any imperfect metal. For Nature does not work backward, nor is it a material that looks toward any impure form, such as the imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. According to this distinction, let it be observed what is described of quicksilver in the following chapter.

### CHAPTER II.

Therefore, in all metals there is a true Mercury and a right sulfur, equally in the imperfect as in the perfect metals. It has only been contaminated and made impure in the imperfect metals, which are those that lack only perfect maturation. For these same reasons, they can be reduced to gold and silver; that is, so that the impurity with which they were defiled may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is within them, and the form of gold or silver may be introduced into them. For they were torn away from nature because they were removed and dug out from their natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth. Therefore, they can no longer have any operation within themselves as if they were still hiding under the earth; nevertheless, as much as is within them, they desire to be perfected.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, was seizing a church of the <term>Novatians</term> <gloss>a rigorous Christian sect following Novatian</gloss> while staying in Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him and urged him to return the church. Leontius answered warmly, saying to him, "You Novatians ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance and shut out the loving-kindness of God." When Leontius had said these and many other such harsh things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "Indeed, no one has ever repented as much as I have." When the other asked again, "How have you repented?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I have seen you."

Once, when John <note>John Chrysostom</note> the bishop was accusing him of something and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "Indeed it does not." When John became angry and said, "Do you see that you are alone? Do you wish to be bishop?" Sisinnius replied, "I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, as I am to all others." John, being provoked by what was said, said, "I will stop you, for you are a heretic." To this Sisinnius wittily replied, "I would even provide a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor." But John, softened by the response, said, "I will not stop you from speaking if speaking grieves you so much."

Sisinnius was thus ready and graceful in his responses. To write and record all his sayings would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown through a few examples what kind of man he was when he undertook to lead. I say this: he was famous for his learning. Because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Moreover, all the illustrious members of the Senate cherished and admired him. He composed many books, but in them he mixes his style with poetic words. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writing. For grace attended him in his face, his voice, his appearance, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all the religious sects, and especially by Bishop Atticus. Such are the matters concerning Sisinnius.

Truly, the unlearned and those of a base nature—to whom the gift of obtaining favor from the gods did not truly come, nor did they possess a notion of the immortal Jove—did not listen to either the gods or divine men. They rejected all the gods, yet they chose not only to follow the forbidden <term>demones</term> <gloss>demons or lesser spirits</gloss> without hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those acts through which alone God is adored. For God, as the father of all, lacks nothing; but it is well for us when we adore Him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to Him through the imitation and seeking of Him. For he says that seeking purifies, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward Him. He preached well concerning God the Father and described the character with which He should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, as the lives of the saints are either praised or blamed therein. But among Christians, there is either as much reality or as much calumny as the demons—whom they think are gods—desire. As if it were difficult for anyone to recall what foul and disgraceful things were performed in theaters and temples in service to the gods, and then to observe what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; from this, understand where the building up and where the ruin of morals lies. Who told him this, or who inspired such a vain and fitting lie—except a diabolical spirit—that the Christians revere rather than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we—as fellow citizens in this mortal pilgrimage—venerate and love alongside the holy heavenly angels and the powers of God, forbids sacrifice. Thundering in His law which He gave to His Hebrew people, He introduced a very threatening command, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone should think it was commanded only that sacrifice not be made to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom that man calls the least or lesser—who in the Holy Scriptures are themselves called gods, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the Gentiles, as the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> clearly placed in the Psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons." Lest anyone should think sacrifice was forbidden to these demons but permitted to all or some of the heavenly beings, He immediately added: "except to the Lord alone." This means to the Lord only, lest perhaps someone hearing "to the Lord alone" <note>original: "domino soli"</note> might believe the sun <note>original: "solem"</note> is the god to whom sacrifice should be made. That it is not to be understood this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher bears such significant testimony, gave a law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language—not obscure or unknown, but now spread abroad among all nations—in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there to search for many things regarding this matter in His law and His prophets? Indeed, there is no need to search, for they are not hidden or rare; rather, it is easy to collect frequent and fitting examples and place them in this disputation of mine, by which it appears clearer than light that He willed sacrifice to be made to no one at all except to Himself, the true and supreme God. Behold this one thing said briefly, or rather weightily, threateningly, but truly by that God whom their most learned men proclaim as so excellent: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the rooting out of the disobedient follow. "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out," He says, "except to the Lord only." Not because He has need of anything, but because it is profitable for us that we should be His possession. For to Him it is sung in the sacred writings of the Hebrews: "I have said to the Lord, You are my God, for You have no need of my goods." Moreover, we ourselves are His most noble and best sacrifice. This is His city, the mysteries of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets proclaimed through oracles that the victims which the Jews offered as a shadow of the future would cease, and that the Gentiles would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun to its setting, just as we now see being done.

# But by meditating on the Supreme, that which is hidden is revealed, for from Him come the soul's bondage and liberation. (3.2.5)

3.2.5

Now, an objection might be raised: The <term>Jiva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss> is a part of the Supreme Self, just as a spark is a part of a fire. This being the case, just as the fire and the spark share the same powers of burning and lighting, so too should the individual soul and <term>Ishwara</term> <gloss>the Lord</gloss> share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Therefore, by the power of the soul's own will, it should be able to create chariots and other objects in the dream state.

To this, we reply: Even though there is a relationship of part and whole between the individual soul and the Lord, it is a matter of direct perception that the soul possesses qualities opposite to those of the Lord.

Does this mean the soul lacks the qualities of the Lord entirely? No, it is not that they do not exist; rather, though existing, they are hidden <note>original: "tirohita"</note> by the intervention of <term>Avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss> and other factors. That which is hidden is revealed only to that creature who, through meditating on the Supreme Lord and exerting effort, has shaken off the darkness. This happens through the grace of the Lord to one who has attained perfection, just as the power of sight, obscured by a cataract, is restored by the power of medicine. It does not happen naturally for all creatures. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, come the bondage and liberation of this soul. Bondage results from the lack of knowledge of the Lord's true nature, while liberation results from the realization of that nature.

As the <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>revealed scripture</gloss> says: By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of afflictions, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, there is a third state: at the dissolution of the body, universal sovereignty is attained, and one becomes absolute, with all desires fulfilled. <note>Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note>

# Or, that concealment results from connection with the body. (3.2.6)

3.2.6

Why is it that the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, has its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It is understandable that burning and lighting are obscured in a spark, but why here?

We reply: This is true. That concealment of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the fire that is inherent in wood <note>original: "arani", the wooden fire-stick</note> has its powers of burning and lighting hidden, or as fire is hidden when covered by ashes, so too the soul's knowledge and sovereignty are obscured due to its connection with the <term>upadhis</term> <gloss>limiting adjuncts</gloss> like the body, which are produced by names and forms set up by ignorance. This leads to the error of failing to discriminate between the soul and the body.

The word "or" in the sutra is intended to dispel the doubt that the soul is something other than the Lord. One might argue: Let the soul be entirely different from the Lord since its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why bother imagining a connection with the body? We say no, because the difference of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. Scripture, beginning with "That Divinity thought," refers to the soul as "this soul which is my Self" <note>Chandogya Upanishad 6.3.2</note>. Furthermore, it teaches the soul its identity with the Lord: "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That thou art, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty become hidden through connection with the body.

Consequently, the creation of chariots in a dream by the soul's mere will is not possible. If the soul could create by its will in dreams, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is unpleasant for themselves. As for the argument that the scriptural comparison to the waking state proves the reality of dreams, that comparison is not intended to imply reality. It would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the <term>Shruti</term> itself shows the absence of real chariots in dreams. The dream appears similar to the waking state only because it is caused by the impressions <note>original: "vasana"</note> arising from the waking state. Therefore, it is established that the dream state is <term>Maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss> alone.

# The absence of that dream occurs in the channels and in the Self, as known from scripture. (3.2.7)

The Section on the Absence of Dreams (3.2.7)

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep <note>original: "sushupti"</note> is examined. Regarding deep sleep, there are these scriptural texts. In one place it is said: When he is fast asleep, composed, and knows no dream, then he sleeps in these channels <note>original: "nadis"</note>. Elsewhere, following a description of the channels, it says: Having crawled back through them, he rests in the pericardium <note>original: "puritat"</note>. In another place, again regarding the channels: In them he remains when, being asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one with the <term>Prana</term> <gloss>vital breath/life-force</gloss> alone. Elsewhere: He sleeps in the space within the heart. Elsewhere: Then, my dear, he is united with the Existent, he has gone to his own Self. And also: Embraced by the conscious Self, he knows nothing without and nothing within.

The doubt arises here: Are these various places—the channels and so on—different, independent locations for deep sleep, or are they collectively one location? What is the initial view? That they are different. Why? Because they serve the same purpose. It is not common for things serving the same purpose to be dependent on one another...

When words reached a point of difficulty and hardship, you will soon see the key to happiness. The messenger returned from Sam <note>Zal's father, a great hero</note> with joy and a fortunate message. He spoke and heard much, and finally Rudaba's mother <note>Sindukht</note> also became part of the story. She quickly handed the reply to the woman <note>the intermediary/nurse</note>, and the woman left her presence and carried the letter away.

She came to Rudaba like the wind, with this joy and noble spirit. The fairy-faced <note>Rudaba</note> scattered silver coins over the woman and seated her on a golden-patterned throne. She said to that resourceful nurse: "Take a suit of clothes as a reward for this good news, and also something for the fortunate Zal from what I have in my treasury."

She brought forward a fine silken head-wrap, so finely woven that the warp and woof were invisible. Its entire surface was covered in red rubies and pearls, so that the gold was hidden by the gems. She also sent a pair of precious rings, shining like the planet Jupiter in the sky, to Dastan-e Sam <note>Zal</note>, along with many blessings and messages.

The woman left the chamber and reached the hallway. Sindukht <note>Rudaba's mother</note> looked and saw her. Her soul became troubled and anxious; she said with a loud voice: "Where are you from, young woman? You pass before me from time to time; you enter the chambers but do not look at me. My bright heart has become suspicious of you. Tell me, are you a bow or a string?" <note>A metaphor asking for her true purpose or nature</note>

The woman turned pale like sandarac <note>a yellow resin</note> out of fear; she grew afraid and kissed the ground. She said to Sindukht: "O beautiful one, hear my words and speak your mind. I am a seeker of means, bringing bread from all sides. I have sold clothes and ornaments to people of substance. I go to the houses of the great; they buy clothes, silver, and jewels from me. Rudaba requested ornaments for this chamber, she wanted precious gems. I brought her a gold-adorned crown and a casket full of royal jewels."

Sindukht said: "Let me see them and show them to me, to ease the suspicion and thought in my heart." The woman replied: "I handed them to Rudaba, and there is more; I will bring it now." Sindukht said: "Bring it and place it before my eyes, to pour water on this anger of mine." The woman said: "The moon-faced one <note>Rudaba</note> will give the silver tomorrow; do not seek an excuse from me today."

Because of her ill-fated words, Sindukht's heart prepared for conflict. She saw through the woman's deceit and shortcomings. When she saw those precious clothes and the ornaments from Rudaba's hand, she became enraged. She seized the woman's hair in her hand, twisted it, and threw her down to the ground. She dragged the resourceful woman by her face, bringing her down and casting her aside. She dragged her through the meadow, pulling her by her hair in humiliation across the rocky ground. She dragged her for a time by her hair and threw her on the dust like one unconscious. She bound her there, striking her with hands and feet.

From there, she entered the palace in a rage, filled with pain, sorrow, and grief. She closed the palace door behind her, troubled by the thoughts revolving in her mind. She commanded her daughter to come forward, and she struck her own cheeks in grief. She washed the two roses <note>cheeks</note> with her watery narcissus <note>eyes</note> until the roses were soaked.

She said to Rudaba: "O precious moon, why did you choose the well over the throne? What was left of kindness in the world that I did not show you, openly or secretly? What did you lack, O moon-faced one? Tell your secret to me. Who is this woman who comes to you? Why does she come? Whatever this man and woman have devised—this beautiful head-wrap and ring—will bring much profit and loss from my great treasury and the Arabs. You will bring a bad name upon us; no daughter like the one I have birthed was ever born."

Rudaba looked at the ground and her feet, remaining in her place out of shame before her mother. Tears of love poured from her eyes, her face adorned with the blood of her two narcissus eyes. She said to her mother: "O wise one, a whole army of grief consumes my soul. If you had not given birth to me at all, mother, no words of good or evil would be spoken of me. The commander Dastan <note>Zal</note> stayed in Kabul, and his love struck such a spark in my heart. The world became so narrow for my heart that I wept both openly and secretly. I do not wish to be alive without his face; my life is in his very scent. Know that he sat with me; we took hand in hand in a covenant. Nothing else happened between us, though a fire was hidden between us. A messenger was sent to the great Sam, and a reply was sent to the mighty Zal. For a time he was troubled and pained, hearing and speaking words of counsel. Finally, he agreed and consulted the ancient priests <note>Mubads</note>."

And a growth developed in the area between the groin and the scrotum. In name <note>referring to the medical term for the condition</note> it grew more bitter toward the internal parts. From this, as the flesh opened up, serous fluids <term>ichores</term> <gloss>watery discharges from a wound or ulcer</gloss> flowed out, emitting a heavy and foul-smelling breath. It reached a point where neither the discharge nor the doctors were able to contain the putrefaction. Instead, an unbearable, continuous, and most pungent sensation consumed the body. It poured out from both the hemorrhoids and the open sores, until the spreading of the disease, having cut its way down to the very internal organs, broke his thread of life. He died in this manner, just as Clearchus <note>Clearchus of Heraclea, a previous tyrant known for his cruelty</note> had died, reflecting that he was being called to account for the cruel and lawless ways he had treated the citizens. For they say he often prayed for death to come to him from any source, but for many days he was consumed by the bitter and heavy disease. Thus the tyrant perished, having lived fifty-six years, twelve of which were spent in his tyranny. At that time, Agesilaus <note>Agesilaus II, the Spartan king</note> ruled the Lacedaemonians.

Timotheus, having taken over the rule, reshaped it toward a milder and more democratic form, so that he was no longer called a tyrant but was named a benefactor and savior for his deeds. For he settled debts by paying the creditors, and he provided for those in need of funds for trade and other means of living without charging interest. He released from the prisons not only his fellow countrymen but even his enemies. He was a judge who was precise yet simultaneously humane, and in other matters he was honorable and did not sell his verdicts. In these affairs, he especially cherished his brother Dionysius, choosing to have him immediately as a partner in the government and later as his successor. Furthermore, he bore himself bravely in military actions with a temperate disposition of both body and soul, and he was both sensible and gracious in the settlement of battles.

to men who hunt with the help of the noble <term>tuphasioi</term> <gloss>a type of water bird, possibly a heron or egret</gloss>.
O Hermes of famous counsel, the fishermen propitiate you above all others; therefore, with cries shared among the gods of the wild, I would come following the fame of your gathered company.
First, let the fisherman have a body and limbs that are both swift and strong; let him be neither overly fat nor, on the other hand, wasted in flesh. For it is often necessary to struggle against powerful fish being hauled in, which possess immense strength as they are tossed and whirled in the embrace of their mother, the brine.
He must be able to leap from a rock and spring back up onto a rock with ease. He must be able to track a long path quickly through the deep-stretching toil of the sea, to dive into the deepest parts, and to remain amidst the swells as if he were lingering over tasks on land, laboring with the enduring heart of a man competing in a contest within the sea.
Let the fisherman’s soul be full of craft and wise; for fish devise many and varied schemes, escaping by means of unexpected deceits.
Let him be especially daring, fearless, and temperate. Let him not love the satiety of sleep, but let him look sharply, being awake in his heart and with wide-open eyes.
Furthermore, let him endure the winter storms of Zeus and the parching season of the Dog Star <note>referring to the extreme heat of midsummer</note>, being steadfast in his desire for labor and a lover of the sea.
For in this way he would be strong and dear to Hermes.
The evening hunt is best during the autumn seasons, and again when the morning star <term>Heosphoros</term> <gloss>the dawn-bringer, or Venus</gloss> rises.
In winter, one should set out together with the spreading rays of the sun; but in the blooming spring, the hunt is favored all day long by every kind of breeze.

# Description of Lima, City of the Kings

<margin>Appearance of the city of Lima.</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one can see into every corner, and on both sides the open fields. Through the greater part of the houses run canals bringing fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort for the citizens, who can thereby water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they keep beautiful and pleasant. Also, in this river lie many water mills of our country's fashion <note>original: "op onse landts aert", referring to Dutch-style mills</note>, where they grind their grain. In short, very wealthy citizens live here, some of whom possess 150,000 ducats. From this city, ships sometimes depart carrying goods worth 800,000 ducats, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which stands a crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep cattle, as well as their pigeon houses and vineyards; however, there are no good grapes due to the nature of the soil. There are beautiful gardens, not only full of all kinds of local fruits, but also those from Spain, such as pomegranates, lemons, citrons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar canes, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. Truly, to pass human life with joy, if the scandalous disagreements and wars were not there, this place would surely be one of the most beautiful in the entire world. The climate thereabouts is so temperate that throughout the whole year there is neither excessive heat nor harmful cold. Also, it has never been seen that hunger or plague occurred there, nor any rain, thunder, or lightning from heaven. On the contrary, there is always a clear, bright, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535 and is called the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Epiphany <note>Three Kings' Day</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as the fruits of the trees and the earth as mentioned, there is no less an abundance of wheat and grain. During the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet it is not unhealthy like ours; for those who have pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase in people and wealth, although many years ago there were over 500 houses, and the city is built so white that 2,000 might well stand there, for the streets are wide and the market square large. Each house has a plot of 80 feet in width and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for it is consumed by worms within two or three years—the houses are built with only one story, yet very costly and magnificent with many rooms and halls suitable for living and hosting foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials that they bake together very thick and fill with earth. They cover the roofs of their houses with painted mats or painted linen, and all around and above

<column-break/>

on the walls they make arbors of reeds where they shelter from the sun. They do not worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trujillo, Huanuco, Chachapoyas, Puerto Viejo, Guayaquil, Popayán, Catchi, San Miguel, and San Francisco. It was previously mentioned that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shores of the sea we have dealt until now, beginning from the Equator <note>original: "die Linea"</note> and Cape Passao to this point. It should also be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima but much further south, the sea coast is very dry and full of large desolate sandy places, where for a distance of ten miles inland it neither thunders, lightens, nor rains; but beyond those ten miles, or as far as the mountains are distant from the sea, it does. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but there are four or five standing waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which originate from the snow and rain falling in the mountains, not from springs, which are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers have been partly described before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from one another, though mostly 7 or 8, by which travelers regulate their journey because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, for a mile's width or sometimes more or less depending on the terrain, there are various fruitful trees and cornfields which are moistened and sown by the people, which they may do throughout the entire year. Also, many kinds of wild trees, corn, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises grow near these rivers. Since the Spaniards took the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through certain canals they lead out of these rivers. Because these rivers run swiftly down from high mountains, one can hardly cross them without help, and many have drowned therein. Those who travel along the flat land usually stay so close to the seaside that they always have it in view. When it is winter in the mountains and rains heavily, it is dangerous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers one must cross, either with certain rafts they have for that purpose or with a net filled tightly with gourds <note>original: "Cauwaerden"</note>, upon which the traveler must lie outstretched while one of the Indians swims ahead, pulling the net or raft with a rope, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of reeds. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to the knees, and an outer garment like a cloak. The women wear a garment of cotton according to the length of the body. Although the fashion of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nonetheless some distinction in the head-dress: some wear single ribbons, some braided, some of one color, others of various colors; and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, all distinguished according to the custom of the land.

### On the shame sought from unworthy praise.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Spare the one who has been praised, for when you are praised unjustly,
> if you then condemn him in turn, it will be a sign of inconstancy.

**Pain:** I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.
<note>A large decorative initial L marks the beginning of the response.</note>
**Reason:** You say you are accused of having praised an unworthy man. Indeed, what is an evil often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people believe others to be just as they are themselves. From this, they are even more inclined toward praising than is fair; and although I admit it is bad to praise the unworthy, to disparage the undeserving is much worse.

**Pain:** I have praised an unworthy man.

**Reason:** If you did this knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another, but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

**Pain:** The praise of another turns into my own infamy.

**Reason:** On the contrary, it is either your own fault or your ignorance. For no infamy, just as no praise, comes from what belongs to another.

**Pain:** I grieve greatly for having praised an unworthy man.

**Reason:** See to it then that you do not have to grieve for this same thing often. Beware lest you leap forward rashly to praise or to disparage. For there is a lust for both things and, to speak accurately, a disease and an itch of a restless tongue that knows no quiet. The restraint and guarding of the tongue are numbered among the works of extraordinary perfection, as the Scripture says:

One who has undergone <term>evacuation</term> <gloss>cleansing of the body through purging or bleeding</gloss> must not rush to consume many or fatty foods, lest <term>nature</term> <gloss>the body's innate healing intelligence</gloss> attract them while they are undigested. If any such food is necessary, it must be taken little by little, gradually, so that what enters the body is well-digested. The goal is a specific evacuation in equal measure. As for an evacuation specific to one <term>humor</term> <gloss>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</gloss> alone, whether in quantity or in corruption of quality, it is not the primary goal. Every excessive evacuation causes fever in most cases. If the cessation of a habitual diarrhea causes an ailment, then repeating that evacuation usually cures it. For example, if the cessation of a nosebleed or ear discharge causes blockages, returning them to their habit removes the blockage. Know that the consequences of leaving a remnant of the matter that needs evacuation are less harmful than being excessive in evacuation and reaching the point where strength fails. Often, nature dissolves that remnant itself. As long as the humor is of the type intended and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to evacuate until fainting occurs. One whose strength is robust but whose humors are many and corrupt should be evacuated little by little. Likewise, if the matter is highly <term>concocted</term> <gloss>matured or ripened for expulsion</gloss> or heavily mixed with the blood, it cannot be evacuated all at once, as is the case in sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that <term>purging</term> <gloss>laxative evacuation</gloss> draws from above and uproots from below; it is suitable for drawing away opposing materials. It is also suitable after the evacuation of materials. If the materials are below, drawing them is contrary to uprooting them from where they are. <term>Vomiting</term> performs drawing and uprooting in the opposite manner. <term>Bloodletting</term> <note>original: "al-fasd"</note> differs in its state according to the sites from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who least need evacuation are those with good nutrition and good digestion. Inhabitants of hot countries have little need for evacuation.

### Chapter Four: On Common Rules for Vomiting and Purging, and an Indication of How Purgative and Emetic Medicines Draw

We say: it is recommended for one who wishes to purge or vomit to divide their food, consuming the daily amount in several portions and making them of different foods and different drinks. For the stomach, in these circumstances, may desire to push what is in it upwards or downwards. As for uniform food consumed upon other food, the stomach is stingy with it, clings to it, and grips it tightly, especially if it is small in quantity. For one who is naturally loose-bodied, none of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not occur in one who follows a good regimen; such a person needs what is lighter than these. Often, exercise, massage, and the bath are sufficient for digestion. If the body becomes full, and most of that fullness is of the best of humors—meaning blood—then bloodletting is what is needed for purification, rather than purging. If necessity dictates both bloodletting and evacuation by means of <term>hellebore</term> or strong medicines, one must begin with bloodletting. This is among the recommendations of <term>Hippocrates</term> in the book <term>Epidemics</term> <note>original: "Abidhimya"</note>, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are viscous and cold, bloodletting may increase their thickness and viscosity; in that case, one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize bloodletting, then evacuate if needed afterward. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform bloodletting. He who prioritizes medicine over bloodletting when bloodletting should have been first has erred. One who has recently undergone bloodletting and needs evacuation, if he drinks medicine, it may be halted in him. Often, drinking medicine when bloodletting was required causes confusion and agitation; if it does not settle with sedatives, know that bloodletting should have preceded it. You should not perform an evacuation required by excessive fullness gently when the greatness of the ailment demands otherwise; fullness is judged by quality, not just quantity. Often, improving one's regimen suffices instead of a required bloodletting at the time. Often, a cause calls for evacuation but an obstacle arises; in that case, there is no trick but fasting, sleep, and correcting the <term>dyscrasia</term> <gloss>imbalance of temperament</gloss> caused by the fullness. Some evacuations are for the sake of precaution, such as what is needed by those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in spring. One needs to take precautions before the time and evacuate the specific humor of the disease, whether by bloodletting or purging. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done for those with dropsy. You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor to be evacuated in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> when you need to evacuate yellow bile; in that case, it must be mixed with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <note>original: "al-halilaj"</note>, to correct any dyscrasia that might occur afterward. In those with internal tumors, their purging and vomiting are weakened; if forced to do so, use for them things like <term>bindweed</term> and <term>safflower</term>. As for <term>musaibihi</term> <note>uncertain botanical term</note> and <term>cassia fistula</term> <note>original: "khiyar shanbar"</note> and the like: Hippocrates said that he whose constitution is easily inclined toward vomiting should prioritize vomiting for purification in summer, spring, or autumn, but not winter. He who is of moderate build, purging is better for him. If a cause calls for evacuation by vomiting, let him wait for summer and avoid it unless necessary. One must precede purging and vomiting by thinning the humor intended for evacuation and widening and opening the channels; this protects the body from exhaustion. Know that habituating nature gently and responding to the desired purging or vomiting easily before using strong medicine is a beneficial regimen. Purging and vomiting during wasting of the body is difficult, exhausting, and dangerous. An emetic medicine may turn into a purgative if the stomach is strong, or if drunk during intense hunger, or if the drinker has a sharp, loose nature, or is unaccustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is heavy in substance and quick to descend. A purgative becomes an emetic due to weakness of the stomach, or intense dryness of the stool, or because the medicine is loathsome, or the person has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge or purges before maturation, stirs up the humor it was meant to purge and spreads it through the body; it then overcomes the body and other humors transform into it, increasing that humor in the system. Some humors respond more quickly to vomiting in most cases, such as yellow bile. Others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Others have varying states, like phlegm, for which purging is generally more appropriate. For one whose humor is descending, such as those with chronic diarrhea <note>original: "zalaq al-am'a"</note>, vomiting them is impossible. The worst purgative medicines are those composed of drugs that differ greatly in their time of purging, causing agitation; the first purges the second before the second can act, or the first purges the second itself. Whenever one undergoes purging or vomiting while the body is clean, they will inevitably suffer dizziness, colic, and general distress, and what is evacuated will be evacuated with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating wastes, there is no agitation; if agitation begins, it is either evacuating something other than waste, or the humor being evacuated has changed, which indicates the body is clean of the intended humor.

Now Radha, distressed by separation, speaks concerning the moon. **In separation:** "Aye" is a tender address. O friend, this moon <term>vidhu</term> <gloss>the moon</gloss> spreads great agony of love in my heart. Of what kind? It is the friend and ally of the mind-born one <note>Kamadeva</note>. She speaks by remembering the state of Murari in separation. Of what kind? Its luster is like the luster of the lotus-face of Murari which is pale <term>pandu</term> <gloss>white or yellowish-pale</gloss> due to separation. Therefore, even while covering or concealing the pain <note>by its cool light</note>, it actually increases it. This is what is meant: Previously, by having the beauty of Murari's face pale from longing for me, it destroyed my pain; but now, as the friend of Desire, it only creates agony. Since the moon was born from the mind of the Supreme Being and Desire is also born of the mind, they are like brothers. As the scripture <term>Shruti</term> says: The moon was born from the mind, and the sun from the eyes. The word <term>vedana</term> <gloss>pain</gloss> can mean both knowledge and suffering. | Even if your place were a mouse hole, the cat's claw would make you drink poison. | Comfort is brought even if the grasp of imagination is long, if those imaginations are beautiful. |
| If long imaginations are terrifying, one becomes like wax melting in the fire. | If in the midst of snakes and scorpions the imagination is a good thought by the help of the Lord of Majesty, |
| Then the snakes and scorpions become companions, because your imagination is the alchemy of copper. | Beautiful imagination shows patience to be sweet, for relief is the description of the state in the presence. |

# The Sign of Virtue’s Fullness <note>original: De Chong Fu</note>

<margin>The principles in this section are subtle and profound.</margin>
<margin>Following this idea, there are two further meanings.</margin>

When piglets suckle <gloss>drink milk</gloss> from their dead mother, after a short while they startle <gloss>their eyes move; this refers to the mother’s eyes moving in death</gloss> <gloss>to blink</gloss>, and they all abandon her and run away. This is because they no longer see themselves in her <gloss>they believe the blinking of the eyes shows she no longer sees them</gloss>, and they feel she is no longer of their kind <gloss>the stiffness of the corpse is no longer like them</gloss>. What they loved about their mother was not her physical form, but that which animated her form <gloss>if the form is not worthy of love, then it is not worthy of dislike</gloss>. When a man dies in battle, he is buried without his feathered fans <gloss>those who die in battle lose their martial prowess, so they are not provided with fans</gloss> <gloss>martial skill is the root of a soldier</gloss>. A man whose feet have been cut off <note>a common punishment in ancient China</note> has no reason to care for his shoes <gloss>feet are the root of shoes</gloss>. In both cases, the fundamental root is gone.

The maidservants of the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> do not trim their nails or pierce their ears <gloss>this is another metaphor; the selected concubines do not cut or pierce themselves to keep their forms whole, so as to attract the gaze of the Most Honorable One</gloss>. A man who has just taken a wife stays outside the court and is no longer sent on official duties <gloss>he is not used for labor for fear of callousing his hands and feet, which would interfere with the rights of the new marriage</gloss>. If people value the wholeness of the physical form this much <gloss>those with whole forms are still able to move others</gloss>, how much more should they value one whose inner virtue is never forgotten!

<summary>Zhuangzi uses metaphors of suckling piglets, fallen soldiers, and palace etiquette to argue that the animating spirit and inner virtue are more fundamental than the physical body. # The Latter Cloud <note>original: "Uttara-megha"</note>

Of the women <note>original: "simantinīnām"</note> and brides. The lexicon of Amara states: "A woman is called simantini or vadhu." **Approached by a friend** <note>original: "suhṛdupanataḥ"</note> means having arrived through the presence of a friend. The word "friend" is used to remove any suspicion of deception. The news of the beloved is the **beloved's news** <note>original: "kāntodantaḥ"</note>. Amara states: "Varta, pravṛtti, vṛttānta, and udanta all mean news or tidings." This news is **slightly less than a meeting** <note>original: "saṃgamāt kiṃcidūnaḥ"</note>, meaning it brings joy almost equal to the actual contact with the beloved.

Now he delivers the message:

->O long-lived one, speak thus to her both by my request and to benefit yourself:<-
->Your companion, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri,<-
->being alive though separated, asks of your welfare, O frail one;<-
->for this is the first thing to be asked of living beings whose calamities are easily found. 41<-

Regarding this verse: O **long-lived one** <note>original: "āyuṣman"</note>. The suffix denotes praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of helping others. **By my request** <note>original: "mama vacanāt"</note> means by my words of entreaty, **and for yourself** <note>original: "ātmanaśca"</note> to **benefit** <note>original: "upakartum"</note>. This means to make yourself fulfilled through the act of helping others. Although "self" is the object of the act of benefiting, the use of the genitive case <note>original: "ātmanaḥ"</note> is not incorrect when only a general relationship is intended. As Bharavi says: "She benefits the fortune by which others are helped." Likewise, Sriharsha says: "To benefit the virtuous, to see fortune, to travel through the sky." Therefore, the statement of Nath that the second case <note>original: "accusative"</note> is seen everywhere is a statement without authority. **Speak thus** to that beloved. What should be said? O **frail one** <note>original: "abale"</note>, **your companion** <note>original: "tava sahacaraḥ"</note>, your husband, **residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri** <note>original: "rāmagiryāśramasthaḥ"</note>, stays in the hermitages of Chitrakuta. **Alive** <note>original: "avyāpannaḥ"</note> means he has not died. He gives the reason for not dying: though **separated** <note>original: "viyuktaḥ"</note> and suffering from the separation, he **asks of your welfare** <note>original: "tvāṃ kuśalaṃ pṛcchati"</note>. The verb "to ask" takes two objects. For indeed, for **living beings** <note>original: "prāṇinām"</note> whose **calamities are easily found** <note>original: "sulabhavipadām"</note> and occur without effort, **this very thing** <note>original: "etadeva"</note>, namely welfare, is the **first thing to be spoken** <note>original: "pūrvābhāṣyam"</note> or must necessarily be asked first.

->With his limb, your limb; with his thin limb, your thin one; with his deeply heated limb, your heated one;<-
->with his tearful limb, your tear-drenched one; with his constantly longing limb, your longing one...<-

<margin>
1. Long-lived one. 2. He should speak. 3. One. 4. Separated (feminine), appointed. 5. First to be comforted... for among beings with perishable bodies, this is the first comfort. 6. O fair-limbed one, and thin. 7. Flow of tears.
</margin>

<summary>The Yaksha instructs the Cloud to deliver a message of welfare to his wife, noting that for those in distress, hearing that a loved one is alive is the greatest comfort. The commentary by Mallinatha justifies the grammatical structure and emphasizes the merit of helping others.</summary>

# The Epistle of Ibn Tufayl

At that point, we saw ourselves as worthy of composing a discourse to be transmitted from us. It became our duty to be the first to present you with what we possess and to inform you of what we have attained, due to the sincerity of your loyalty and the purity of your devotion. However, if we were to cast upon you the ultimate conclusions we have reached before establishing their principles with you, it would benefit you no more than a general, traditional acceptance <note>original: "amr taqlidi mujmal"; referring to knowledge accepted on authority rather than through personal experience or proof</note>. This would only occur if you thought well of us based on affection and agreement, rather than because we deserve to have our word accepted on its own merit.

We do not desire for you anything less than the highest rank. We are not satisfied for you to remain at a level that does not even guarantee salvation, let alone the attainment of the highest degrees of success. Rather, we wish to lead you along the paths that we have previously trodden and to have you swim in the sea that we have already crossed, so that it may lead you to what we have reached. Thus, you may witness what we have witnessed and realize through your own inner insight <term>basirah</term> <gloss>spiritual or intellectual vision</gloss> everything that we have realized. You would then be free from binding your knowledge to what we have known.

This endeavor requires a specific and significant amount of time, freedom from distractions, and a total dedication of one's resolve <term>himmah</term> <gloss>spiritual ambition or intense focus</gloss> to this art. If your determination is sincere and your intention is sound to strive <note>original: "al-tashmir"; literally to tuck up one's sleeves in preparation for hard work</note> toward this goal, then at dawn you will praise your night's journey <note>a classical Arabic proverb meaning that hard work is rewarded when the goal is reached</note>, and you will obtain the blessing of your effort. You will have pleased your Lord, and He will have pleased you. I am at your service to help you reach what you desire of your hope and what you aspire to with your resolve and your whole being. I hope to lead you along the most direct path, safest from perils and calamities, even if I now present only a brief glimpse to stir your longing <term>al-tashwiq</term> <gloss>the awakening of desire or yearning for knowledge</gloss>.

<summary>Ibn Tufayl addresses a seeker, explaining that true knowledge must be gained through personal insight and experience rather than blind imitation of authority. He emphasizes the need for total dedication and a systematic approach to reach spiritual enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>Ibn Tufayl, enlightenment, insight, basirah, himmah, spiritual path, taqlid, philosophical method</keywords>

They cannot bring about misfortune or blessing, and they maintain that there are no omens of good or evil. Consequently, the administration falls into disorder and the state is endangered. Master Mozi addressed Gongmengzi, saying: Regarding funeral rites, for a ruler, parents, wife, or the eldest son <gloss>the heir</gloss>, there is a three-year period of mourning. For paternal uncles, brothers, and cousins, it is one year. For distant relatives, it is five months. For paternal aunts, elder sisters, maternal uncles, and sisters' sons, there are all specific months of mourning. Furthermore, during the intervals when one is not actively mourning, one is expected to recite the three hundred Odes, play the three hundred Odes on stringed instruments, sing the three hundred Odes, and perform the three hundred dances. If your words were followed, when would a gentleman find the time to attend to the government? When would the common people find the time to attend to their work?

Gongmengzi replied: When the state is in disorder, one governs it. When it is well-governed, one performs the rites and music. When the state is stable, one attends to business. When the state is wealthy, one performs the rites and music.

Master Mozi said: The order of a state <margin>Lu says five characters are missing here: "is the result of governing it, therefore it is orderly"</margin> depends on governance. If governance is abandoned, then the order of the state is also abandoned.

The ruler of this city is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>original: "Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman", with the letters Qaf and Ra carrying the short 'a' vowel</note>. It previously belonged to his brother Musa, who ceded it to King al-Nasir <note>the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent an emir and an army there, but Sultan Badr al-Din later seized control, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this Sultan outside the city as he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted my animal for him, so he dismounted his animal as well and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they dismount for him; they admire this gesture and increase their hospitality toward him. However, if the traveler greets them while remaining mounted, they are offended and displeased, which leads to the traveler being denied any favors. This happened to me with one of them, and I shall mention it later. When I had greeted him and we both remounted, he asked about my circumstances and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be given the finest lodging. He used to send abundant food, fruit, and sweets on silver platters, along with candles. He provided me with clothing and a mount, and treated me with great kindness. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray <note>original: "Aqsara", pronounced with a short 'a' on the Alif, a silent Qaf, and a short 'a' on the Sad and Ra</note>.

Aksaray is among the most beautiful and well-built cities of the land of the Romans <note>Anatolia</note>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and gardens on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through the houses. It contains many trees and grapevines, and there are many orchards within its walls. The famous carpets known by its name are manufactured there from sheep's wool; they have no equal in any other country. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq <note>the Ilkhanid Mongol ruler</note>. We stayed there at the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>hospice or Sufi lodge</gloss> of Sharif Husayn, who is the deputy there for Emir Artana. Artana is the deputy of the King of Iraq over the conquered territories of Anatolia. This Sharif is one of the <term>fityan</term> <gloss>members of the Akhi youth brotherhoods</gloss> and has a large following. He showed us ultimate hospitality and performed the same noble deeds as those before him.
