<margin>The chieftain Bononiana accompanies the chieftain in a secure manner.</margin> Having summoned the sick men whom we mentioned were left behind, the chieftain Bononiana, who was located midway on the direct route, kindly received them as they passed through. He gave them twenty pounds of pure, carved gold and provided an abundance of food suitable for eating. He refused to leave our men until he had escorted them from his palace into the territory of Pacra. He himself held all the vessels in his right hand like a faithful deposit, saying as he handed them over: "Behold your fellow soldiers, O bravest of men; behold, I deliver them to you in the same state as my palace received them upon their arrival. I wish they were in better health, but he who sends thunder and lightning upon wicked men, and who provides us with juice <note>likely referring to plant sap or fermented drink</note> and maize out of his goodness through the clemency of the seasons, answers for you and your companions." Saying this and lifting his eyes to heaven, he pointed toward the sun. "By suppressing our violent and proud enemies, you bring tranquility of mind to us and our homes. You tame monsters; we believe you and your companions, men outstanding in virtue, were sent from on high, so that under the protection of your <term>maccana</term> <gloss>a wooden sword or club used by indigenous peoples</gloss> we may live our lives without fear. We shall give perpetual thanks to the Giver of goods for this great care brought to us." The interpreters said that the chieftain Bononiana delivered this and other similar speeches. Vasco <note>Vasco Núñez de Balboa</note> returned equal thanks to him for his escort and his beneficence toward our men; indeed, he honored Bononiana with many gifts that were very pleasing to them. Vasco writes that he learned much from this chieftain regarding the wealth of those regions, which he says he wishes to pass over for the present, referring them to the eventual outcome. I do not understand what this implicit hyperbole means. He seems to promise great things, and it should not be judged foreign to his promise that immense riches can be hoped for from there, since they entered no house of the inhabitants in which they did not find golden breastplates or pectorals, or golden necklaces for the neck or arms. I make a conjecture from the houses of our own people. If someone, stimulated by a desire for iron, were to betake himself with a strong hand into Italy or Spain, what iron would he find in the houses? In one place an iron frying pan, in another an iron pot and tripods placed over the fire for the necessity of the kitchen. Nowhere will he find anything made of iron that is not fit for use, nor will he obtain a great abundance of iron. It will be conjectured from these finds that iron exists in those regions. They perceived that those natives value raw gold no more than our people value raw iron. These things I, Blessed Father <note>referring to Pope Leo X, the dedicatee</note>, have concerning those matters from the reports of Vasco and the letters and living voice of his fellow soldiers; however, time, which uncovers all hidden things, will reveal them more clearly. They were unable to accomplish anything extraordinary in searching for gold mines, because out of the one hundred and ninety men whom we mentioned Vasco led out from Darien, he used only seventy, or at most eighty, for conducting affairs. The rest were always left behind in the houses of the chieftains; but he says those especially fell into various diseases who had recently been brought from Hispaniola. These men were unable to endure such great calamity, as they had to nourish their stomachs, accustomed to better foods, being content only with provincial bread <note>cassava or maize bread</note> and wild herbs without salt, often with river water, and sometimes even lacking that which is healthy. The earlier residents of Darien, however, had hardened themselves to endure all evils and extreme hunger. Whence he jokingly boasts that he has observed a longer and sharper Lent than your Holiness commands to be observed by the institution of the ancestors. For he says that for four continuous years, he and his companions were rarely sated with the fruits of the earth or trees; they used fish more rarely, and meat most rarely of all. He laments that it came to the point that they were forced to eat mangy dogs and filthy toads and other things of this sort in place of delicate feasts and fine dishes when they could obtain them. We have written more extensively about these things in previous sections; I call the "earlier Darienites" those who first took the land to inhabit under the leaders Nicuesa and Hojeda, of whom few were survivors. Let us now dismiss these matters, and let the victorious Vasco be led back again over the high peaks of the mountains.

Other episodes occurred in this prison, some concerning the cheerfulness of his life, others so remarkably decent that they are worthy of my serious attention. A man who spoke Greek entered the prison and asked, "Where is the man of Tyana?" Taking him aside, he said, "Tomorrow the Emperor will speak with you." It seemed he had heard this from Aelian <note>Casperius Aelianus, the Praetorian Prefect who was secretly a friend to Apollonius</note>. He had rushed to tell him this in secret, for he alone knew of it. "Furthermore," he said, "the prison warden has been told to provide you with everything you might require." Apollonius replied, "You act kindly; but I lead the same life now as I did before these events. I will talk about whatever happens, but I will live by eating; for," he said, "I do not need advice, but is it likely that you will speak with the Emperor?" "By Zeus," he said, "unless he intends to punish me." "And what if he does not look down on you," he asked, "but rather you look down on him?" "You give excellent advice," he said, "and I have so persuaded myself."

"I am glad to see you prepared," he said, "when they bring you in. But you must also be prepared for the Emperor's voice and the harshness of his face. For he speaks with a heavy tone, even when he speaks mildly; and his eyebrow hangs over the character of his eye. His cheek is full of bile, for this he shows most of all. Let us not be terrified by these things, O man of Tyana, for they are more a matter of nature and are always the same."

Apollonius replied, "Odysseus, when he entered the cave of Polyphemus <note>The Cyclops from Homer's Odyssey</note>, had neither heard where he came from before, nor what he ate, nor how his voice thundered, yet he took courage against him, though he was afraid at first, and he left the cave having proven himself a man. It is better for me to be self-sufficient, saving both myself and my companions, for whose sake I am in danger." Having spoken such things to the visitor, and having reported them to Damis <note>Apollonius's loyal disciple and chronicler</note>, he went to sleep.

Around dawn, a secretary of the imperial court arrived and said, "O Apollonius, the Emperor commands you to come to the palace when the market is full <note>mid-morning</note>, not yet to make your defense, but because he wishes to see who you happen to be and to meet with you alone." "Why then do you speak to me about these things?" he asked. "For it is not you," he said, "but he who commands." "By Zeus," said the man of Tyana. "To whom then should I say these things?" The answer to the first point is clear. Just as there is no doubt that men can kill by God’s permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member or others. But in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches who are currently being discussed. The solution to the second point is also clear through this. However, regarding the argument that because God permits the generative power to be harmed by witchcraft for certain reasons, therefore it is also permitted that a member be truly and really removed, this does not hold. It does not mean this always happens, for it would not occur by way of witchcraft, nor do witches intend this when they perform such acts, as they do not have the power to restore the member when they wish and know how. From this, it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by <term>prestigiosa arte</term> <gloss>the art of illusion/deception</gloss>. Regarding the third point, concerning the transformation of Lot’s wife, we say it was true and not by the art of illusion; however, we are now speaking of the art of illusion. Regarding the fourth point, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them, it is said concerning the magicians of Pharaoh that they made true serpents. Demons can produce certain effects upon some imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do upon humans, for whom God has greater care, according to the saying: "Is God concerned about oxen?" Nevertheless, as has been said, they can always, by God’s permission, harm men truly and really, or even by the art of illusion, and through this, the solution to the final argument is also clear.

What need is there in this law of His and in His prophets to search out many things regarding this matter? Or rather, not to search, for they are not abstruse or rare, but to gather the open and frequent ones, and to place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God has willed that sacrifice be made to no one at all except to Himself alone. Behold this one thing, briefly—or rather, grandly and threateningly, but truthfully—spoken by that God whom their most learned men preach so excellently: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest destruction overtake the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out," He says, "except to the Lord alone." Not that He is in need of any thing, but because it is profitable for us that we be His property. For to Him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for You do not need my goods." But the most excellent and best sacrifice of this God is we ourselves. AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

Celsus says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt, having never accomplished anything noteworthy, and that they were never held in any account or number. Now, regarding the fact that they were not fugitives and were not Egyptians, but Hebrews who had resided in Egypt, we have spoken in the preceding pages. If he thinks that their being held in no account or number is established by the fact that their history is not found at all among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to look closely at their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were people who displayed a shadow of a heavenly life upon earth. Among them, nothing else was considered God except the One who is over all, and no one who made images held citizenship. For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in their commonwealth, as the law cast out all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues, which entices the foolish among men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, a law among them such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under the heaven, a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters beneath the earth." And the law indeed intended that they, by communing with the truth regarding each thing, should not fashion things other than the truth, lying about what is truly male or what is truly female, or the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or the kind of creeping things or fish. Solemn and noble among them also is the command: "Do not, having looked up to the heaven and seen the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, be led astray and worship them and serve them."

What kind of commonwealth was that of an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for effeminacy to appear? It is also wonderful that the incitements of the young, the prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of the most just judges, and they had given much proof of a healthy life.

# Through meditation on the Supreme, that which is obscured [is revealed]; from Him, indeed, arise the bondage and liberation of this [individual soul]. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued that the individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss>) is merely a part of the Supreme Self (<term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>the Lord/Supreme Being</gloss>), just as a spark is a part of fire. If this is the case, then just as the spark and the fire both possess the powers of burning and illumination, the individual soul and the Supreme Lord should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream would be possible for the individual soul through its own will. To this, we reply: even though the individual soul and the Supreme Lord stand in the relation of part and whole, the individual soul’s nature is observed to be the opposite of the Lord’s. Does the individual soul then not possess the same nature as the Lord? It is not that it does not possess it; rather, that nature is obscured by the veil of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>) and the like. This obscured nature is revealed only to a being who meditates upon the Supreme Lord, who strives, and who has cleared away the darkness—much like the power of vision, obscured by cataracts, is restored by the potency of medicine—through the grace of the Lord. It is not revealed to all beings by nature. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, arise the bondage and liberation of this individual soul: bondage arises from not knowing the nature of the Lord, and liberation arises from knowing that nature. Thus, the scripture says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. By meditating upon Him, at the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state, the sovereignty of the universe, and becomes one whose desires are fulfilled," and so on.

# Or [it is obscured] due to connection with the body. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why, then, does the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It would be logical for these powers to remain unobscured, just as the burning and illuminating powers of a spark are not obscured. We reply: this is true; however, this obscuration of the individual soul’s knowledge and sovereignty occurs due to its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects of experience. There is an analogy here: just as the burning and illuminating powers of fire, though inherent, are obscured when it is contained within the wood, or as when it is covered by ashes, so too is the individual soul’s knowledge and sovereignty obscured by its connection with the limiting adjuncts (<term>upadhi</term> <gloss>limiting adjuncts</gloss>) of the body and the like, which are created by name and form imposed by ignorance, and by the confusion arising from the lack of discrimination between them. The word "or" is used to exclude the doubt that the individual soul is something other than the Lord. One might argue: let the individual soul be something other than the Lord, since its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why assume a connection with the body? We reply: it is not so; the individual soul cannot be other than the Lord. The scripture begins with "That Divinity thought" and continues with "having entered into this by this individual soul as the Self," referring to the individual soul with the word "Self." Furthermore, it instructs the individual soul about its identity with the Lord, saying, "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Thou Art, O Svetaketu." Therefore, the individual soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured due to its connection with the body. Consequently, the creation of chariots and the like in a dream by the individual soul’s will is not tenable. If the creation of chariots in a dream were a matter of will, no one would ever see an undesirable dream, for no one wills an undesirable thing. As for the argument that the scripture regarding the waking state indicates the reality of the dream state, that comparison is not intended to establish reality, as it would contradict the self-luminous nature of the soul, and the scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and the like in a dream. The comparison is intended to show that the dream appears similar to the waking state because it is constructed from impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious impressions</gloss>) born of the waking state. Therefore, it is established that the dream state is merely an illusion (<term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss>).

# Its absence is in the nerves, in the Supreme Self, according to scripture. || 3.2.7 ||

The Section on the Absence of That [Dream State]. || 3.2.7 ||

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>deep sleep</gloss>) is examined. Regarding this, there are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep. In one place it is heard: "When a person is thus asleep, fully composed, and serene, and does not know any dream, he has entered into these nerves." In another place, after mentioning the nerves, it is heard: "Having moved through them, he rests in the pericardium (<term>puritat</term> <gloss>pericardium</gloss>)." Similarly, in another place, after mentioning the nerves: "He is in them when, being asleep, he does not see any dream; then he becomes one with the vital breath (<term>prana</term> <gloss>vital breath</gloss>) alone." Likewise, in another place: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Similarly, in another place: "Then, O gentle one, he becomes united with the Existent, he has attained his own Self." And also: "Embraced by the omniscient Self, he knows nothing external or internal."

Here a doubt arises: are these—the nerves and the rest—separate places of deep sleep, independent of one another, or are they a single place of deep sleep, dependent upon one another? What is the conclusion? They are separate; why? Because they have the same purpose, and things with the same purpose are not found to be dependent upon one another in any context.

<summary>This passage discusses the nature of the individual soul's obscured knowledge and sovereignty due to its connection with the body, refutes the idea that dream objects are willed creations, and introduces the inquiry into the location of the soul during deep sleep.</summary>

## Thence come speed of mind, independence from the body, and mastery over nature. 48

Speed of mind is the attainment of unsurpassed movement for the body. Independence from the body <term>vikaraṇabhāva</term> <gloss>the state of functioning without the physical senses</gloss> is the ability of the senses to operate in any desired place, time, or object, even when separated from the body. Mastery over nature is the control over all manifestations of <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primordial matter</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolic</gloss>. These are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the senses. 48

## Mastery over all states of existence and omniscience belong to one who possesses only the discriminative knowledge between <term>sattva</term> <gloss>the pure aspect of mind</gloss> and the <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>the pure self</gloss>. 49

For one who has cleansed the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia</gloss>, who rests in the highest clarity, who abides in the supreme state of mastery, and who is established solely in the discriminative knowledge between <term>sattva</term> and the <term>puruṣa</term>, there arises mastery over all states of existence. Regarding the accomplishments arising from the mastery of the five forms of the senses, he says: **Thence come speed of mind, independence from the body, and mastery over nature.** The state of functioning without the physical senses is the ability of the senses to operate independently of the body. Place refers to regions like Kashmir; time refers to the past and future; object refers to subtle elements and the like. Mastery over nature is the control over all manifestations of <term>prakṛti</term>, achieved through the mastery of the senses along with their causal connections. These accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> by those expert in the science of yoga. One might ask: if the senses are mastered, they may become subject to control regarding their objects, but how does this extend to their causes, such as <term>pradhāna</term> <gloss>the primary cause of matter</gloss>? To this he says: **These are...** This refers to the mastery of the five forms of the senses, such as perception. The meaning is that these accomplishments do not arise from the mastery of the senses alone, but from the mastery of their five forms, which include their causes like <term>pradhāna</term>. 48

These <term>saṃyamas</term> <gloss>concentrated meditations</gloss>, which are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action, lead directly or indirectly to the goal. He now shows the intermediate powers of that discriminative knowledge between <term>sattva</term> and the <term>puruṣa</term>, which is the purpose of the faith cultivated by these accomplishments: **Mastery over all states of existence and omniscience belong to one who possesses only the discriminative knowledge between <term>sattva</term> and the <term>puruṣa</term>.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>. From that comes the supreme state of mastery. The mind-stuff, when clouded by <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>, was not under control; but when they are pacified, it becomes subject to the yogi who has attained mastery. In that state of mastery, for the yogi established solely in the discriminative knowledge between <term>sattva</term> and the <term>puruṣa</term>, there is mastery over all states of existence. <margin>Commentary by Su</margin> If one does not know the Way but strives to learn, knowledge and experience will increase daily, yet without a unifying principle, this inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said, "To hear much, select the good and follow it; to see much and remember it, this is the second level of knowledge." If one realizes the Way, one looks back at all artificial actions and sees them as false. To discard falsehood and return to one's true nature is what is meant by "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it with a single thread." To discard falsehood in order to return to one's true nature can be called diminishing. Yet, if the intention to discard falsehood still remains, one has not reached the end. When one forgets even this intention, the heart becomes pure nature with nothing left over. Only then can one act without failing to be in a state of non-action. People all have a desire to grasp the principles of the world, so they create affairs and seek them. When the heart is revealed externally, things will resist it, and thus it can never be attained. The Sage practices non-action, so he has no affairs. His heart is not revealed externally, and things are at peace with him. Although he does not seek to grasp the principles of the world, he acts, and the principles of the world become orderly and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> Those who "pursue learning" are those who have not yet heard the Way. Not having heard the Way, they must seek it broadly, so they increase daily. Those who "pursue the Way" are those who have already heard the Way. Having heard the Way, they practice it, aiming only for non-action. Thus, they diminish daily. However, those who still focus on "diminishing" are still involved in "action." One must even diminish the act of diminishing itself, and only then reach the state of non-action. Non-action is what is called being silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" means that when stimulated, one penetrates all the reasons of the world. To pursue the Way until reaching this state is called "learning that is not learning," "freedom from worry," and "spirit without fixed form." It is like the <term>I Ching</term> <gloss>Book of Changes</gloss> having no fixed body. If it is not the most spiritual thing in the world, who could participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, one can see that to take the world, one must always use non-action. If one uses action, it is not enough to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning, so learning seeks to increase daily. Once one is transformed, one can speak of the Way, so the Way seeks to diminish daily. Increasing allows one to advance in seeking, while diminishing may be difficult to force. Only those with supreme clarity can suddenly cast off attachments and reach the realm of non-action. Thus, they can do nothing and yet leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they are more than sufficient.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> Pursuing learning is for the sake of seeking knowledge, so it increases daily. Pursuing the Way is for the sake of removing falsehood, so it diminishes daily. If knowledge does not reach the ultimate, then the diminishing is not complete. Therefore, increasing is the foundation for diminishing. If one diminishes and diminishes again, falsehood is removed and truth is complete, then there is non-action. When one reaches the state of non-action, there is nothing one does that is not non-action. This can no longer be discussed in terms of increasing or diminishing. When one reaches the ultimate of non-action, even if the world is vast, it is unified by a single thread. If one creates affairs out of a desire to act, even a single object before one's eyes will become tangled and contradictory, let alone the vastness of the world.

The Sage has no fixed heart; he makes the hearts of the common people his heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, and thus virtue is good. To those who are faithful, I am faithful; to those who are not faithful, I am also faithful, and thus virtue is faithful. Elsewhere, I saw Arsaces murdering his wife, and the eunuch Arbaces drawing his sword against Arsaces. Spatinus the Mede was being dragged out of the banquet by the guards, his brow crushed by a golden cup. Similar things to these were to be seen in Libya, and among the Scythians and Thracians in their royal palaces: men committing adultery, murdering, plotting, plundering, perjuring themselves, living in fear, being betrayed by their own kin. Such was the spectacle the kings provided for me. The affairs of private citizens were much more ridiculous. For I saw them too: Hermodorus the Epicurean perjuring himself for a thousand drachmae; Agathocles the Stoic litigating against his student over a fee; Cleinias the orator stealing a bowl from the Asclepieion; and Herophilus the Cynic sleeping in a brothel. Why should I even mention the others who were breaking into houses, litigating, lending money, or demanding payment? The sight was altogether varied and of every kind. "Indeed, Menippus, these things were well worth telling, for it seems they provided you with no small delight." "To go through everything in order, my friend, is impossible, since even to see them was a task. However, the main points of the events appeared as Homer describes those on the shield: for in one place there were feasts and weddings, elsewhere courts and assemblies; in another part someone was sacrificing, while in the neighborhood another appeared mourning. Are being and substance different? Is being that which is stripped of other things, while substance is being together with other things, such as motion, rest, sameness, and difference, and are these the elements of that substance? Is the whole, then, substance, while each of those things is, one being, another motion, another something else? Motion, then, is being by accident. But is substance also by accident, or is it that which completes substance? Or are substance itself and all things there also substance? How, then, is it not so here? Or is it because there all things are one, while here, since the images are divided, one thing is separate from another? It is as in the seed, where all things are together, and each thing is all things, and there is no hand without a head, whereas here, they are separated from one another, for they are images and not true. Shall we say, then, that the qualities there are substances, being differences concerning substance, or concerning being, and that they make differences between substances in relation to one another, and in relation to substance as a whole? Or is this not absurd? But concerning the qualities here, some are differences of substances, such as two-footed and four-footed, while others, not being differences, are called qualities only. And yet, the same thing becomes a completing difference in one case, and not a difference in another, where it does not complete.

First, let the body and limbs of the angler be both swift and strong, neither too fat nor lacking in flesh. For it is often necessary to struggle with powerful fish that possess overweening strength, as they twist and thrash in the embrace of their mother, the brine. He must be able to leap from a rock and spring upon a rock with ease. He must be able to traverse the long path of the deep sea quickly when the labor is intense, to dive into the deepest parts, and to remain amidst the swells just as one lingers on land, working at tasks that men with enduring hearts perform in the sea.

The angler must be very cunning and intelligent, since fish devise many varied schemes when they encounter unexpected snares. He must be especially daring, fearless, and prudent. He should not love the satiety of sleep, but should watch keenly, with an alert heart and wide-open eyes. He should bear well both the winter of Zeus and the thirsty season of the Dog Star <note>original: "Seirios"</note>, and he should desire labors and love the sea. For thus he will be successful in his catch and dear to Hermes.

### **Torah Light**
These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Service, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah is the commandment of "You shall not add and you shall not subtract," <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note> which points to the perfection of the Torah. As the philosophers have said, a thing that is perfect in the ultimate sense cannot have anything lacking or anything in excess. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it were to receive an addition, it would be found not to have been perfect. Therefore, the definition of the perfect is that it has neither lack nor excess. It is known that the Torah depends on His Great Name, which is the Tetragrammaton, as it is written: "The Torah of the Lord <note>original: "YHVH"</note> is perfect," <note>Psalm 19:8</note> as I have elaborated upon this in my tractate *Shevuot*, in the chapter "Torah Light." And as it is written in the *Zohar* regarding this verse: "This is My Name and this is My memorial." <note>Exodus 3:15</note> The letters YH with "My Name" equal 360. The letters VH with "My memorial" equal 248. And it is written: "I am the first and I am the last." <note>Isaiah 44:6</note> He is the Absolute Perfect; there is no deficiency in Him nor addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note> This is a warning against erasing the Name or tearing a stone from the Temple. The letters of the Name are the house in which He, may He be blessed, dwells, and likewise the Temple. It is written: "I am the Lord, My Name is the Holy One, blessed be He; I am One and My Name is One." The letters are like a body for the house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul within them. He who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service refers to the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The commandment came to have a fixed place specifically in the Chosen House, and it states the reason: "To His habitation you shall seek, and you shall come there." <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note> "To His habitation" hints at the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>the indwelling presence of God</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name of the Tetragrammaton, as it is written: "And the Lord is in His holy temple," <note>Habakkuk 2:20</note> which is the secret of the Name Adonai, which is the Divine Presence. For in the Temple, the Glory is unified in the splendor of His strength, and this is "to place His Name there," as the Aramaic translation <note>Targum Onkelos</note> says: "to cause His Divine Presence to dwell." Around the place of holiness, the wicked walk, for they are the <term>kelipah</term> <gloss>shell/husk of impurity</gloss>. ### **And sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inward. This is the secret of the commandment to be diligent in bringing the offering from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch is returned to its root, and it is written regarding them: "There you shall offer," <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note> meaning there they shall have an ascent, and not outside. Since the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, is where holiness resides, we were commanded to be "turn from evil" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. Our Sages of blessed memory hinted at this secret: "The nations outside the Land are not idolaters." The matter is that the nations who are in the Land of Israel, under the dominion of the Honored Name, worship God by "cutting the shoots" <gloss>a metaphor for heresy or undermining the divine unity</gloss>, and this is true idolatry. However, those outside the Land are under the dominion of the external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against tearing one stone from the holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eradicate a "wayward city" <note>Deuteronomy 13:13</note> and not to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Likewise, an inciter and a seducer must be uprooted and eradicated, for he is from the impurity of the primordial serpent who was an inciter, and the Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said: "Cursed is the serpent." Therefore, one does not argue in favor of the inciter. The commandment came not to love him and to hate him, as is said regarding the serpent: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman." <note>Genesis 3:15</note> A false prophet is also like an inciter. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first fruits, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first fruits, which are the beginning, indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they shall go to a holy place, and from there the priests, who are holy to their God, shall take them and eat them in Jerusalem. The secret of the "lesser holy things" and the "second tithe" is that their consumption is in Jerusalem, and this is "like the grain, the wine, and the oil," which are the fathers of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat the lesser holy things until after the blood is dashed, for the blood is the soul. Afterward, the body is permitted for enjoyment. Know that just as the service, which is the offering, is an offering to the Lord, so too is the one who serves. For the essence of the service is that he offers himself, in the secret of "When a man among you brings an offering." <note>Leviticus 1:2</note> The burnt offering is entirely consumed, for it comes because of the thought, the secret of the mind, which is spiritual, and "it shall be burning all the night," <note>Leviticus 6:2</note> for "he devises iniquity upon his bed." <note>Psalm 36:5</note> The lesser holy things are the perfection of the soul and the body.

### **The secret** of the unblemished firstborn is the secret of the holy people of Israel, who are called "My son, My firstborn, Israel." <note>Exodus 4:22</note> They are the unblemished, the perfect congregation, and are called "the sheep of My pasture." <note>Psalm 79:13</note> Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating the holy things when they have developed blemishes and have been redeemed is that the holy people of Israel are called "man" <note>Ezekiel 34:31</note>, and he was holy. Afterward, a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," <note>Genesis 3:21</note> but he has a redemption, in the secret of "And I will give a man in your stead." <note>Isaiah 43:4</note> This was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>the scapegoat</gloss>, "and it shall bear their iniquities." <note>Leviticus 16:22</note> Our Sages of blessed memory said: "The iniquities of the unblemished, which fall upon his head and upon his people." But we were commanded not to cause a blemish in the holy things in order to eat them, for then one is casting a blemish upon the holy things by his own choice. Also, there is the prohibition of work and shearing the holy things, for even the broken tablets are holy.

### **In summary**, the service is the offering, but the internal offering is the man. Likewise, his soul is offered after his death on the altar above, and Michael is the High Priest. Everything is the secret of "For in the image of God He made man." <note>Genesis 9:6</note> Therefore, there is a great warning to be careful in capital cases not to put a man to death except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then he dies by the hand of Heaven, in the secret of "He is the witness and He is the Judge," for the Holy One, blessed be He, is a true witness and a true judge. Likewise, the Sanhedrin must be like this; just as they are true judges, they must be true witnesses. I mean that the truth of the testimony must be clarified to them with absolute clarity, which is the inquiry and investigation. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death." <note>Psalm 116:15</note>

### **And since** "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death," for the holy people of Israel are holy by virtue of their souls, which after their death cleave to the heights, therefore the commandment came: "You shall not cut yourselves, you shall not make any baldness," etc., <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note> "for you are children to the Lord your God." <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note> This is not so for the nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, for it is appropriate for them, since in their death they go to perdition and have no portion in this world or the world to come. This is not so for us; we are children to the Lord. When one departs from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, then on the contrary, we have a permanent dwelling above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to increase mourning and to perform these acts.

### **Let us return** to the matter that the man who serves is himself the offering, as it is written: "When a man among you brings an offering." <note>Leviticus 1:2</note> There is another secret in this: it happens that even below, the man is offered, in the secret of reincarnation. "Man and beast You save, O Lord." <note>Psalm 36:7</note> Therefore, even in the eating of ordinary meat, the meat of desire, we were commanded regarding slaughter and given a great warning against any nick in the knife, for then it is a carcass, and it becomes a carcass in Israel. For who knows what reincarnation is within it? "Love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note> means to choose for him a good death, which is slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies by itself, then the power of impurity spreads and takes hold of it. But when one slaughters it while it is healthy, and there is a spark of holiness in the domestic animal, the wild animal, or the pure bird, then its soul departs in purity.

### **And he who eats** a limb from a living creature is like one who eats from the flesh of his brother when there is a reincarnation of a soul there. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." <note>Deuteronomy 12:23</note> Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure domestic animals, wild animals, and birds all point to the spark that spreads within them, whether it is from the side of impurity or from the side of holiness. I have elaborated on this in the portion of *Shemini*. When Israel conducts themselves in holiness, it is written about them: "And they shall make Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among them," <note>Exodus 25:8</note> for they themselves are the Tabernacle. For so is man in his three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies, the heart corresponds to the Holy Place, and from the belly downward corresponds to the Courtyard of the Holy, as I have elaborated in the portion of *Terumah*. When one eats foods that are from the side of holiness, then they are like offerings brought upon the altar. Regarding this, our Sages of blessed memory said: "Now a man's table atones," as I have elaborated in its place.

### **The matter** of the commandments of the festivals and their offerings, I have written about each one in its special place. The commandment came to rejoice during the festivals and to make the pilgrimage, and "three times a year every male of yours shall appear." <note>Deuteronomy 16:16</note> Our Sages of blessed memory said: "Just as he comes to see, so he comes to be seen." Therefore, if he wishes to be seen in the Temple, where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> and be a faithful servant to his Creator. For without this, it is forbidden to look at a wicked man, and how could he wish to be seen before Him, may He be blessed? He brings a burnt offering of appearance, and then he himself is an offering through the offering that he brings. It is said: "Three times a year he shall appear"—Isaac, who was a perfect burnt offering.

Description of Lima, City of the Kings.

<margin>Appearance of the city of Lima.</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one can also see into every corner, and on both sides is the flat land. Through most of the houses run canals, which bring fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort to the citizens, who can thereby water all their orchards and vegetable gardens, which they keep clean and pleasant. Also,

<margin>Many water mills, with which they grind their grain.</margin>
there are many water mills in this river, in our country's style, where they grind their grain. In short, very rich citizens live here, some of whom have 150,000 ducats. And from this city, ships sail at times with goods worth 800,000 ducats, and some even worth a million. On the east side, high up in the city, is a high mountain on which a crucifix stands. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their beasts, and their dovecotes, their vineyards—though no good grapes, due to the nature of the land—and beautiful gardens, not only full of all kinds of fruits of that land, but also

<margin>Description of the fertility of the land.</margin>
of the Spanish kind, such as figs, pomegranates, limes, lemons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar cane, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. And truly, if the scandalous discord and war were not there, this place would certainly be one of the most beautiful in the entire world to pass one's human life with joy: for the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the entire year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. Also, one has never seen hunger or plague there, or any rain, or claps of thunder, or lightning from the heavens

<margin>Why the City of Kings received its name, and it was built in the year 1535.</margin>
striking: but on the contrary, always a bright, clear, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535. It is named the City of Kings because the people were brought into it on the day of the Three Kings <note>original: "drie Coningen dagh", referring to Epiphany</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish, which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as meat and fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. And the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist falls every day before noon, like a fog, though not unhealthy as it is with us: for those who have pain in the head, washing themselves with this get relief. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will increase daily in people and wealth, even though for many years there were over 500 houses,

<margin>The width and length of the houses of Lima.</margin>
and the city is built very widely, so that there could well be 2,000, because the streets are wide and the market square is large. Each house has 80 feet of land frontage and 160 feet of length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for it is eaten by worms within 2 or 3 years—the houses are built with only one story, yet still very

<margin>Appearance of the houses.</margin>
costly and magnificent with many rooms, halls, and parlors, suitable for living and for hosting foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials that they bake together very thick, and they fill them with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen, all around and above.

<column-break/>

On the walls, they make small arbors of branches where they hide from the sun. They do not need to worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Carchi, S. Michael, S. Francisco. It has been said before that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. We have dealt with the flat land on the shore of the sea until now, starting from the Linea <note>referring to the Equator</note> and Cape Passao to here. It is also to be known that from Tumbes onwards, not only to Lima but much further, the sea coast to the south is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places, where for 10 miles of distance it neither thunders, lightnings, nor rains; but beyond those 10 miles, it does, or as much more or less as the mountains lie from the sea. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but there are 4 or 5 stagnant waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with the water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which take their origin from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from springs, which are few in the mountains. The distances of these rivers have been described here before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from each other, though mostly 7 or 8, by which travelers regulate themselves because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, a mile wide or even wider, sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the situation of the land, there are different fertile trees and grain lands that are cultivated and sown by the people, which they can do throughout the entire year. Also, many kinds of wild trees, cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and lilies, etc., grow around these rivers. And after the Spaniards took the land, they also sowed wheat, making the land moist through some canals that they lead from these rivers, which, because they flow rapidly from high mountains, one can hardly cross without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who travel along the flat land generally keep so close to the sea side that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and it rains a lot, it is dangerous to travel there because of the swelling of the rivers that one must pass, either with certain rafts that they have for that purpose, or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out, and one of the Indians swims in front, pulling that net or the raft with a rope, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of branches. The men wear shirts and cloths to the knees and extending over them, and an upper garment like a cloak. The women wear a dress of cotton according to the length of the body, and although the style of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nevertheless some difference in the adornment of the head: for some wear single cords, some braided, some of one kind, others of different colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, and all are distinguished according to the custom of the land.

Why, then, did he not call the soul the midpoint between intellect and sensation? Because he says that intellect and sensation are certain cognitive powers; but he wishes to convey the mediation that exists in their substances, not that which exists in their powers. And why did he not call it the midpoint between the Idea and the things formed by the Idea? Because it was not his purpose now to teach what its form is, but its substance; and it is not the same thing to speak of the substance of something and its form; he is presenting such a substance. Why did he not place it as the midpoint between intelligible and sensible numbers? Because he will provide the harmony in the following arguments, according to which it holds the midpoint between the separate numbers and the separate harmony, and the sensible numbers and the inseparable harmony of the underlying things. For the soul is neither self-harmony itself, nor is it in the things that are harmonized, according to Plato's thought; rather, self-harmony is uniform, separate, and removed from all things that are harmonized in any way, being only this very thing which is called harmony; but that which is in the harmonized things belongs to others and is naturally moved by others; the harmony of the soul is the midpoint between both; for this is what is primarily harmonized; therefore, it also imparts harmony to others; for that which is able to impart something to another is either the form itself, or has participated in it primarily. It is therefore subordinate to the intelligible harmony, and subordinate to the intelligible numbers; and being superior to the sensible harmony, it is also superior to the sensible numbers. And if one must speak briefly about each of these, each of them is fourfold; for the number is first the divine, second the essential, third the psychic, and last the physical; the one is uniform, the next is unmoved, the next is self-moved, and the next is moved by another. And the harmony is first that which is in the gods, second that which is in the things that truly are, third that which is in the souls, and last that which is in the things harmonized by others. If, therefore, it had been Plato's purpose now to speak about the psychic harmony, he would have said that it is the midpoint between the indivisible and the divisible harmony; but since the discussion at present is about substance, he says that it has grasped the midpoint of the Same and the Other and substance. One must also observe that, just as he has made a return in these matters of the progressions of the psychic substance to the principles; for since the type of mixtures is twofold, one consisting in the mixture of the extremes, as we have in the case of substance, sameness, and otherness, and the other in the gathering of the means back into one whole, in the former he began from substance and ended at the other, but in the latter, conversely, he first harmonized the other with the same, then both with substance, and ended at the substance from which he set out in the progression; and everywhere he holds to the two principles after the One; for even when he was making the soul from the indivisible and the divisible, he placed the indivisible analogous to the limit, and the divisible to the infinite; <unclear>for the infinite is the cause of plurality</unclear>, and the limit of unification; and when he placed the other as in the genera of being, it was of the series of the infinite, and the same, of the limit; and when he mixed these with substance; for substance is uniform, but these are dual and opposed to each other; and he did not cease gathering the plurality until he made the whole one; for the One is superior even to substance itself and the two principles. Since the mixture is twofold, as we have said, one being the constitutive of the elements themselves, and the other of that which is from the elements, Porphyry rightly asked whether he made both of these in the mixing bowl, or one outside the bowl and the other within it; and he decided that he mixes the elements without the bowl <unclear>acting</unclear>; but since the generation of the means occurred according to the meeting of the extremes, the extremes could not at all come together into the same; but in producing that which is from all the middle elements, he uses the mixing bowl, casting the elements into it and mixing them, so that the soul might be one in all things, and of the same color as itself, and homogeneous, with all the genera having permeated through everything, and so that the soul might receive the form, and that which is from the mixing bowl; for the form of each is according to the whole, so that, being a soul-maker, the mixing bowl creates the totality of the soul within itself; therefore, the second mixture is in the mixing bowl alone. Our teacher also agreed with this distinction. Plato also seems, in the arguments concerning the partial souls, to indicate this by saying: and again, into the former mixing bowl, in which he was mixing the soul of the universe, he poured the remainders of the previous things, mixing them; into which he says the soul of the universe was also cast, but not its elements, and in the case of our own, the remainders of the previous things are mixed within it; and these were the means, clearly the second mixture occurring in the mixing bowl <unclear>after another</unclear> than the first according to the creative cause, and the second also according to the life-giving cause, already making the soul from the middle genera; for it was necessary for the creator to act both before the mixing bowl, and with the mixing bowl, just as also after the mixing bowl, using the creative divisions, and the other activities concerning the soul; for after the totality of the soul, the

### On the shame felt from undeserved praise.
## D I A L. XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you are praised unjustly,
> If you condemn it later, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Reason.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy person.

<note>A large ornamental initial L marks the beginning of the response.</note>

*Joy.* It is indeed an evil that often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they are themselves, imagine others to be the same. Hence, they are even more prone than is fair to offer praise: and although I admit that praising the unworthy is a bad thing, it is much worse to disparage the deserving.

*Reason.* I praised an unworthy person.

*Joy.* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if you were ignorant, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another, but to deceive is the crime of the deceiver himself.

*Reason.* The praise of another turns into my own infamy.

*Joy.* On the contrary, it is your own fault or ignorance. For just as there is no praise to be gained from another, there is no infamy to be gained from them either.

*Reason.* I grieve greatly that I praised an unworthy person.

*Joy.* See to it, therefore, that you do not often grieve for that very thing. Beware of rushing rashly into praising or disparaging. For there is a desire for both: and (to speak precisely) it is a disease and a certain itch of a restless tongue that is ignorant of quiet; the bridle and guard of which are numbered among the works of supreme perfection, as Scripture says:

If there is no faithfulness in the flower, why do you go toward every flower?
All trust is placed in You, for You are the pillar and the support.

If they cut their hands at the sight of Joseph’s face,
You have cut two hundred Josephs of the soul from heart and intellect.

From filth and from goodness, You create the form of a person,
So that he flees two leagues away from the scent of filth.

Make him food for the earth, so that he may become pure greenery;
He escapes from impurity when You have breathed the spirit into him.

Come, O heart, go to the sky, go to the pasture of God;
You have grazed long enough in the pasture of beasts.

Place all your desire upon that for which there is no hope,
For it is from that first hopelessness that you have arrived at this side.

Be silent, for the Lord who grants speech will speak,
For He is the one who made the door and the lock, and He is the one who made the key.

It is also used for those suffering from uterine troubles. It is also applied as a liniment, and bull’s gall mixed with opium is applied in doses of two obols. It is beneficial to fumigate the uterus with stag’s hair. They report that hinds, when they feel they are pregnant, swallow a small stone, which, when found in their excrement or in the uterus (for it is found there too), is kept by the pregnant woman as an amulet. Small bones are also found in the heart and uterus that are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. For we have already spoken of the pumice stone found in the uterus of cows in the same way in the section on the nature of cattle. Wolf’s fat applied as a liniment softens the uterus. It relieves pains in the liver. Eating the flesh of a wolf is beneficial for those about to give birth. Or, if they are beginning to go into labor, it should be near them while they eat. It is so effective that it even works against harmful substances applied to the skin. However, for it to arrive <note>meaning to be brought near or consumed</note> is considered fatal. The hare is of great use to women. Dried lung, when drunk, aids the uterus. The liver, with Samian earth and water, is drunk for excessive menstrual flow. The rennet is used for the afterbirth. They avoid bathing for a day. A liniment made with saffron and leek juice, applied on wool, expels dead fetuses. If hare’s uterus is eaten, it is believed that male children will be conceived. This is also achieved by their testicles and rennet. It is said that a hare’s uterus, removed and given to those who have ceased to bear children, brings back fertility. But it is also used by the Magi for conception, and they give it to the husband to drink. Likewise, nine grains of dung are given to a virgin so that her breasts may remain firm forever. Rennet is also used. For this reason, they smear it with honey where they do not want hair to grow back after it has been plucked. For inflation of the uterus, boar’s or pig’s dung applied with oil is beneficial. It is more effective if flour of dry dung is sprinkled into a potion, or if pregnant women or those who have just given birth are in pain. Sow’s milk drunk with honeyed wine aids the labor of women. Drunk by itself, it replenishes the failing milk of nursing mothers. The same substance, when smeared with the blood of a female pig, prevents the breasts from growing too large. If they are painful, they are soothed by drinking ass’s milk. This, taken with added honey, also aids their purgations. The aged tallow of the same animal heals ulcerations of the uterus, and when applied on wool, it softens the hardness of the uterus. When fresh or aged and applied with water, it acts as a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>a depilatory or hair-removing agent</gloss>. The aged spleen of the same animal, applied with water, increases the flow of milk in the breasts. Fumigation corrects uterine issues. Fumigated ass’s hooves hasten labor, so that it may even induce an abortion; it is not used in any other way, as it kills the living fetus. If the fresh dung of the same animal is applied, it is said to stop excessive bleeding remarkably well. The ash of the same dung is also used, which is also beneficial when applied to the uterus. Horse foam applied for forty days before the hair grows prevents it from returning. Likewise, a decoction of stag’s horn. It is better if the horns are fresh. Just as an architect chooses assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work, but will work together with him in the best way, so the statesman, being a master craftsman according to Pindar, and a creator of good order and justice, will not immediately choose friends who are like-minded, and servants who are enthusiastic with him for the good, but rather those who are suited to the specific need at hand, lest they bend him unjustly and violently. For he will appear no different from a builder or carpenter who, through inexperience and error, uses squares, rules, and levels that would cause the work to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking instruments of political men. And one must not slide along with them when they transgress, but must take care that they do not commit errors even out of ignorance. 

This is what disgraced Solon and brought him into disrepute with the citizens. For when he conceived the idea of lightening the burden of debts and the <term>seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking off of burdens</gloss>—which was a euphemism for introducing a cancellation of debts—he shared this with his friends. But they did a most unjust thing; they borrowed a great deal of money beforehand, and a short time later, when the law was brought to light, they were seen to have purchased brilliant houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon was accused of being a partner in the injustice, though he had been wronged. 

Agesilaus, regarding the requests of his friends, became weak and humble himself, like the Pegasus of Euripides, <margin>he would wish</margin> cowering, yielding more than he would wish. And by helping them in their misfortunes more readily than he should have, he seemed to make himself complicit in their injustices. For he saved Phoebidas, who was on trial for seizing the Cadmea without orders, saying that such things should be done spontaneously. And he also saved Sphodrias, who was fleeing trial for an illegal and terrible act; for he had invaded Attica while they were friends and allies. He managed to get him acquitted, softened by the amorous pleas of the boy, and a letter of his to a certain potentate is still circulated, saying: "If Nicias is not guilty, acquit him; if he is guilty, acquit him for my sake; but in any case, acquit him." 

But Phocion would not even join his son-in-law Charillus, who was on trial regarding the Harpalus affair, but saying, "I made you my son-in-law for all that is just," he walked away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not dissuade his brother from tyranny through teaching and entreaty, cooperated with those who killed him. For one must not be a friend "up to the altar" in order not to perjure oneself, as Pericles once said, but up to the point of law, justice, and the common good. When this is overlooked, it leads to great and common harm, just as the failure to punish Sphodrias and Phoebidas led to the ruin of Sparta in the Leuctrian War. 

Since the statesman is not forced by reason to be harsh in dealing with the moderate mistakes of friends, he may even provide for their safety by using the surplus of public affairs to help his friends, and to stand by and work with them. There are also favors that are not subject to reproach, such as helping a friend toward an office, or entrusting him with a glorious administration or a humane embassy, such as one holding the honors of a leader, or an interview with a city on behalf of friendship and harmony. If there is a difficult, prominent, and great task, he should assign it to himself first, and then choose his friend as an associate, as Diomedes did: "If you command me to choose a companion myself, how then could I forget the godlike Odysseus?" And he in turn returns the praise in a fitting manner: "Old man, you ask about these horses, which are new arrivals, Thracian; the good Diomedes killed their master, and twelve companions, all the best." For this yielding to friends adorns the praisers no less than those who are praised.

Epaminondas was the best of men; when he refused Pelopidas's request to release a pimp from prison, and shortly after released him when his mistress asked, he said, "Such favors, Pelopidas, are fitting for mistresses, not for generals." Cato, however, was harsh and stubborn; when Catulus the censor, who was one of his closest friends and acquaintances, asked for the release of one of those being judged by him while he was treasurer, he said, "It is shameful, you who ought to be disciplining us young men, to be cast out by our own servants." For he could have refused the favor by deed, and removed the harshness and bitterness from his words, so as not to appear to be inflicting the pain of the act willingly, but necessarily, because of the law and justice. 

There are also ways in politics to help friends in need of money that are not ignoble. For example, Themistocles, after the battle, seeing a dead man wearing gold necklaces and bracelets, passed by himself, but turning to his friend, said, "Take these, for you have not become Themistocles." For circumstances often give the statesman the opportunity to help his friends; for not everyone is a Menemachus. To one, entrust a paid advocacy on behalf of justice; to another, introduce a wealthy man in need of care and protection; to another, assist in some contract or lease that has profit. Epaminondas, when a friend approached a certain rich man, told him to ask for a talent, as if he himself had ordered it to be given. When the one asked came and inquired about the reason, he said, "Because this man is good, but poor; and you are rich, having stolen much from the city." And Xenophon says that Agesilaus took pride in enriching his friends while he himself was superior to wealth. 

Since, according to Simonides, every lark must have a crest, and every state brings some enmities and differences, it is not least appropriate for the statesman to have considered these matters as well. Most people praise Themistocles and Aristides for laying aside their enmity at the borders whenever they went out on an embassy or a military command, and then taking it up again. To some, the conduct of Cretinas the Magnesian is also exceedingly pleasing. For while he was in political opposition to Hermeias, a man who was not powerful but ambitious and brilliant in spirit, when the Mithridatic War gripped the city and he saw it in danger, he ordered Hermeias to take over the leadership and manage affairs while he himself withdrew. If he wishes to be the general, he should go out of the way, lest by being ambitious toward each other, they destroy the city. The proposal pleased Hermeias, and saying that Cretinas was more warlike than himself, he withdrew with his children and wife. When this was said, the Blessed One replied to Manjushri, the youth: "Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva should proclaim this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, by being established in four things. To represent three water jars, or heaven and earth pouring forth water, they depict the water jar as a heart possessing a tongue. They use the heart because, among them, it is the governing part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of the Egyptian land. They use the tongue because, being always in moisture, they call it the generator of existence. They use three water jars, neither more nor fewer, because the process of the rising <note>referring to the annual flooding of the Nile</note> is, according to them, threefold. They assign one to the Egyptian land, since it is by its own nature generative of water. Another they assign to the ocean, for water comes from there into Egypt during the time of the rising. A third they assign to the rains, which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the time of the Nile's rising. This is what the Sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said that the son of David will only come in a generation that is entirely guilty, and so on. This is the secret of "it has all turned white; he is clean" <note>Leviticus 13:13</note>. In this way, understand that the Fear of Isaac <note>a title for the attribute of Gevurah</note> has no power or dominion when the Supernal Crown <term>Keter</term> <gloss>the highest divine emanation</gloss> shines its face downward, because its great light dims the light of the eyes of the Fear of Isaac. This is the secret of "The Lord make His face shine upon you, and be gracious to you" <note>Numbers 6:25</note>. What is "and be gracious to you"? It means that if you are not worthy of mercy at the time He shines His supernal face, He will give you a gift of grace <note>a free gift not based on merit</note>. This is the secret of "The Lord make His face shine upon you, and be gracious to you."

I will now enlighten your eyes further, with the help of God. Know that wherever you find the light of the face from above, it is a great secret. There are three hundred and ten faces of wrath, and they are all attached to the Fear of Isaac. When the attribute of the Crown shines its face and brings out a banner of mercy, upon which is engraved the attribute of <term>El</term> <gloss>God/Mercy</gloss>—which is the secret of the tithes of the faces of wrath—then all the faces of wrath turn to shine, and they are all transformed into mercy. This is also "Happy is the people that know the joyful shout; O Lord, they walk in the light of Your countenance" <note>Psalm 89:16</note>. One should not rush to consume large amounts of raw food after evacuation, as the body’s nature may draw it in undigested. If something must be consumed, it should be in small, gradual portions so that what enters the body is well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for the blood. As for the evacuation of a humor that has increased in quantity or corrupted in quality, this is distinct from phlebotomy. Any excessive evacuation usually induces fever. If the cessation of a habitual discharge, such as earwax or nasal mucus, causes an obstruction, then resuming that evacuation usually cures it. Know that leaving a remainder of the matter that needs to be evacuated is less harmful than exhausting the evacuation to the point where strength fails. Often, nature will dissolve that remainder. As long as the humor is of the appropriate type and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess. Sometimes you may need to evacuate until the point of fainting. If a person has strong vitality but a large amount of poor humors, evacuate them little by little. The same applies if the matter is highly viscous or strongly mixed with blood, making it impossible to evacuate all at once, as in cases of sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, or chronic boils. Know that diarrhea draws from above and clears from below, so it is suitable for both opposing and corresponding attractions. It is also effective after the materials have settled; if the materials are below, it draws them in the opposite direction and clears them from where they are. Vomiting acts by attraction and clearing in the reverse manner. The state of phlebotomy varies according to the sites from which blood is drawn, as you have learned. Those least in need of evacuation are those with good nutrition and good digestion. Inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say: It is recommended for one who intends to purge or vomit to space out their food, consuming the total amount intended for the day in several sittings, and to make these different foods and different drinks. The stomach, in this state, is prompted to desire the expulsion of its contents either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, taken upon other food, the stomach clings to it, holds it back, and grips it tightly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with a naturally loose constitution, none of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not arise in one who manages their health well; they require something milder. Often, exercise, massage, and bathing are sufficient. If the body is full, and it is filled with the best of humors—namely blood—then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, not diarrhea. If necessity dictates both phlebotomy and evacuation with substances like hellebore or strong medicines, one must begin with phlebotomy. This is among the recommendations of Hippocrates in the book *Epidemics*, and it is the truth. The same applies if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood. However, if the humors are viscous and cold, phlebotomy may increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In general, if the humors are balanced, prioritize phlebotomy; if one prevails later, evacuate it. If they are unbalanced, evacuate the excess first until they are balanced, then perform phlebotomy. Whoever prioritizes medicine over phlebotomy when phlebotomy should have been prioritized for a few days, or whoever has recently undergone phlebotomy and needs evacuation, finds drinking medicine more appropriate. Often, taking purgative medicine when phlebotomy was required leads to fever and agitation. If this does not subside with sedatives, know that phlebotomy should have been performed first. Not every evacuation is needed due to excessive fullness; rather, the severity of the illness may demand it, and the fullness is judged by quality, not quantity. Often, improving one's regimen suffices instead of the phlebotomy required at the time. Often, a need for evacuation arises but is met with an obstacle; in such cases, the only remedy is fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance caused by the fullness. Some evacuation is done as a precaution, such as that needed by those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. One must take precautions before the time arrives and perform the evacuation specific to the illness, whether it be phlebotomy or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. You may be forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as scammony when you need to evacuate bile. In that case, you must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purgation, such as myrobalan, and correct any imbalance that may occur afterward. In patients with tumors of the viscera, their diarrhea and vomiting are weakened. If you are forced to do so, use substances like ivy and safflower. As for polypody, cassia fistula, and the like, Hippocrates said: "Whoever is thin, their nature is easily prompted to vomit." Therefore, it is better to use vomiting for their purification in summer, spring, or autumn, rather than winter. For those with a moderate constitution, diarrhea is more appropriate. If a need for vomiting arises, wait for the summer and avoid it when not necessary. It is necessary to precede diarrhea and vomiting by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and by widening and opening the passages, as this protects the body from exhaustion. Know that accustoming the body to be loose and responsive to the desired diarrhea or vomiting before using strong medicine is one of the successful methods of management. Diarrhea and vomiting in the presence of abdominal emaciation are difficult, exhausting, and dangerous. An emetic medicine may act as a purgative if the stomach is strong, if it is taken during intense hunger, if the drinker has a naturally loose constitution, if they are not accustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is heavy in substance and descends quickly. A purgative may become emetic due to a weak stomach, the extreme dryness of the waste, the unpleasantness of the medicine, or if the person has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge or if it purges matter that is not "cooked" <note>matured/digested</note>, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it through the body, where it takes hold and other humors are transformed into it, increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting in most cases, such as bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some vary, such as phlegm. For a feverish patient, diarrhea is safer in itself. For those whose humor is descending, such as those with intestinal slippage <note>diarrhea/dysentery</note>, vomiting is impossible. The worst purgative medicines are those composed of ingredients that differ strongly in their timing of action, as this disturbs the bowels; the first ingredient purges the second before the second can act, or the first ingredient may purge the second itself. Whoever undergoes diarrhea and vomiting while their body is already clean will inevitably suffer from dizziness, colic, and distress, and what is evacuated will be evacuated with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating waste, there will be no agitation. When agitation begins, it is evacuating what is not waste. If the evacuated humor changes from one type to another during vomiting or diarrhea, it indicates that the body has been cleansed of the humor intended for evacuation.
