One descends into a state of ritual impurity through intention, but one only ascends from that impurity through a change in action. An action removes the status of a previous action and a previous intention, but an intention does not remove the status of an action nor of an intention. If you say that this rule applies only to vessels, which are significant, but that handles <term>yadot</term> <gloss>handles/projections of food</gloss>, which exist for the purpose of eating, are made impure by intention and purified by intention—but have we not learned in a <term>Mishnah</term> <gloss>the foundational text of the Oral Law</gloss>: "All handles of food that were threshed in the threshing floor are pure (and Rabbi Yose declares them impure)." This is understandable according to the one who says "threshed" means "loosened their bundles," but according to the one who says "what does 'threshed' mean? It means literally threshed," what can be said? Here, too, it means they were literally threshed. If so, what is the reasoning of the "others" who say it is like Rabbi Yose? For we learned: "Rabbi Yose declares them impure." What is this? It is understandable there that the reasoning of Rabbi Yose is appropriate for the statement of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who said: "Since they are fit to be turned with a pitchfork." But here, for what are they fit? They are fit for when one gathers them, to hold them by their stalks. The core text: "All handles of food that were threshed in the threshing floor are pure, and Rabbi Yose declares them impure." What does "threshed" mean? Rabbi Yochanan said: "Literally threshed." Rabbi Eliezer says: "He loosened their bundles." It is understandable according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says "threshed" means "loosened their bundles," that this is why Rabbi Yose declares them impure. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, who says "literally threshed," why does Rabbi Yose declare them impure? Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: "Since they are fit to be turned with a pitchfork." Rabbi Eliezer said: "Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork? To tell you that just as this pitchfork turns the grain on the threshing floor from one place to another, so too the prayer of the righteous turns the mind of the Holy One, blessed be He, from the attribute of cruelty to the attribute of mercy."

Third article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

To the third point, we proceed as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things which are prior and better known by nature are posterior and less known to us. But universals are prior by nature, because that from which the consequence of being does not convert is prior in subsistence. Therefore, universals are posterior in the cognition of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us than simple things. But universals are simpler; therefore, they are known later to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined thing falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition. But more universal things are parts of the definition of less universal things, just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "human." Therefore, universals are known later to us. Furthermore, we arrive at causes and principles through effects. But universals are certain principles. Therefore, universals are known later to us. But against this is what is said in the first book of the *Physics*, that it is necessary to proceed from universals to singulars. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive cognition. And because sense is of singulars, but intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. Now, everything that proceeds from potency to act arrives at an incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and act, before it arrives at a perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately. The incomplete act, however, is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known in a certain respect in act, and in a certain way in potency. Hence the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics* that things are first manifest and certain to us in a more confused way. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both the universal whole, in which parts are contained in potency, and the integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in a universal whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing, just as to know "animal" indistinctly is to know animal insofar as it is animal. But to know "animal" distinctly is to know animal insofar as it is rational or irrational, which is to know a human or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "human." And the same reason applies if we compare any more universal thing to a less universal thing. And because sense exits from potency into act just as the intellect does, the same order

of cognition appears in the sense. For according to sense, we judge the more common before the less common, both according to place and according to time. According to place, indeed, just as when something is seen from a distance, it is grasped as being a body before it is grasped as being an animal; and it is grasped as being an animal before it is grasped as being a human, and a human before Socrates or Plato. According to time, because a child from the beginning distinguishes a human from a non-human before they distinguish this human from another human. And therefore, children from the beginning call all men "fathers." Later, however, they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*. And the reason for this is manifest: because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potency to know the principle of distinction, just as he who knows the genus is in potency to know the difference. And thus it is clear that indistinct cognition is intermediate between potency and act. Therefore, it must be said that the cognition of singulars is prior to us than the cognition of universals, just as sensitive cognition is prior to intellectual cognition. But both according to sense and according to intellect, the cognition of the more common is prior to the cognition of the less common. To the first, therefore, it must be said that the universal can be considered in two ways. In one way, according to which the universal nature is considered together with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality—namely, that one and the same thing has a relation to many—proceeds from the abstraction of the intellect, it is necessary that in this way the universal is posterior. Hence, in the first book of *On the Soul*, it is said that the universal animal is either nothing or is posterior. But according to Plato, who posited subsistent universals, according to this consideration, the universal would be prior, because particulars according to him are only through participation in subsistent universals, which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself, namely of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus it must be said that there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, according to which way those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more common is prior by nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of a human and an animal. For an animal is generated before a human, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior by nature to potency, and the perfect prior to the imperfect. And in this way, the less common is prior by nature than the more common, such as a human is prior to an animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a human. To the second, it must be said that the more common universal is compared to the less common as a whole and as a part: as a whole, indeed, insofar as in the more universal, not only is the less universal contained in potency, but others as well—as under "animal" not only human but also horse; as a part, however, insofar as the less common contains in its definition not only the more common but also others, as "human" contains not only "animal" but also "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition than "human." But "human" is prior in our cognition than the fact that "animal" is a part of its definition. To the third, it must be said that any part can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing prevents knowing the parts before the whole, such as stones before a house. In another way, according to what they are as parts of this whole, and thus it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. O friend, this moon intensifies the agony of love in my heart. What is it like? It is a friend to the mind-born one, that is, Kama <note>the god of love</note>. She speaks out of the memory of the state of separation from Murari. What is it like? It possesses a radiance like the radiance of Murari's lotus-face, which is pale from separation. Therefore, even though it conceals the pain, it does so. This is what is meant: although it destroys my pain by possessing the luster of Murari's face, which was pale from my separation, as a friend of desire, it certainly causes pain. Even though it is not to be accepted, because he is situated in relation to it, there was no sorrow; now, knowing him to be attached to another, I cannot remain.

"Hamsalilaka" <gloss>swan-like play</gloss> and so on. "Lava, lesa, kana, arnava" <gloss>a small amount, a particle, a drop, an ocean</gloss> is from the <term>Amara</term> <gloss>Amara-kosha, a Sanskrit lexicon</gloss>. <7> Regarding "Sri Jayadeva": The love-play of Hari, that is, Krishna, composed by Sri Jayadeva, may it cause the impurities of the Kali age, that is, the sins of the listeners and readers, to be pacified, that is, destroyed. <8> Now she says that even this moon causes greater distress: "In separation." "Aye" is used in sorrow. This moon, which is visible, intensifies, that is, expands, the agony of love, that is, the suffering of desire, in my heart to such a degree. What is it like? It possesses the radiance of the lotus-face of Murari, that is, Krishna, which is pale, that is, grey, due to separation from me. And thus, by seeing the moon, which is like the lotus-face of such a Krishna, great agony arises due to the memory of Krishna's lotus-face. What is it doing? It is concealing the pain. And thus, by seeing the moon, such a destruction of discernment occurs that the mind remembers only him, even though he has committed an offense through his methods. She states the reason for it being a cause of distress: "Of the mind-born one." It is a friend to the mind-born one, that is, Kama. And thus, because I did not follow Krishna even though he was nearby, Kama has become my enemy due to the transgression of his command. The moon, wishing to assist his friend, also causes distress. The moon is famous as being born from the mind of Krishna, and Kama is famous as being born from the mind. Because of their brotherhood, there is friendship between Kama and the moon; hence, the word "manobhuva" <gloss>mind-born</gloss> is used for Kama. And thus the <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>Vedic scripture</gloss> says: "The moon was born from the mind, the sun was born from the eye." "Vedana" <gloss>pain</gloss> refers to both knowledge and suffering. It also refers to fear, anger, sorrow, confusion, and memory, according to the <term>Vishva</term> <gloss>a lexicon</gloss>. "Tiro" <gloss>concealment</gloss> is used in the sense of disappearance and in the sense of being oblique. <5>

When the lion awoke the next morning, the judge entered with a group of his prominent companions, carrying a document containing what Dimna had said in his excuses. The lion took the document and ordered them to leave him.

Then he sent for his mother and read the document to her. It distressed her, and she said, "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The lion said, "I will not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said, "I do not see that you know what harms you from what benefits you. I believe that Dimna, through your prolonged consideration of his case, will stir up against you matters you will be unable to withstand or overcome."

She then stood up and left in anger. The next day, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing.

The judge said to him, "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life once the accusation is fixed in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt. This will free you from the consequences of the afterlife, and a good reputation may return to you for two reasons: first, your ability to find exits and fabricate excuses that defend yourself; and second, your confession of guilt, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: death in a state of honor is better than life in a state of disgrace."

Dimna answered him, saying, "Judges do not judge based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. You know that suspicion does not replace the truth in any way. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself better than you do, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My case has only appeared ugly to you, if that is indeed the case, because you suspected that I strove to commit this."

A commotion fell upon the entire court,
A tumult seized the mind of that Sultan.

The hearts of the city's elite and commoners were lost,
Wondering what distress and calamity had occurred.

Is a powerful enemy intent upon us,
Or has a deadly plague arisen from the unseen?

For the jester had arrived with harsh speed,
Having killed several Arabian horses along the way.

The people gathered at the King's palace,
Asking why the jester had come in such haste.

From his haste and his frantic gestures,
A clamor and anxiety fell upon Termez.

One man was striking his knees with both hands,
Another was crying "Woe!" out of fear.

From the clamor, the strife, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart was lost to a hundred kinds of imagination.

Everyone was casting omens based on conjecture,
Wondering what fire had fallen into the garment.

He sought a path, and the King quickly granted him one;
When he kissed the ground, the King asked, "What was it?"

Whoever asked him about his sour state,
He would place a finger on his lips, signaling, "Be silent."

His demeanor increased the King's anxiety;
Everyone became bewildered and stunned by his state.

The jester signaled, "O King of generosity,
Grant me a moment to catch my breath,

So that my reason may return to me for a moment,
For I have fallen into a world of wonders."

After an hour, when the King's throat and mouth
Had become bitter from anxiety and suspicion—

For he had never seen the jester like this,
And there was no companion more pleasant to him than he;

He was always making jokes and witticisms,
Keeping the King happy and laughing.

He would make him laugh so much while sitting
That the King would hold his belly with both hands,

For from the force of laughter, his body would sweat,
And he would fall forward from his laughing.

Yet today, he was so pale and sour,
Placing his hand on his lips, saying, "O King, be silent."

Anxiety upon anxiety, and imagination upon imagination,
What calamity would come to the King?

For the King's heart was filled with grief and caution,
Because the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty.

He had killed many kings in that region,
Either by trickery or by the power of that stubborn one.

This King of Termez was in anxiety because of him,
And the jester's art only increased that anxiety.

He said, "Speak quickly, what is the situation?
From whom is this tumult and clamor of yours?"

He said, "I heard in the village that the King
Had a herald proclaim on every highway:

'I seek someone who will ride for three days
To Samarkand, and I will give him treasures.'

'I will give him treasures in return,
When the purpose is achieved through his message.'

I rushed to you for that reason,
To tell you that I do not have that ability.

Such agility does not come from one like me;
Do not fasten the thread of this hope upon me."

Now he delivers the message:

Tell her this, O long-lived one, to do a favor for me and for yourself:
Speak thus, your companion, residing in the hermitage of Ramagiri,
Alive and well, asks after your welfare, O delicate one, though separated.
For this is the first greeting for living beings prone to misfortune. (41)

"Tell her this": O long-lived one. The suffix <term>matup</term> is used here in praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of helping others. "By my word," that is, by my request, "and to do a favor for yourself," meaning to fulfill yourself through the act of helping another. Even though the self is the object of the act of helping, the genitive case is not contradictory here, as in the expression "he helps him." As Bharavi says, "That wealth is useful by which one helps others." And Sriharsha says, "To help the virtuous, to see wealth, to travel through the sky." And the statement of the master, "Because the accusative is seen in some places, it is so for all," is a statement of the master, not the masterless. Speak thus to her, your beloved. What should he say? "O delicate one, your companion, your husband, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, that is, Chitrakuta, is alive," meaning he has not died. He gives the reason for his survival: "Separated," being unhappy due to the separation, "he asks after your welfare." The verb "to ask" takes two objects. Indeed, for living beings whose misfortunes are easily attained, this very inquiry about welfare is the first thing that must be asked. The suffix <term>nyat</term> is used in the sense of necessity.

Xiangling smiled and said, "No wonder I often take an old book of poetry and read a poem or two in my spare time. Some are matched perfectly, while others are not. If this determination is sincere on your part, and your intention to strive in this pursuit is sound, you will praise your journey at dawn and attain the blessing of your endeavor. If he leaves two sisters and a wife, and he bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the wealth after the bequest, the method for this is to establish the estate at twelve shares. Each sister receives one-third of what remains of the wealth after the bequest. This is wealth minus a bequest. You know that one-eighth of what remains, together with the bequest, equals the portion of a sister. So, one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest. One-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest, together with the bequest, equals the portion of a sister. That is one-eighth of the wealth and seven-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals three-eighths of the wealth and one-third of the bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. Subtract three-eighths of the wealth from the wealth, and five-eighths of the wealth remains, which equals three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals five bequests and four-fifths of a bequest. The wealth is twenty-nine, the bequest is five, and the portion is eight.

Its sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman (with a fatha on the qaf and the ra). Before him, it belonged to his brother Musa, who ceded it to King al-Nasir in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent an emir and an army there, but then Sultan Badr al-Din seized it, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this sultan outside the city as he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my mount for him, so he dismounted from his, and I greeted him. He received me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a visitor dismounts for them, they dismount for him; they are pleased by this action and increase their honor toward him. If he greets them while mounted, it displeases them and does not satisfy them, which can be a cause for the visitor being deprived of favor. This happened to me with some of them, and I will mention it. When I greeted him, he remounted and I remounted. He asked me about my situation and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be lodged in the best of lodgings. He would send much food, fruit, and sweets in silver platters, as well as wax candles. He provided me with clothing, a mount, and treated me well. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray (pronounced with a fatha on the hamza, a sukun on the qaf, and a fatha on the sad and the ra). It is one of the most beautiful and well-constructed cities in the land of Rum <note>Anatolia</note>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and gardens on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through its houses. It contains trees and grapevines, and there are many gardens inside it. Carpets are made there, attributed to the city, from sheep's wool, which have no equal in any other land. From there, they are transported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the obedience of the King of Iraq. We stayed there at the hospice of the Sharif Husayn, who is the deputy there for the Emir Eretna. Eretna is the deputy for the King of Iraq in the lands of Rum that he has seized. This Sharif is one of the <term>fityan</term> <gloss>young men/knights of the chivalric orders</gloss>, and he has a large following. He honored us with extreme hospitality and performed the same actions as those who preceded him. Then we traveled to the city of Nigde (pronounced with a fatha on the nun, a sukun on the kaf, and a fatha on the dal). It is one of the cities of the King of Iraq, a large and populous city, though some of it has fallen into ruin. There are waterwheels on it, both inside and outside, from which the gardens are irrigated. Fruits are abundant there. They dug a pit, covered it with hurdles and earth, and scattered the excess soil <margin>what about the tiger</margin> elsewhere. The male tiger, coming along incautiously, fell into the pit and was impaled on sharp stakes fixed at the bottom of the trench. It stunned the entire neighborhood with its roaring, and the mountains echoed with that screeching. It was killed by huge stones thrown from the edges of the trench onto the beast, which was already pierced by the stakes. It shattered the spears, which had been fixed by hand and thrown from above, into a thousand splinters and a thousand fragments. Half-dead and bloodless, it filled those watching with terror, considering what it might have done had it been free and unharmed. A certain Juan de Ledesma, a man from Seville, a friend of Vasco <note>referring to Vasco Núñez de Balboa</note> and his companion in labors, confessed to me that he had eaten of that tiger. When asked why they call it a tiger, those who have never seen a tiger respond that they judge it to be a tiger from its spots, its ferocity, its dexterity, and other signs given by authors, although many of them claim to have seen spotted leopards and panthers themselves. After the tiger was killed, they followed its tracks toward the mountains and reached its den, its marital home.

In the absence of the mother, they took two cubs that were still dependent on their mother's milk. Changing their plan—for they had intended to send them to Spain once they were grown—they carefully placed iron chains around their necks and returned the little ones to the mother's den to be suckled. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty, with the chains left exactly where they had been placed. They believe the cubs were torn to pieces and carried off by the mother in a rage, so that no one else could enjoy them. They assert that they could not have been freed from the chains alive by any means. The skin of the killed tiger was stuffed with dried herbs and straw and sent to Hispaniola to the Admiral and the leaders from whom these new lands expect laws and aid. Both those who suffered inconveniences from the tiger and those who handled its skin related these things to me; we accept what is given. We must return to Pacra, from whom we departed. Having entered the deserted <term>boios</term> <gloss>houses</gloss> of Pacra, Vasco strives to attract Pacra. Through envoys <margin>Pacra returns</margin> he signifies to Pacra the same things we mentioned were signified to the others. For a long time, Pacra refused. Threats were added to his refusal. Finally, he came, accompanied by three chieftains. Vasco writes that Pacra was so deformed, filthy, and foul that he confesses he had never seen anything more hideous. He says that nature had granted him only a human form; otherwise, he was a brute, wild, and monstrous animal. He says his morals matched his appearance and features. He was abusing the daughters of four neighboring chieftains, whom he had seized by force, with detestable lust. Many things regarding the obscene morals of Pacra and injuries of another kind were hurled by the neighboring chieftains before Vasco, as if before a praetorian judge or Hercules the avenger; they demanded that punishment be inflicted upon Pacra. He threw the monstrous beast, along with the three chieftains themselves who obeyed Pacra and suffered from the same diseases, into the jaws of the war dogs, and ordered their mangled corpses to be burned. Miraculous things are reported about the dogs with which they enter battles. They rush at armed natives just as precipitously as they do at fleeing deer or wild boars if they are pointed out with a finger. It sometimes happened that there was no need for swords, arrows, or other weapons to rout the enemies encountered; for when the signal was given and the dogs were released to lead the column, the enemies, terrified by the grim appearance and unusual barking of the mastiffs, <margin>wonders about the dogs</margin> abandoned the battles and ranks, stupidly stunned by the prodigious invention. ### CHAPTER LXVI.

**How another day we sent messengers to the Caciques of Tlascala, entreating them for peace, and what they did regarding it.**

After the battle I have recounted had passed, in which we captured the three principal Indians, our Captain Cortes sent them off immediately, and with the two who were in our camp who had gone other times as messengers, he ordered them to tell the Caciques of Tlascala that we entreated them to come at once in peace, and to grant us passage through their land to go to Mexico, as we had sent to tell them other times: and that if they do not come now, we will kill all their people, and because we love them much, and wish to have them as brothers, we would not wish to anger them, if they had not given cause for it, and many flattering words were said to them to attract them to our friendship: and those messengers went willingly at once to the capital of Tlascala, and delivered their embassy to all the Caciques, already named by me: whom they found gathered with many other elders and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and they were very sad, both from the bad outcome of the war, and from the death of the captains who were their relatives or sons who died in the battles, and it is said that they did not wish to listen to them willingly; It seemed that he had heard this from Aelianus. "I understand," he said, "the secret matter. For he alone knows it." "Indeed," he said, "it has been announced to the one in charge of the prison that you are to have whatever you find necessary." "Not even someone to advise you," he said, "on how to speak to the king, Apollonius?" "By Zeus," he said, "unless he tries to persuade me to flatter him." And Apollonius said, "Odysseus, when he entered the cave of Polyphemus, without having heard beforehand how large he was, or what he ate, or how his voice thundered, took courage, even though he was afraid at first, and left the cave having been deemed a man. For me, it is sufficient to depart, having saved myself and my companions, for whose sake I am in danger." Having discoursed in this way to the visitor, and having reported it to Damis, he slept.

At dawn, a secretary from the royal courts arrived and said, "The king commands you, Apollonius, to come to the palace when the market is full, not yet to make your defense, but because he wishes to see who you are, and to speak with you alone." "Why then," he said, "do you speak to me about these things? Are you not Apollonius?" "By Zeus," said the man from Tyana, "I am." "To whom then," he said, "should I say these things?" Once found, we identify the day of the week for the beginning of the year and its nature. Once we know the beginning of the year and its nature, and we combine that nature with the common or intercalary status, we can determine the start of the following year.

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The goal of alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>
He has destined them to penetrate. From these things, gather that it is necessary to proceed according to my prescription, and by no means according to yours. Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still thunder many things against me, my Monarchy will nevertheless stand, while yours goes to ruin. I do not write so prolixly about Alchemy in vain, but I do it with this mind and purpose, that from these things you may know closely and solidly what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended by the fact that neither gold nor silver comes from it. But rather, this must be carefully attended to, that through it secrets may be discovered, and the deceptions of the <term>seplasiarii</term> <gloss>perfumers or apothecaries who sell adulterated drugs</gloss> may be exposed, by which the crude common people are deceived, while they serve them for one florin what they would not redeem for a single coin. Such are their precious secrets.

<margin>Poison exists even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is forced to admit this. If this is therefore true, I ask you now whether poison should not be separated from the good and useful, and the good accepted, and the evil left behind? Indeed, it is necessary. If, therefore, it is necessary, I ask you to explain to me how this is separated in your workshops? For among you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted to admit that poison lies hidden there, and you are asked where it finally goes, you then bring forth I know not what about corrections, which extract and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is ventilated.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, after Diagridium <note>a purgative preparation of scammony</note> is mentioned. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it was at first? And yet you boast in the meantime that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it escaped to?
<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test this, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know that not sluggishly. Thus you also correct Turbith <note>a purgative root</note>, and call it Diaturbith. These are your kinds of corrections, which would befit rustics and should be given to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see whether you will not feel the poison.
<margin>What "correcting" means to physicians.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* Whoever is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who has been punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; it lies with them, not with you. Now, in this case, the Physician has nothing more to consider than that the poison should be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without any harm. The same is to be understood equally of all other things, namely, that a similar separation is necessary. That not yet being done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your place, or the greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will remain.

Now, therefore, at last, if that true foundation is necessary which removes the poison, how does Alchemy perform this? For it is necessary that this be done in such a way that, if Mars <note>iron</note> is in the Sun <note>gold</note>, Mars should be removed, and if Saturn <note>lead</note> dwells in Venus <note>copper</note>, it should be separated from it. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist in them. But those bodies which are contrary, it is necessary that some of them be entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety may be removed, and the evil which you seek may be taken away from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so much less useful is Medicine which does not pass through fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into another generation, which ought to conduce to and assist man. And should this not deservedly be considered the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to apply poisons, but secrets.
<margin>Workshops criticized.</margin>
But all those workshop preparations, however many there are, do not contribute even a letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are occupied simply in correcting, just as if a dog has farted in a room, and that stench is quieted either by troches and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask, does the stench not remain in the room afterwards just as it did before? And although it may not be perceived by smell, is it therefore permitted for anyone to say that the stench has been separated and no longer remains? Indeed, it is present, but corrected by fumigation. Thus, therefore, the fumigation and the stench enter the nostrils together. Such also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who dull an <term>aleopathic</term> <gloss>a term used by Paracelsus to denote a harsh or harmful medicine</gloss> with sugar, so that it may inflict no harm. Thus, sugar and honey are their master-work. Thus they also correct gentian with theriac <note>a complex medicinal antidote</note>. But are these not works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the princes of Physicians. But who is so stupid that he does not immediately smell that these things are worth nothing? What else, I ask, can they boast of regarding their remedies, other than to say, *This Electuary is sweet, made of aromatics, sugar, and honey.*

The answer to the first point is clear. There is no doubt that just as men can kill by God’s permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member or others. But in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches who are currently being discussed. The solution to the second point is also clear through this. However, the argument that because God permits the generative power to be bewitched for certain reasons, therefore it is also permitted that a member be truly and really removed, does not hold. This is because such a thing would not happen by way of witchcraft, nor do witches intend this when they perform such acts, as they do not have the power to restore the member when they wish and know how. From this, it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by illusory art. Regarding the third point, concerning the wife of Lot, we say: it was true and not by illusory art, whereas we are now speaking of illusory art. Regarding the fourth point, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said, concerning the magicians of Pharaoh, that they made real serpents. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen cannot exist anywhere, no illusory deception can occur in the eye of the observer, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. Furthermore, if it is said that that form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be. First, because air is not receptive to any form or figure. But the unlearned, and even the philosophers themselves, to whom the truth of the Lord’s gifts has not truly proceeded, nor do they have the knowledge of the immortal Jupiter, not listening to both the gods and divine men, have indeed rejected all the gods, but they have chosen not only not to hate the demons, who are forbidden, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform the only things through which God is adored. For God, as the Father of all, needs nothing, but it is good for us when we adore Him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to Him through imitation and instruction from Him. For instruction purges the intellect, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward Him. He indeed preached well about God the Father and said with what morals He should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whether the life of the saints is praised or blamed. But it was only among the Christians, or it is slandered as much as the demons—whom they think are gods—desire, as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in the theaters and temples for the sake of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to God, and from this to understand where there is a building up and where there is a ruin of morals. But who said this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and fitting lie, that Christians would rather revere than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we, in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love along with the celestial holy angels and the powers of God, whom we consider most blessed as fellow citizens, forbids sacrifice in His law which He gave to His people, the Hebrews, and He threatened it very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone think that it was commanded not to sacrifice to the worst demons and earthly spirits, whom he calls mimes or lesser ones, because they themselves were also called gods in the holy scriptures, not of the Hebrews

but of the Gentiles, which the seventy interpreters clearly placed in the psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons," lest anyone therefore think that it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, but that it was permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones, either all or some, he immediately added: "except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only, lest perhaps someone, because he says "to the Lord alone," might believe that God is the only one to whom he thinks he must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood in that way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this philosopher gives such great testimony, gave a law to His own people, the Hebrews, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but already spread among all nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there in this law of His and in His prophets to search for many things about this matter, or rather, not to search? For they are not hidden or erased, but are clear and frequent to collect, and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that He willed that sacrifice be offered to no one at all except only to Himself, the true and supreme God. Behold, this one thing, briefly or rather grandly, menacingly, but truthfully said by that God whom their most learned men preach: let it be heard, feared, and fulfilled, lest the eradication follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," He says, "shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." Not that He needs any thing, but because it is expedient for us that we be His. For it is sung to Him in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for You do not need my goods." But the most excellent and best sacrifice of Him is we ourselves. This is His city, the mystery of which thing we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have disputed in the preceding books. For the prophets of the Hebrews interpreted the oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future were to cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting, as we now see happening, were to offer one sacrifice.

AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

Celsus says that the Christians are fugitives from Egypt, who have never done anything noteworthy, and have never been of any account in speech or in number. Regarding the claim that they were not fugitives, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had resided in Egypt, we have spoken in the preceding sections. If he thinks that their being of no account in speech or in number is established by the fact that their history is not particularly found among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to dwell upon their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were people who demonstrated a shadow of a heavenly life upon earth. Among them, nothing else was considered God except the One who is over all, and no one who made images held citizenship. For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in their commonwealth, as the law cast out all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues, which draws the foolish among men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, a law among them such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under the heaven, a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters underneath the earth." And the law indeed intended that they, by communing with the truth regarding each thing, should not fashion things other than the truth, misrepresenting the truly male or the truly female or the nature of beasts or the race of birds or the kind of fish. It is also solemn and noble among them that one should not "look up to the heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, and be led astray and worship them and serve them."

What kind of commonwealth was that of an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for effeminacy to appear? It is also wonderful that the incitements of the young, the prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of the most just, and they had given much proof of a healthy life.

# But by meditation on the Supreme, that which is obscured [is revealed]; from Him, indeed, are the bondage and liberation of this [individual soul]. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued: The individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss>) is merely a part of the Supreme Self (<term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>the Lord/Supreme Being</gloss>), just as a spark is a part of fire. If this is so, then just as the spark and the fire both possess the powers of burning and illumination, the individual soul and the Supreme Lord should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, due to the soul's power of knowledge and sovereignty, the creation of chariots and the like in dreams would be possible through mere will. To this, we reply: Even though the individual soul and the Supreme Lord stand in the relation of part and whole, the difference in their nature is directly perceived. Does the individual soul then not possess the same nature as the Lord? It is not that it does not possess it; rather, that nature, though present, is obscured by the obstruction of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>) and the like. This obscured nature is revealed only to a person who meditates on the Supreme Lord, who is striving, and whose darkness has been dispelled—just as the power of vision, obscured by cataracts, is revealed by the potency of medicine—through the grace of the Lord. It is not revealed to all beings by nature. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, proceed the bondage and liberation of this individual soul: bondage arises from the lack of knowledge of the Lord's true nature, and liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. Thus, the scripture says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of afflictions, birth and death cease. By meditation upon Him, at the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state, the universal sovereignty, and becomes one whose desires are fulfilled," and so on.

# Or [it is obscured] due to connection with the body. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why, then, does the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It would be logical for knowledge and sovereignty to remain unobscured, just as burning and illumination are in a spark. We reply: This is true; however, this obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs due to its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experiences of objects. There is an analogy here: just as the burning and illuminating powers of fire, though inherent, are obscured when the fire is contained within the wood, or as when it is covered by ashes, so too is the knowledge and sovereignty of the soul obscured by its connection with the body, which is created by name and form imposed by ignorance, and by the confusion of identity resulting from that. The word "or" (<term>va</term>) is used to exclude the doubt that the soul is distinct from the Lord. One might object: Let the soul be distinct from the Lord, since its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why assume a connection with the body? We reply: It is not so; the distinctness of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. The scripture begins with "That Divinity thought" and continues with "having entered [the body] with this living self," referring to the soul as the Self. Furthermore, it instructs the soul in its divinity, saying, "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Thou Art, O Svetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured due to its connection with the body. Consequently, the creation of chariots and the like in dreams by the soul's will is not possible. If the creation of chariots in dreams were by will, no one would ever see an undesirable dream, for no one wills an undesirable thing. As for the argument that the scripture regarding the waking state declares the reality of dreams, that statement of similarity does not imply reality, as it would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and the like in dreams. That statement is intended to convey that dreams are similar to the waking state because they are caused by impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious impressions</gloss>) arising from the waking state. Therefore, it is established that dreams are mere illusion (<term>maya-matra</term> <gloss>mere illusion</gloss>).

# Its absence [is] in the nerves and in the Self, according to the scripture. || 3.2.7 ||

The Section on the Absence of That [Dream State]. || 3.2.7 ||

The state of dreaming has been examined; now the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>deep sleep</gloss>) is to be examined. Regarding this, there are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep. In one place it is heard: "When a person is thus asleep, completely serene, and knows no dream, he has then entered into the nerves." In another place, after mentioning the nerves, it is heard: "Moving along these, he rests in the pericardium (<term>puritat</term> <gloss>pericardium</gloss>)." Similarly, in another place, after mentioning the nerves: "He is in them when he is asleep and sees no dream; then he becomes one with the vital breath (<term>prana</term> <gloss>vital breath</gloss>) alone." Likewise, in another place: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Similarly, in another place: "Then, O gentle one, he becomes united with the Existent, he has attained his own Self." And also: "Embraced by the omniscient Self, he knows nothing external or internal."

Here a doubt arises: Are these, the nerves and the rest, independent and distinct places of deep sleep, or are they one place of deep sleep, being mutually dependent? What is the conclusion? They are distinct; why? Because they have the same purpose—and things with the same purpose are not mutually dependent anywhere.

<summary>This passage discusses the nature of the individual soul as a part of the Supreme, explaining that its divine powers are obscured by the body and ignorance, and introduces the state of deep sleep as a return to the Self.</summary>

## Thence comes speed of mind, the state of having no instruments, and mastery over nature. 48

Speed of mind is the attainment of unsurpassed movement for the body. The state of having no instruments <term>vikaraṇabhāva</term> <gloss>the ability of the senses to function independently of the physical body</gloss> is the attainment of the functioning of the senses in accordance with one's desired place, time, and object, even when separated from the body. Mastery over nature <term>pradhānajaya</term> <gloss>control over the primary cause of matter</gloss> is the state of having power over all manifestations of nature. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolic</gloss>. These are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the senses. 48

## Mastery over all states of existence and omniscience belong to one who possesses only the discriminative knowledge between the purity of consciousness <term>sattva</term> and the Self <term>puruṣa</term>. 49

For one whose intellect <term>buddhisattva</term> <gloss>the pure, luminous aspect of the mind</gloss> has been cleansed of the impurities of passion <term>rajas</term> and inertia <term>tamas</term>, who resides in the highest clarity and the supreme state of mastery, and who is established solely in the discriminative knowledge between the purity of consciousness and the Self, there arises mastery over all states of existence. All qualities <term>guṇas</term> are essentially...

<column-break/>

He states the accomplishments resulting from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **Thence comes speed of mind, the state of having no instruments, and mastery over nature.** The state of having no instruments is the functioning of the senses when separated from the body. Place refers to regions like Kashmir; time refers to the past and so on; object refers to subtle things and so on. Mastery over nature is the power over all manifestations of nature, resulting from the mastery of the senses in their causal state. These accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> by those skilled in the science of Yoga. One might ask: if the senses are mastered, they may become obedient along with their objects, but what does this have to do with their causes, such as the primary nature <term>pradhāna</term>? To this, he says: **These are attained...** through the mastery of the five forms of the senses, such as perception. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not arise from the mastery of the senses alone, but from the mastery of their five forms, which include their causes, such as the primary nature. 48

These are the <term>saṃyamas</term> <gloss>concentrated meditations</gloss> that are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action, both directly and indirectly, through the faith generated by the attainment of their respective accomplishments. He now shows the intermediate manifestations of that discriminative knowledge between the purity of consciousness and the Self, which is the goal of these practices: **Mastery over all states of existence and omniscience belong to one who possesses only the discriminative knowledge between the purity of consciousness and the Self.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of passion and inertia. From that comes the supreme state of mastery. The mind-stuff <term>cittasattva</term> was previously overwhelmed by passion and inertia and was not under control. When those are pacified, it becomes subject to the yogi who has attained mastery. In that state of mastery, the yogi who is established solely in the discriminative knowledge between the purity of consciousness and the Self attains mastery over all states of existence. He explains this further: **All qualities are...**

<margin>Commentary by Su</margin> To not know but strive to learn, to increase one's hearing and seeing day by day without a way to unify them, is to inevitably become burdened. Confucius said, "To hear much, select the good and follow it; to see much and remember it, this is the second level of knowledge." If one knows the Way, then one looks back at all false actions and realizes they are nothing but delusion. To remove delusion and return to one's nature is what is called "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it with one thread." To forget the mind in order to return to pure nature is what is meant by diminishing. If one does not yet reach the point of forgetting even the act of forgetting, then this mind is not yet purely returned to nature. There is no remainder, and only then can one act without losing the state of non-action. People all have the desire to take the world and finish the affairs of principle, so they create affairs and seek them. When the mind is revealed externally, things will resent it, making success impossible. The Sage practices non-action, so he has no affairs. His mind is not revealed externally, so things are at peace. Even if he does not seek to take the world's affairs and principles, he acts upon them, and the world's affairs and principles become smooth and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> "Practicing learning" refers to those who have not yet heard the Way. Not having heard the Way, one must be broad in study, hence it is said "to increase." "Practicing the Way" refers to those who have already heard the Way. Having heard the Way, one must practice non-action, hence it is said "to diminish." To "diminish and further diminish" means one has not yet avoided having actions. One must even diminish the act of diminishing itself, and only then reach the state of non-action. Non-action is what is called being silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing, yet nothing is left undone" refers to being moved and thereby penetrating all the reasons of the world. To reach non-action from non-action is what is called the constant. Learning without worry is called spirit. The method of spirit is what is called the Way. Who can reach this level of ultimate spirit? Viewed from this perspective, it is clear that one who takes the world by constantly using non-action will find that when one resorts to action, it is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning, so learning seeks to increase day by day. Only after doing everything can one speak of the Way, so the Way seeks to diminish day by day. However, "increasing" can be pursued progressively, while "diminishing" may be difficult to force. Only those with ultimate clarity can suddenly cast off their burdens and reach the realm of non-action. Thus, they can do nothing, yet there is nothing they cannot do, and their application in the world is inexhaustible and abundant.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> Practicing learning is for the sake of seeking knowledge, hence it increases day by day. Practicing the Way is for the sake of removing delusion, hence it diminishes day by day. If knowledge does not reach the ultimate, then the diminishing is not complete. Therefore, "increasing day by day" is the foundation for "diminishing day by day." If one diminishes and diminishes again until delusion is removed and truth is complete, then one reaches non-action. When one reaches non-action, there is no action that is not non-action. This is no longer a matter of simple increase or decrease. When one reaches the ultimate of non-action, even if the world is vast, one unifies it with a single thread. If one creates affairs out of having affairs, it is difficult to find leisure. If one is still entangled and confused by a single object, how much more so with the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no constant mind. He takes the minds of the common people as his own mind. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, for the virtue of goodness is attained. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, for the virtue of trust is attained. In this way, poetry relates to philosophy. For poetry is a different kind of philosophy: in time it is ancient, in harmony it is metrical, and in its judgment it is mythological. Philosophy, on the other hand, is something else: it is ethical, in time it is more recent, in harmony it is less rhythmic, and in its judgment it is clearer. Therefore, when one considers the time and the way they are brought together, how might one practice distinguishing between them, especially in what each says about the divine, both the poets and the philosophers? Or, if we consider the inquiry itself, let us say it is like this: just as someone who considers medicine, which he possesses from the beginning, and compares it to the new medicine applied to current diseases, he might judge which of the two is better or worse. Asclepius <note>the Greek god of medicine</note> would say to him: time does not change simple arts. For those things whose need is constant, their works are also simple. But medicine, if it follows the nature of the body, is not a fixed thing, nor is it uniform. Instead, it changes and shifts according to the food currently consumed, finding remedies sufficient for the patient, at one time using one thing, at another time another, suitable for the current diet. Therefore, do not think that the one who cuts out ulcers with a knife, or the one who treats gout, is not using the same art as the one who applies later methods. These wise and varied remedies are sharp. But when the art deals with bodies that are not sickly, nor complex, nor entirely weakened, it handles them easily, and its work is simple, such as applying mild drugs. However, when it treats bodies that are now becoming more complex and of a poor constitution, the art itself becomes varied, and it changes from its former simplicity into something multifaceted. Let both the poet and the philosopher answer to another Asclepius regarding their practices. This one will be indignant if anyone ignores Homer, Hesiod, or Orpheus, or anyone else who speaks of the same things, or claims that Aristotle is wiser.

Hermes of the deep counsels, you whom the fishers honor above all others. Therefore, calling upon you alongside the gods of the headlands, I go forth to seek celestial glory.

Observe the body of the fisherman, and his land, and his swiftness, and his strength. Let him lack nothing, neither in flesh nor in spirit, for necessity often compels him to struggle against fish being hauled up by the hooks, those which possess overweening strength, until they are twisted and tossed in the embrace of their mother, the salt sea. Let his skin be such that he may leap across and spring back with ease, and let his hands be hardened by the labor of the deep. Let him quickly discern the long path, and dive into the deepest parts, and remain among the swells, as if he were performing tasks upon the land, for the man who possesses a steadfast heart must labor twice as hard in the sea.

The fisherman must be cunning and intelligent in his soul. For fish are very numerous and devise many shifting tricks when they encounter unexpected snares. He must be especially vigilant, alert, and prudent. He must not love the satiety of sleep, but must keep his heart sharp and his eyes wide open. He must endure both winter and the shivering cold of the season, and he must love his labors and love the sea. For thus he lives as a friend to strength and to Hermes.

The hunt is most fitting in the seasons of autumn, when the morning star rises. In winter, he must go forth as the rays of the sun scatter, and throughout the day in the flourishing spring, he must strive with all manner of nets when the time is right.

When the god had declared these things, they immediately cast lots among all the maidens of the Aepytid line. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. Ephebolus the seer forbade this, claiming she ought not to be sacrificed, for she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus; rather, the woman who lived with Lyciscus, being unable to bear children, had passed the girl off as her own. While he was explaining these matters, Lyciscus took the maiden and deserted to Sparta. The Messenians were disheartened when they learned of Lyciscus’s flight. At this point, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytid lineage and more distinguished than Lyciscus in reputation and military matters, voluntarily offered his own daughter for the sacrifice. Human affairs are often obscured by fate, and the lot was covered by river mud. Even then, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, an obstacle arose. A certain Messenian man (whose name is not recorded) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. He was about to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since he had betrothed her, Aristodemus no longer had authority over the girl, and that by betrothing her himself, he had become more authoritative than the father. When he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameless argument, claiming that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. In the end, he drove Aristodemus to such a state of madness and rage that he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and showed that she was not pregnant. Ephebolus, who was present, ordered that someone else be provided to be sacrificed; for the death of Aristodemus’s daughter had gained them nothing, as the father had killed her, but they had not sacrificed her to the gods as the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said this, the multitude of Messenians rushed to kill the suitor of the girl, as he had brought an unholy stain upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain. This man had been a very close friend of Euphais. Euphais persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the girl’s death, and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the Aepytid line agreed that he spoke the truth. The fear they felt regarding the daughter ceased, and everyone hastened to act. The kings, persuaded by this advice, dismissed the assembly, and from that point, they turned to sacrifices and the festival of the gods. The Lacedaemonians, having heard of the oracle given to the Messenians, were themselves disheartened, and the kings hesitated to begin the battle.

In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (for the omens were favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to be no longer present with them. For that which is not good by choice is not praiseworthy, even if it is desirable. For that person is worthy of praise who, by his own zeal and not without struggle and conflict, embraces the good through the free choice of his will.

For honor and glory are prepared for that which can be converted to the good; on the other hand, Gehenna and punishment are prepared for that same mutable nature, which is indeed able to avoid evil and incline toward the good and the right side. ### **Torah Light**
These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Service, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah is the commandment of "You shall not add and you shall not subtract," <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note> which points to the perfection of the Torah. It is as the philosophers said: a thing that is perfect in the ultimate sense of perfection cannot be called lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it were to receive an addition, it would be found not to have been perfect. Therefore, the definition of the perfect is that it has neither lack nor excess. It is known that the Torah depends on His Great Name, which is the <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>, as in "The Torah of the Lord is perfect," <note>Psalm 19:8</note> as I have elaborated upon this in my tractate <term>Shevuot</term> <gloss>Oaths</gloss>, chapter "Torah Light." And as it is written in the <term>Zohar</term> <gloss>Book of Splendor</gloss> regarding the verse "This is My name and this is My memorial": <note>Exodus 3:15</note> <term>Yah</term> <gloss>the first two letters of the Name</gloss> with "My name" equals 365; <term>Vav-He</term> <gloss>the last two letters of the Name</gloss> with "My memorial" equals 248. And it is written, "I am the first and I am the last," <note>Isaiah 44:6</note> and He is the absolute perfect, having no deficiency nor addition. Regarding this comes the warning, "You shall not do so to the Lord your God," <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note> a warning against erasing the Name or smashing a stone from the Temple. The letters of the Name are in the house where He, may He be blessed, dwells, and likewise the Temple. It is written, "I am the Lord, My name is..." The letters are like a closure for the house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul for them. He who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service refers to the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The commandment came to have a fixed place, and it came to the Chosen House, and it said a word with a reason: "To His habitation you shall seek and you shall come there." <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note> "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Yod-Vav</term>, as it is written, "And He descended upon Mount Sinai." <note>Exodus 19:20</note> And as it is written, "Do not fear, for it will dwell with me," <note>referencing the indwelling of the Divine</note> for in the Temple the Glory is unified in the splendor of His people. This is "to His name, His name there," as the <term>Targum</term> <gloss>Aramaic translation</gloss> says: to cause His <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> to dwell. And around the place of holiness, the wicked walk, for they are the <term>Kelipah</term> <gloss>husk/shell of impurity</gloss>. Therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in any place that you see." <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>

### **And sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outside, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inside. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborn of the sacrifice from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written regarding them, "There you shall offer," <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note> meaning, there they shall have an ascent, and not outside. Since the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, is where holiness resides, we were commanded to be "turn from evil" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate after them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. Its secret hints at the ten nations whose power is not that of idolaters. The matter is that the nations who are in the Land of Israel, under the dominion of the Honored Name, worship the Name by "cutting the shoots," <note>a metaphor for heresy</note> and this is true idolatry. However, those in the lands outside the Land are under the dominion of the external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against smashing one stone from the holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eradicate an apostate city and not to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Likewise, a seducer and enticer must be uprooted and eradicated, for he is of the impurity of the primordial serpent who was a seducer. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the serpent," <note>Genesis 3:14</note> therefore the powers of the seducer are not revived. The commandment came not to love him and not to listen to him, as the matter stated regarding the serpent, "And I will put enmity between you and the woman." <note>Genesis 3:15</note> Also, a false prophet is like a seducer. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first fruits, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first fruits, which are the beginning, point to great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they shall go to a holy place, and from there they shall take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. The secret of the lesser holy offerings and the second tithe is that their consumption is in Jerusalem. This is the grain, the wine, and the oil, which are the fathers of the fathers of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat the lesser holy offerings until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul. Afterwards, there is permission to eat and to enjoy. Know that just as the service, which is the sacrifice, is a sacrifice to the Lord, so is the servant, for the essence of the service is that he sacrifices himself, in the secret of "When a man among you brings an offering." <note>Leviticus 1:2</note> And the burnt offering is entirely consumed, for it comes because of the thought of turning away from the mind, which is spiritual, and he keeps it all night, etc., the serpent does not hinder him. And the lesser holy offerings are the perfection of the soul and the body.

### **And the secret** of the firstborn is the secret of Israel, who are called holy, as it is said, "Israel is My firstborn." <note>Exodus 4:22</note> He has compassion on them, "And you shall guard them," and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." <note>Psalm 79:13</note> Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating the holy offerings corresponds to the fact that they have blemishes and defects, for Israel are holy and Israel are called "man." This is the secret of holiness; afterwards, a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in garments of skin, but he has a redemption, in the secret of "And I will give a man in your stead." <note>Isaiah 43:3</note> This was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <note>the scapegoat</note>, "And he shall bear their iniquities," <note>Leviticus 16:22</note> meaning, their iniquities are those that fall upon his head and upon his people. But we were commanded not to cause a blemish in the holy offerings in order to eat them, for he who causes a blemish in the holy offerings does so by his own choice. Also, there is a prohibition of work and shearing on the holy offerings, for even the broken tablets are holy.

### **In summary**, the service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the man. And likewise, his soul is called after his death to the altar above, and Michael is the High Priest. The matter is the secret that "in the image of God was man created." <note>Genesis 9:6</note> Therefore, the warning came to be careful in his life regarding the taking of lives, not to kill a man except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then it is in the hands of Heaven, in the secret of "He is the witness, He is the judge," for the Lord, blessed be He, is a true witness and a true judge. So must the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <gloss>High Court</gloss> be; just as they are true judges, so must they be true witnesses. I mean that they must have the clarification of the truth of the witnesses in complete clarity, that is, the inquiry and investigation. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death." <note>Psalm 116:15</note>

### **And since** it is precious in the eyes of the Lord, for Israel are holy by virtue of their souls, which after their death adhere to the souls above, therefore the commandment came, "You shall not cut yourselves, you shall not make any baldness," etc., <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note> for "you are children to the Lord your God." <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note> This is not so for the nations; the cutting and the baldness are from their customs, for it is appropriate since in their death they go to perdition and have no portion in this world nor in the world to come. This is not so for us, the children of the Living God. And when one departs from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, on the contrary, we have a permanent dwelling above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to increase mourning and to perform these acts.

### **Let us return** to the matter, for the man who serves is himself the sacrifice, as it is said, "When a man among you brings an offering." And there is another secret in this, for the sparks that were scattered, even below, the man, that is, in the secret of the transmigration, "Man and beast You shall save, O Lord." <note>Psalm 36:7</note> Therefore, even in the eating of ordinary meat, the meat of desire, we were commanded in the slaughtering and in great care without a notch, for then it is a carcass, and then it becomes a carcass in Israel. For who knows what transmigration is in it? "Love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note> means to choose for him a good death, that is, slaughtering without a notch. And if the beast dies by itself, or it spreads and the power of impurity takes hold of it, but when he slaughters it properly, and there is in the beast, its sacrifice, and like a pure bird, a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **And he who eats** a limb from a living creature is like one who eats from the flesh of a person when there is a transmigration of a soul there. This is the secret of "The soul shall not be eaten with the flesh." <note>Deuteronomy 12:23</note> And likewise the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure beasts, animals, and birds, all point to the spark that spreads in them, whether it is from the side of impurity or from the side of holiness. I have elaborated on this in the portion of <term>Shemini</term> <gloss>Eighth</gloss>. And Israel, when they conduct themselves in holiness, it is written about them, "And they shall make Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among them," <note>Exodus 25:8</note> for they themselves are the Tabernacle. For here the man is like three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies, the heart corresponds to the Holy Place, and then from the belly downwards corresponds to the Courtyard of the Holy Place, as I have elaborated in the portion of <term>Terumah</term> <gloss>Contribution</gloss>. And when he eats foods that are from the side of holiness, then they are like a sacrifice offered upon the altar. Regarding this, the Sages of blessed memory said: now a man's table atones, as I have elaborated in its place.

### **And the matter** of the commandments of the festivals and their sacrifices, I have written the matters of each one in its special place. And the commandment came to rejoice on the festivals and to ascend for the festival, "Three times a year shall all your males appear." <note>Exodus 23:17</note> And it does not say "to see," but in the way he comes to see, so he comes to be seen. Therefore, if he wishes to be seen in the Temple, where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> and be a faithful servant to his Creator. Without this, it is forbidden to enter the hall of the wicked, and how can he wish to be seen before Him, may He be blessed? And he brings a burnt offering of appearance, and then he himself is a sacrifice through the sacrifice that he offers. And it said, "Three times a year shall he appear." Isaac, who lived, is a perfect burnt offering.
