# Description of Lima, City of the Kings.

<margin>Appearance of the city of Lima.</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one can also see into every corner. On both sides of the flat land, and through most of the houses, canals run out, bringing fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort to the citizens, who can thereby water all their orchards and vegetable gardens, which they keep clean and pleasant. Also,

<margin>Many water mills with which they grind their grain.</margin>
there are many water mills in this river, in the manner of our own country, where they grind their grain. In short, very rich citizens live here, some of whom possess 150,000 ducats. And from this city, ships sail at times carrying 800,000 ducats worth of goods, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain on which a crucifix stands. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their livestock, and their dovecotes, their vineyards—though no good grapes, due to the nature of the land—and beautiful gardens, not only full of all kinds of fruits of that land, but also

<margin>Description of the fertility of the land.</margin>
of Spanish fruits, such as figs, pomegranates, limes, lemons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar cane, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. And truly, to pass human life with joy, if the scandalous disagreements and wars were not there, this place is certainly one of the most beautiful in the whole world. For the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the entire year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. Also, one has never seen hunger or plague there, or any rain, or thunderclaps, or lightning from the heavens

<margin>Why the City of Kings received its name, and it was built in the year 1535.</margin>
striking; but on the contrary, always a bright, clear, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535. It is named the City of Kings because the people were brought into it on the day of the Three Kings <note>original: "drie Coningen dagh", referring to Epiphany</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish that they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as meat and fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. And the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist, like a fog, falls every day before noon, though it is not unhealthy as it is with us; for those who have headaches, washing themselves with this find relief. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will increase daily in people and wealth, even though for many years there were only 500 houses,

<margin>The width and length of the houses of Lima.</margin>
and the city is built very white, so that there may well be 2,000 houses, because the streets are wide and the market square is large. Each house has 80 feet of land width and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for it is eaten by worms within 2 or 3 years—the houses are built with only one story, yet they are very

<margin>Appearance of the houses.</margin>
costly and magnificent with many rooms, halls, and parlors, suitable for living and for hosting foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials that they bake together very thick, and they fill them with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen, all around and above

This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Catchi, S. Michael, S. Francisco. It has been said before that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Regarding the flat land on the shore of the sea, we have dealt with it until now, starting from the Linea <note>the Equator</note> and Cape Passao to here. It is also to be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima, but much further, the sea coast to the south is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places, where for 10 miles of the way the city does not thunder, lightning, or rain; but beyond those 10 miles it does, or as much more or less as the mountains lie from the sea. There are also no fountains or wells in this flat land, but rather 4 or 5 stagnant waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with the water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which take their origin from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from fountains, which are few in the mountains. The distances of these rivers have been described here in part; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from each other, though mostly 7 or 8, by which traveling people regulate themselves because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, a mile wide or even wider, sometimes more, sometimes less, according to the situation of the land, there are different fertile trees and grain lands that are cultivated and sown by the people, which they can do throughout the whole year. Also, many kinds of wild trees, cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and lilies, etc., grow around these rivers. And after the Spaniards took the land, they also sowed wheat, making the land moist through some canals that they lead from these rivers, which, because they run down quickly from high mountains, one can hardly cross without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who make their journey along the flat land generally keep so close to the sea side that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and it rains a lot, it is dangerous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either with certain rafts that they have for that purpose, or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out, and one of the Indians swims in front, pulling that net or the raft with a rope, and another steering from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of reeds. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to the knees and extending over them, and an outer garment like a cloak. The women wear a course of cotton according to the length of the body, and although the style of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nevertheless some difference in the adornment of the head; for some wear single cords, some braided, some of one kind, others of different colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, and all are different according to the custom of the land.

### On the shame felt from undeserved praise.
## D I A L. XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you are praised unjustly,
> If you condemn it later, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Joy.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy person.
<note>A large ornamental initial L marks the beginning of the response from Reason.</note>
*Reason.* You are accused of having praised an unworthy person. That which is evil often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they are themselves, imagine others to be the same. Hence, they are even more prone than is fair to offer praise; and although I admit that praising the unworthy is a bad thing, it is much worse to disparage the deserving.

*Joy.* I have praised an unworthy person.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another, but to deceive is the crime of the deceiver himself.

*Joy.* The praise of another turns into my own disgrace.

In this way, the eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth. For the one states that equal bases subtend equal sides and angles, while the other states that equal sides placed upon equal bases contain equal angles. The conclusion regarding equal bases was the result of the former, while the condition of equal sides being placed <note>as a premise</note> was one of the hypotheses assumed in that same theorem. Now, since there are two such conversions, the primary one is uniform and definite, while the other is varied and proceeds into a large number of theorems, not converting in one instance but in many, due to the multitude of hypotheses in composite theorems. Often, we also convert a theorem that begins from two <note>or more</note> hypotheses, whenever the hypotheses are not all definite but some are indefinite.

One must also observe in these matters that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions. For example, every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangle is a hexagonal. The reason is that the one is more general, while the other is more specific.

Then, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Manjushri addressed the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult, what these bodhisattvas-mahasattvas have endured out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should these bodhisattvas-mahasattvas expound this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period?"

When this was said, the Blessed One replied to the bodhisattva-mahasattva Manjushri: "Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva should expound this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, by being established in four things. In which four? Here, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva should expound this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, by being established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association.

"And how, Manjushri, is a bodhisattva-mahasattva established in proper conduct? When, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva is patient, disciplined, has attained the stage of the disciplined, has a mind that is not terrified or agitated, and is free from envy; and when, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva does not dwell on any phenomenon, but observes the true nature of phenomena as they really are. This lack of fixation and lack of conceptualization regarding these phenomena is called the conduct of the bodhisattva-mahasattva, Manjushri.

"And what, Manjushri, is the sphere of association for a bodhisattva-mahasattva? When, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva does not associate with kings, nor with princes, nor with high-ranking royal ministers, nor with royal officials; he does not serve them, does not frequent them, does not wait upon them, and does not approach them. He does not associate with other sectarians, wandering ascetics, mendicants, or Jains; he does not serve them, does not frequent them, and does not wait upon them. He does not associate with those devoted to poetic treatises, nor does he serve, frequent, or wait upon those who hold to materialistic mantras or materialists, nor does he engage in conversation with them. He does not associate with outcasts, butchers, swineherds, poultry farmers, hunters, meat-sellers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not approach other places of amusement for others, nor does he engage in conversation with them. If he approaches them, he teaches the Dharma from time to time, but he teaches it without being dependent on them.

"He does not associate with monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who follow the path of the disciples <note>original: "shravakayaniyan"</note>; he does not serve them, does not frequent them, does not wait upon them, and does not engage in conversation with them. He does not share a common sphere of association with them, whether in walking or in dwelling. If he approaches them, he teaches the Dharma from time to time, but he teaches it without being dependent on them. This, Manjushri, is the sphere of association for a bodhisattva-mahasattva."

To signify a divine water-vessel, or water gushing forth from heaven and earth, they represent the water-vessel as a heart possessing a tongue. It is a heart because, among them, this is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. It is a tongue because, existing always in moisture, they call it the generator of good. They represent the water-vessel as having force, neither more nor less, because the process of the inundation is twofold according to them. They assign one part to the land of Egypt, since Egypt is by its nature productive of water. The other part they assign to the ocean, for from it water arrives into Egypt during the time of the inundation. They represent grain by means of rains, which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the time of the Nile’s inundation. That Egypt generates water is possible to learn from this: in the rest of the climate of the world, the flooding of rivers is completed in the winter.

# The Fourth Art

->Chapter Four: On the General Rules for Vomiting and Purging, and an Indication of How to<-
->Attract the Purgative Medicine and Vomiting<-

One should not rush to consume many poor-quality foods, as the body’s nature will draw them in without proper digestion. If any such thing is necessary, it must be done little by little, gradually, so that what enters the body is well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for blood. As for evacuation specific to a humor that has increased in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is something other than phlebotomy. Every excessive evacuation usually causes harm. If the cessation of a habitual purge causes a recurrence of the ailment, that evacuation should be repeated, as is often the case with those who suffer from the cessation of a nosebleed or a blockage. Repeating the process will resolve it. Know that the remainder of the matter that needs to be evacuated is less susceptible to being completely removed, and pushing it to the point of exhaustion weakens the strength of the body. Often, nature itself dissolves that remainder. As long as the humor is of the appropriate type and the patient can tolerate it, do not fear excess. Sometimes you may need to evacuate until the patient feels faint. If a person has strong constitution and a large amount of bad humors, evacuate them little by little. The same applies if the matter is highly mature or strongly mixed with blood, such that it cannot be evacuated all at once. This is the case in sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that purging draws from above and clears from below, so it is consistent with the natural process of attraction. It is also appropriate after the materials have settled. If the materials are below, the opposite action draws them toward it and clears them from where they are, and vice versa. The state of phlebotomy varies according to the locations from which blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who digest well have the least need for evacuation, and people in hot climates have little need for it.

We say that it is recommended for one who wishes to purge to consume or space out their food in portions. They should determine the amount they intend to test in a day, and make the foods and drinks varied. The stomach is stimulated by this to push what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, but rather a single type, the stomach becomes satisfied with it, relaxes, and grips it tightly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with a naturally loose constitution, none of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not arise in one who manages their health well; they require something milder. Exercise, massage, and cupping may suffice. If the body becomes filled with an excess of the best humors, meaning blood, then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, not purging. If necessity dictates phlebotomy or evacuation, such as in autumn, and the patient is weak, then vomiting is preferred over phlebotomy. This is one of the recommendations of Hippocrates and the books that follow it, and it is the truth. The same applies if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood. If the humors are uniform, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy might increase their thickness and viscosity, so one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are uniform, prioritize phlebotomy; if they become unbalanced after that, then evacuate. If they are not uniform, evacuate the excess first until they are balanced, then perform phlebotomy. Whoever prioritizes medicine over phlebotomy should have performed a small phlebotomy first. If someone has recently undergone phlebotomy and needs evacuation, and then takes medicine, it should be stopped. Often, taking medicine when phlebotomy was required causes faintness and distress. If it does not subside with sedatives, phlebotomy should have been performed first. There is no evacuation required for excessive fullness that is not also called for by the severity of the ailment and the fullness in terms of quality and quantity. Often, proper management prevents the need for phlebotomy at the time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but an obstacle prevents it; the solution then is fasting, sleep, and correcting the temperament of the body. Some evacuation is done as a precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a specific time, especially in the spring. One must take precautions before the time arrives and perform the specific evacuation, whether it be phlebotomy or purging. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. You may need to use a medicine that is compatible with the humor being evacuated in terms of quality, such as scammony when you need to evacuate yellow bile. In that case, you must mix it with something that differs in quality but agrees in purging, such as myrobalan. Correcting the temperament if it occurs later in patients with visceral tumors weakens their purging. If you are forced to do so, use things like ivy and safflower. As for the purgative and cassia, Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a constitution that easily responds to vomiting, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in the summer or spring." This relieves the body of fatigue. Know that a person accustomed to a loose constitution or one not accustomed to vomiting should avoid it when not necessary. One must prepare before purging by softening the humor one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages. Know that a person accustomed to a loose constitution or one not accustomed to vomiting should, before using strong medicine, follow one of the mild regimens. Purging while the abdomen is emaciated is difficult and tiring. A medicine intended for vomiting may act as a purgative if the stomach is strong, if it is taken on an empty stomach, if the person is accustomed to a loose constitution, or if the medicine is heavier in substance and descends quickly. A purgative may cause vomiting due to a weak stomach, excessive weight, the medicine causing distress, or the person having indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge due to lack of maturity, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it throughout the body, taking hold of the body and attracting other humors to it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting, such as yellow bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a state like milk and stars, where purging is more appropriate for them. Those whose humor is descending, such as those with intestinal slippage, find that the gripping of the intestines hinders the purgative medicine. What is composed of medicines that differ greatly in the time of purging causes the purging to be disturbed, and the first may purge the second before the second acts, or the first may purge the second itself. Whoever undergoes purging and their body is not cleansed of it, they will suffer from colic and distress, and what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, if the medicine evacuates the waste, there will be no disturbance. If it is taken and there is disturbance, it is either evacuating something other than the waste, or the evacuated humor has changed to another humor, which indicates the body has been cleansed of the humor intended for evacuation.

But have we not learned: * All handles of food that are in the basket in the threshing floor are pure (and Rabbi Yose declares them impure). It is well for the one who says "in the basket," for it is taught "their bundles," that is fine. But for the one who says "what is in the basket," in the basket literally, what is there to say? Third article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universals are prior by nature. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us, and simple things are posterior. But universals are prior, therefore they are known later to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition, and the parts of the definition are less universal, just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are known later to us. Furthermore, effects are known before causes and principles. But universals are known later to us. But if it is as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*, we must proceed from the universal to the singular. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition takes its beginning in some way from sensitive cognition. And because sense is of singulars, and intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is a middle between potency and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately. The incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potency, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: things are first manifest and certain to us in a more confused way. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both the whole in which parts are contained in potency and the integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing, just as knowing "animal" indistinctly and knowing the animal in which there is rationality or irrationality, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and to know "man." And if I compare any more or less universal thing, just as sense proceeds from potency to act, so does the intellect; this is the order

<column-break/>

of cognition that appears in sense. For in sense, one distinguishes more and less, and when a thing is known remotely, it is perceived as a body, and then as an animal; and it is perceived more as an animal than as a body, and prior as a body than as a man. Or it is clear that a child from the beginning distinguishes a man from a non-man; and children from the beginning call all men "father." Later, however, one terminates at each one, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: things are manifest and one knows something indistinctly still and in potency, or one knows the genus and the principle, and thus one knows the species and the parts. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is the middle between potency and act. And so the cognition of singulars is prior to us, and the cognition of universals is posterior to sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If one considers both sense and intellect, the cognition of the less universal is prior to the cognition of the more universal. To the first, it must be said that this can be considered in a twofold way. One way is to consider the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth is that the true and the same have a relationship to many things, and the abstraction of the intellect is the end of this process, while the truth is posterior. In the first book of *De Anima*, it is said that the universal is either nothing or is posterior; but Plato posited universals as substances, and in this consideration, it is true, because particulars are not except by participation in the universals subsisting, which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the less universal is prior in nature, which appears manifest in the generation of man and animal. For the animal is generated before the man, as the Philosopher says in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. Another is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior to potency in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is being perfected; and in this way, the more universal is prior in nature, for the animal is prior to man. The intention of nature does not stop at the generation of the animal, but intends to generate man. To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole, it is made more universal, not only containing man and horse, but also the less universal, and it contains in the future not only the more universal but also others, as man is not only animal but rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition than "man." If "man" is prior in our cognition, it is because of its definition. To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. One way is absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is known of the house. In another way, as it is a part of this whole, and stones are necessary, we must know the whole before the parts. For we know the house in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the definition to be considered absolutely is prior to the defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified by those things, but rather by the parts.

The judge said to him, "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. This will relieve you of the burden of the afterlife, and you may regain a good reputation for two reasons: first, your ability to find exits and fabricate excuses that defend yourself; and second, your voluntary confession of guilt, choosing the safety of the afterlife over the safety of this world. "O long-lived one, at my request and for your own benefit,
Speak thus to her: 'Your companion, residing in the hermitage of Ramagiri,
Though separated, is alive and asks after your well-being, O delicate one.'
For this is the first greeting among beings prone to misfortune." (41)

"To her": O long-lived one. The suffix <term>matup</term> is used here in a sense of praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of helping others. At my request and for your own benefit, meaning to fulfill yourself through the act of helping another. Although the self is the object of the act of helping, the use of the genitive case <term>ātmanaḥ</term> <gloss>of the self</gloss> is not contradictory, as in the expression "he helps him." As Bharavi says: "That wealth is truly useful which helps others." Similarly, Sri Harsha says: "To help the virtuous, to see wealth, to travel through the sky." Thus, the commentator's remark that "sometimes the second case is not seen, so it is the same for all" is merely a statement of the obvious. Speak thus to that beloved. What should be said? "O delicate one, your companion, your husband, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, is alive, meaning he has not died." He provides the reason for his survival: "Though separated, suffering from the pangs of separation, he asks after your well-being." The verb "to ask" takes two objects because of the state of suffering. Indeed, for beings whose misfortunes are easily attained, this inquiry about well-being is the first thing that must be asked. The suffix <term>ṇyat</term> is used here to denote necessity.

Xiangling smiled and said, "Now that I have come in, I have some free time. If you could teach me how to write poetry, it would be my great fortune!" Daiyu smiled and said, "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not an expert, I can certainly teach you the basics." The middle development and transition are two pairs of couplets: level tones must be matched with oblique tones; empty words must be matched with solid words, and solid words with empty words. If you truly have a brilliant line, even if the level and oblique tones or the empty and solid words do not match, it is still acceptable."

Xiangling smiled and said, "No wonder I often took a book of old poetry to read a few lines in secret. Some were matched perfectly, and some were not. I also heard people say, 'The first, third, and fifth characters do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be clear.' Now that I hear you say this, it turns out these rules are not important at all; it is only important that the words and phrases are fresh and novel." Daiyu said, "That is exactly the principle. Words and phrases are ultimately secondary; the most important thing is to establish the intent. If the sentiment is genuine, even if the words and phrases are not polished, it is naturally good. This is called 'not letting the words harm the meaning'."

Xiangling said, "I only love Lu Fangweng's lines, 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, the fragrance lingers long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is truly vivid and interesting!" Daiyu said, "Because you do not know poetry, you love these shallow and easy things. You will then witness what we have witnessed, verify with your own insight everything we have verified, and have no need to tether your knowledge to what we have known. This requires a certain, not insignificant, amount of time, freedom from distractions, and the application of your entire resolve to this art. You know that one-eighth of what remains, together with the bequest, equals a sister's portion. So, one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest. Therefore, one-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest, together with the bequest, equals a sister's portion. That is one-eighth of the wealth and seven-eighths of the bequest. The entire wealth equals three-eighths of the wealth and one-third of the bequests and five-eighths of the bequest. Subtract three-eighths from the wealth, and five-eighths of the wealth remains, which equals three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals five bequests and four-fifths of a bequest. The wealth is twenty-nine, the bequest is five, and the portion is eight.

In another aspect of bequests: a man died and left four sons, and he bequeathed to a man the equivalent of one of his sons' portions, and to another one-fourth of what remains of the third. Know that the bequest is only from the third.

### CHAPTER LXVI.

**How the next day we sent messengers to the Caciques of Tlascala, entreating them for peace, and what they did regarding it.**

After the battle I have recounted had passed, in which we captured the three principal Indians, our Captain Cortes sent them off immediately, along with the two who were in our camp who had gone as messengers other times. He ordered them to tell the Caciques of Tlascala that we entreated them to come at once in peace, and to grant us passage through their land to go to Mexico, as we had sent to tell them other times. And that if they did not come now, we would kill all their people, and because we loved them much and wished to have them as brothers, we would not want to anger them if they had not given cause for it. Many flattering words were said to them to attract them to our friendship. Those messengers went willingly to the capital of Tlascala and delivered their embassy to all the Caciques I have already named. They found them gathered with many other elders and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and they were very sad, both from the bad outcome of the war and from the death of the captains who were their relatives or sons who died in the battles. It is said they did not want to listen to them willingly. What they agreed upon regarding this was that they immediately ordered the calling of all the diviners and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and others who cast lots, which they call <term>Tacalnagual</term> <gloss>sorcerers</gloss>, who are like wizards. They told them to look through their divinations and spells and charms to see what kind of people we were, and if we could be defeated by waging war on us by day and by night continuously, and also to know if we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>gods or demons</gloss>, just as those from Cempoal said, which I have already said other times are evil things like demons, and what things we ate, and that they should look at all this with great diligence. Because, as it seemed, the friendly Indians we brought from Cempoal made them believe that we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>gods or demons</gloss>, and that we ate the hearts of Indians, and that the cannons threw lightning like that which falls from the sky, and that the greyhound was a tiger or lion, and that the horses were for lancing the Indians when we wanted to kill them. And they told them many other childish things. But let us return to the <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>. A courtesan who refuses to approach a man by the order of the King shall receive one thousand lashes, or a fine of five thousand <term>panas</term> <gloss>units of currency</gloss>.
If she accepts payment but develops an aversion, the fine shall be double the payment.
If she misappropriates the payment for her residence, she shall pay eight times the amount, unless the cause is illness or a fault in the man.
If she causes distress to a man who has sought her company, or if she attempts to drown herself, she shall be punished.
Whoever steals the ornaments or the payment of a courtesan shall be fined eight times the value.
A courtesan must report her income, her future prospects, and the men she associates with.
By this rule, the regulations for actors, dancers, singers, musicians, professional storytellers, rope dancers, jugglers, wandering bards, women who trade in their own bodies, and secret agents are also explained.
They shall pay a fee of five <term>panas</term> for a public performance by visiting artists.
Women who live by their beauty shall pay a monthly tax equal to twice their daily earnings.
A courtesan must ensure that her female slaves and those who live by performing on stage are trained in singing, instrumental music, recitation, dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing the lute, flute, and drum, as well as the knowledge of psychology, perfumery, garland-making, hypnotism, massage, and the arts of a courtesan. They shall earn their livelihood from the King's circle. The sons of courtesans and those who live by the stage should be trained to be leaders. They must also be trained in all rhythmic movements and musical measures.
Women who know secret languages and codes should be employed by them among those who are not their own kin, for the purpose of espionage, assassination, or detecting negligence.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the Superintendent of Courtesans, in the Book of Superintendents.

He spoke to him about himself, and about the water, and he discussed his own simplicity in the face of the man. A certain listener to his lectures, who had been sent by Domitian, fell in. He seemed to be a good sort, and he claimed to be in great danger. He possessed a tongue that was not uneducated, such as those who are prone to slander use for speeches or lawsuits. Apollonius, for his part, spoke of whatever happened to come to mind, things that did not advance the other man’s cause. For he spoke to them even while looking at wild beasts and trees, by which some were held and others were moved. When the man tried to lead him into slanders against the tyrant, he said, "My good man, say whatever you wish. You will not be slandered by me. As for the complaints I have against the king, I will speak them to him directly." Other episodes occurred in this prison, some involving plots, others generally so great that they are not worth my recording. In the evening, he mentioned them, having left nothing out. The matters concerning the discourse follow after the fifth day of his confinement.

A man who spoke Greek came to the prison and said, "Where is the man from Tyana?" Having taken him aside, he said, "Tomorrow the king will speak with you." It seemed that he had heard this from Aelianus. He then withdrew into secrecy, for he alone seemed to know of it. "Everything regarding the prison has been foretold," he said, "and it is for you to reach the end of the trial." "You do well," he said, "but I, in the life I lead and in the way I live, do the same. I will speak on behalf of those who have fallen into misfortune, and I ask for his favor." "For in this way," Apollonius said, "will you advise me on how to speak to the king?" "By Zeus," he said, "if he is not persuaded by flatterers." "And why does he overlook me," he said, "and not even despise me?" "You advise excellently," he said, "and I have convinced myself of it."

As he was leaving, he said, "I have come, and I rejoice that I am prepared to see you. I have prepared you for the king’s voice and for the surliness of his face. For he speaks with a heavy tone, even when he speaks gently; his brow hangs over his eyes; his cheek is full of bile, for these things reveal his character most of all. Do not be struck by these things, man of Tyana. For they are a matter of nature and are always the same." And Apollonius said, "Odysseus of old, singing of his many wanderings, and having heard beforehand all that there was to hear, did not fear even the way he ate, nor how his voice thundered. He took heart, even though he feared him at the beginning, and he left the flute behind. But for me, it is sufficient to save myself and my companions, for whose sake I am in danger." Having spoken such things to the visitor, and having reported them to the one who needed to know, he slept.

At dawn, a secretary from the palace came and said, "The king commands you, Apollonius, to come to the palace when the market is full, not yet to make your defense, but because he wishes to see who you are and to speak with you alone." "Why then," he said, "do you speak to me about these things? Are you not Aelianus?" "By Zeus, I am," said the man from Tyana. "To whom then," he said, "should I say these things? I will say them to those who are leading me. For I must go out as if from a prison." "It has been ordered," he said, "in addition to those other things; for I will arrive later than the appointed time. I came to give instructions to someone. For these things have been ordered for you." The man then departed.

Apollonius, having rested himself on his bed, said, "I need sleep. The night has been difficult for me, as I wished to remember what I once heard from Phraotes." And I, if I were to stay awake, would perhaps have been better prepared, as if he had already been warned himself, for it was a great matter. "And how could I prepare myself," he said, "not knowing what he will ask you? Will you not allow me to speak about your life?" "By Zeus," he said, "I must. I will use it for that very purpose. But I wish to share with you what I always remember of Phraotes. For the present situation is good, and it will seem so to you as well. Phraotes advises that one should neither play with the lions that men tame, for they will hold a grudge if they are struck, nor should one coddle them, for they become unruly by nature. Rather, one should call them forth while striking fear into them, so that they may become manageable. We were not studying this for the sake of training wild beasts, but for how one should deal with tyrants. By using this method, one would not fall, for that is the middle path."

"This advice," he said, "has been spoken excellently regarding tyrants. But there is also the lion in Aesop, the one in the cave. Aesop says that he was not sick, but he pretended to be, so that the beasts who visited him would come straight to him." "And why, Apollonius," he said, "do we not use this, so that one might not be caught by guile, nor lack any of the necessary skills?" And Apollonius said, "But I consider the fox wiser. For when she approached and saw, she did not go inside, but left the cave, having observed the tracks of her own kind." Having said these things, he gave himself over to a short sleep, as much as came to his eyes. When day broke, having prayed to the sun, as is customary in prison, he spoke to those who approached him about whatever they asked. When the market was full, the secretary arrived and said, "It is time to go to the doors, lest we be called too late." He said, "Let us go," and he rose and went forth. As he walked, four guards followed him, and many others approached.

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The end of alchemy is not gold and silver, but arcana <gloss>secret remedies</gloss>.</margin>
has destined, let them penetrate. From these things, gather that it is necessary to proceed according to my prescription, and by no means according to yours. Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still thunder many things against me, my Monarchy shall nevertheless stand, while yours will utterly perish. I do not write so prolixly about Alchemy in vain, but I do it with this mind and purpose, that you may know closely and solidly what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended by this, that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it: but rather, this must be taken care of, that through it the <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret remedies</gloss> are uncovered, and the deceptions of the <term>seplasiarii</term> <gloss>apothecaries/perfumers</gloss> are exposed, by which the rude common people are deceived, while they serve them for one florin what they would not redeem for a single coin. Such are their precious <term>arcana</term>.

<margin>Poison exists even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies and exists even in the best things? All are forced to admit this. If this is true, then I ask you whether poison should not be separated from the good and useful, and the good accepted, and the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I ask you to explain to me how this is separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted to admit that poison lies there, and you are asked where it finally goes, you then bring forth I know not what about corrections, which extract and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is ventilated.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or after Diagridium <gloss>a purgative preparation of scammony</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it was at first? And yet you boast in the meantime that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it gone?
<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test this, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know this not sluggishly. Thus you also correct Turbith <gloss>a purgative root</gloss>, and call it Diaturbith. Such are your corrections, which would befit rustics and should be given to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see whether you will not feel the poison.
<margin>What it means to correct a physician.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* Whoever is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who is punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; it is situated with them, not with you. Now, in this case, the physician must consider nothing more than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation: as, for example, a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without harm. The same must be understood equally of all other things, namely, that a similar separation is necessary. That not yet being done, you cannot be secure in your operation: unless it happens that nature supplies your place, or the greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will remain.

Now, therefore, if that true foundation is necessary which removes the poison, how does Alchemy perform this? For it is necessary that this be done in such a way that, if Mars <gloss>iron</gloss> is in the Sun <gloss>gold</gloss>, Mars is removed, and if Saturn <gloss>lead</gloss> is in Venus <gloss>copper</gloss>, it is separated from it. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist in them. But as for the bodies that are contrary, it is necessary that some of them be entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety may be removed, and the evil which you seek may be taken away from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so much less useful is a Medicine that does not pass through fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through fire into another generation, which ought to conduce to and assist man. And should this not deservedly be considered the proper foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to apply poisons, but <term>arcana</term>.
<margin>Workshops criticized.</margin>
But all those workshop preparations, however many there are, do not contribute even a letter to this doctrine: but they are occupied simply in correcting, just as if a dog has farted in a room, and that stench is suppressed either by troches and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask, does the stench not remain in the room afterwards just as it was before? And although it may not be perceived by smell, is it therefore permitted for anyone to say that the stench has been separated and no longer remains? Indeed, it is present, but corrected by fumigation. Thus, therefore, the fumigation and the stench enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who dull an <term>allopathic</term> <gloss>remedy acting by contraries</gloss> with sugar, so that it may inflict no harm. Thus sugar and honey are their masteries. Thus they also correct gentian with theriac <gloss>a medicinal electuary</gloss>. But are these not works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the princes of physicians. But who is so stupid that he does not immediately smell that these things are worth nothing? What else, I ask, can they boast of regarding their remedies, than to say, *This Electuary is sweet, made of aromatics, sugar, and honey.*

Regarding the fourth point, that demons can induce some substantial forms and therefore can also remove them, it is said regarding the magicians of Pharaoh who created real serpents, that demons can produce certain effects concerning some imperfect creatures with the aid of another agent, which they cannot do concerning humans, for whom God has greater care. Fourthly, the truth itself is declared where they also transform humans into beasts. Regarding how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. In the 17th Question, 5th Chapter, "Bishops," from the Council of Ancyra: "Whoever believes that any creature can be changed or transformed for the better or the worse into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an infidel and worse than a pagan." And let us use the arguments of Saint Thomas in the second book of the Sentences, distinction 8, "Whether demons can imprint upon the bodily senses by deluding them with illusions." Where he first argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must be somewhere, but it cannot be only in the sense, because the sense does not have any species unless received from things, and there is no true beast there according to the authority of the canon cited. Nor, again, can it be in the thing that is seen, such as a woman appearing as a beast, because two substantial forms cannot be in the same thing at the same time and in the same way. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen cannot be anywhere, no deceptive illusion can occur in the eye of the viewer, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. Furthermore, if it is said that that form is in the surrounding air, this cannot be. First, because air is not receptive to any form or figure. Second, because the air around that person cannot remain one and the same due to its fluidity, especially since it is in motion. Third, because such a transformation would be seen by everyone, which does not happen; why do demons not appear to deceive the visions of holy men at least? Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportionate to it. The active thing proportionate to the sense is twofold. One is as the originator of the act, namely the object. The other is as a referent, such as the medium. The form that is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor can it be the medium as a carrier. Regarding the first, that it cannot be the object, it cannot be taken from any thing, as touched upon in the previous argument, since it is not in the sense as received from a thing, nor in the thing itself, nor even in the air itself as a referring medium, as touched upon in the third argument. He often avoided the cleverness required for debate. His lifestyle was simple, yet he maintained a luxurious standard with great temperance. He delighted in white clothing and bathed twice daily in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why, as a bishop, he bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I cannot manage to do it a third time." Once, when he saw the bishop approaching Arsatius, he was asked by one of Arsatius’s attendants why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a clergyman should dress in white. He replied, "You tell me first where it is written that a bishop must wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius turned the argument back upon him. "You will not be able to show," he said, "that a clergyman must wear black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white.' And the Savior in the Gospels appears wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles wearing white." Having readily said these things and many others, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, was seizing a Novatian church while visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius approached him and urged him to return the church. Leontius responded heatedly, saying to him, "You Novatians ought not to have churches, as you reject repentance and shut out the philanthropy of God." When Leontius said these and many other such things against the Novatians, Sisinnius replied, "Indeed, no one repents as much as I do." When Leontius asked again, "How do you repent?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you."

When John <note>John Chrysostom</note> once complained to the bishop, saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "It does not have two." When John became angry and said, "Do you see that you are alone? Do you wish to be bishop?" Sisinnius replied, "I do not mean that, but rather that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, as I am to others." John, indignant at what was said, replied, "But I will stop you from being a heretic." To this, Sisinnius replied wittily, "I will even pay you a reward if you relieve me of such great labor." Pleased by the reply, John said, "I will not stop you from speaking with me, if you are so pained by what you say."

Thus, Sisinnius was ready with his replies and witty. It would be a long task to write down and record everything he said. Therefore, I have shown in a few words what kind of man he was, as I deemed it necessary. I will add that he was renowned for his education. AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

Celsus claims that the Jews were runaways from Egypt, that they never accomplished anything of note, and that they were never significant in either influence or number. Regarding the claim that they were not runaways, but Hebrews who had resided in Egypt rather than being Egyptians, we have already spoken in the preceding sections <note>See Origen, *Contra Celsum* III 5–8</note>. If he thinks their lack of significance in influence or number is proven by the fact that their history is not widely found among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to examine their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, they would find that these people existed as a shadow of a heavenly life upon earth <note>See Job 8:9; Hebrews 10:1</note>. Among them, no one was considered God except the One who is over all, and no one who made images held a position in the state. For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in their commonwealth, as the Law cast out all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues, which draw the foolish among men and drag the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, a law among them such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under the heaven, a likeness of any reptile that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters beneath the earth" <note>Deuteronomy 4:16–18</note>. Indeed, the Law desired that they, while communing with the truth regarding each thing, should not fashion things other than the <margin>525</margin> truth, falsifying what is truly male, or what is truly female, or the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or the kind of reptiles, or of fish. Also solemn and noble among them is the command: "Do not, having looked up to the heaven and seen the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, be led astray and worship them and serve them" <note>Deuteronomy 4:19</note>.

What kind of commonwealth was it, that of an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for a womanish man to appear? It is also wonderful that the incitements of the young, the prostitutes, were to be removed from their commonwealth <note>See Deuteronomy 23:1, 17</note>. There were also courts of the most just judges, and they had given much proof of a healthy life <note>See Exodus 18:21–22; Deuteronomy 1:15</note>.

Now, in accordance with the request of your honor, we shall again mention some of these expressions in these pages, so that perhaps they may guide the thirsty in the deserts of remoteness toward the station of nearness, and lead the lost in the wilderness of separation and estrangement to the tents of proximity and union. May there flow from this Pen that which will quicken the hearts of the people, so that all may arise from their beds of heedlessness and listen to the melodies of the Dove in the Paradise, from the Lote-Tree that was in the Most Glorious Garden, singing and watching by the hands of Power, by the permission of God.

If the path were known and clear, it would be understood that when the slender moon of the Christian dispensation burned away the veil of limitation and form, and the command of that Blessed Beauty became in some measure manifest upon this earth, one day that Unseen Beauty spoke to some of the spiritual companions of separation and kindled the fire of longing. He said, "I go, and I will come again." And in another station, He said, "I go, and another will come who will say what I have not said, and will complete what I have said." In truth, these two expressions are one, if you are among those who perceive the Manifestations of Oneness. If one observes with the eye of spiritual insight, it is in truth the promise of the Seal.

# But because of meditation on the Supreme, that which was obscured [is revealed]; from Him, indeed, come the bondage and liberation of this [individual soul]. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued: the individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss>) is merely a part of the Supreme Self (<term>ishwara</term> <gloss>the Lord/Supreme Being</gloss>), just as a spark is a part of fire. If this is so, just as the fire and the spark both possess the powers of burning and illumination, the individual soul and the Lord should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, due to the soul's power of knowledge and sovereignty, the creation of chariots and the like in dreams would be possible through mere will. To this, it is replied: even though the individual soul and the Lord stand in the relation of part and whole, the individual soul’s nature is observed to be the opposite of the Lord’s. Does the individual soul then not possess the same nature as the Lord? It is not that it does not possess it; although it exists, it is obscured by the obstruction of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance/nescience</gloss>) and the like. This obscured nature, however, becomes manifest in some rare beings who meditate upon the Supreme Lord, who are disciplined, and whose darkness has been washed away—just as the power of vision, obscured by cataracts, is restored by the potency of medicine—through the grace of the Lord. It does not manifest by nature in all beings. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, come the bondage and liberation of this individual soul. Bondage arises from a lack of knowledge of the Lord’s true nature, and liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. The scripture also says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. By meditating upon Him, at the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state, the universal sovereignty, and becomes one whose desires are fulfilled," and so on.

# Or [it is obscured] due to connection with the body. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why does the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It is logical that the powers of knowledge and sovereignty should be obscured, just as the burning and illuminating powers of a spark are obscured when it is within the wood. It is replied: this is true. This obscuration of the soul’s knowledge and sovereignty occurs due to its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy here: just as the burning and illuminating powers of fire, though inherent, are obscured when it is contained within the wood, or as when it is covered by ashes, so too is the knowledge and sovereignty of the soul obscured by its connection with the limiting adjuncts (<term>upadhi</term> <gloss>limiting adjuncts/conditions</gloss>) of the body and the like, which are created by name and form imposed by ignorance, and by the confusion of identity resulting from them. The word "or" is used to exclude the doubt that the individual soul is something other than the Lord. One might ask: let the individual soul be something other than the Lord, since its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why assume a connection with the body? It is replied: no, the otherness of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. The scripture begins with "That Deity thought" and continues with "having entered into this by this individual soul as the Self," referring to the individual soul with the word "Self." Furthermore, it instructs the individual soul in its divinity, saying, "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Thou Art, O Svetaketu." Therefore, the individual soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured due to its connection with the body. Consequently, the creation of chariots and the like in dreams by the soul’s will does not hold. If the creation of chariots in dreams were by will, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills an unpleasant thing. As for the argument that the scripture regarding the waking state declares the reality of the dream state, that statement of similarity is not intended to imply reality, as that would contradict the soul’s nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and the like in dreams. The comparison is intended to show that the dream appears similar to the waking state because it is constructed from impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious impressions</gloss>) born of the waking state. Therefore, the dream state is merely an illusion (<term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion/magic</gloss>).

# Its absence [of dream experience] is in the nerves, as stated by scripture, and in the Self. || 3.2.7 ||

The Section on the Absence of That [Dream Experience]. || 3.2.7 ||

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>deep sleep</gloss>) is to be examined. Regarding this, there are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep. In one place it is heard: "When a person is thus asleep, having become fully serene and knowing no dream, he then sleeps in the nerves." In another place, after mentioning the nerves, it is heard: "Having moved along them, he rests in the pericardium." Similarly, in another place, after mentioning the nerves: "He resides in them when he is asleep and sees no dream; then he becomes one with the vital breath (<term>prana</term> <gloss>vital breath/life force</gloss>) alone." Likewise, in another place: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Similarly, in another place: "O gentle one, then he becomes united with the Existent, he has attained his own Self." And also: "Embraced by the intelligent Self, he knows nothing external or internal."

A doubt arises here: are these, the nerves and the rest, separate places of deep sleep independent of one another, or are they a single place of deep sleep dependent upon one another? What is the conclusion? They are separate; why? Because they have the same purpose. Things with the same purpose are not dependent upon one another in any context.

### Thence come speed of mind, independence from the body, and mastery over nature. || 48 ||

Speed of mind is the attainment of supreme swiftness for the body. Independence from the body is the attainment of function for the senses, independent of the body, according to one's desire for a specific place, time, or object. Mastery over nature is the control over all manifestations of the primary cause <term>pradhāna</term> <gloss>primordial matter</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhu-pratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolic</gloss>. These are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the senses. || 48 ||

### For one who possesses only the discriminative knowledge of the purity of the self and the intellect, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience. || 49 ||

For the one whose intellect has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>, who abides in the highest clarity and the supreme state of mastery, and who is established solely in the discriminative knowledge of the distinction between the intellect and the self, there is sovereignty over all states of existence. All aspects of the <term>guṇas</term> <gloss>qualities of nature</gloss> are <column-break/>

The author speaks of the accomplishments resulting from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **Thence come speed of mind, independence from the body, and mastery over nature.** The functioning of the senses without the body is independence from the body. Place refers to regions like Kashmir; time refers to the past and so on; object refers to subtle things and so on. Mastery over nature is the control over all manifestations of primordial matter, achieved through the mastery of the senses in their causal state. These accomplishments are called <term>madhu-pratīkā</term> by those expert in the science of Yoga. One might ask: if the senses are mastered, the senses with their objects may become controlled, but what does that have to do with their causes, such as primordial matter? To this, he says: **And these.** This refers to the mastery of the five forms of the senses, such as perception. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not arise from the mastery of the senses alone, but from the mastery of their five forms, which include primordial matter and the rest. || 48 ||

These are the causes of the powers of knowledge and action. Through the <term>saṃyama</term> <gloss>concentrated focus</gloss>, both direct and indirect, and through the faith generated by the attainment of these accomplishments, he shows the intermediate powers of that discriminative knowledge of the distinction between the intellect and the self, which is the goal: **For one who possesses only the discriminative knowledge of the purity of the self and the intellect, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>. From that comes the supreme state of mastery. The intellect was previously subject to <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>, but upon their subsidence, it becomes subject to the Yogi who is the master. For that Yogi who is established solely in the discriminative knowledge of the distinction between the intellect and the self, there is sovereignty over all states of existence. Su’s Commentary: If one does not know the Way but busies oneself with learning, one’s knowledge and perceptions will increase daily, yet one will have no way to unify them, and one will inevitably become burdened. Confucius said, "To hear much, select the good and follow it; to see much and remember it, this is the second level of knowledge." If one day one knows the Way, one looks back at one's previous artificial actions and sees that none were not delusions. To cast away delusion and return to one's true nature is what is called "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it with a single thread." To cast away delusion to purify one's nature and return to the state of "no-thought" is what is called diminishing. Yet, the intention to cast away delusion still remains. When one reaches the point of forgetting even this intention, so that one's nature is purely and completely restored, then one acts, and nothing is lost to the state of non-action. People all possess the desire to grasp the principles of the world, so they create affairs and pursue them. Their minds are revealed externally, and things resent this, so in the end, they cannot attain their goals. The sage practices non-action, so he creates no affairs. His mind is not revealed externally, and things are at peace with him. Although he does not seek to grasp the principles of the world, he acts, and the principles of the world become harmonious and peaceful.

Lü’s Commentary: Those who "learn" are those who have not yet heard the Way. Because they have not heard the Way and seek it, they do not attain it; because they do not attain it, they seek to broaden their knowledge, hence "daily increase." Those who "practice the Way" are those who have already heard the Way. Having heard the Way, they practice it, but they have not yet attained the state of non-action, hence "daily diminish." Yet, those who diminish still cannot avoid having an intention to act. Only when one diminishes even the act of diminishing does one reach the state of non-action. Non-action is what is called being silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" refers to being moved and thereby penetrating all the reasons of the world. To reach the state of leaving nothing undone is called "abandoning learning and having no worries." This is called the mystery of the spirit. The <term>I Ching</term> <gloss>Book of Changes</gloss> has no fixed form; if it were not the most spiritual thing in the world, who could participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, one can know whether one can take the world. If one uses non-action as the basis, one can succeed; if one relies on intentional action, one is not sufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

Huang Maocai’s Commentary: Only when one knows everything can one speak of learning. Therefore, learning seeks daily increase. Through increase, one can advance in one's search and undergo transformation, and only then can one speak of the Way. Therefore, the Way seeks daily diminution. However, that which is increased can be cast off until one reaches non-action. Some find this difficult to force; only those who are perfectly enlightened can suddenly cast off the world and be at ease.

Xizhai’s Commentary: Learning is the means to seek knowledge, hence "daily increase." Practicing the Way is the means to cast away delusion, hence "daily diminution." If knowledge does not reach its limit, then the diminution is not complete. Therefore, "daily increase" is the foundation for "daily diminution." If one diminishes and diminishes again, until delusion is cast away and truth is complete, then one reaches non-action. When one reaches non-action, all that exists is as if it did not exist. This is no longer easy to discuss in terms of increase or diminution. When one reaches the ultimate of non-action, even if the world is vast, it is unified by a single thread. If one creates affairs and generates tasks, one will have no time to spare. Even a single object would be tangled and contradictory, let alone the vastness of the world.

The sage has no fixed mind; he takes the minds of the common people as his own. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, for virtue is good. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, for virtue is trustworthy. In this way, I consider poetry to be related to philosophy. For what is poetry, if not philosophy? It is ancient in time, metrical in its harmony, and mythological in its judgment. And what is philosophy, if not poetry? It is more recent in time, more prosaic in its harmony, and clearer in its judgment. Therefore, since these things differ from one another only in time and form, how could one distinguish the difference between them, regarding what each says about the divine—both the poets and the philosophers? Or to what should we compare this inquiry? Let us say it is like this: if someone were to consider the original medicine of the past in relation to the new medicine, which is now prescribed for the bodies of the present, and were to examine which of the two is better or worse, Asclepius <note>the Greek god of medicine</note> would answer him that time does not alter other arts, for the needs of those arts are always the same, and their works remain unchanged. But medicine, following the nature of bodies—a thing that is not stable or consistent, but which changes and shifts according to the foods in one's diet—must discover remedies and diets that are appropriate to the current nourishment. Therefore, do not think that those men of old, or Machaon and Podalirius <note>legendary physicians and sons of Asclepius</note>, were wiser in healing than those who later applied themselves to the art and discovered these wise and varied remedies. Rather, at that time, the art dealt with bodies that were not nourished by complex foods, nor were they entirely weakened, so it handled them easily, and its task was simple: to soothe the sick with mild medicines. But now, as bodies have slipped into a more complex diet and a poor constitution, the art itself has become complex and has changed from its former simplicity into a varied form. Come, let both the poet and the philosopher answer like Asclepius regarding their pursuits. If someone were to think that Homer and Hesiod, or even Orpheus, or any other man of that time, was less wise than Aristotle, he would be mistaken in his understanding.

ON FISHING, BOOK III

<note>The text begins with a fragmented line, likely a remnant of the previous section: "to the man, the noble herons of the deep."</note>

Hermes of glorious counsel, the fishermen propitiate you above all others. Therefore, they invoke you alongside the rustic deities, as we seek the fame of the great gathering.

First, let the fisherman’s body and limbs be both swift and strong. Let him be neither too fat nor lacking in flesh, for it is often necessary to struggle with powerful fish that possess overwhelming strength, and at times they writhe and thrash in the embrace of their mother, the salt sea. He must be able to leap from a rock and spring back onto it with ease. He must be able to endure the strain of the deep, to traverse long paths through the water with speed, to dive into the greatest depths, and to remain among the swells as if he were laboring on land, like a man of steadfast heart competing in the sea.

Let the fisherman be cunning and intelligent, for fish devise many varied schemes, escaping from unexpected traps. Let him be especially daring, fearless, and temperate. Let him not love the satiety of sleep, but let him watch keenly, awake in heart and with wide-open eyes. Let him endure the winter of Zeus and the thirsty season, and let him love his labors and desire the sea. For in this way, he shall be strong and dear to Hermes.

Fishing in the evening is best during the seasons of autumn, and when the morning star rises. In winter, one should set out when the rays of the sun are spreading, and in the flourishing spring, one should labor throughout the entire day, as the season increases with every kind of breeze.

<summary>This passage outlines the physical and mental requirements for a successful fisherman, emphasizing the need for agility, endurance, and cunning, while also noting the best times of day and year for fishing.</summary>

But the god, who does not least of all delight in the affairs of men, conceals what is fated in such matters, and the lot fell upon the river Ilius. Where even then, a struggle arose for the Messenians to save Aristodemus, and an obstacle was introduced as follows. A man of the Messenians (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. He was then about to take the woman as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, claiming that since he had betrothed her, Aristodemus was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, having betrothed her, had become more entitled to her than he. When the seer had said these things, the multitude of the Messenians rushed to kill the suitor of the girl, as he had brought an unholy stain upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain.
