**Torah Light** These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Service, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah is the command of "You shall not add and you shall not subtract," <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note> which indicates the perfection of the Torah. It is as the philosophers say: a thing that is perfect in the ultimate sense cannot have anything lacking or anything extra. For if it were lacking, they would say it lacks beauty, and if it were extra, they would say it was not perfect to begin with. Therefore, the definition of "perfect" is that it has neither lack nor excess. It is known that the Torah depends on His Great Name, which is <term>Yod He Vav He</term>, as it is written, "The Torah of the Lord is perfect," <note>Psalm 19:8</note> as I have elaborated upon this in my tractate <term>Shevuot</term>, chapter <term>Torah Or</term> <gloss>Torah Light</gloss>. And as it is written in the <term>Zohar</term> regarding the verse, "This is My name and this is My memorial" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>: <term>YH</term> with "My name" equals 365, and <term>VH</term> with "My memorial" equals 248. And it is written, "I am the first and I am the last." <note>Isaiah 44:6</note> He is the Absolute Perfect, having no deficiency and no addition. Regarding this comes the warning, "You shall not do so to the Lord your God," <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note> a warning against erasing the Name or tearing down a stone from the Temple. The letters of the Name are the house in which He, may He be blessed, dwells, and so too is the Temple. It is written, "I am the Lord, My name," and "My name is the soul of the letters." The letters are a covering for the revelation of His Name, and His Name is the soul for them. He who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service refers to the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came to have a fixed place specifically in the Chosen House, and it is forbidden to do otherwise, for the reason: "To His habitation you shall seek, and you shall come there." <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note> "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is a palace for the Lord, as it is written, "And He will descend into His holy palace, the Lord from the heavens." <note>Zechariah 2:17</note> The <term>Shekhinah</term> in the Temple will unify the Glory in the splendor of His strength, and this is "to His habitation, His name there," as the <term>Targum</term> <gloss>Aramaic translation</gloss> renders it: "to cause His <term>Shekhinah</term> to dwell." Around the place of holiness, the wicked walk, for they are the <term>kelipah</term> <gloss>husk/shell of impurity</gloss>. Therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in any place that you see." <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>

**And sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inward. This is the secret of the commandment to be diligent in bringing the sacrifice from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the one who returns is attached to his root, and it is written regarding them, "There you shall ascend," <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note> meaning there they shall have an ascent, and not outside. Since the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, is where holiness resides, we were commanded to be "turn from evil" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped, and one must uproot and eradicate them. This was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. Regarding "turn from evil," our Sages of blessed memory said that the nations outside the Land are not considered idolaters. The matter is that the nations who are in the Land of Israel, under the government of the Honored Name, worship the Lord by "cutting the shoots" <note>a metaphor for heresy</note>, and this is true idolatry. However, those outside the Land are under the government of the external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against tearing one stone from the holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eradicate a "perverted city" <note>Deuteronomy 13:13</note> and not to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Likewise, one who incites or leads astray must be uprooted and eradicated, for he is from the impurity of the primordial serpent who was an inciter, and the Holy One, blessed be He, cursed the serpent. Therefore, we do not seek merit for the inciter. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, as in the matter of "I will put enmity between you and the woman" <note>Genesis 3:15</note> regarding the serpent. Also, a false prophet is like an inciter. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the command that the priests have no permission to eat until the offering is brought to the Chosen House. For the firstlings, which are the "first," indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they must go to a holy place and take their sustenance from there, and also because they are holy, they must be eaten in Jerusalem. This is the secret of the "lesser holy things" and the tithes that are eaten in Jerusalem, and this is the grain, the wine, and the oil, which are the fathers of all foods. It is forbidden to eat the lesser holy things until after the blood is sprinkled, for the blood is the soul. Afterwards, the body is permitted to derive benefit. Know that just as the service, which is the sacrifice, is an offering to the Lord, so too is the one who serves, for the essence of the service is that he offers himself, as in the secret of "When a man among you brings an offering." <note>Leviticus 1:2</note> The burnt offering is entirely consumed, for it comes because of a thought, the secret of the mind, which is spiritual, and it is kept all night, for there is no darkness upon his resting place. The lesser holy things represent the perfection of the soul and the body.

**And the secret** of the unblemished firstling, and the secret of "Israel is holy," and He called them "My son, My firstborn, Israel." <note>Exodus 4:22</note> They are the holy congregation and are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating holy things when they have developed blemishes and have been redeemed: for Israel is holy, and Israel is called "man" (<term>Adam</term>). He is a holy living being; afterwards, a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," but he has a redemption, in the secret of "I will give a man in your stead." <note>Isaiah 43:4</note> This was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>the scapegoat</gloss>, which carries their iniquities. Our Sages of blessed memory said that they are "fierce" (<term>azut</term>), for they rest upon the "strength" (<term>oz</term>) of His people. But we were commanded not to cause a blemish in the holy things in order to eat them, for "a blemish is in them" <note>Leviticus 22:25</note> in their holiness, in their choice. Also, there is a prohibition against working or shearing the holy things, for even though they have fallen, they still possess the life of holiness.

**The conclusion** of the matter is that the service is the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is the human being. His soul is also offered after his death on the altar above, and Michael is the High Priest. The secret is that "in the image of God, man was made." Therefore, there is a great warning regarding the judgment of souls, not to put a man to death except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then he dies by the hand of Heaven, in the secret of "He is the witness, He is the judge," for the Holy One, blessed be He, is a true witness and a true judge. So too must the Sanhedrin be; just as they are true judges, they must be true witnesses. I mean that the truth of the testimony must be clarified for them with complete clarity, which is the inquiry and investigation. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and it will be established in the eyes of the Lord, the altar.

**And since** it is precious in the eyes of the Lord, for Israel is holy by virtue of their souls, which after their death attach to the souls above, therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, you shall not make a bald spot," etc., <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note> for "you are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the nations; the cutting and the baldness are from their customs, for it is appropriate since at their death they go to destruction and have no portion in this world or the world to come. Not so for us; we are children to the Lord. When one departs from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, on the contrary, we have a permanent dwelling above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to increase in mourning and to perform these acts.

**Let us return** to the matter that the person who serves is himself the sacrifice, as it is written, "When a man among you brings an offering." There is more in the hidden aspect, for it is prepared that he is offered even below, the human being, in the secret of the reincarnation: "Man and beast You save, O Lord." <note>Psalm 36:7</note> Therefore, even when eating ordinary meat of desire, we were commanded regarding the slaughter and warned greatly against any blemish, for if it is a blemish, it becomes a carcass (<term>nevelah</term>) in Israel. For who knows what reincarnation is in it? And "Love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note> means to choose for him a good death, which is slaughter without blemish. If the animal died by itself, it is spread and seized by the power of impurity. But when we slaughter with purity, and there is in the beast, the animal, and the bird a purity of a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

**And he who eats** a limb from a living creature is like one who eats from the flesh of a man when there is a reincarnation of a soul there. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." <note>Deuteronomy 12:23</note> Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of the pure beasts, animals, and birds all point to the spark that spreads within them, whether it is from the side of impurity or from the side of holiness. I have elaborated on this in <term>Parashat Shemini</term>. When Israel conducts themselves in holiness, it is written about them, "And they shall make Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among them," <note>Exodus 25:8</note> for they themselves are the Tabernacle, for they are the human being, as it were, in parts. The head corresponds to the Holy of Holies, the heart corresponds to the Holy Place, and from the belly downwards corresponds to the Courtyard of the Holy. As I have elaborated in <term>Parashat Terumah</term>, when one eats foods that are from the side of holiness, they are like a sacrifice offered upon the altar. Regarding this, our Sages of blessed memory said, "Now a person's table atones," as I have elaborated in its place.

**The matter** of the commandments of the festivals and their sacrifices, I have written their matters, each in its own place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals, to ascend for the festival, and "three times a year, every male shall appear." <note>Deuteronomy 16:16</note> And "he shall not appear" <note>a play on words: 'yera'eh' (shall appear) vs 'yireh' (shall see)</note>—in the way that he comes to see, so he comes to be seen. Therefore, if he wishes to be seen in the Temple, where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. For without this, it is forbidden to look at a wicked person, and how could he wish to be seen before Him, may He be blessed? He brings a burnt offering of appearance, and then he himself is a sacrifice through the sacrifice that he offers. And it is said, "Three times a year he shall appear." # Description of Lima, City of the Kings.

<margin>Appearance of the city of Lima.</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all coming straight onto the market, from where one can also see into all the corners, and on both sides the flat land. And through the greater part of the houses go canals bringing fresh water from the river, and very great convenience and comfort for the citizens; they can hereby water all their orchards and vegetable gardens, which they have beautiful and pleasant. Also

<margin>Many watermills, with which they grind their grain.</margin>
there lie in this river many watermills in our country's style, on which they grind their grain. In short, very rich citizens live here, some of whom have 150,000 ducats. And from this city, ships sail at times worth 800,000 ducats, and some even of a million. On the east side, high up in the city, is a high mountain on which a crucifix stands. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep the animals, and their dovecotes, their vineyards—though no good grapes, because of the nature of the land—and beautiful gardens, not only full

<margin>Description of the fertility of this land.</margin>
of all kinds of fruits of that land, but also of the Spanish ones, such as figs, pomegranates, lemons, citrons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar cane, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. And truly, to pass human life with joy, if the scandal, disunity, and war were not there, this place is certainly one of the most beautiful in the entire world: for the landscape there is so tempered that throughout the entire year there is no excessive heat or terrible cold. Also, one has never seen that there is hunger or plague, or any rain, or thunderclaps, or lightning from the Heavens

<margin>For what reason the city of the Kings received its name, and was built in the year 1535.</margin>
struck: but on the contrary, always a bright, clear, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535. It is called the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on the day of the Three Kings <note>original: "drie Coningen dagh", referring to Epiphany</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as also the remaining fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. And the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these 4 winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet not unhealthy as with us: for those who have pain in the head, washing themselves with this, find relief. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase in people and wealth, even though for many years there were over 500 houses

<margin>The width and length of the houses of Lima.</margin>
and the city is built very white, so that there may well be 2,000 standing, for the streets are wide and the market square is large. Each house has 80 feet of land, and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for it is consumed by worms within 2 or 3 years—the houses are built of only one story, yet very

<margin>Appearance of the houses</margin>
costly and magnificent with many rooms, halls, and parlors suitable for living and for hosting foreign guests. The walls are made of some materials that they bake together very thick, and fill them with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen, and all around and above

<column-break/>

on the walls they make small arbors of reeds where they shelter from the sun. For the rain, they do not worry, for it does not rain there. This city has under it all these cities where Bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Catchi, S. Michael, S. Francisco. It has been said before that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: in flat land by the sea, in mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and in land over the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea, we have treated until now, beginning from the Linea <note>the Equator</note> and Cape Passao to here. It is also to be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima, but much further, the sea coast to the south is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places, where for 10 miles of distance it neither thunders, lightnings, nor rains; but beyond those 10 miles it does, or as much or more as the mountains lie from the sea. There are also no fountains or wells in this flat land, but indeed 4 or 5 standing waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants maintain themselves with the water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which take their origin from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from fountains, which are few in the mountains. The distance of these rivers is partly described here; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from one another, though mostly 7 or 8. According to which the traveling people regulate themselves, because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, they are a mile wide or even more, sometimes more, sometimes less, according to the location of the land; there are different fertile trees and chosen lands that are watered and sown by the people, which they can do throughout the entire year. Also, around these rivers grow many kinds of wild trees, cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and lilies, etc. And after the Spaniards have taken the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through some canals that they lead from these rivers, which, because they run down quickly from high mountains, one can hardly sail across without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who make their journey along the flat land generally keep so close to the sea side that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and it rains much, it is dangerous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either with certain rafts that they have for that purpose, or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out, and one of the Indians swims in front, pulling that net or the raft with a cord, and another steering from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of reeds. The men wear shirts and cloths to the knees, and over that stretching an upper garment like a cloak. The women a dress of cotton to the length of the body, and although the style of the clothing is almost everywhere the same, there is nevertheless some difference in the adornment of the head: for some wear simple caps, some braided, some of one color, others of different colors, and there is no one who does not wear a cap on the head, and all distinguished according to the custom of the land.

### On the shame felt from undeserved praise.
### DIAL. XXVI.

> *Praise sparingly, for when you are praised unjustly,*
> *If you condemn it later, it will be a sign of fickleness.*

*Reason.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy person.

<note>A large decorative initial L marks the beginning of the response.</note>

*Joy.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy person. That which is an evil often springs from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they are themselves, imagine others to be the same. Hence, they are even more inclined than is fair to offer praise: and although I admit that to praise the unworthy is a bad thing, it is much worse to disparage the deserving.

*Reason.* I have praised an unworthy person.

*Joy.* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy: but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another; but to deceive is the crime of the deceiver himself.

*Reason.* The praise of another turns into my own infamy.

*Joy.* On the contrary, it is your own fault or ignorance. For just as there is no praise to be gained from another, so there is no infamy.

*Reason.* I grieve greatly that I have praised an unworthy person.

*Joy.* See to it, therefore, that you do not often grieve for this very thing. Beware of rushing rashly into praising or disparaging. For there is a desire for both: and (to speak properly) it is a disease and a certain itch of a tongue that is restless and ignorant of quiet; the bridle and guard of which are numbered among the works of supreme perfection, as Scripture says:

In this way, the eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth. For the one states that equal bases subtend equal sides and angles, while the other states that equal sides placed upon equal bases contain equal angles. Of these, the conclusion regarding equal bases was the result of the former, while the condition of equal sides being placed <note>as a premise</note> was one of the hypotheses assumed in that former theorem. Now, since there are two such converses, the primary one is uniform and definite, while the other is varied and proceeds into a large number of theorems, not converting in one instance but in many, due to the multitude of hypotheses in composite theorems. Often, we also convert one theorem from that which begins with two <note>or more</note> hypotheses, when the hypotheses are not all definite but some are indefinite.

One must also observe in these matters that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions. For example, every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangular number is a hexagonal number. All of them in the whole world, <term>shaquf</term> <gloss>transparent/clear</gloss>, meaning boldness. "From standing before the Lord of all the earth." **In which are.** The black ones. And he also mentioned the black ones because the kingdom of Babylon had already passed. And the kingdom of Media and Persia went forth first to the north country, for they were in all of Assyria and a portion of them ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth. And the white ones, which were the kingdom of Greece, went forth after them, for the kingdom of Greece was <unclear>bright</unclear>, for Alexander of Macedon, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him and reigned, and a portion of them ruled after him over the whole world. And the grizzled ones went forth into the south country, which was a holy portion, because Rome is to the south, and Julius Caesar, who reigned over Rome, began to fight against the kingdom of Greece, and at the beginning of his wars he went forth to the land of Egypt, which is to the south, and in all the provinces where the sons of Greece were reigning. And Julius Caesar overcame them, and he transferred the kingdom from the sons of Greece and returned it to the Romans.

Then the bodhisattva-mahasattva Manjushri said to the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult for these bodhisattva-mahasattvas to have endured so much out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should these bodhisattva-mahasattvas proclaim this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period?"

When this was said, the Blessed One replied to the bodhisattva-mahasattva Manjushri: "Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva should proclaim this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, by being established in four things. Which four? Here, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva should proclaim this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, by being established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association.

"And how, Manjushri, is a bodhisattva-mahasattva established in proper conduct? When, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva is patient, disciplined, has attained the stage of the disciplined, has a mind that is fearless and unperturbed, and is free from envy; and when, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva does not dwell on any phenomenon, but observes the true nature of phenomena as they really are. This lack of attachment and lack of conceptualization regarding these phenomena is called, Manjushri, the conduct of a bodhisattva-mahasattva.

"And what, Manjushri, is the sphere of association of a bodhisattva-mahasattva? When, Manjushri, a bodhisattva-mahasattva does not associate with kings, does not associate with princes, does not associate with high-ranking royal officials, does not associate with royal servants, does not serve them, does not honor them, does not approach them. He does not associate with followers of other sects, wandering ascetics, naked ascetics, or those who follow the path of worldly scriptures, nor does he serve them, honor them, or approach them. He does not associate with those who hold to materialistic philosophies, nor does he serve them, honor them, or approach them, nor does he engage in conversation with them. He does not associate with butchers, those who raise animals for slaughter, those who raise pigs, those who raise chickens, hunters, meat-sellers, actors, dancers, wrestlers, or boxers. He does not approach other places of worldly amusement. He does not engage in conversation with them. If they approach him, he teaches them the Dharma from time to time, but he teaches it without being dependent on them. He does not associate with monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who follow the path of the <term>shravaka</term> <gloss>disciple/hearer</gloss>, nor does he serve them, honor them, or approach them, nor does he engage in conversation with them. He does not share a common sphere of activity with them, whether in walking or in dwelling. If they approach him, he teaches them the Dharma from time to time, but he teaches it without being dependent on them. This, Manjushri, is the sphere of association of a bodhisattva-mahasattva."

<margin>They use this sign in all things. A heart with a tongue in the Egyptian language.</margin>
Three water jars, or heaven and earth pouring forth water; they liken the water jar to a heart possessing a tongue. A heart, because among them it is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. A tongue, because it exists always in moisture, and they call it the generator of being. There are three water jars, neither more nor fewer, because the process of the rising <note>referring to the annual flooding of the Nile</note> is, according to them, threefold. They assign one for the land of Egypt, since Egypt is by its own nature generative of water. Another is for the Ocean, for from it water arrives into Egypt during the time of the rising. A third is for the rains, which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the time of the Nile's rising. That Egypt generates the water is possible to learn from this: in the rest of the climate of the world, the flooding of rivers occurs in the winter.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic meaning of three water jars in Egyptian hieroglyphs, representing the threefold nature of the Nile's annual flood as originating from Egypt, the Ocean, and the rains of Ethiopia.</summary>

Regarding this, it is said, "And it came to pass, when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see" <note>Genesis 27:1</note>, speaking of his attribute. Therefore, the Lord, blessed be He, at the time of harsh judgment, has mercy on His world and says, "For My own sake, for My own sake, I will do it" <note>Isaiah 48:11</note>. For how could He profane [His name]? This is the mystery of the verse, "The Lord is gracious and full of compassion" <note>Psalm 111:4</note>. Every "gracious" <term>chanun</term> <gloss>gracious/merciful</gloss> is a turning of the face, for the face is turned to the other side. In this way, the <term>Sefirah</term> <gloss>divine emanation</gloss> of <term>Pachad Yitzchak</term> <gloss>Fear of Isaac</gloss> is established with power and dominion, in the sense that the Supreme Crown turns its face downward, because its great light covers the light of the eyes of the Fear of Isaac. This is the mystery of, "The Lord make His face shine upon you, and be gracious unto you" <note>Numbers 6:25</note>.

What is "and be gracious unto you"? It is the drawing down of mercy, in the sense that the Supreme Face, blessed be He, turns toward you as a free gift. This is the mystery of, "The Lord make His face shine upon you, and be gracious unto you." Now, I will turn your eyes again to this: know that in every place where you find the light of the face from above, this is a great mystery. It is that there are three attributes and a crown of faces of wrath, and all of them are for the righteous, as in the Fear of Isaac. The attribute of the Crown turns its face and removes the banner of wrath, and the attribute of <term>El</term> <gloss>God</gloss> is established within it. This is the mystery of the crowns of the faces of wrath.

And all the faces of wrath, the decrees, are turned and poured out here into mercy. This is the mystery of, "God is jealous and the Lord avenges" <note>Nahum 1:2</note>. This is the mystery of, "Blessed are the people who know the joyful shout; O Lord, they walk in the light of Your countenance" <note>Psalm 89:16</note>. Thus, the mystery of, "And it came to pass, when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see," is established. And here you will understand the mystery of, "Blow the horn at the new moon, at the covered time for our feast day" <note>Psalm 81:4</note>. And the mystery of, "Blessed are the people who know the joyful shout; O Lord, they walk in the light of Your countenance," will be understood as that which is the horn of the power of Isaac. When you understand your eyes in this way, you will enter into the mystery of the "remembrances" <term>zichronot</term> <gloss>remembrances/memorials</gloss> that turn back. And the "remembrances of sins." Here you will understand what is the difference between the remembrances that turn back and the remembrances of sins. For the creation of the remembrances is a drawing from the great mercies from above, in the mystery of, "God is jealous and the Lord avenges." And the remembrances of sins are those that draw from the attribute of <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God (as Judge)</gloss>, from the attribute of the drawing, as it is said of it, "He draws upon the face of the deep, and remembers light and flees darkness." Therefore, the attribute of <term>El</term> <gloss>God</gloss> turns downward, which is included in the attribute of <term>Elohim</term>, which is the mystery of the <term>Selah</term> <gloss>pause/forever</gloss>. This is the mystery of, "The Lord make His face shine upon you, and be gracious unto you."

After I have made this known to you, I have come to inform you of the mystery of the attribute of the name <term>El</term> <gloss>God</gloss>, blessed be He, which mediates in the middle and prevents the destruction of His world. The synonyms of <term>El</term>, blessed be He, that stand in the middle are the inner paths, the <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss> that divides the judgment, and they are included in the middle between <term>Chesed</term> and <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>. These synonyms that are in the middle are called the synonyms of mercy, and of them it is said, "And the Lord our God is the Merciful One," and the Holy One, blessed be He. Now I will choose this: know that all the Holy Names, the synonyms, and the attributes—whether they are called <term>Chesed</term>, whether they are called <term>Rachamim</term> <gloss>Mercies</gloss>, whether they are called <term>Din</term>—there is not one among them that is pure <term>Chesed</term>, or pure <term>Din</term>, or pure <term>Rachamim</term> that does not have a mixture, and all this is from the middle and below. ### Chapter Four: On the Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and an Indication of How to Draw with Purgative and Emetic Medicines

We say: It is recommended for one who intends to purge or vomit to divide their food, consuming the total amount they would eat in a day in several portions, and to make them different foods and different drinks. The stomach is prompted by these variations to desire to expel what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, taken upon other food, the stomach clings to it, holds it back, and grips it tightly, especially if it is small in quantity. As for those with a loose nature, none of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not occur in one who has good management; they require what is less frightening than those. Often, exercise, massage, and bathing are sufficient for digestion. Furthermore, if their body is full, it is more often full of the best humors, meaning blood. Thus, bloodletting is what is needed for purification rather than diarrhea. If necessity dictates bloodletting and evacuation with substances like hellebore and strong medicines, one must begin with bloodletting. This is one of the recommendations of Hippocrates in the book *Epidemics*, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood, and if the humors are viscous and cold, bloodletting might increase their thickness and viscosity. Therefore, it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In summary, if the humors are equal, prioritize bloodletting; if a humor prevails after that, evacuate it. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform bloodletting. Whoever prioritizes medicine over bloodletting when bloodletting should have been prioritized has no excuse. Whoever has recently undergone bloodletting and needs to evacuate, if they drink medicine, it will be stopped for them. Often, drinking the necessary medicine when bloodletting was required has resulted in fainting and distress. If it does not subside with sedatives, know that bloodletting should have been prioritized. There is no evacuation needed for excessive fullness that is done gently, which the magnitude of the ailment and the fullness—according to quality, not quantity—call for. Often, improving management is sufficient instead of the bloodletting required at the time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but a counter-indication prevents it, so the only remedy is fasting, sleep, and correcting the bad temperament by addressing the fullness. Some evacuation is by way of precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. It is necessary to take precautions before the time and perform the evacuation specific to their illness, whether it is bloodletting or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous to the humor being evacuated in quality, such as scammony when you need to evacuate bile. In that case, you must mix it with something that is contrary to it in quality but compatible in its purgative effect, such as myrobalan, and correct any bad temperament that might occur afterward. In patients with visceral tumors, their diarrhea and vomiting are weakened. If you are forced to do so, use for them things like colocynth and safflower. As for *mizaj* <gloss>mixtures</gloss>, *cassia fistula*, and the like: Hippocrates said that whoever has a nature that easily responds to vomiting, the best way to purify them is to use vomiting in summer, spring, or autumn, but not winter. For one with a moderate constitution, diarrhea is more suitable. If a need for vomiting arises, wait for the summer and avoid it when not necessary. It is necessary to precede diarrhea and vomiting by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and by widening and opening the passages, as this secures the body from fatigue. Know that accustoming the nature to respond easily to what is desired in terms of diarrhea or vomiting before using strong medicine is one of the beneficial management practices. Diarrhea and vomiting with physical emaciation are difficult, exhausting, and dangerous. An emetic medicine may become a purgative if the stomach is strong, if it is drunk during intense hunger, if the drinker has a loose nature, if they are not accustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is heavy in substance and descends quickly. A purgative becomes an emetic due to a weak stomach, the extreme dryness of the waste, or because the medicine is repulsive and the person has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge or if it purges matter that is not mature, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it throughout the body, taking control of the body and transforming other humors into it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting in most cases, such as bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have varying states, such as phlegm. For a feverish patient, diarrhea is more appropriate in itself. For one whose humor is descending, such as those with intestinal slippage, vomiting is impossible. The worst purgative medicines are those composed of medicines that are highly contradictory in the time of their purgative action, as they disturb the bowels; the first might purge the second before the second acts, or the first might purge the second itself. Whoever is subjected to diarrhea and vomiting while their body is clean will inevitably suffer from dizziness, colic, and distress. In summary, what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating excess matter, there is no distress with it. When it begins to cause distress, it is either evacuating something other than the excess, or if the evacuated humor changes during vomiting or diarrhea to another humor, it indicates the body is clean of the humor intended for evacuation.

This. Sacrifice. Extended. By the All-Creator. Come. Gods. Being of good mind. || 5 ||

This verse has been explained previously (Atharva Veda 2.35.5). I offer the senses, beginning with the eye, as being related to the mental sacrifice; I make them inclined toward that. The summary is: may the gods, being of good mind—that is, acting as if they are of good heart—come to and reach this mental sacrifice, which is extended or spread out by the god <term>Vishvakarma</term> <gloss>the All-Creator</gloss>.

> Those who are the priests of the gods, and those who are worthy of sacrifice, and those for whom the oblation is made as their portion.
> May all the gods, as many as there are, being mighty, come with their wives to this sacrifice and rejoice. || 6 ||

Those. Of the gods. Priests. Those. And. Worthy of sacrifice. For whom. Oblation. Is made. Portion.
This. Sacrifice. With. Wives. Having come. As many as. Gods. Mighty. Rejoice. || 6 ||

Among the gods, those who are the priests are those who perform the sacrifice at the proper time. And those who are worthy of sacrifice are those who are to be worshipped. For both these groups of gods, the oblation, which is in the form of a share, is made or given. May all the gods, as many as there are in number, being mighty, come to this sacrifice with their wives—such as <term>Indrani</term> <gloss>the wife of Indra</gloss> and others—and rejoice, becoming satisfied by the acceptance of the oblation.

Now, Radha, tormented by separation, speaks regarding the moon: "Viraha..." <note>regarding separation</note>. "Aye" is an expression of sorrow. "O friend, this moon intensifies the agony of love in my heart. What kind of moon? It is a friend to the god of love <note>Manobhuva</note>. She speaks while remembering the state of separation from Murari. What kind of moon? One whose radiance is like the radiance of Murari's lotus-face, which is pale from separation. Therefore, even though it conceals the pain, it still causes pain because it is a friend to the god of love. The meaning is this: previously, because it possessed the radiance of Murari's face, which was pale from my separation, it destroyed my pain; but now, as a friend of desire, it causes pain. Knowing that he is now attached to another, I cannot remain..."

<note>The commentary continues: "Hamsalilah" <gloss>the play of the swan</gloss>. "Lavalekha" <gloss>a particle or drop</gloss>. Regarding "Shri Jayadeva...", the play of Hari </note><note>Krishna</note> sung by Shri Jayadeva should destroy the sins of the Kali age for the listeners and readers. Now, she says that even this moon causes greater agony: "Viraha..." <note>regarding separation</note>. "Aye" is in sorrow. This moon, which is visible, intensifies the agony of love in my heart. What is it like? It has the radiance of the lotus-face of Murari, which is pale from separation from me. Thus, the sight of this moon, which resembles Krishna's lotus-face, causes great agony because it reminds me of his face. What is it doing? It is concealing the pain. Thus, the sight of the moon causes the uprooting of discernment; even though Krishna has committed an offense, the mind remembers him. She gives the reason for it causing agony: "Manobhuva..." <note>of the mind-born one</note>, a friend to the god of love. Thus, because I did not follow Krishna even when he was nearby, the god of love has become my enemy due to my transgression of his command. The moon, wishing to assist him, also causes agony. The moon is famous as the brother of the god of love, and because of their kinship, they are friends; hence the use of the term "Manobhuva" <note>born of the mind</note>. As the Shruti says: "The moon was born from the mind, the sun from the eye." The word "vedana" <gloss>pain</gloss> refers to knowledge or suffering, and also to fear, anger, sorrow, confusion, and memory.

This will free you from the consequences in the afterlife and restore a good reputation to your name for two reasons: first, your ability to find exits and fabricate excuses to defend yourself; and second, your voluntary confession of guilt, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. Dimna answered him, saying, "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. It has come in a tradition that the Glorious Creator
Created the inhabitants of the world in three kinds.
One group is entirely reason, knowledge, and existence;
That is the angel, who knows nothing but prostration.
There is no greed or passion in its essence;
It is pure light, alive through the love of God.
Another group is devoid of knowledge,
Like an animal, fat from fodder.
It sees nothing but the stable and the grass;
It is heedless of misery and of honor.
This third one is the human being and mankind;
Half is angel, and half is donkey.
The donkey half is inclined toward the base;
The other half is inclined toward the sublime.
Those two groups are at rest from war and strife,
But this human is in torment with two opposites.
And this human, too, was divided by trial;
They are human in form, but became three communities.
One group has become completely immersed in the Divine,
Joined with the angels like Jesus.
The form is Adam, but the meaning is Gabriel,
Freed from anger, passion, and idle talk.
Freed from asceticism, piety, and holy struggle,
As if they were not born of human kind.
Another group joined with the donkeys;
They became pure anger and absolute desire.
The Gabrielic quality was in them and departed;
That house was narrow, and that quality was heavy.
The person who is without the Beloved becomes dead;
He becomes a donkey when his soul is without Him.
Because the soul that does not have Him is base;
This is a true saying, the Sufi has spoken it.
He performs more soul-work than the animals;
He does intricate tasks in the world.
The deceit and trickery that he knows how to weave,
That does not appear from other animals.
Weaving gold-embroidered garments,
Finding pearls in the depths of the sea,
The minute details of the science of geometry,
Along with astronomy, medicine, and philosophy,
Since his attachment is only to this world,
He has no path to the seventh heaven.
All this knowledge is the foundation of the end,
Which is a support for the cow and the camel.
For the sake of sustaining the animal for a few days,
The confused ones called these mysteries.

The Glorious Creator brought forth the creation,
He created the creatures in three parts.
One group with reason and existence,
That is the angel, which is in the state of prostration.

It became a manifestation of the lights of God's love.

It became an animal, desiring through instinct.

Joined to the host of angels, like the station of Jesus.
The form is Adam, but the meaning is Gabriel,
Freed from anger, passion, and idle talk.
Those who are simple-hearted through piety and asceticism,
As if they were not born of human kind.
The last group is of the nature of beasts;
Pure anger and absolute desire, the same.
The Gabrielic quality in them met with decline;
The house was narrow, and that high quality was complete.
That person who is without the Beloved becomes dead;
He becomes a donkey when that soul is without the Beloved.
Since the soul that is without the Beloved is base,
This is the word of Truth, hold this saying fast.
Deeper than the animal soul, he is immersed;
Every intricate work in the world is his work.
The form of knowledge, deceit, trickery, and guile;
Other animals cannot perform such work.

He draws forth gems from the depths of the sea.
He makes many designs in the science of geometry;
Also the known sciences of philosophy, medicine, and astronomy.
Attachment and connection to the worldly is total;
There is no passage to the seventh heaven.
This knowledge is tied to the manger;
He provides for himself with the cow and the camel.
The purpose is the sustaining of the animal for a few days;
Those fools have called these mysteries.

When the young feed upon their dead mother, after a short while, she blinks <gloss>the eyes move; it means the mother is dead but her eyes move</gloss>, and they all abandon her and run away. They no longer see her as their mother, and they no longer perceive her as one of their own kind. What they loved in their mother was not her physical form, but that which animated her form. For those who die in battle, their burial does not include the use of ceremonial fans. One does not cherish the shoes of a man who has had his feet cut off, for in both cases, the foundation is gone. The various attendants of the Son of Heaven do not trim their nails and do not pierce their ears. Those who take a wife are kept outside and are no longer employed in service. If preserving the physical form is enough to achieve such things, how much more so is it for one who has perfected their virtue!

<margin>This means the blinking of the eyes is no longer seen as the mother.</margin>

<margin>The stiffness of the body is no longer perceived as one of their own kind.</margin>

<margin>If the physical form is not worth loving, it is not worth loathing.</margin>

<margin>Those who die in battle lack martial spirit, therefore they are not honored with ceremonial fans.</margin>

<margin>War takes martial spirit as its foundation.</margin>

<margin>Shoes take the feet as their foundation.</margin>

<margin>Another analogy is provided: those selected as imperial concubines do not trim their nails or pierce their ears, so as to keep their forms complete and receive the gaze of the supreme ruler.</margin>

<margin>They are not kept in official service for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would prevent them from exercising the influence of a new marriage.</margin>

<margin>Those who are physically complete are still enough to move others.</margin>

<summary>This passage from the Zhuangzi uses the analogy of animals reacting to a dead mother and the physical requirements of imperial attendants to argue that the essence of a being lies in its animating spirit rather than its physical form, emphasizing the superiority of those who have perfected their inner virtue.</summary>

<term>Tam</term> <gloss>her</gloss>. O long-lived one. The suffix <term>matup</term> is used here in the sense of praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of helping others. [**<term>Vacanat</term>**] <gloss>from the words</gloss>. From my request, and also to do a favor to yourself. The meaning is to fulfill yourself through the act of helping another. Even though the self is the object of the action of helping, the use of the genitive case <term>atmanah</term> is not contradictory, as in the phrase "he helps himself." As <term>Bharavi</term> <gloss>a classical Sanskrit poet</gloss> says: "That wealth is useful by which one helps others." And <term>Sriharsha</term> <gloss>a classical Sanskrit poet</gloss> says: "To help the virtuous, to see wealth, to travel through the sky." Thus, the statement of <term>Natha</term> <gloss>referring to the commentator Mallinatha</gloss> that "the second case is seen somewhere, so it is the same for all" is a statement of the master, not of the ignorant. Speak thus to that beloved. What should be said? He says: O delicate one, your companion, your husband, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri—that is, being a dweller of the Ramagiri hermitage—is <term>avyapannah</term> <gloss>not dead</gloss>. He gives the reason for his survival: being separated and suffering, he asks after your welfare. The verb "to ask" takes two objects. ->May you obtain the unbroken love of your husband,<-
->thus addressed by them, Uma bowed low.<-
->But by her, who shares half the body of him,<-
->even the blessings of loved ones were surpassed. || 28 ||

*Akhaṇḍitam* (unbroken) etc. **Uma**, having bowed, **was addressed by them** (the virtuous women) saying, "**May you obtain the unbroken** (undiminished) **love of your husband** (Shiva)." The use of the present tense with *sma* indicates the past tense. **By her**, Gauri, who **shares half the body** of **him** (Hara), **even the blessings of loved ones** (friends and relatives) **were surpassed** (rendered inferior). The meaning is that she attained a result even greater than those blessings.

->Having completed the task of his daughter,<-
->befitting his own desire and resources,<-
->the mountain, a man of action, stood in the assembly,<-
->occupied by friends, awaiting the arrival of the Bull-emblemed one. || 29 ||

*Icchā* (desire) etc. **The mountain** (Himavan), who is **a man of action** (skilled), and **a member of the assembly** (worthy of the court), **having completed the task** of **his daughter** (Parvati) in a manner **befitting** both his **desire and resources**, **stood** in the **assembly occupied by friends**, **awaiting the arrival of the Bull-emblemed one** (Hara).

->Meanwhile, on the mountain of Kubera,<-
->adornments befitting that former marriage ceremony<-
->were brought by the Mothers and placed<-
->before the Punisher of the City. || 30 ||

*Tāvat* (meanwhile) etc. **Meanwhile**, at the very time Gauri was being adorned, **on the mountain of Kubera** (Kailasa), **adornments** (ornamental materials) **befitting that former marriage ceremony** were **brought by the Mothers** (the seven divine mothers, such as Brahmi) and **placed before the Punisher of the City** (Shiva).

### The Nahidiyya Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham told us, saying:

I inclined with a group of my companions toward the courtyard of a tent, seeking hospitality from its people. A short, stout man came out to us and said: "Who are you?" We said: "Guests who have not tasted food for three days." He cleared his throat and said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of a <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of crushed wheat and meat</gloss> as large as a bald man's head, in a wide bowl, crowned with choice dates from the orchards of a tyrant, the single one of which fills the mouth? From a group of five thirsty ones, in which the molar disappears, as if its pits were birds' tongues. They scoop the <term>nahida</term> with bowls milked from aged, fat-laden camels. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it." The old man laughed and said: "And your uncle also desires it." Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of fine flour like pieces of bullion, sifted onto a silk tablecloth, smelling of <term>qarz</term> <gloss>a type of acacia bark used for tanning and scenting</gloss>? A nimble, clever, light-footed youth jumps to it, kneads it without shaking or startling it, separates it without soft kneading, then moistens it with clarified butter or whey, a generous moistening. Then he proceeds to twist it and leaves it in the corner of the <term>sayda</term> <gloss>a type of cooking hearth</gloss>. When it has risen without being sparse, he takes the wood of the <term>ghada</term> <gloss>a desert tree used for fuel</gloss> and lights a fire in it. When its fire dies down, he prepares the bed for his dough, then he flattens it after having thoroughly moistened it, then he spreads it over it, then he covers it. When it has risen and puffed, he piles on it hot stones that meet the two heats, until he covers them on the hearth with a lid. It splits open, its crust mimics thin bread, and its redness is the redness of the Hijazi <term>busr</term> <gloss>unripe dates</gloss> famous for the 'Mother of Rats' or the 'Ibn Tab' cluster. He pours over it white butter like snow until it settles into the crevices of the dough. The core of the flour drinks what is on it of the butter. I present it to you, and you gulp it down in mouthfuls of <term>juwayn</term> or <term>zankal</term> <gloss>types of small, quick bites</gloss>. Do you desire it, O youths?" He said: Everyone of us stretched toward his description, our saliva flowed, and we smacked our lips. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it." He laughed and said: "And your uncle, by God, does not hate it." Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of a Najdi she-kid, highland and wild, that has eaten the <term>baram</term> and the Najdi wormwood, the <term>qaysum</term> <gloss>southernwood</gloss> and the dry brush, and has sipped the hot water, and filled itself with <term>qasis</term> <gloss>a type of desert plant</gloss> until its marrow is hidden and its fat is rich? It is slaughtered and then plunged into a cauldron until it is cooked without burning or overcooking. Then it is presented to you, its skin removed to reveal white fat on a tray arranged with flatbreads like spread-out Coptic linen or dyed red fabric. If he leaves two sisters and a wife, and he bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the wealth after the bequest, the method for that is to establish the estate <note>original: "الفريضة" <gloss>the obligatory share/estate distribution</gloss></note> from twelve shares. For each sister is one-third of what remains of the wealth after the bequest. This is wealth minus a bequest. You know that one-eighth of what remains with the bequest equals the portion of a sister. So, one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest. One-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest, together with the bequest, equals the portion of a sister. That is one-eighth of the wealth and seven-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals three-eighths of the wealth and one-third of the bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. Subtract three-eighths from the wealth, and there remains five-eighths of the wealth, which equals three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals five bequests and four-fifths of a bequest. The wealth is twenty-nine, the bequest is five, and the portion is eight.

In another aspect of bequests: a man died and left four sons, and he bequeathed to a man the equivalent of the portion of one of his sons, and to another one-fourth of what remains of the third. Know that the bequest is only from the third.

Its sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman (with the *qaf* and *ra* vocalized with a *fatha*). Before him, it belonged to his brother Musa, who ceded it to King al-Nasir in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent an emir and an army there, but then Sultan Badr al-Din seized it, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this sultan outside the city as he was returning from hunting. I dismounted from my mount for him, so he dismounted from his, and I greeted him. He received me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a visitor dismounts for them, they dismount for him; they are pleased by this action and increase their honor toward him. If one greets them while mounted, it displeases them and does not satisfy them, and it becomes a cause for the visitor to be deprived of favor. This happened to me with some of them, and I will mention it. When I greeted him, he mounted and I mounted. He asked me about my situation and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be lodged in the best accommodation. He would send much food, fruit, and sweets in silver platters, along with wax candles. He clothed me, provided me with a mount, and treated me well. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray (vocalized with a *fatha* on the *hamza*, a *sukun* on the *qaf*, and a *fatha* on the *sad* and the *ra*). It is one of the finest and most well-constructed cities in the land of the <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia/Byzantine territories</gloss>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and gardens on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through its houses. It contains trees and grapevines, and there are many gardens inside it. Carpets attributed to the city are made there from sheep's wool, which have no equal in any other land. From there, they are transported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the obedience of the King of Iraq. We stayed there at the hospice of the Sharif Husayn, who is the deputy there for the Emir Artaw Arta, who is the deputy for the King of Iraq in the lands of the <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia</gloss> that he has conquered. This Sharif is one of the <term>fityan</term> <gloss>members of a chivalric youth order</gloss>, and he has a large following. He honored us with the utmost honor and acted better than those who preceded him. Then we traveled to the city of Nigde (vocalized with a *fatha* on the *nun*, a *sukun* on the *kaf*, and a *fatha* on the *dal*). It is one of the cities of the King of Iraq, a large and populous city, though some of it has fallen into ruin. It is traversed by the river known as the Black River, which is one of the major rivers. There are three bridges over it, one inside the city and two outside. There are waterwheels (<term>nawa'ir</term>) <gloss>large water-lifting wheels</gloss> on it, both inside and outside, from which the gardens are irrigated. Fruits are abundant there. ### CHAPTER LXVI.

#### How the next day we sent messengers to the Caciques of Tlascala, asking them for peace, and what they did about it.

<note>A decorative initial D, typical of the period, marks the beginning of the chapter.</note>

After the battle I have recounted had passed, in which we captured the three principal Indians, our Captain Cortés sent them off immediately. Along with the two who were in our camp, who had gone as messengers other times, he ordered them to tell the Caciques of Tlascala that we begged them to come at once in peace, and to grant us passage through their land to go to Mexico, as we had sent to tell them other times. We told them that if they did not come now, we would kill all their people, and because we liked them much and wished to have them as brothers, we would not want to anger them if they had not given cause for it. Many flattering words were said to them to attract them to our friendship. Those messengers went willingly to the capital of Tlascala and delivered their embassy to all the Caciques I have already named. They found them gathered with many other elders and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and they were very sad, both from the poor outcome of the war and from the death of the captains who were their relatives or sons who died in the battles. It is said they did not want to listen to them willingly. What they agreed upon was to immediately order the calling of all the diviners and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and others who cast lots, whom they call <term>Tacalnaguat</term> <gloss>sorcerers</gloss>, who are like wizards. They told them to look through their divinations, spells, and lots to see what kind of people we were, and if we could be defeated by waging war on us day and night, and also to know if we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>gods or demons</gloss>, just as those from Cempoal said, which I have said other times are evil things like demons, and what things we ate, and to look

A courtesan who refuses to approach a man by the order of the King shall receive one thousand lashes or a fine of five thousand <term>panas</term> <gloss>units of currency</gloss>.

When we find it, we discover alongside it the beginning of the year in the week and its nature. When we know the beginning of the year and its nature, and we combine that nature with the common or leap status, we know from that the passage of the beginning of the next year.

Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still thunder many things against me, my Monarchy will nevertheless stand, and yours will utterly perish. I do not write so prolixly about Alchemy in vain, but I do it with this intention and purpose, that from these things you may know closely and solidly what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood.

<margin>The end of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but arcana <gloss>secret remedies</gloss>.</margin>
Nor should you be offended by the fact that neither gold nor silver comes from it. Rather, this must be carefully attended to: that through it, arcana may be discovered, and the deceptions of the apothecaries <note>original: "seplasiariorum"</note> exposed, by which the crude common people are deceived, while they serve them for one florin what they would not redeem for a single coin. Such are their precious arcana.

<margin>Poison exists even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is forced to admit this. If this is true, then I ask you now: should poison not be separated from the good and useful? And should the good be accepted and the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it must be so, I ask you to explain to me how this is separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted to admit that poison lies hidden there, and you are asked where it finally goes, you then bring forth something about corrections that extract and remove the poison, just as the quince is said to correct scammony, after the manner of <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>a purgative preparation of scammony</gloss>.

<margin>The correction of physicians is examined.</margin>
What kind of correction is that, truly? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it was at first? And yet you boast in the meantime that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. Where has it gone? It remains in the <term>Diagridium</term>. Test this, if you are wise: exceed the dose, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it without delay.

<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>a purgative root</gloss>, and call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. These are your kinds of corrections, which would befit rustics and should be given to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see whether you will not feel the poison.

<margin>What it means for a physician to correct.</margin>
*To correct is to take what is corrected.* If someone is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who is punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; it is up to them, not up to you. Now, in this case, the physician must consider nothing more than that the poison should be removed. This must be done through separation. For example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted as food. If you remove the poison from it, you will eat it without harm. The same must be understood equally of all other things, namely, that a similar separation is necessary. That not yet being done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless it happens that nature supplies your place, or the greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will remain. Now, therefore, if that true foundation is required which removes the poison, how does Alchemy accomplish this? For it must be done in such a way that, if Mars <note>alchemical symbol for iron</note> is in the Sun <note>alchemical symbol for gold</note>, Mars is removed; and if Saturn <note>alchemical symbol for lead</note> dwells in Venus <note>alchemical symbol for copper</note>, it is separated from it. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist in them. But those bodies which are contrary must be entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is removed, and the evil which you seek is taken from the good. Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so medicine is much less useful if it does not pass through the fire.

<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
For it is necessary for all things to pass through fire into another generation, by which it ought to benefit and assist man. And should this not deservedly be considered the sound foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to employ poisons, but arcana.

<margin>Workshops are criticized.</margin>
But all those workshop preparations, however many there are, do not contribute even a single letter to this doctrine. They are simply occupied with correcting, as if a dog were to break wind in a room, and that stench were to be quieted by troches, incense, or juniper wood. I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room just as much afterwards as before? And although it may not be perceived by the sense of smell, am I therefore to be allowed to say that the stench has been separated and no longer remains? Indeed, it is present, but corrected by the fumigation. Thus, the fumigation and the stench enter the nostrils together. Such also are the corrections of the pharmacists, who dull <term>Aleopaticum</term> <gloss>a purgative medicine</gloss> with sugar, so that it inflicts no harm. Thus, sugar and honey are their mastery. In this way, gentian also corrects theriac. Are these not the works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the principal physicians. Who is so stupid that he does not immediately smell that these things are worth nothing? What, I ask, can they boast of their remedies other than to say, *This electuary is sweet, made of aromatics, sugar, and honey*

He often avoided the cleverness required for formal debate. His lifestyle was simple, yet he maintained it with great temperance. He indulged in white clothing and bathed in the public baths twice daily. Once, when someone asked him why, as a bishop, he bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I do not have time for a third." On another occasion, when he saw Arcadius the bishop, one of Arcadius's associates asked him why he wore clothing unbecoming of a bishop, and where it was written that a clergyman must wear white. He replied, "Tell me first, where is it written that a bishop must wear black?" When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius approached him and said, "You will not be able to show that a clergyman must wear black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels appears in white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles wearing white." Having readily said these things and many others, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, was taking away a church from the Novatians while visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius came to him and urged him to return the church. Leontius replied heatedly, saying to him, "You Novatians do not deserve to have churches, as you abolish repentance and exclude the philanthropy of God." As Leontius continued to speak ill of the Novatians in this and similar ways, Sisinnius said, "Indeed, no one has ever repented as much as I have." When Leontius asked, "How did you repent?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you."

Once, when John <note>John Chrysostom</note> was complaining to the bishop and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "It does not have two." When John became angry and said, "Do you see that you are alone? Do you wish to be bishop?" Sisinnius replied, "I do not mean that, but rather that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, as I am to others." John, indignant at what was said, replied, "I will stop you from this, for you are a heretic." To this, Sisinnius wittily replied, "I will even pay you a reward if you relieve me of such great labor." Softened by this reply, John said, "I will not stop you from speaking with me, if speaking at all causes you such grief."

Thus, Sisinnius was ready with his replies and full of wit. It would be a long task to write down and record everything he said. Therefore, I have shown in a few words what kind of man he was, as I considered it necessary. I will add that he was renowned for his education. Because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Furthermore, all the prominent members of the Senate cherished and admired him. He wrote many books. In them, he mixes poetic language with his own. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writing. For he possessed grace in his face, his voice, his posture, his gaze, and in the entire movement of his body. He was therefore loved by people of all religions, and especially by the bishop Atticus. These are the things concerning Sisinnius.

The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, for the life of the saints is either praised or blamed. But among Christians, there is only as much slander as the demons—whom they consider gods—desire. It is as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were performed in theaters and temples in honor of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in churches, or what is offered to the true God. From this, understand where the building of morals lies and where the ruin. Who, moreover, said this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, with such a vain and fitting lie: that Christians revere rather than hate the demons whose worship the Hebrews were forbidden to practice? But that God whom the wise Hebrews worshipped, and to whom we offer sacrifice along with the heavenly holy angels and the virtues of God—whom we venerate and love as most blessed fellow citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage—forbids it, thundering in His law which He gave to His Hebrew people. He added, with great menace, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone think that it was not commanded that sacrifice should be withheld from the worst demons and earthly spirits—whom this man calls the least or lesser ones—who are even called gods in the holy scriptures, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations, which the seventy interpreters clearly set down in the Psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the nations are demons." Lest anyone think, therefore, that sacrifice was forbidden to these demons, but permitted to be offered to the heavenly ones, either all or some, He immediately added: "Except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only. This is so that no one who hears "to the Lord alone" might believe that it is the sun <note>original: "solem"</note> to whom one thinks sacrifice should be offered. That this is not to be understood in that way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this philosopher gives such great testimony, gave a law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure or unknown, but now spread among all nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there in this, His law and His prophets, to search out many things on this matter? Indeed, there is no need to search, for they are not hidden or rare, but rather fitting and frequent to collect and place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that He wished sacrifice to be offered to no one at all except to Himself, the true and supreme God. Behold this one thing, briefly—or rather, sternly and menacingly, but truthfully—spoken by that God whom their most learned men proclaim: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the disobedient meet with eradication. "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out," He says, "except to the Lord only." Not that He is in need of any thing, but because it is profitable for us that we be His possession. Celsus claims that the Christians say the Jews were runaways from Egypt, that they never accomplished anything noteworthy, and that they were never significant in speech or in number. Regarding the claim that they were not runaways, but Hebrews who had resided in Egypt, we have already spoken in the preceding sections. If he thinks their lack of significance in speech or number is proven by the fact that their history is not widely found among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to examine their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, they would find that these people were a shadow of a heavenly life on earth. Among them, no one was considered God except the One who is over all, and no one who made images held a position in their society. For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in their state, as the Law expelled all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues, which attract the foolish among men and drag the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, a law among them such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under the heaven, a likeness of any reptile that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters beneath the earth." The Law indeed intended that they, while engaging with the truth of each thing, should not fashion things other than the truth, falsifying what is truly male or what is really female, or the nature of beasts, or birds, or the race of reptiles, or of fish. Also solemn and noble among them is the command: "Do not, having looked up to heaven and seen the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, be led astray and worship them and serve them."

What kind of constitution was that of an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for effeminacy to appear? It is also wonderful that the incitements of the young, the prostitutes, were removed from their society. There were also courts of the most just judges, and they had given much proof of a healthy life.
