# Through meditation on the Supreme, the obscured [powers] are revealed; from Him, therefore, come the bondage and liberation of this [individual soul]. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued that the individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss>) is merely a part of the Supreme Self (<term>atman</term> <gloss>Self</gloss>), just as a spark is a part of fire. If this is the case, just as the spark and the fire both possess the powers of burning and illumination, the individual soul and the Lord (<term>ishwara</term> <gloss>Lord/God</gloss>) should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, due to the soul's own knowledge and sovereignty, the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream would be a result of its own will. To this, it is replied: even though the individual soul and the Lord stand in the relation of part and whole, the individual soul clearly possesses attributes contrary to those of the Lord. Does the individual soul then possess no attributes equal to the Lord? It is not that they do not exist; they exist but are obscured by the obstruction of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>) and similar factors. This obscured power is revealed only to a person who meditates on the Supreme Lord, whose mind is focused, and whose darkness has been dispelled—much like the power of vision, obscured by cataracts, is restored through the potency of medicine—by the grace of the Lord. It is not revealed to all beings by nature. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, come the bondage and liberation of this soul. Bondage arises from a lack of knowledge of the Lord's true nature, and liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. The scripture (<term>shruti</term> <gloss>revealed scripture</gloss>) also says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. Through meditation on Him, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state, universal sovereignty, and all desires are fulfilled," and so on.

# Or, that [obscuration] is due to the connection with the body. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why does the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It would be logical for these powers to remain unobscured, just as the burning and illuminating powers of a spark are not obscured. It is replied: this is true, but the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs due to its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy here: just as the burning and illuminating powers of fire, though inherent, are obscured when it is contained within wood, or as when it is covered by ash, so too is the knowledge and sovereignty of the soul obscured by the connection with the limiting adjuncts (<term>upadhi</term> <gloss>limiting adjuncts</gloss>) of the body and the like, which are created by name and form imposed by ignorance. This obscuration is caused by the confusion of distinguishing the soul from these adjuncts. The word "or" (<term>va</term> <gloss>or</gloss>) is used to exclude the doubt that the soul is something other than the Lord. One might ask: why not assume the soul is something other than the Lord, given that its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured, rather than imagining a connection with the body? It is replied: the soul cannot be other than the Lord. The scripture begins with "That Divinity thought" and continues with "having entered into this by this individual soul as the Self," referring to the soul with the word "Self." Furthermore, it instructs the soul, "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Thou Art, O Svetaketu," teaching that the soul is indeed the Lord. Therefore, the soul, being non-different from the Lord, has its knowledge and sovereignty obscured due to its connection with the body. Consequently, the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream by the soul's will is not tenable. If the creation of chariots in a dream were a matter of will, no one would ever see an undesirable dream, for no one wills an undesirable thing. As for the argument that the scripture regarding the waking state declares the reality of the dream state, that comparison is not intended to imply the same degree of reality, as that would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and the like in a dream. The comparison is intended to suggest that the dream is similar to the waking state in its appearance, as it is caused by impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious impressions</gloss>) derived from the waking state. Therefore, it is established that the dream is merely an illusion (<term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion/magic</gloss>).

# Its absence is in the nerves, in the Self, according to the scripture. || 3.2.7 ||

The Section on the Absence of That [Dream State]. || 3.2.7 ||

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>deep sleep</gloss>) is to be examined. Regarding this, there are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep. In one place it is heard: "When a person is thus asleep, completely serene, and does not know any dream, he has entered into the nerves." Elsewhere, after mentioning the nerves, it is heard: "Having moved through them, he rests in the pericardium." Similarly, in another place, after mentioning the nerves: "He enters into them when he is asleep and sees no dream; then he becomes one with the vital breath (<term>prana</term> <gloss>vital breath</gloss>) alone." Likewise, in another place: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Similarly, in another place: "O gentle one, then he becomes united with the Existent, he has attained his own Self." And also: "Embraced by the omniscient Self, he knows nothing external or internal."

Here a doubt arises: are these—the nerves and the others—separate places of deep sleep, independent of one another, or are they a single place of deep sleep, dependent on one another? What is the conclusion? They are separate. Why? Because they have the same purpose; things with the same purpose are not found to be dependent on one another in any context.

ON FISHING, BOOK III

<note>The text begins with a fragmented invocation, likely referring to the noble herons or similar avian observers of the sea.</note>
Glorious Hermes, counselor of renown, the fishermen honor you above all others. For this reason, they call upon you alongside the rustic deities, as we seek the fame that comes from the vast sea.

First, the fisherman must possess a body and limbs that are both swift and strong. He should be neither excessively fat nor lacking in muscle, for it is often necessary to struggle against powerful fish that possess immense strength, sometimes thrashing and twisting in the embrace of their mother, the salt sea. He must be able to leap from rock to rock with ease, and when the labor of the deep demands it, he must be able to swim swiftly through the long passage, diving into the deepest waters and remaining there amidst the swells, just as one toils on land, for the man who labors in the sea must possess a steadfast heart.

The fisherman must be cunning and intelligent, for fish are very numerous and devise many shifting tricks, escaping from unexpected snares. He must be, above all, courageous, fearless, and temperate. He should not love the satiety of sleep, but should watch keenly, alert in heart and with wide-open eyes. He must endure the winter storms of Zeus and the thirsty season of summer, and he must love his labors and desire the sea. For in this way, he will be strong and dear to Hermes.

Fishing is best in the evening during the autumn season, and again when the morning star rises. In winter, one should set out when the rays of the sun are spreading, and in the flourishing spring, one should spend the entire day, as the sea is favored by breezes of every kind.

# Description of Lima, City of the Kings.

<margin>Appearance of the city of Lima.</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one can also see into all corners. On both sides of the flat land and through the greater part of the houses, canals run, bringing fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort to the citizens, who can thereby irrigate all their orchards and vegetable gardens, which they have in abundance and beauty. Also, there are many water mills in this river, in the manner of our own country, where they grind their grain. In short, very wealthy citizens live here, some of whom possess 150,000 ducats. And from this city, ships sail at times carrying 800,000 ducats, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which a crucifix stands. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their livestock, their dovecotes, and their vineyards—though they have no good grapes due to the nature of the soil—and beautiful gardens, not only full of all kinds of fruits of that land, but also of Spanish ones, such as apples, pomegranates, lemons, citrons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar cane, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. And truly, if it were not for the scandals, disagreements, and wars, this place would certainly be one of the most beautiful in the entire world, for the climate there is so temperate that there is no excessive heat or harmful cold throughout the entire year. Also, one has never seen hunger or plague there, nor any rain, thunder, or lightning striking from the heavens; but on the contrary, always a bright, clear, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535 and is called the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on the day of the Three Kings <note>Epiphany</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish, which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as the fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. The four months that are summer in Spain are winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, though it is not unhealthy as it is with us, for those who have pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will increase daily in people and wealth, even though for many years there were only about 500 houses; and the city is built very white, so that there may well be 2,000 now, for the streets are wide and the market square is large. Each house has 80 feet of land width and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for it is consumed by worms within two or three years—the houses are built with only one story, yet they are very costly and magnificent with many rooms, halls, and parlors suitable for living and for hosting foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials that they bake together very thick and fill with earth. They roof their houses with painted mats or painted linen, and all around and above

<column-break/>

on the walls, they make arbors of reeds where they take shelter from the sun. They do not worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Catchi, S. Michael, S. Francisco. It has been said before that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. We have dealt so far with the flat land along the seashore, starting from the Line <note>the Equator</note> and Cape Passao up to this point. It is also to be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima, but even much further, the seacoast to the south is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places, where for 10 miles it neither thunders, lightnings, nor rains, but beyond those 10 miles it does, or as much or more as the mountains are from the sea. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but there are four or five stagnant waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which take their origin from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from springs, which are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers have been described in part before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from one another, though mostly 7 or 8, by which traveling people regulate themselves because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, a mile wide or even wider—sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the situation of the land—there are various fertile trees and grain lands that are irrigated and sown by the people, which they can do throughout the entire year. Also, many kinds of wild trees, grain, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises, etc., grow around these rivers. And after the Spaniards took the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through some canals that they lead from these rivers, which, because they run down quickly from high mountains, are difficult to cross without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who make their journey along the flat land usually keep so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and it rains a lot, it is dangerous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either with certain rafts they have for that purpose or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out, and one of the Indians swims in front, pulling that net or raft with a cord, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of reeds. The men wear shirts and cloths to the knees, and over that, an outer garment like a cloak. The women wear a <term>cora</term> <gloss>a type of tunic</gloss> of cotton to the length of the body, and although the style of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nevertheless some difference in the adornment of the head, for some wear single small caps, some braided, some of one color, others of different colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, and all are distinguished according to the custom of the land.

### Chapter Four: On Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and an Indication of How to Administer Purgative and Emetic Medicines

We say: It is recommended for one who wishes to purge or vomit to space out their food, consuming the amount they would normally eat in a day over several sittings, and to make these different foods and different drinks. The stomach is then prompted by these variations to desire to expel what is inside it, either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied and is taken on top of other food, the stomach clings to it, holds it back, and grips it tightly, especially if the amount is small. As for those with a loose constitution, this is not necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not arise for one who has a good regimen; they need what is lighter than these. Often, exercise, massage, and bathing are sufficient for digestion. If their body is full, and it is the most full of the best humors, meaning blood, then bloodletting is what is needed for purification, rather than diarrhea. If necessity dictates bloodletting and evacuation with substances like hellebore and strong medicines, one must begin with bloodletting. This is one of the precepts of Hippocrates in the book *Epidemics*, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood, and if the humors are viscous and cold, bloodletting might increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize bloodletting; if a humor dominates after that, evacuate it. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform bloodletting. Whoever prioritizes medicine over bloodletting when they should have prioritized bloodletting is wrong. Furthermore, whoever has recently had bloodletting and needs evacuation, and then drinks medicine, it will stop for them. Often, drinking the medicine when bloodletting was required causes confusion and disturbance. If it does not subside with sedatives, know that bloodletting should have been prioritized. There is no evacuation needed for excessive fullness that is done gently, which the severity of the ailment calls for, and fullness is according to quality, not quantity. Often, improving the regimen is sufficient instead of the bloodletting required at the time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but an obstacle prevents it, and the only solution is fasting, sleep, and correcting the bad temperament caused by the fullness. Some evacuation is by way of precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other such conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. They need to take precautions before the time and perform the evacuation specific to their illness, whether it is bloodletting or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external desiccants and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. You may be forced to use a medicine that is similar in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as scammony when you need to evacuate bile. In that case, it must be mixed with something that is contrary in quality but similar in purgative effect, such as myrobalan, to correct any bad temperament that might occur afterward. In patients with visceral tumors, their diarrhea and vomiting are weakened. If you are forced to do so, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for <term>mastic</term> <gloss>a resin used for digestion</gloss> and cassia and the like, Hippocrates said: Whoever has a constitution that easily responds to vomiting, the best way to purify them is to use vomiting in summer, spring, or autumn, but not winter. For those of moderate constitution, diarrhea is better for them. If a need for vomiting arises, wait for summer and avoid it when not necessary. It is necessary to precede diarrhea and vomiting by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and by widening and opening the passages, as this protects the body from fatigue. Know that accustoming the body to respond to what is desired, whether diarrhea or vomiting, easily before using strong medicine is one of the methods of management. Diarrhea and vomiting with emaciation are difficult, tiring, and dangerous. An emetic medicine may become a purgative if the stomach is strong, or if it is drunk on an empty stomach, or if the drinker has a loose constitution, or is not accustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is heavy in substance and descends quickly. A purgative becomes an emetic due to a weak stomach, or the intensity of the dryness of the waste, or because the medicine is unpleasant, or the person has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge or purges matter that is not mature, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it through the body, taking control of the body and transforming other humors into it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting in most cases, such as bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have varying states, such as phlegm, and diarrhea is more correct for it in itself. For someone whose humor is descending, such as those with intestinal slippage, vomiting is impossible. The worst purgative medicines are those composed of medicines that are highly contradictory in the time of their purgative action, as they disturb the bowels, and the first may purge the second before the second acts, or the first may purge the second itself. When diarrhea and vomiting occur and the body is clean, there is inevitably dizziness, colic, and distress. In general, what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating the waste, there is no disturbance with it. When it begins to disturb, it is either evacuating something other than the waste, or if the evacuated humor changes by vomiting or diarrhea into another humor, it indicates the body is clean of the humor intended for evacuation.

The young ones feed at their dead mother. After a short while, she blinks, and they all abandon her and run away. They do not see their mother in her, and they do not recognize their own kind in her. The reason they loved their mother was not because they loved her physical form, but because they loved that which animated her form. Those who die in battle are not buried with ceremonial fans. Those who serve as attendants to the Son of Heaven do not trim their nails and do not pierce their ears. Those who take a wife are kept outside and are no longer employed in service. "To her" <note>original: "तामिति"</note>. O **long-lived one** <note>original: "आयुष्मन्". The suffix implies praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of his service to others.</note>. **By my request** and **for your own benefit** as well. The meaning is to fulfill yourself through the act of helping another. Although the object of the verb "to help" usually takes the second case, the use of the sixth case here is not contradictory, as it indicates a general relationship. As Bharavi says, "She serves fortune who serves others." And Sri Harsha says, "To help the virtuous, to see fortune, to travel through the sky." Thus, the statement by Nath <note>original: "नाथवचन". Refers to a commentator.</note> that the second case is seen everywhere is an unsupported claim. **Speak thus** to that beloved. What should he say? "O **delicate one** <note>original: "अबले". Literally "powerless one," a term of endearment.</note>, **your companion**—your husband—**residing in the hermitage of Ramagiri**—staying in the hermitages of Chitrakuta—**remains alive**—meaning he has not died." He provides the reason for his survival: **separated**—suffering from the state of separation—**he asks after your well-being**. The verb "to ask" takes two objects. Indeed, for **living beings** who are **prone to misfortune**—those whose calamities occur without effort—**this very thing**—asking about well-being—**is the first greeting** that must be addressed. The suffix <term>nyat</term> <gloss>a grammatical suffix indicating necessity</gloss> is used here to denote necessity.

At that point, we considered ourselves worthy of setting down words that would be transmitted from us. It became incumbent upon us to be the first to present you with what we possess and to reveal to you what we have attained, due to the sincerity of your devotion and the purity of your clarity. However, if we were to present you with the ultimate conclusions we have reached before establishing their foundations with you, it would provide you with nothing more than a matter of general imitation. This is true if you hold a favorable opinion of us based on our friendship and agreement, but not in the sense that we deserve to have our word accepted. We are not satisfied for you with anything less than a rank higher than this, nor are we content for you with this rank, as it is insufficient for salvation, let alone for attaining the highest degrees.

We wish to lead you along the paths upon which we have preceded you, and to have you swim in the sea we have already crossed, until it leads you to where we have arrived. You will then witness what we have witnessed, verify with your own insight everything we have verified, and have no need to tether your knowledge to what we have known. This requires a specific, not insignificant, amount of time, freedom from distractions, and the application of your entire resolve to this discipline. If this determination is sincere on your part, and your intention to gird yourself for this pursuit is sound, you will praise your journey at dawn, attain the blessing of your endeavor, and you will have pleased your Lord, and He will have pleased you. I am for you wherever you desire in your hope, and wherever you aspire with your resolve and your entire being. I hope to guide you along the most direct path, the one safest from perils and calamities. If you are now prepared, I shall offer a brief glimpse to inspire your longing.

Its sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman (with the *qaf* and *ra* vocalized with a *fatha*). Before him, it belonged to his brother Musa, who ceded it to King al-Nasir in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent an emir and an army there, but then Sultan Badr al-Din seized it, built his royal residence there, and established his rule. I met this sultan outside the city as he was returning from hunting. I dismounted from my mount for him, and he dismounted from his. I greeted him, and he received me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a visitor dismounts for them, they dismount for him, are pleased by his action, and increase their honor toward him. If he greets them while mounted, it displeases them, does not satisfy them, and becomes a cause for the visitor to be deprived of favor. This happened to me with some of them, and I will mention it. When I greeted him, he remounted and I remounted. He asked about my condition and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be lodged in the best accommodation. He would send much food, fruit, and sweets in silver platters, along with candles. He clothed me, provided me with a mount, and treated me well. Our stay with him did not last long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray (vocalized with a *fatha* on the *hamza*, a *sukun* on the *qaf*, and a *fatha* on the plain *sad* and the *ra*). It is one of the most beautiful and well-constructed cities in the lands of the Romans <note>original: "bilad al-Rum," referring to Anatolia</note>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and gardens on every side. Three rivers cut through the city, and water flows through its houses. It contains trees and grapevines, and there are many gardens inside it. Carpets attributed to the city are made there from sheep's wool, which have no equal in any other land. From there, they are transported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the obedience of the King of Iraq. We stayed there at the hospice of the Sharif Husayn, the deputy there for the Emir Eretna. Eretna is the deputy for the King of Iraq in the lands of the Romans that he has seized. This Sharif is one of the <term>fityan</term> <gloss>young men of chivalry/knightly brotherhood</gloss>, and he has a large following. He honored us with the utmost honor and performed the same deeds as those who preceded him. Then we traveled to the city of Nigde (vocalized with a *fatha* on the *nun*, a *sukun* on the *kaf*, and a *fatha* on the plain *dal*). It is one of the cities of the King of Iraq, a large and populous city, though some of it has fallen into ruin. It is cut through by the river known as the Black River, which is one of the major rivers. There are three bridges over it, one inside the city and two outside. There are waterwheels on it, both inside and outside, from which the gardens are irrigated. Fruits are abundant there. <margin>The chieftain Bononiana is treated with kindness by the chieftain.</margin>The chieftain, who was in the middle of the journey, kindly received those who were passing through, whom we said had been left behind, and he gave them twenty pounds of chased pure gold, and provided them abundantly with food suitable for eating. He did not wish to abandon our men at all until he had led them from his own palace to Pacra, and he himself held them all by the hand as if they were a faithful deposit, saying to the one to whom he was handing them over: "Behold your fellow soldiers, most brave man; behold the kind of men my palace received as they arrived, such I deliver to you. I would wish them to be in better health, but he who sends thunder and lightning against wicked men, and who provides us with juice <note>likely referring to cassava juice or similar plant-based sustenance</note> and maize out of his goodness through the mildness of the seasons, answers for you and your companions." Saying this, and stretching his eyes toward heaven, he was pointing to the sun. "By crushing our violent and proud enemies, you bring peace of mind to us and our homes. You tame monsters; we believe you and your companions, men excelling in virtue, were sent from on high, so that under the protection of your <term>maccana</term> <gloss>a wooden sword or club used by the indigenous people</gloss> we may be allowed to live our lives without fear." The interpreters said that the chieftain Bononiana had spoken these and other things of this kind. Vaschus returned equal thanks to him for his companionship and kindness toward our men; indeed, he adorned Bononiana with many very welcome gifts. Vaschus writes that he learned much from this chieftain about the wealth of those parts, which he says he wishes to pass over for the present, and he cites the outcome for those things. I do not understand what this implied hyperbole means. He seems to promise great things, and it should not be judged alien to his promise that huge riches are to be hoped for from there, since they did not approach any house of the inhabitants in which they did not find breastplates or golden pectorals, or golden necklaces for the neck or arms. I make a conjecture from the houses of our own people. If anyone, stimulated by a desire for iron, were to betake himself with a strong hand into Italy or Spain, what iron will he find in the houses? There, they have sharpened an iron frying pan, a pot made of iron elsewhere, and tripods placed on the fire, a supply for the needs of the kitchen. Nowhere will he find anything not suitable for use made of iron, nor will he obtain a great supply of iron. Iron will be conjectured to be in those regions from the things found. They sensed that those natives value raw gold no more than our people value raw iron. This is my opinion. I, Father, have these things about those matters from the letters and the living voice of Vaschus and his fellow soldiers; but time, revealing all hidden things, will make them clearer. They could accomplish nothing extraordinary in searching for gold mines, because of the one hundred and ninety men whom we mentioned Vaschus had led out from Darien, only seventy or so were used when he employed his efforts in conducting affairs, the others being always left behind in the houses of the chieftains. But he says that those who had recently been brought from Hispaniola fell especially into various diseases. Indeed, they could not tolerate such great calamity, so that they were content to nourish their stomachs, accustomed to better food, with only provincial bread and wild herbs without salt, often with river water, and sometimes even that healthy water failing. The earlier Darienites, however, had hardened themselves to endure all evils and the ultimate hunger. Whence he jokingly boasts that he had observed a longer and harsher Lent than your Holiness might order to be observed according to the custom of the ancestors. For he says that he and his companions spent four continuous years rarely satisfied with the fruits of the earth or trees, rarely using fish, and most rarely meat; and he laments that it came to such a point that when they could obtain them, they were forced to eat scabby dogs, muddy toads, and other things of this kind as if they were delicate feasts and sumptuous dishes. We have written more extensively about these things above; I call those "earlier Darienites" who first captured the land to be inhabited under the leadership of Nicuesa and Fogeda, of whom few were survivors. Let us now leave these things aside, and let Vaschus be led back again as a victor over the high peaks of the mountains.
